    Carol's finger hovered over the backspace, the cursor blinking like a countdown. The clock read 2:37 AM and Helen had gone to bed hours ago, Carol following in theory.

    She didn't hit the key yet. 

    Raban was there in the paragraph in front of her, leaning against the mast, topcoat thrown over one shoulder.

    She closed her eyes. In Carol's mind, and in the hundreds of legal pad pages stashed in a desk drawer, Raban had always been a woman. Dark eyes and dark hair tied back badly, or not at all. Capable and proud of it, restless and wistful, set against Lucasia's strict rules and careful lines. Carol felt a sour twist of irritation at how easily she'd dreamed them. How goddamn sincere.

    She opened her eyes and stared at the bright screen. As she thought about saving the document and sending it to Helen's little list of publishers, the old resistance came up, sticky and instinctive. It tarred her palms with sweat, a lingering residue that even years of a happy marriage hadn't washed away. She trusted publishers about as far as she trusted most people, which was to say, not at fucking all. The list was a row of mouths waiting to say what was wrong with it, with her. 

    When she was sixteen, her mother had driven her three hours to hell. 

    Inside it smelled like disinfectant and old carpet. At the desk, a woman with sprayed hair smiled hard and slid over a clipboard. YOU ARE SAFE HERE, said the poster behind her.

    They took Carol's bag, her shoelaces, asked if she understood why she was there. Carol said no. Her mother didn't look at her.

    Her days were a circle of folding chairs, and a man quoting the Bible, saying we all have temptations.The other kids traded stories in the breaks, clustered in cliques, whispering like it was summer camp. One of them laughed at something and Carol smiled reflexively, then realized she hadn't been included. The circle had a gap where she sat.

    "Identity issues," the counsellors said, and Carol would think: you're the ones who've got issues. They said "struggling with sin," and Carol wanted to stand up and shout: I'm not struggling, I loved every fucking second of it.

    The first time she mouthed off, the counsellors acted shocked; like she was some delicate flower who'd accidentally held hands with a girl, like she hadn't spent half of ninth grade with her face between Becky M's thighs in the gym storage closet.

    They marched her down the hall to a little room with no window, and a man she hadn't seen before shut the door and asked for details in a soft voice that made her skin crawl. How long had she felt this way. What exactly had she done, with whom. He made her say things she would rather have died than describe to him, and each time she faltered he waited, pen poised, making the silence push her into finishing. Then smaller questions; where had they touched, whether she liked being touched. After that, he kept asking, until the answers started to feel filthy in her mouth. 

    He wrote it all down while she sat there hot with shame, aware of the closed door at her back and the sick sense that he could ask anything he liked and no one would stop him. By the end, Carol understood that making her say it was the point.

    After that, she gave them nothing real, nothing more they could use, and by the second week, she was saying different things that she knew weren't true. When she repeated the right phrases, they smiled, and told her they were proud of her. 

    Nobody had ever said that to Carol before.

    Carol's starving heart lunged at it before she could refuse. It felt better than she wanted to admit, more frightening than any punishment. Warmth spread through her, sickly, like the whisky she'd been stealing since seventh grade, and while it was spreading she could feel herself dissolving. Being liked meant she was disappearing. She could have it or she could have herself.

    She kept saying the lies and stopped believing the warmth. She wasn't stupid.

    At night, she lay on a bunk bed that smelled of bleach. Through the wall, someone cried every night at almost exactly the same time as she did.

    She stared at the slats and pictured their heaven. No fear, no loneliness, no pain. She wiped her face with both hands. It was all bullshit, the sin and the salvation, but if you really believed there was somewhere the hurting stopped—she understood how someone might want to skip the wait.

    She thought about what they'd told her: she deserved to be free of this burden, the person He intended was waiting on the other side of her struggle, and what they meant: she was never going to be a person anyone wanted. The girl that deserved heaven and happiness could only be born once this one was buried.

    On visitation day, the room filled with parents, siblings, church friends, carrying paper cups and grocery store cookies. Kids who'd spent all week pretending not to care suddenly went bright.

    Carol sat in her folding chair and waited.

    What she got was a letter from her mother. Saying she had sent Carol there because she loved her, because she could not bear the thought of Carol burning in hell. Carol folded the letter once, then again and again, until the edges went soft. A small and hard splinter fixed into place and never left.

    She moved out the first chance she got. Then farther, then farther still. Used the money left to her by Nana to pay through college. New Mexico for grad school finally felt far enough; the horizon so wide you could see anything coming, like a blank page, room enough to write oceans out of sand. And then she met Helen. For the first time in her life, Carol said I love you, something true, to someone who wanted to hear it.

    Years later, that was still why she whispered the fear to Helen. It won't sell, she'd claimed the night before, and hated that it felt like the same old lesson. Common sense dictated a debut needed a broad appeal, a marketable romantic lead. A brooding male love interest would be the safe bet. He would never raise eyebrows.

    So Raban became a man. 

    She spent the next four hours systematically stripping any femininity. With every stroke of the backspace key, she carved the she out of sentences. Shoulders broadened and the accent sank lower, the un-selfconscious authority coarsened. She kept the square jaw, but added a beard. She was stitching a new skin over the old, creating a man out of a woman's ribs. 

    Carol scrolled her way down the document with mindless efficiency, scanning Lucasia's surrender to Raban. Carol surgically deleted it. In the new version, his hands on Lucasia's waist were firm but safe. He kissed her. Deeply, the prose said. His hands stayed on her waist. When they broke apart, Lucasia's cheeks were flushed. The end. No one's fingers inside anyone.

    You wrote what you knew, and she'd spent a long time knowing what not to say. By the time the sun began to bleed through the curtains, she'd finished the edit, the coffee, and whatever nerve she might have started with.

    He caught her gaze, a spark igniting in the chaos of the cyclacane. 'Join me, ma cherie,' Raban's voice was a baritone growl, a challenge and a promise. 'Forget their laws and sail with me. Be free.'

    She should really stop letting herself write when she was drunk. She made a mental note to delete 'ma cherie' later. Jesus Christ. 

    When Helen walked into the room with a peppermint tea, she leaned down to kiss Carol's shoulder. "How's it coming? Did you finish Raban's intro?"

    Helen was wearing the gray tank top, the one that meant she'd woken up wanting Carol and was testing the waters. Carol knew that signal. On a normal morning, she'd already be tilting, chair pushed back, face up, waiting for Helen to close the distance and do whatever she wanted with the rest of the hour.

    But right now, sad and bitter, Carol couldn't even meet her eyes. "Yeah," she said, her voice a dry rattle in her throat. Carol didn't look up. She couldn't.

    She watched the cursor blink one, two, three, and tried to delude herself into ignoring a sinking certainty. She had just closed the door on the only version of her story she would ever love. The Raban who was meant to be Lucasia's shore, now lost to the depths of the sea.

    Coffee wafted past her shoulder that was definitely instant and her nose twisted. Her own thermos, coffee ground fresh from beans she'd brought aboard, had been empty for an hour. She'd kept unscrewing the lid and checking, hopeful, as though it might regenerate. A laminated sign above the controls said NO FOOD ON CONSOLES, and she'd taped her last cookie to it.

    Zosia felt her ears warm. She lifted her chin a fraction anyway, jaw sharp above the uniform collar. "With all due respect, Chief, my shift's not finished." She didn't argue because she enjoyed arguing. She argued because words mattered and she was usually correct.

    The dark reflective surface of the bridge's windows caught her profile as she turned: cheekbones catching the console light and her dark shoulder-length hair tied back, always making her look more severe than she felt. He sighed with relief, and because she couldn't help it, she added, "It's kind of cool—" she tried to stop herself from sounding too pleased— "I know, but remember the squall is visible and a blind spot too." The man nodded with open admiration, so Zosia kept walking before it could turn into a conversation.

The sky was still dark but thinning at the edges, stars hanging on where the cloud cover broke. Underneath it was the smell she'd come out here for: salt and spray, sharp enough to sting. The schooner had been invited to Tangier as part of a cultural exchange and traditional sailing circuit, which was a long way of saying there would be civilian visiting hours.     Zosia checked her clipboard and then the small group of tourists who had been assigned to her. Six people. She was dressed in the navy version of approachable: white short-sleeved shirt with shoulder insignia, but no neck tie, and hair loose.     This was not what her job usually consisted of, mercifully—she taught ensigns who had no idea what they didn't know yet—but she'd made the mistake of learning to be fluent in more languages than Polish.

    "This is a training ship," she said, in French and then again in English, because it looked like a couple needed it. "Three masts. The rig is traditional. The work is not." She made sure her voice was low and authoritative. "If you stay with me and don't wander off, nobody will have to go diving for you."

    "Yeah," Carol said. "Exactly. I'm all about discipline now."

    Carol saw his mouth twitch. He left the house with her phone in his pocket. She stood there, staring at the spot where the phone had been, and felt her whole body sag with relief. She went to the bar, opened the cupboard, found a bottle, poured. She stared at the glass.

    Tomorrow mattered. If she got wrecked tonight like she'd been planning, she'd wake up foggy and mean and shaky. She set the glass down. Her lip curled with irritation at herself, which was insane. Who gets mad about doing the smart thing? Jesus.

    The problem was, not being plastered left room to think. Room for Zosia's voice, which she did not have access to anymore, thank god. Room for her brain to replay every stupid romantic moment, then rate how down bad she was on a scale from one to biblical.

It was supposed to be about the stem cells, the joining, the theft of choice, and it was, but underneath it was the miserable admission that they had loved her badly, not falsely. Certain they knew what was best, willing to follow through by any means, all in the name of love. Carol had survived that before, and it hadn't killed her, but it hadn't left her capacity for forgiveness fully intact either.

    Carol exhaled hard through her nose, like she could blow the thoughts out. She walked out of the front door before she could change her mind.

    Manny's porch light was on. Carol knocked once, then again, because he probably had three different weapons within reach and would still take two seconds to decide whether the knock was a trick.

    The door cracked open and his eyes glanced like he was scanning for a sniper.

    Carol crossed her arms. "Relax. It's just me, the world's least stealthy predator."

    His shoulders dropped, which counted as warmth, for him. He opened the door with a half-eaten empanada in his hand.

    "What," he said, chewing.

    "I'm not drinking tonight," she said, as if accusing him personally. "Which means I'm going to be alone with my thoughts, and I don't want to be." She barreled on before she lost momentum. "Do you want to watch a movie? Like… a normal human thing. We can sit six feet apart and glare at the same screen."

    His gaze narrowed. "Movie."

    "Yeah," Carol shrugged. "With a beginning, middle, end. No radios. No—" she waved a hand vaguely— "whatever the fuck tomorrow is." He kept chewing long enough that she nearly turned around, but then, he stepped back to let her in. Carol sighed. "Something with explosions, okay? We need to feel better about not having set one off yet."

    Chapter 2

    People said that ignorance was bliss.

    So was oblivion.

    Zosia's first sensation was cold. Sweat cooling on her skin. Sound came next: her own breathing, ragged and thin.

    Then there was pain. It had been gone, numbed, but now it flooded in as if a membrane had ruptured, raw and ruthless. Her throat burned, her lungs worked, and the air hurt. Everything hurt.

    Each sensation came alone, and that was wrong—they were supposed to be together, everything was supposed to be together, and she couldn't remember what that meant.

    Her eyes cracked open and bright light hit her, unforgiving. She was lying on a mattress with a corrugated deckhead above her. Sick bay of a ship? Suddenly there was a bang from the wall, a concussive thud that stabbed through her. Loose anchor?

    She closed her eyes against it and her breath came shallow, insufficient. Her memories were jumbled; fragments that didn't cohere, edges of faces, sensations, words she couldn't place. And then, like a single thread pulling at the fraying fabric of her mind; she remembered her dying crewmate. 

    She wanted to sit up, to shout, demand answers, but every muscle felt sealed shut, as if moving was pulling her apart, piece by piece. 

    There was a presence beside her, hovering just out of reach. "Zosia?" The voice was tentative. A woman. The name sounded strange to her ears, but it was hers.

    "Gdzie.." she rasped, the word feeling strange in her mouth.

    She forced her eyes open again. Zosia turned her head, her neck screamed at the motion, and the woman sitting beside her had a face she couldn't place. She tried to reach for a name, a memory, but everything slipped through her fingers like water.

    "Gdzie jestem?" Her mouth was dry, her tongue useless. She coughed and her body convulsed with it. The woman's face swam, doubled.

    The woman didn't say anything. She was holding herself back, arms crossed in front of her body. "I... I'm sorry," she said eventually. 

    English. American. Where was she? The woman—doctor?—seemed to shrink in on herself.

    Zosia narrowed her eyes. She wasn't a doctor. This wasn't a sick bay. She parted her dry lips and forced her thoughts into coherent English. "What happened?" The bulblight hurt. The walls were too close, too stark. "Where… where am I?"

    The blonde woman's brow furrowed then smoothed as if searching for the right words. She knelt by Zosia's side.

    "You're—okay. You're okay. You're in—" Her hands were shaking. She pressed them together. "I fucked up. I'm going to explain, I just—I don't know where to—"

    Zosia's chest rose and fell unevenly, as she took in the words, trying to make sense of them. Her mind kept drifting somewhere else; a warmth, a place where nothing had edges, nothing was separate, and she hadn't needed her own lungs to breathe.

    "What?" Zosia rasped. Her throat was so dry. She looked up at the woman hovering over her.

    "You were—there was—everyone got connected. Like, their thoughts. Everyone on earth. And you were—you were in it, and we—I took you out. We took you out. That's what just happened."

    Zosia didn't know what that meant. She tried to recall, stretch her mind, but there were no images, no memories. She didn't have the words for it, but the emptiness was deafening, the severed end of something that had been continuous, a cord cut, and she could still feel the place where it had been attached. The last thing she remembered, clearly, was the deck of Iskra. All the blood. The hot, salty air. Then—nothing.

    Zosia blinked through her confusion, her body still feeling strange and alien. She tried to lift her hand but her limbs were sluggish. The woman's hand reached out, just above hers, not quite touching her. She looked a mess; tear tracks ran through her cheeks, blotchy, her eyes red. What had happened? 

    Zosia looked up at the ceiling, her mind spinning. "Water," she murmured hoarsely. She couldn't turn but heard the woman scrabble around the floor, on hands and knees, cursing under her breath. An open bottle appeared in her periphery and some water spilled out onto her shoulder as the woman handled it, the sensation strange. She noticed then, she wasn't in her uniform, or a hospital gown, but civilian clothes. In a tiny metal-walled room, a shipping container?

    "Shit! Fuck. Sorry. It's just—it's just water."

    Who was this inept woman? 

    Zosia tried, more forcefully, to sit up again. Pain shot through her, but it wasn't as sharp. She managed to push herself into a half-sitting position and her body felt new and unreliable, borrowed, as if she hadn't finished inhabiting in it.

    Zosia took the bottle weakly. She heard noise moving from outside the room, container, whatever they were in. Metal scraped against metal, maybe. She coughed as the water went down and the woman's hand hovered again.

    Zosia cleared her throat. "I do not understand," her voice sounded desperate to her own ears. There was a strange urgency to her emotions she wasn't used to feeling. "I was on Iskra. Kowalski—I was trying to save him. I—"

    The woman interrupted her gently, her hand hesitating at her side. “You're in America now," the woman said it like an apology. "It's been—it's been a while. Months. Since wherever you were. I know that doesn't—" She exhaled hard. "I know."

    Zosia's mind spun again. She'd been in a coma. That was the dream she'd been torn from? Why was she in America? Nothing added up.

    She jumped as she heard another bang from outside and the start made her muscles jerk painfully.

    The woman moved to stand. "It's okay. The door's gonna open."

    Zosia followed her lead, trying to stand. Her legs wobbled slightly, but she kept her posture, chin raised. She wasn't going to lean on anyone. The woman stopped and watched her, but didn't move. "I am fine," she said to the woman and to herself. She could feel the pull of dizziness in her head. She took a small, unsteady step forward, testing her balance.

    Her knees buckled.

    She stumbled, too slow to respond, and her arm went out grasping for something—anything—but before she could fall, the woman's hand shot out to hers to steady her.

    The touch brought a strange comfort—and a name surfaced, sudden and certain. This woman was Carol. How did she know that?  "Carol," she whispered, almost to herself, in disbelief, the word slipped out.

    Carol froze. Her hand was still there supporting, but her face came apart, past shock.

    Zosia stared back. Before she could ask, a sudden clatter made both of them jump.

    The door swung open. Zosia squinted as the brightness of the world beyond pierced through the small space. It opened further and she saw houses, a street outside. A man stood there, framed by the sunlight beaming in, his silhouette sharp against it. Zosia looked out and tried to map this man, this place, onto anything she remembered. Only fragments rose and fell: brightness with no source; voices in harmony; a sensation of being held from the inside out. Then the violent absence of it, skull empty and her body screaming alone. Her hand clenched Carol's tighter.

    He looked at Carol, then to Zosia, and a faint furrow appeared on his brow. The moment stretched. His eyes dropped to their hands and the pause was brief, but Zosia felt it like a spotlight. She pulled her hand free and positioned it at her side, parade rest, as if she'd never needed the support.

    The man looked at Carol directly. "Did it work?" he asked, his voice low, accented.

    Carol nodded slowly, "It worked."

    The man's expression shifted and his lips curled upward. It almost looked out of place on his features. He stepped forward and clapped Carol lightly on the shoulder, and Zosia watched Carol receive it like a blow. "Good," he said, his tone lighter. "Now we get to work."

    Carol's shoulders straightened. "Work?"

    The man's eyes narrowed. "Like we talked. She has been in. Intelligence. We start with that."

    Carol stiffened beside her. "She... She doesn't have anything. Not anymore."

    He stopped, frowning. He looked at Zosia. "You don't have anything?" He sounded skeptical.

    She glanced at Carol involuntarily then put a full meter between them. If this man was going to interrogate her, he would address her as herself, not as an extension of whatever she was to this woman. "I do not remember," she said flatly, her eyes meeting his without hesitation. 

    He didn't say anything at first. His eyes searched her, the silence heavy. He looked at her hand, still hovering just above her side, suspiciously. "Why hold her hand, if you don't remember her?" he asked, bluntly.

    She should've pulled away sooner…why had she held on in the first place? Her fingers curled into her palm, the muscles tensing as she broke her gaze away from him and turned her face to the ground, giving him nothing. Zosia's fingers twitched at her side, the urge to step further back from Carol even stronger now. "I did not want to fall over," she muttered. 

    He didn't look convinced. His eyes narrowed, but there was no anger, just calculation, his mind making conclusions about her. Military, she judged—or at least he dressed similarly, and how he scrutinized her…Who the hell were these people? 

    Carol opened her mouth, clearly unsure, but before she could speak, Zosia took another step away from Carol, and held herself as upright as she could, not letting the pain show on her face.

    "I don't remember anything, sir," Zosia said again, louder this time, more firm.

    Carol looked at Zosia, her brows furrowing. Zosia still didn't understand how she knew Carol's name. She didn't understand anything right now.

    The man paused at the honorific. "Okay. We figure out." Then he moved quickly, his footsteps purposeful towards the house. His eyes flicked over Zosia, noting the tension in her posture, and when he saw her scan the surroundings, he folded his arms. "This is... home, for now," he said, then added, "No need—" he made quote marks with his fingers— "Sir."

    Like she'd done something strange. Not military, then. His tone was detached, but how he studied her, like looking for familiarity and finding none...but she didn't know either of these people.

    She followed them into the house. The entryway alone was bigger than her quarters on Iskra.

    "You should rest. Decompress." he said, like it was a new word he had just learned. "Maybe feel different."

    She scoffed at his performative kindness. Condescending asshole. "Rest?" she echoed, her voice biting. "I have just come out of the longest sleep of my life. I want some answers. What the fuck is going on?"

    Carol glanced at her, eyebrows raised, but stayed silent.

    The man grunted in response, not arguing, but his gaze lingered on Carol for a moment too long, his eyes narrowing just slightly before he spoke again. "You two need talk. I will go." 

    He left with no further word. The door shut behind him, and she felt another sudden sense of emptiness, a strange cavity in her gut, a craving to be around as many people as possible, more overwhelming than the physical pain. She didn't want the asshole to leave. Was she going insane?

    She'd always been fine alone. She'd preferred it, actually. Hadn't she?

    Carol turned to her, rocking onto her toes before awkwardly gesturing with her thumb toward the kitchen, and Zosia felt a quiet urge to follow her, anything to not be left alone. Carol pulled open a cabinet and retrieved a bottle of vodka. She wasn't the biggest drinker but she needed something strong to numb the edges of whatever this was, the confusion and pain still pounding at her skull.

    "I need that," Zosia demanded.

    Carol didn't respond immediately. She paused with her back turned to Zosia, her hand hovering near the bottle. The thought of being denied sent a wave of irritation through Zosia, but Carol grabbed a glass, and poured just enough for something to sip. Carol's voice was a little hoarse as she turned. "Right, uh—yeah, here you go." She handed the drink over with a tight smile.

    Zosia took the glass from her, the cold a small comfort against her hand, and knocked back the majority of it. She didn't ask for an explanation behind Carol's decision to offer it, didn't care. Zosia leaned into the counter and closed her eyes, the burn cutting a clean line through the noise.

    She opened her eyes. Carol was putting the bottle away, her back turned, her shoulders drawn in. Zosia sipped the remainder of her drink, and then, almost without thinking, she said, "I don't know what is happening." She hated the vulnerability in it, but she needed to know.

    Carol turned again. "I don't—" she stopped, and turned inward, her lips pressing into a thin line. She nodded to herself. "I'm here to help," she said. "Whatever you need."

    Zosia frowned. The concern might be real but the delivery was atrocious. She'd heard that tone on every harbor pilot who assumed she couldn't moor her own vessel. She set the glass down hard enough to feel the counter through her palm, and crossed her arms.  "I need to know what the fuck is going on."

    "Sure, but we'll take it step by step, okay?" Carol's jaw was too tight for it. She couldn't perform patience any better than she could hold still—everything gave her away. She was steering herself word by word through a line she'd clearly rehearsed, because she thought Zosia needed it.

    "I don't need steps. Tell me all of it. How do you know my name?" Zosia's voice stayed level. Everything underneath it was not. “How do I know yours? I don't remember anything. I do not even know you."

    Carol turned to fill her own glass with water from the tap. "You know me."

    Zosia had no memory to justify it and no framework to explain it and she wanted, badly, to stop feeling it. Whatever Carol thought she knew belonged to a woman Zosia couldn't remember being. "I don't. Stop talking as though I should. Whoever knew you is not here. Talk to the one who is."

    Carol's hand stilled on the faucet. She turned on her toes and looked up and Zosia saw her take in her crossed arms, the refusal to be condescended to, and for the first time Carol looked at her like she was seeing a stranger. Good. Zosia was a stranger. It should have felt like solid ground and it didn't. She kept her arms folded and her chin level because those were the only parts still answering to her.

    Carol's jaw worked. "Alright. I'll tell you what the hell is going on, but there's a lot, and some of it's—" 

    Zosia eyed her sharply. "I don't know who you think I am, but I am not some delicate weak thing. Tell me now. I can handle it."

    Carol stared at her tight-lipped for a moment. "Okay. The world fucking ended." She raised her eyebrows. "That snappy enough for you?"

    Zosia's stomach twisted, but she didn't look away.

    Carol exhaled. "Let's sit down for the rest of it."

    "I'll sit when I decide to sit."

    Carol's eyes narrowed. "Suit yourself," she muttered, and turned down the hallway without checking whether Zosia followed.

    Zosia followed. Her legs decided before her pride could weigh in. Alone with the refrigerator, her chest clenched like a fist. Now, two steps behind Carol, the knot loosened with every step. She hated it. She kept walking.

    She followed Carol to a living room—how many living rooms did one house need?—and Carol hunched into a chair to continue explaining, dragging Zosia further into a nightmare she didn't want to face. The virus, the psychic glue. Zosia's fingers tightened around her glass, her eyes scanning Carol's face for any hint of lie. It looked more like she was checking a list off in her head.

    A part of her wanted to shout, to throw up, to throw something, and she wasn't sure if it was anger, fear, or grief. Everything rose too fast, too eager, and it startled her. She was used to keeping her feelings tightly wound, now it all came unspooled so easily. She kept her posture rigid. If she held herself correctly, nothing could get loose. She was not going to fall apart in a stranger's living room. She was not going to fall apart at all.

    Carol kept talking and she wasn't measured about it, corrected herself, doubled back, swore when she lost her place and started over. Her hands moved constantly; fingers drumming the armchair, picking at a seam, gripping her own knee, then pressing flat against her thigh as if she'd caught them misbehaving. She flung information like emptying a sinking boat, fast and desperate to get the weight out before it dragged her under. Zosia sat on the couch with her back to the window. Light through the blinds striped the room and Carol's face in bars, picking out every crease and shadow. 

    The room was enormous. The whole house was enormous, tiled floors and vaulted ceilings and she was in New Mexico, apparently. She knew almost nothing about it beyond Roswell, and the aliens Carol was describing were a different kind—no little green men, just DNA and every mind on earth folded into one. The shadow of a tree moved across the wall in a slow, indifferent sway.  Outside, a bird was singing. Zosia listened to a stranger describe the end of the world in a living room bigger than a wardroom, and whatever was in her that should've been shouting went calm instead.

    It was the worst situation report Zosia had ever received and yet something in Carol's gracelessness steadied her. Every flaw in the delivery was more proof that she was incapable of pretending. Whatever Carol was telling her, she believed it.

    Carol paused. "Are you—"

    "This is what happened to the world," Zosia said. "Now tell me what happened to me. I woke up in a container."

    Carol seemed relieved to explain the container. The rest of the immune were comfortable with the situation and Carol and Manousos—she learned the man's name—had used her as the first guinea pig for their 'unjoining' theory. Carol talked through it quickly, and Zosia heard her own extraction described in the language of a plan, a procedure. She had been a procedure.

    Zosia waited for the anger. It was there, she could feel it circling, but Carol's voice had cracked and her thumbnail was scoring a white line into a fingertip, and it wasn't coming. Zosia's mask was thinning now, she could feel it, and she didn't know when it had started to wear. She didn't want to feel calmed by someone who had ripped her apart and was describing the process over tap water.

    She leaned forward from her perch on the end of the couch. "I do not know what the hell—" She stopped herself. It wasn't Carol's fault, not entirely—and there it was, the strange feeling Zosia didn't want to admit to, that felt more intimate than it should. "I don't know what you expected," she said, and heard her own voice come out quieter, "but I was happy. I was part of something."

    "But you didn't choose any of it." Carol's hands were tapping the glass; an arrhythmic, anxious drumming. Zosia watched the movement and felt an urge to still them that made no sense. She didn't know this woman. 

    "You don't know me, you have no idea what I'd choose."

    "I know what came back." Carol's hand swept toward Zosia, palm up, like she was presenting exhibit A. "This, right now. You telling me I'm wrong. You told Manny to fuck off with one look and you'd rather fall flat on your face than let someone help you. You won't sit when I tell you to, you—" Carol's mouth pulled tight. Her hand dropped to her knee. "A week ago you would've agreed with anything I said, and if I told you to bring me a drink you'd have smiled while you poured it." Carol looked at the floor. “You never said no to anything." Her face had gone white.

    Zosia's jaw locked. She couldn't argue with it. That didn't sound like her. She wanted to say: this isn't who I am either, but saying that meant admitting she was afraid, and admitting that meant admitting why—the feeling in her that had no origin and no justification and would not leave.

    "That obviously wasn't you," Carol said. "That was a—" Carol searched, her neck flushing— "a pleasant fucking screensaver with your face." Her voice splintered and she pressed her lips shut. Carol's breathing was audible, ragged, and Zosia could hear the anger pointed at this hivemind—the warm dream—and at herself. Carol's hands came up and covered her eyes and stayed there, and when she spoke again it was from behind them, muffled. "I should've done this sooner." She dropped her hands. Her face was blotched and raw. "And I didn't want to."

    Carol was angry for her, and Zosia could not claim in herself the fury that should've been there at being treated as a lab rat. She'd entered this house with enough to burn it down and somewhere it had bled out of her. Carol was blaming herself for something Zosia had felt from the inside, and the inside had been different. Instead of anger, Zosia found that she couldn't let Carol sit there with a version of events that wasn't even half the story. 

    "It wasn't—" Zosia stopped. She was trying to describe a color to someone who'd only seen the negative. "It wasn't blank. There was so much. Everyone—" Zosia's voice cracked before she could stop it, "Everyone was happy, everyone was loved. I was content, for first time—" her English faltered, and she fought her way back. "Now I am hurting again." 

    It was shameful how quickly she got upset now. This joining had made emotion shared and painless. Now it belonged to her again, and it was louder than she remembered. 

    "I never meant to hurt you," Carol said. "I did this to give you a choice. If you—if you want to go back, we can find a way."

    Zosia closed her eyes, trying to hold fast against the constant pain and confusion that threatened to split her. Going back should've been obvious, and yet despite the agony, her instinct also said no. Underneath her reasoning, she'd already decided, and the decision wasn't freedom matters or any principle she could defend rationally.

    "I am not saying you did wrong," Zosia said. "I don't want to be asleep, now I'm here. But it didn't feel like that then, it felt like I didn't matter, and that was how it should be. Now I'm alone again, and there is no one in it with me."

    Carol's eyes changed, a glimmer of empathy. She understood, in some way, Zosia thought, feeling a bitter relief. 

    She kept trying to name what else she felt, and every label came up wrong. It wasn't trust. It wasn't even liking, not yet. Zosia didn't have enough information for either of those. 

    Her pulse softened when Carol spoke, even when she'd been describing an alien invasion. It made her defensive on principle. Carol wasn't a threat in the physical sense—she was shorter and tense in a way that suggested more bark than bite—but there was something else about her that felt dangerous.

    "It—it wasn't easy for me, either." Carol gave a humorless laugh. "If that makes you feel any better."

    What Zosia had was a strange, stubborn patience that existed independent of her opinion.

    Zosia needed an explanation and she lined up the facts she'd learned. Carol had said she was immune, the immune had chaperones, Zosia was in Carol's house, had been extracted on Carol's driveway, and her hand somehow knew Carol's name before her brain did. This one piece, at least, wasn't difficult to guess.

    "So I was yours," Zosia said.

    Carol's hand stopped tapping. There was a moment of silence. "My—chaperone, yeah." Carol's mouth twisted. "They needed someone to talk to me without me shouting every time, so they sent you."

    "Why me?" Zosia asked. "I was in Maroko. Morocco."

    Carol sighed hard, a sound like she was letting go of a rope and watching it fall. "Okay," she said, "Okay. Uh—" She pointed at Zosia with one finger then pulled it back like it burned. "Wait here. Just—" Carol was already standing, leg bumping into the coffee table. "Don't move. Don't—" Carol frowned at herself, clearly aware she sounded crazy. "Give me a second."

    Zosia watched her disappear into the hallway and waited. The patience in her chest stayed. Infuriating. Her eyes flicked around, taking inventory. Lamps. Books. Framed art. The house was not luxurious in any fancy way, just… expensive. Too much air between objects. 

    Carol came back a few seconds later carrying a hardback book with both hands. She held it out between them and then hesitated. "I—" Carol stopped. Her face had gone from pale to red again. "This is going to sound so fucking stupid."

    Zosia looked at the cover. Stormshadow of Wycaro. Her stomach dropped so hard it felt like she missed several rungs. Carol Sturka.Zosia's vision narrowed so fast she thought she might pass out. 

    She knew those books. She knew those books almost as well as she knew rigging plans. She'd read them in the hours after watch rotations, spine cracked open against her chest like a prayer, carried them across the world, kept them under pillows. This Carol had written them. 

    Zosia stared. She couldn't blink. She couldn't say You're her without sounding like a child. There was no version of a sentence that didn't make her sound like what she was: lonely enough that these books had mattered more than they should.

    Zosia's mouth opened, then closed. Her face went hot. She looked up at Carol, and suddenly her whole being made no sense. This was the author of Wycaro? This tense, foul-mouthed, clumsy woman? Zosia felt like a myth had walked into the room wearing stained sweatpants. 

    "You're—" It came out strangled. Zosia shut her mouth. She felt the floor tilt beneath her, except the floor wasn't a deck, it was dry and level and the rolling was inside her.

    Carol exhaled. "Okay, look." She shoved the book a fraction closer on the table between them. "You look like… that." Carol's eyes flicked up to check her reaction and then away again, as if she couldn't stand to watch.

    "Like what?" Zosia heard herself ask, distantly, and her voice came out thin.

    Carol's shoulders rose in another defensive hunch. "Raban, my pirate hero," she said with sarcastic cheer. Her shoulders dropped. "You look like—like the character I wrote for this story. Close enough that when they—when they did the whole…The first time you showed up, I thought I was going insane." Carol's voice got rougher, like she was pushing through it. "They chose you because you fit whatever—" Carol made a vague gesture around her face— "and because they knew it would work on me."

    Zosia didn't understand.

    Carol's eyes stayed on the table. "They knew I'd be more likely to listen if they put a face in front of me I liked." Carol finally looked up, eyes bright. "So, yeah. That's why you. The ugly truth." Carol's laugh came out wrong. "Congratulations, you were my weak spot."

    Zosia was aware, dimly, that she should say something. Anything. A question. Carol was watching her with wary attention like she expected a punch to the face. But Zosia was stuck on something else... She forced her eyes down to the book. Raban was a man. She was a woman.

    She realized then. An awful, humiliating understanding. They did this for me.

    Not only for Carol. They would've obviously sent a man if it was just for Carol. If this hivemind had all her thoughts and memories—then it would've known. It would've known about the books and about Raban and how Zosia had wanted, when she was younger and naive, to be like him; how she'd loved the dream of sailing beyond rules and borders. It would've known how easily her stupid heart was hooked by it. 

    Maybe—Zosia's face flamed hotter—it had been… a kindness. A perverse one. The hivemind letting her meet the creator of the books she'd loved. Handing her Raban's coat and letting her wear it. The thought made her want to crawl out of her skin. 

    Carol was still watching her, waiting. Zosia could not say any of this out loud. She reached for the book and flipped it open like she needed proof it was real. The paper smelled faintly of dust. Zosia had only ever read the paperbacks, the strict weight limit for life at sea prohibiting anything heavier than it needed to be. She flipped to the back flap and there it was: the author photo.

    Carol Sturka, professionally lit, hair styled, face set in an expression that suggested controlled charm. She looked polished. Zosia studied it, then slowly lifted her eyes to the Carol sitting across from her.

    This Carol looked like she'd been through the wringer and wasn't pretending otherwise: hair a mess, a blotchy bruised shadow under both red-rimmed eyes like she'd had no sleep for a week. Her posture was collapsed—shoulders up, spine curved, bracing for impact. She sat pigeon-toed and jittery, hands too busy to rest. A real person, not a brand.

    The thought rose, uninvited and absurd: I like this one more. Zosia closed the book too quickly as if she'd been caught stealing. "That photo," she said, and her voice came out flat, "doesn't look like you."

    A flinch and a smile fought across Carol's face. "Yeah," she said. "Marketing. Helen picked it." Carol leaned forward, "Listen," she said, and there was a steadiness in it, like she'd made a decision. "If you want to shout, curse me out, punch me in the face—go ahead, I'm right here. I deserve all of it."

    Zosia's hands tightened around the book. Some part of her had already decided Carol was not something to break, and more awful, her chest warmed at Carol saying I'm right here.

    Zosia's gaze dropped, and she opened the book to a random page. She thought of herself on Iskra, wedged into her bunk with the curtain drawn, lamp dimmed low. She saw the condolence messages, then the silence after. Sasha's laugh replaced by nothing at all, and the world still turning, indifferent. These books had been silly and impossible and, in the middle of grief, useful. They had given her somewhere to go. A port in a storm.

    The memory sharpened the shame and softened the other feeling. Zosia's eyes read one passage, and without meaning to, she heard it in Carol's voice. She snapped the book closed again.

    Carol was still waiting. Her fingers fidgeting against her glass again, impatience trying to disguise fear. Zosia swallowed. She could not say you're my favorite author like a teenager, your books kept me sane like that wouldn't make Carol recoil, I wanted to be Raban without dying on the spot.

    Zosia forced herself to breathe. The patience in her chest was still there, deep and stubborn. The fondness worse now, because it had a name and books behind it.

    She looked at Carol again. The tension in her jaw, bracing for rejection. She moved her head and a slat of sunlight crossed Carol's eyes, and the guarded gray burned off like fog, into a startling blue. Zosia felt herself tilt inside, subtle as a compass needle.

    A crush, she realized, with absolute horror.

    Of course it was. Of course. It was so painfully typical of her: alone again in her own head, newly raw, immediately finding the most inconvenient woman and developing a humiliating attachment. She wanted to vanish into the floor. She locked her spine and tucked her chin. She could feel her own face still hot, betraying her, but she hoped Carol would attribute it to anger. Her heart was hammering. 

    Zosia slid her gaze sideways, searched for something to latch onto that wouldn't expose her. The question that came surprised her. "Why couldn't they send someone you knew? The other immune, you said their chaperones were people from their life. Why this?" She tapped the book, still hardly believing it.

    Carol's gaze cut away, down to her own hands, her fingers worrying a hangnail. "They…" She exhaled through her nose. "They didn't have much to work with," she said finally.

    Carol's mouth tightened while Zosia reached for the most obvious. If this hivemind used family, friends… then Carol must not have had them, or not anymore. The thought made Zosia ache, which was ridiculous, she barely knew her, she didn't—"Did you…not have anyone?"

    Carol's face pinched, like the question found a bruise. "I did," she said, and her throat worked, her eyes went glassy for a second, then cleared with effort. "She died. When it happened. Helen."

    The name from earlier. Zosia's anger lost the rest of its edge. She'd been telling herself she was the one stolen from, but Carol had been robbed first. 

    "My wife," Carol added.

    Zosia froze. Wife.

    The word rearranged the room. The shock hit Zosia like a sudden gust, making the crush she was trying to dampen flare up horribly. Her face burned, and for one terrible second every thought she had was the wrong one, and the sympathy she felt tangled with something far less generous.

    Of course. A theoretically possible but categorically impossible crush on a woman who had lost the love of her life. One person, as her whole world. Zosia had lived like that too. She'd buried Sasha and carried it like ballast for years, and she knew what Carol's face would be doing right now without needing to look.

    She inhaled slowly as part of the fondness in her shifted and steadied into recognition. Zosia's hand lifted an inch from the sofa, a reflex to reach across—anything that said I get it—

    Carol caught the movement and her expression tightened. "I don't want—" Carol's jaw clenched. "It's fine," she sighed. "So yeah," her voice less defensive. "They sent you. When I first wrote it, Raban was a woman, and the romance was between two women."

    Zosia's attention narrowed to that sentence—two women, Raban was a woman—and the implications bloomed outward like ink in water.

    Why she'd recognized herself in Raban, how the romance had made her feel seen—the reasons she'd clung to the book beneath the sailing and the nonsense. She'd always told herself it was just because she was lonely.

    Now it made perfect sense. Her throat burned. "And they knew," Zosia said, voice low. "It knew that."

    "Yep." 

    Zosia looked down again at the thick hardback in her hands. The book felt heavier now.

    Her crush—humiliating—shifted again. It wasn't just Carol Sturka, author of Wycaro. It was Carol Sturka, the woman who wrote a love story between two women and had to hide it in plain sight, who had lost her wife at the end of the world, who was sitting across from her now, braced to be laughed at.

    Zosia's gaze dropped to Carol's fidgety hands. "I don't want to punch you," she said softly. Carol's shoulders sagged. "You don't—" Her accent felt thick. "You don't understand."

    Carol's eyebrows went up. "Try me."

    Zosia didn't look at her. If she did, she might do something idiotic, like cry. "After my best friend died—" she said, and her mouth went careful. She chose the version that wouldn't start a fire, that would keep things simpler— "husband, technically..." She'd been saying it that way for so long it had worn a groove, and she followed the path of least exposure. "I couldn't sleep. I could not… be alone with myself." She held the book a little tighter. "These books got me through it."

    The silence that followed was dense. When Zosia finally made herself glance up, Carol was looking at her drink.

    "Okay," Carol said, nodding at something, accepting it. "I'm sorry."

    The mortification returned in a fresh wave. She had just confessed her private coping mechanism to the author.

    Carol leaned back, rubbed her palm over face. "Okay. Jesus," and gave a short, shocked laugh. "You've read my books."

    Zosia wanted a pit to open under her, but she looked at Carol's lopsided smile and felt the fondness hold. In the empty space where everyone used to be, where oblivion made everything easy, Zosia felt something difficult take root.

    That evening, Carol found Zosia in the living room, legs tucked underneath her on the sofa, foot tapping against the arm. 

    After she'd shown Zosia the guest bedroom, she had asked, offhand, if Zosia had read Bloodsong yet. Like she didn't actually care. Zosia said she'd been waiting for the paperback, for whatever reason, so Carol had pulled out an author copy—still crisp—and shoved it into Zosia's hands before she could change her mind. 

    It was an attempt at giving Zosia space to process that wasn't just Carol retreating into the furniture, and truth was, Carol needed the space too. The day had scraped her down, and she didn't trust what stupid shit would come out of her mouth if she tried to fill every silence. Carol swore to herself that tomorrow she would be a Good Host, be here for Zosia, ask about her old life and Be Cool about it.

    Zosia had said her husband died, and that was clearly the person she'd mentioned in Montana. The implication had been plain enough for Carol to seize on, like her brain was grateful for an excuse to stop hoping and start being miserable. She was straight.

    The lamp in the corner threw warm light across Zosia and caught the edge of her jaw. She'd been reading for hours, turning pages with such intense focus it made Carol self-conscious. Carol had checked, twice, from the hallway, pretending to look for something in a console cupboard both times. Now a third time. She wanted to get a bottle out so badly. Carol turned for the kitchen and nearly pivoted and turned back when Zosia glanced up.

    "Hi," Carol said, caught. She dithered at the edge of the living room. "It's late."

    Zosia closed the book on her thumb and pushed her hair back behind both ears. Her eyes were tired. "I know. I wanted to finish the chapter." She paused. "Chapters."

    Carol's gaze went to the makeshift bookmark—one of Zosia's own hairs, dark against the paper—and tried to calculate where she was without being obvious. "How far did you get?" Carol asked, like it didn't matter.

    "Raban is in the cave," Zosia said. "With the healer. Lucasia has just found him."

    Carol knew the scene. Lucasia lifting the candle wearing Raban's coat, seeing his face, her heart filling with hope for the first time in months. And Raban looking up at her and saying Have you mistaken me for someone you know.

    "Right," Carol said, gulping. She leaned against the doorframe and crossed her arms, attempting cool and casual. "What do you think so far?"

    Zosia closed the book properly, squaring it on her knee. "It is better than book three."

    Carol waited for the spike of shame, from being damned with faint praise, but it didn't hit. Larry had told her, with a straight face, that this shit was as good as Shakespeare. This was one woman with sleepy eyes and real opinions she was too polite to say. The concept of criticism existed again, finally, and it didn't have to mean rejection of the whole.

    Carol came into the room and slouched on the arm of the opposite chair. "Low bar."

    "It is not a low bar," Zosia said, offended on her behalf, apparently. She straightened her back and then looked almost annoyed at herself for what she said next. "But the physics of the ship-handling is always… melodramatic."

    "Melodramatic? In my pirate soap opera?"

    She should've rolled her eyes, but instead she found herself fond. She used to roll them at the mansplainers correcting minutiae, as if any of it mattered when the ship was sailing on purple fucking sand. She didn't have to guess why her reaction was the opposite when it came from Zosia.

    Zosia's lips pressed together in one corner. "Yes," and then, as if precision required it, "I notice it more every time I re-read…" She moved straight into the critique, face gone pink, saying something about angles like she could outrun the blush, and Carol didn't hear a word of it. Every time I re-read. Plural. Habitual. Nobody re-reads stories they don't love.

    Zosia looked down at the book, then up again, like she was deciding whether to say the next part. "It also… it changed for me after you told me."

    "Told you what?"

    Zosia didn't hold her gaze. "That Raban was a woman," she said. "Now I can't read it the same. It feels like it was always supposed to be that."

    Yep. There it is. Straight woman prefers straight romance. Carol forced herself to nod. "Makes sense," she said, instead.

    "I can see now you are doing something different with Raban."

    Carol didn't know what to say to that so she waited, wiping her palms on her sweatpants. Zosia's voice had never been this accented before. 

    "This scene where Lucasia finds him," Zosia said, and her words went more deliberate. She was probably thinking in Polish and translating on the way out. "He looks at her and sees a stranger, and she cannot even be angry, because it is not his fault."

    Carol gripped her kneecap hard enough to leave a bruise. She could feel the fictional frame bending under what Carol actually wanted to ask. "So what do you think happens next?" Carol said. She cleared her throat. "I mean—what do you think Lucasia will do? Tell him who he was?"

    Zosia looked up. "She shouldn't."

    Carol's stomach dropped. "Huh?"

    "It would ruin him." Zosia's accent thickened around the consonants. "If she tells him, he will try to be that person for her. He is loyal." Zosia frowned, but it was a reader's frown, annoyed at a problem in the story, not at Carol. "She would be giving him a story that belongs to her. He would…" She searched. "It would be like wearing someone else's coat."

    "And if she doesn't?" Carol asked, and her voice broke embarrassingly on the last word.

    "Then she is deciding for him what he can bear." Her thumb pressed into the book's spine. "That's Lucasia at her worst. In book two she does the same with the mutiny—she decides what the crew can handle and she's wrong every time."

    Jesus. Zosia was pulling from two books back, cross-referencing Lucasia's pattern, arguing from the text. She wasn't thinking about Carol at all. "So either way, she's fucked."

    Zosia's mouth twitched. "I would not say it like that." She set the book down on the arm of the sofa, spine aligned with the edge. "I'm thinking," she said slowly, and there was fatigue, under the careful formality, "that Lucasia loves him and does not know what to do. If she tells him to get him back, she loves him more than she respects him. If she keeps it to herself because she thinks he can't take it, she respects him less than she claims to…" Zosia trailed off. She looked at the framed black-and-white print on the wall, her reflection faintly visible.

    Zosia looked back. She studied Carol's face, and Carol could see her noticing her tight jaw, the white-knuckled grip on her own knee. She frowned and dropped her head to the book again. Her hair fell forward and she impatiently pushed it back behind an ear. 

    Carol had told Zosia she looked like Raban, but the resemblance had been skin-deep until now. The Zosia she had known moved through the world so poised, like nobody Carol had ever imagined. Now, she was restless, just like Raban: the hair push, the tapping, the jaw jumping while she thought. They had delivered the face and left out the friction. 

    "I don't know yet," Zosia said, with a finality that ended discussion. "Maybe Raban remembers on his own or Lucasia finds a middle way. I have not finished. Do not tell me spoilers."

    "Sure," Carol said. "Take your time."

    Zosia stood and the movement was stiff as she walked past Carol, then paused in the doorway. "Good night."

    "Night," Carol said, too fast. Zosia's fingers caught the doorframe on the way out—two taps, quick and absent—and Carol listened to her even footsteps on the stairs, to the guest room door shutting. She sat in the empty room with her arms wrapped around herself.

    Every time I re-read.

    Carol thought of Helen in the car after a signing, scrolling through her phone while Carol replayed every interaction. Did that lady really cry? Carol had asked derisively, and Helen had smiled sideways and said Your readers love it, babe and your readers had drawn a gentle line. Cotton candy, Larry had told her, confirming what she'd suspected and Helen had loved her too much to say. She'd read every draft Carol handed her, with a pencil in her mouth and notes that were always about pacing and never about meaning.

    Zosia, before, had loved Wycaro and loved Carol and loved everyone and everything else too, and still, the part of Carol that Helen had never been able to reach, that wanted someone to love the work not just the worker, had responded hungrily. Carol's words were the last novelty left for everyone on Earth, and Zosia had been their theater, and Carol had basked in the spotlight of it.

    This Zosia loved Wycaro the same way Carol did: privately and probably more than it deserved. Nobody blushes about liking Shakespeare. She loved Carol's cotton candy enough to be embarrassed by it.

    Helen had loved her and not the books. Everyone had loved everything so meant nothing. Now Zosia loved the books and not her.

    Nothing about any of this whole fucked up situation had been built to hold any kind of love story, but she'd wanted it anyway, pathetically, obviously, and none of it mattered because Zosia was straight. It had always been a long shot, she'd known that, and been too afraid to look at it. 

    She could live with it. Loss and heartbreak and every other wretched fucking feeling weren't new. She'd been living with them for months. She could try to be an adult about it, stop angling herself toward a door that would never open, and even if it hurt, she could still be glad Zosia was her own person again. It just meant she had to live with the fact that the decision had cost her something she'd secretly wanted to keep.

    She thought about telling Zosia everything. Sitting her down and saying: you loved me, or something that looked like it. You made me write the true version of Raban, the one I'd been too scared to write again for twenty years, and I did it because you made me happy enough, or stupid enough, and I can't tell the difference anymore.

    She thought about not telling her. Letting this Zosia, imperious and unreadable, become whoever she was, without the weight of Carol's mess on top of her own.

    Lucasia loves him and does not know what to do.

    Carol rubbed her eyes with both hands, and stayed there for a long time.

    In the dream, Zosia came to herself as everyone.

    She was everyone, but it didn't feel like a chorus. It felt like drifting; the current already decided.

    She was on the Iskra. Its familiar grooves under her boots, the salt-worn railing under her palm, her feet found the deck's pitch—except there was no pitch. The ship was still, no harbor noise carrying across the water. The air smelled of diesel and rust.

    She walked off the gangway because the dream had already decided she would. Her actions were inevitable and unarguable, and she reached for a folded piece of fabric from a market stall and her arms slipped into the sleeves. She felt the texture and knew it simultaneously, too precise to be sensation and too rough to be information, her skin's memory and theirs overlapping

    The street should have been full. Vendors, tourists, the dense pedestrian stream of a cosmopolitan port city. Instead there was stillness and silence and bodies, dropped mid-stride, mid-gesture, a woman's hand still clenched around the handle of a pram tipped sideways.

    She bent to pick up a corpse.

    Her arms took the load and her knees angled with someone else's practice. She carried the child toward a truck where others were lifting and loading, and there was no grief, none, the weight distributed across so many that each share was almost nothing, and underneath the nothing, a constant balm: not alone.

    That was the strangest part. Being in the dream and being held by it. She couldn't control where it was headed, but she also didn't have to carry the burden of choosing or consequences. The peace was blissful, even while she handled the evidence of an apocalypse. Pain, panic, grief, loneliness—all of it belonged to someone she had been excused from being.

    Zosia felt the odd sensation of being selected, like a hand had reached into a crowd and closed around her. A tug and turn. A new heading. The assignment carried a name she knew and something responded as recognition, or maybe it was everyone's satisfaction at a good match. The dream didn't distinguish, and by the time she reached for it, the feeling had already dissolved into the task.

    Then, as dreams do, it jumped. Between, time existed and she knew what she had lived, but it was carried without seeing, like a river carrying sediment it never surfaces. The sky became another and the air shifted, still dusty but dry. Albuquerque, she somehow knew. She was landing an airplane, the runway heat shimmering, and then she was driving through streets that should have had traffic and didn't, the silence sunlit, toward a house that felt like a fixed point.

    She stepped up into a yard and Carol was there. Her eyes hit Zosia and hardened. Her grief was fresh, and so was the feeling that climbed in Zosia at the sight of her, a lurch of devotion towards their unexpected charge. Thirteen times across the world, the same impulse, the same open wound. 

    Keep her well, they said, she agreed, and it made Zosia's mouth move—words came—her voice higher and more upbeat than in years.

    The same book she'd held the night before came up between them and Zosia felt herself stand to attention. They reached for the gentlest proof they had, something meant to comfort her, not corner her. Tell her it was love that placed you here. "We just want you to be happy." Comfort her. "Should we tell you how much she loved you?"

    Carol's grief surged up, and they learned: this comfort hurts her. The shouting continued, and the anger struck Zosia's body, and even as the collective braced for the crash—her muscles locking, her vision going—even as it happened, Zosia could feel the absolution. It's not personal. 

    The world around her, around them, went down too, a synchronized seizure, the hive's defensive reflex, and then death: systems failing while bodies were offline, vehicles still rolling, people falling at the wrong angle from the wrong height. Ordinary ways to die, multiplied by millions.

    The dream didn't allow her to feel it, only to know it. The loss passed through every mind at once, held by all of them together, and over it ran the same soothing refrain: we'll adapt, we'll continue.

    Then the dream contracted without warning—the whole world, and then one grave, one woman, her jaw tight. Carol turned away and vomited onto the turned earth, her body folding forward, shoulders heaving. Comfort her. Zosia's hand went to Carol's back and her thumb brushed once across the top of her spine. In the dream, Zosia couldn't tell who had moved it.

    They returned to what they could safely offer Carol: competence, hands, an excavator. Zosia completed a task Carol couldn't finish alone and the shared pleasure of service moved through her chest like a long exhale.

    Carol stared at the ground and apologized, voice raw with the effort of it, the words graceless and blunt and meaning: you're a human and I treated you like a wall to throw things at. Zosia felt it move through her like warm water, and as Carol choked on a scoff, the feeling swelled, vast and uncomplicated: a love that wanted nothing back and would give Carol everything and take her pain as soon as possible.

    Then her own thought rose, stubborn: Let her keep it. It startled her even in the dream. She couldn't tell if the thought had been hers then, or if it was hers now, dreaming and annotating in the margin. It was an instinctive respect for autonomy, sharpened by years of mourning and a career of being watched and managed. Carol's grief didn't need to be erased, she needed someone to stand by her while it existed.

    She turned toward the smell of fuel and was already in the recycled air of a cockpit, her fingers finding switches with calm competence. She held no heading, the heading held her. Hours had passed between the grave and this seat, she could feel them stacked behind her, lived and unshown, full of moments the dream had weighed and found less essential.

    Zosia walked to the back in a suit she hadn't chosen—civilian, but a ghost of her dress blues, stripped of every anchor and star. Her shoulders sat low and loose beneath it, the rigid set she'd trained into them gone. Carol kept making little noises—huffs, scoffs, muttered curses—that made her smile. Their fondness pressed through her bones, watching Carol through billions of eyes that all wore hers, like standing with her back to a wall built of people who wouldn't let her fall.

    In the airport, the other immune gathered for Carol. Zosia regarded them with fascination and patience, as though they were rare animals who might eventually come closer to the fence. She watched Carol carefully, who was trying not to need anyone while her eyes searched faces anyway. Zosia's own face was doing something she could feel but couldn't steer—turned toward Carol with an attentiveness that didn't falter when Carol looked back. The expression belonged to everyone and also felt, in a way she couldn't separate out, like it belonged to her. It was her face.

    The immune filled Air Force One's board room with voices, and Zosia felt her attention narrow on Carol, outside their circles, conspicuously unacknowledged. She felt the pull before the words came—a current that lifted her voice to the tone that carried without shouting. "If we could have everyone's attention, please," and gestured toward Carol with an open palm. Everyone turned. She'd done it so many times in Iskra's wardroom the hive hadn't needed to reach for the skill. Carol briefly looked at her, surprised and grateful. In the dream Zosia couldn't tell if the satisfaction was all of theirs or her own—the old trick of bringing a room to heel, repurposed now for Carol's benefit, fit so well in her that the difference between steered and volunteered felt indistinguishable.

    A dinner table. Carol sat with a glass of wine in one hand and her other hand flat on the table. Zosia stood close enough that if Carol leaned sideways she'd touch her. She liked the proximity. She couldn't tell, again, whether the feeling was theirs, had been hers then or was hers now. The dream didn't care.

    Laxmi told Carol the true number and Zosia felt regret rise and they diffused it almost instantly, distributed among billions until it was diluted to nothing. Carol stormed across the gravel and her foot caught on something and Zosia was already moving— onto her knees, hands reaching for Carol's face before the thought caught up. Sailor's reflex, or everyone's. She couldn't tell.

    "Carol?" In the dream her voice sounded gentler than she'd ever heard it in her life and she held Carol's face, cold in her palms. The hive's serenity steadied her grip and she couldn't tell whether the care in her hands was their's or her own, and the world stuttered black and the dream jumped before either let go.

    Koumba leaned against the armchair with an easy looseness, and smiled at Zosia like they already shared a secret. He was the only one who hadn't left Carol. Zosia thought he was trying, in his way, to keep Carol from splintering. Zosia watched Carol's face darken, repulsion and protection tangling.

    "That's your idea of paradise?" Carol snapped, eyes cutting to Zosia, wanting confirmation, needing Zosia to say no so she could justify her fury.

    Zosia felt the urge press through her: keep Carol calm. Don't let her anger spike.

    I want to stay with her, she thought, and immediately she doubted—was it her thought then, or hers now, sleeping alone in a guest bedroom? 

    Koumba was right there, Zosia could feel his disappointment before it happened, waiting behind his eyes. She didn't want to cause it. She must keep everyone from hurting. She let the current make the choice for her, and the dream didn't linger. It pulled away—window, sunlight, Carol's scoffing surrender—everything smearing like wet paint.

    Zosia woke up.

    For a second she didn't know where she was. The bedroom's ceiling beams blurred above her. Her body hurt everywhere, unmoored from them and anchored to nothing.

    She lay still, her jaw sore from clenching, and took inventory. She'd dreamed, and the dream had been full of answers she'd been desperate for.

    The hivemind's full archive was gone—its omniscient knowledge of everything, of Carol—too much for one mind to hold without the network. What remained was first-person: her own eyes, her own sequence of days, compressed and fragmented but hers. She'd been one node, and she got one node's account. It was a start.

    The only loose thread, spoiled and stripped of every surprise she'd been saving it for, was the ending of Bloodsong of Wycaro. No scene in the dream was attached to its acquisition, no book in her hands, just lodged in her recall now, knowledge with no origin. It was the only sign they had left a deeper residue beneath the dreams. The same as how Carol's name had come, in the container, when they'd touched hands.

    But she was getting answers. That was more than she'd had yesterday, which had been nothing; just the blank fact of being free and no way to use it. Now she had a course. Night by night, if this kept up, she'd have the whole picture, or her piece of it at least. Yesterday her spine had done all the work of keeping her together, letting procedure fill the space where purpose should have been. Now the relief of having a heading was so physical it loosened muscles she hadn't known she'd been tensing, and her pain eased slightly.

    She lay there while her pulse slowed. Had she been having private thoughts underneath? She was living those memories again now, knowing how they ended, already unfortunately compromised on the subject of Carol, so who knew what she was reading back into it. How could she know if any thoughts were hers then? The question didn't frighten her. It was genuinely interesting. She had time.

    The house made settling sounds. A distant clink that might've been Carol moving around the kitchen. She was embarrassingly aware she was looking forward to it. 

    Carol had shown her the guest bedroom with a stiff little gesture, like a flight attendant pointing emergency exits. "If you need anything," Carol said, and the words sounded rehearsed again, "I'm here." 

    Zosia had nodded and thanked her, because she didn't know what else to do with I'm here beside tamp down her crush like it was a fire on deck: smother it and starve it of oxygen. It was ridiculous. Unattainable, she told herself, with the familiar resignation. She was used to it. Carol was still grieving.

    She had lay down fully clothed, because undressing felt too intimate in Carol's house, and exhaustion had taken her quickly.

    Now, she sat up slowly, ribs aching. The painkillers had worn off into a dull throb. Her limbs felt heavy, but also… different. She walked to the small dresser and opened the duffel bag Carol had offered. The folded clothes stared back, neat and impersonal. She picked out something familiar, dark slim trousers, a white button up, underwear that wasn't hers but fit.

    She pulled it all on, movements careful because her body protested. She tied her hair and paused, staring at her reflection in the mirror. She looked younger, like herself and not herself, and her mind thought of a word for it—离奇的.

    She gasped. She looked at her hands, and thought of the plane controls, and felt her hands remember them, like muscle memory. She whispered, experimentally, a sentence in Hindi. She somehow knew her English was more extensive than it had ever been, her French faster.

    Her mouth knew. Her hands knew. Zosia had used the knowledge in the dream like a tool: pick it up, apply it, set it down, and the tools were still in her. Subconscious procedural memory, left behind.

    Zosia stared at herself, eyes wide, a smile growing. She could fly a plane, operate an excavator, fluently speak five more languages she hadn't known before. She felt a laugh rise up unexpectedly and the sound startled her with how easy and close to the surface it was. 

    She left her room and stepped into the hallway, and paused with her hand on the wall, like she used to, to orient herself by a ship's vibration. The house didn't move. It was just there, a luxury of space she still wasn't used to. Her nose followed the smell of coffee—instant, ugh—like a towline.

    The framed photo stopped her. Two women against the railing of a boat, in afternoon light. Carol, younger, smiling at something out of frame, her eyes the same impossible blue she'd seen yesterday, matched by the water behind her. The woman beside her was darker haired, hand raised against the sun. Helen. Zosia felt her mind automatically reach out before she'd finished looking, the same reflex that had once returned the current air temperature before the thought completed. Nothing came.

    She felt her face go warm in shame. She'd spent her life keeping her own privacy guarded, stepped out of a consciousness that had everything about everyone, and her first instinct had been to use the skill that wasn't there any longer to be nosy. The blankness that came back was the better answer. It wasn't hers. It was Carol's, Helen's, and she couldn't touch it.

    She looked again at Carol. In the dream, her grief had stopped them cold, and Zosia had been sent to manage her loneliness. Consolation prize were the words Carol had used. 

    Zosia stood in the borrowed socks and looked a moment longer at Helen's raised hand. They had been married. She understood, abstractly, that some women like them could have this. She'd deferred the dream years ago, alongside a fabled retirement plan, as implausible. For a version of herself in different circumstances, in a different time and place, even if she'd found the right woman.

    Carol had found hers. The evidence was right there: the smile, the light, the hand against the sun. Zosia followed the coffee.

     

    Chapter 3

    Carol had woken up braced for the worst, her default setting now: jaw already tight, brain already writing a list of ways things could go to shit; but as she'd sat up, hair in her face, one leg hanging off of the couch, she'd found she was…not in a bad mood.

    Zosia was alive, still in one piece, and when Carol had looked in on her late last night with the door ajar, a crease of tension had smoothed out of her brow and she'd been asleep. Carol had actually left and not stared at her for more than the four breaths she'd counted, like a normal person.

    She'd gone back to the living room and sat on the couch where Zosia had been, staring at the ceiling. The day's exhaustion had eventually caught up to her and she'd fallen asleep right there using Stormshadow to prop a cushion up.

    Carol padded to the kitchen in whatever she'd pulled on in the dark after her shower—the gray pants that had been on the chair, blue sweater. Helen used to leave things out for her when she fell asleep at the desk. Carol still blindly reached for the same chair when she was tired, the gesture outliving her, and by now the flinch had scabbed to almost nothing.

    She was hardly feeling rested at all, but she'd come to a verdict last night on the couch and it had the bleak comfort of a closed case. The Zosia she'd been a mess over hadn't been a person. She'd been an imaginary friend: a happy puppet moving through Carol's rooms, looking like a character she'd carved out of her book; sewn together with only a handful of scraps from the actual woman, who was formal and foreign and straight. Whatever Carol felt would eventually burn itself out for lack of reciprocal fuel. The relief of a ceiling, of knowing it had already been as bad it was going to get, felt almost like rest.

    The kitchen was cold, the tile biting through her socks, and she moved on autopilot to pour a finger of the vodka, then stopped. Today required a clear head, or at least a head that could pretend. Vodka wouldn't help with either. She forced herself to open the jar of instant coffee and pick up the kettle instead, went to switch the faucet on, then stopped again, hand hovering. 

    Footsteps on the stairs. Carol tensed. The early sun had found the kitchen window and lay flat across the counter in a pale strip, warming nothing.

    Zosia appeared in the entryway and looked… better. It looked like her joints were protesting every step, but her eyes were clearer, leaning forward even while the rest of her held back—an anticipation she hadn't had yesterday, and Carol couldn't tell if it was for the caffeine or for the sheer novelty of waking up as herself.

    Her hands were shoved into her front pockets and the gesture was so unlike the Zosia Carol knew, who had moved through the house with such gentle inevitability. This Zosia looked unsure of where to put her elbows, like she'd woken up in someone else's life and was trying not to touch anything. On the other hand, standing there with weight on the balls of her feet, restless, this Zosia nudged the stool leg a fraction, aligning it with the tile seam, then looked faintly annoyed at herself for caring. Carol didn't know whether to be happy or sad.

    Then Zosia looked up and gave her an awkward, tight-lipped smile, not the full, serene one she was used to. It made her nose scrunch. It made her look—God, it made her look a way Carol didn't want to think about—different from before, but the feeling it produced was the same and she couldn't summon her guilt fast enough to cover it. The difficult day ahead dissolved for one stupid second, and Carol forgot to brace for it. 

    Carol tried to play it off with a cheerful "Morning!" and turned back to the counter.

    "Morning," Zosia replied, and the word was slightly awkward too, like she was testing how it sounded. "Do you have a spare toothbrush? There wasn't one in the bag."

    Carol was pouring the kettle and her mouth answered before her brain caught up, "Yours is still in the bathroom."
