    She froze. The domestic implication hung there between them, loud as a dropped pan. At least she hadn't specified master bath. She chanced to glance sideways at her.

    Zosia's eyebrows had lifted. She stared at the counter like it had suddenly become fascinating. "Oh. Did I…" she cleared her throat. "Did I stay over often?"

    Carol could hear the hesitation. She couldn't square it. Learning the world had ended should've surely sharpened her, made her meaner. Not… whatever this was today.

    She set the kettle down too hard. She'd told herself she had been manipulated and seduced. All of that was true, but it wasn't the whole truth. She could hear how it would sound and felt ill. She willed herself to keep her expression neutral. "Some nights," she said. Technically true. God, she was a coward.

    Zosia nodded too quickly like she'd expected worse. Carol swerved, "Are you okay with those clothes?" she asked, then immediately regretted it as her brain supplied: I have others I pulled off of you and kept. She gulped. "I mean—I might have other things. If you want options."

    Zosia smiled a little. "They're not-not my style," she said, and the double negative made her sound shy…and American. Carol noticed then her accent was back like it used to be. Weird. Zosia tugged lightly at the hem of the white shirt. "I don't really get a chance to have any style, but this is close to what I usually wear."

    Carol frowned. "What do you mean?"

    Zosia glanced down at herself, then back up, as if deciding whether the detail mattered. "Uniform," she said simply. "I'm Polish Navy."

    For a second, Carol refused. Navy. This Zosia, blushing as she tugged at her shirt? But then she remembered her yesterday, spine like a fucking flagpole: demanding answers with authority, the Mercator critique, the sir.

    Decades she'd been writing sailors, and all along, Zosia had been a real one. The kid who hadn't had two coins had got herself onto one of those ships under her own steam. Her chest felt warm and sore at the same time and she smiled before she could stop it.

    Zosia straightened. "What?" she asked. "What's so funny?"

    Carol shook her head once, trying to dislodge whatever she was feeling. "Nothing," she said, but then—shut up shut up shut up—she added, "You told me once you wanted to know all about the ships leaving Gdansk. And now you do."

    Zosia looked thrown, as if Carol had reached across a gap she hadn't known existed. Her eyes searched Carol's face and her tone was half wonder. "You know something about me?"

    "It's not—" Carol sighed and gave up on explaining.

    "What else do you know?" Zosia asked, and there was an eagerness in it that made Carol want to put her head through the wall. It should have been a good thing, Zosia happy, Zosia free and smiling.

    She forced a scoff. "Not much," she said. "Don't worry."

    Zosia took her hands out of her pockets and stood straighter, like she'd been waiting to say what came next. "Carol. I have a report." The word was funny—a report, in a kitchen—but Zosia said it without irony. "I remembered you, too. When I slept. And the skills I used are still in me."

    Carol's whole body locked. Fuck. Fuck. "Jesus Christ. Okay. Remembered what?" she asked, keeping her voice neutral. 

    "My… joined life," Zosia said, and then corrected herself. "The first days. I think it'll happen every night. It was in chronological order, like I was living it again." If Carol had learned one thing yesterday, it was that Zosia had that bravery: she would walk straight toward something if it meant she got answers. "Like my brain is thawing, and this is how it's doing it."

    Carol matched her breathing to the kettle's cooling click. Zosia hadn't remembered anything that made her angry. Yet.

    Zosia started listing skills off, reporting like a professional, except her eyes were sparkling with the delight of finding a twenty in a pocket. Carol leaned on the counter and watched her flex her hands open and closed, like testing the memory in her tendons. 

    "So it's all in there again," Carol said. "Everything they knew?"

    Zosia looked at Carol like she'd asked if Zosia could still breathe underwater. "No. That would be too much for one brain. I had access to all of it through the network, and without the network..." She shrugged. "I can only remember what I lived and used. The rest's gone." 

    "Right," Carol nodded, "Obviously." The encyclopaedia was gone, an Earth's worth of trivia crammed into one skull, of course it couldn't hold. But she'd heard what she needed to hear: Zosia remembered what she'd lived and used, and what had she used more thoroughly than everyone's knowledge of Carol? I remembered you, too.

    Carol drank her coffee and her shoulders dropped an inch. She'd been assigned a woman to manage her loneliness, hated it, and underneath that had been so grateful to be seen that it made her sick to remember. The idea that Zosia could understand the whole ugly mess of her without Carol having to explain—she hadn't wanted to lose that. She wouldn't have to start from scratch, and Zosia was downstairs making eye contact like none of it disqualified Carol from company.

    But chronological order meant every night was closer to the parts Carol couldn't say aloud, and if Zosia reached them first, the silence would be its own violation on top of the first. That felt unforgivable. Only, telling her now felt like blowing the fuse on the one fragile good thing Zosia had: waking up with some spark in her eyes, choosing to be free and seeming weirdly happy about it today.

    She would tell her, she decided, before the dream did it for her, just… not like this. She'd wait for Zosia to find her footing, not right now when she was freshly free. It sounded like avoidance, but maybe timing mattered, maybe it was the difference between honesty and cruelty. 

    Coward.

    Carol's fingers tightened around the counter. Zosia watched the movement. If there was another thing she'd learned about this Zosia: she noticed everything.

    "That's great," Carol said. It was great. It was also not great.

    Zosia's eyebrows rose again, but before Carol could dig herself in deeper shit, there were three sharp raps at the front door. Manousos. Carol's shoulders loosened because at least he was a known quantity: righteous asshole. Carol went to open the door and he stood there with his backpack like he'd been up since dawn.

    "Status," he said immediately.

    "Good morning to you too."

    Manny's eyes cut past her into the house. "Zosia," he said, curt. 

    Zosia had been leaning against the counter with her hands back in her pockets, more relaxed than Carol had seen her yet. Manousos stepped over the threshold, and Carol watched as her spine found its full height, chin lifting, the shy hands disappearing to one wrist clasped in the other hand, and whatever had been tentative about her a second ago was gone.

    The shift from shy to commanding hit Carol somewhere it had no business hitting in the same room as Manousos. She'd seen it yesterday too and it had rattled her then for reasons she'd chalked up to adrenaline.

    Leftover feelings she could handle—she'd solved that last night on the couch, she told herself—but want was a different animal, untouched by logic, and it had just watched Zosia snap to attention and rolled over like a dog. Orientation, reciprocity, basic dignity, none of it had been invited to the conversation. The sight of her was the same problem it had been since day goddamn one, and the only thing she could do was not a goddamn thing.

    Carol gritted her teeth and turned to Manny, wanting to start a fight with him for no reason other than she needed somewhere to put the feeling. "Boots," she barked, pointing at his feet, because if she couldn't fuck Zosia she could at least be rude to a man. "She's remembering," Carol added grudgingly, as he shuffled his feet.

    His eyes cut to her. "Todo?"

    "No," Carol said, and felt vaguely ill again. The good mood she'd woken up with was a distant memory. 

    Manny's gaze went to Zosia with barely-contained urgency. "You remember?"

    Zosia nodded once. "Some." She didn't elaborate.

    Manny let out a hard breath through his nose, as if he could exhale now without the whole plan collapsing. "What do you know?" he asked, already halfway into the next step.

    Zosia's eyes drifted up and to the side, "I remembered joining day," she said slowly, testing the phrase. "Flying here. Meeting Carol." Her gaze flicked over to Carol and away again, quick as a touch. "Then meeting the other immune, and the next day when Carol let me go."

    What?

    "I didn't—" Carol started, "I didn't let—"

    "Good," Manousos cut in, as if Carol's correction would be an irrelevant detour. He made an approving sound. "Yes. It will come," he said, "I believe." He turned his attention fully to Zosia, voice going brisk, "Then we use you."

    Carol's head snapped up. "She could've died yesterday."

    Manny finally met her eyes. He didn't blink. "She is alive," he said. "And she is remembering. That was the plan."

    Carol almost laughed. As if any of this was a plan. As if Carol hadn't been playing the most fucked-up emotionally-fraught one-woman improv show ever since the bubble burst.

    "He's not wrong." Zosia said. She glanced again at Carol. "I can help."

    Carol had felt her temper rise on reflex, but Zosia was standing there offering herself up with a stubborn sense of purpose. Carol made her jaw unclench. "You don't have to—"

    "I want to," Zosia said simply. "If I'm useful I can think clearly." Manny nodded once, satisfied. And then—because Zosia was a person now with her own wants—she added, "But first, I want coffee."

    Manny's eyebrows lifted. "Coffee."

    "Coffee," Zosia repeated, in the same tone she'd applied to solving the apocalypse. She looked at Carol. "Do you have any beans? Kona, Colombian?"

    Carol tried to be normal. "There's a can in one of the cupboards, no idea where it's from." 

    Manny's expression did something bizarre. "Colombian?" he asked, and there was a note in his voice Carol didn't know.

    Zosia's gaze went to him, assessing. "You like it?"

    "Of course," Manny said, like she'd asked if he knew the sun rose. "It is grown where I grew up. It is the best." 

    "What altitude?" Zosia asked, like that was a usual question to ask a person. Carol looked between them like they were talking in a foreign language.

    His eyebrows rose again. "Huila. One thousand seven hundred meters. Good body. Good acid if you do not do it over." 

    Zosia made a low hum of approval and Carol's insides flipped, then soured, because the sound was for Manny and his stupid fucking altitude beans. "It's 'overdo' it," Carol grumbled.

    Manousos ignored her with practiced ease. Zosia had opened a cupboard and found the can with a speed that suggested she was operating on her new brain-map of the house. She set it down and reached for the grinder, then hesitated, glancing at Carol like she'd just realized she was in someone else's home. 

    Carol gave her a stiff nod. Then Zosia moved like she was running a drill: she set the grinder down, checked the lid, checked the counter, positioned the press. She lifted the can, shook it once, then pried it open. The scent hit the air, different from the instant; rich and almost chocolatey. 

    Carol was yanked backward in time. That same smell, same morning light. Carol sitting there, wrecked, trying to pretend the night before wasn't a big deal. Like she hadn't come more times in one night than ever before, like she hadn't written a chapter faster than ever before. Zosia moving around her with the same competence.

    Carol's hand tightened around the edge of the counter to concentrate on here and now. Zosia was weighing the beans in her palm, eyes narrowing.

    It should've been unnerving, yanked Carol back again. Instead, Zosia did something the old-her had never done. She tipped a few beans back into the can, shook it and picked two more, like she was choosing specific soldiers for a formation. She didn't look at any instructions. She adjusted the grind finer than the markings suggested, then stopped, listened to the motor, and nudged it again. 

    She was making decisions that were too small to explain and too exact to be random. Carol used to do that. At a keyboard, two in the morning, in the drafts no one would see. Small decisions made on feel, trusting some interior sense of when a line was done.

    Zosia notched the water off the boil too early and waited, counting under her breath in Polish, then poured in a weird jerky spiral. This was an art too, like her writing. Before, Zosia had followed process like scripture: perfectly executed and repeatable, every barista on earth averaged. This Zosia was making the tiny irrational choices that consensus would have eliminated, because no committee comes to weird jerky spiral.

    She turned toward the cupboard and Carol saw it. The Shrek mug, ugly as fuck, green grin mocking her from the shelf. Zosia's hand grabbed it from among the many mugs without thinking and slid it toward Carol without looking.

    Carol froze with it halfway between them, her fingers not moving to accept it. Zosia seemed to realize at the same time, her hand paused on the ceramic then withdrew, and she tucked her hair behind her ear with a briskness like she was reprimanding herself. Carol grabbed the mug before Zosia could take it back because leaving it there between them felt like making it a bigger deal than it was. 

    Helen had found him at a gas station in Tucumcari and laughed so hard at Carol's face she'd had to pull over. She used to salute him—morning, handsome—every day Carol had used it since. Carol gripped the mug with both hands, held it there, let the painful warmth press back, and didn't look up for a second.

    She hadn't told anyone it was her favorite. She hadn't needed to. Helen had known, so they knew, and now Zosia knew again, and the facts sat side by side and none cancelled the others out.

    "Thanks," Carol said. She attempted a joke and failed. "Funny taste you've got."

    Zosia looked up. "Hm?"

    "This one." Carol lifted it. "It's my favorite."

    "I—" Zosia looked away and frowned. "I don't know how I knew that."

    Carol should let it go, change the subject, anything except keep poking. "I don't mind," Carol said instead. "That you know things. It doesn't bother me."

    Zosia didn't move. "It should."

    So Zosia was going to be too polite to mention everything she knew. "But it doesn't."

    Zosia looked away again, busying herself putting away the coffee like it was suddenly urgent. Carol took a sip. It wasn't the coffee Zosia had made before, that was delicious. 

    This was transcendent. Carol stared at Zosia over the rim of the mug like she'd witnessed a magic trick. 

    Zosia caught the look, ears pinking. "What?"

    Carol swallowed. "It's… amazing."

    Zosia fought a smile, one corner lifting. "Yeah?" she said, proudly, and then a tiny shrug. "It should be."

    Manousos, oblivious or pretending to be, had been reorganizing his backpack like an asshole that turns even a coffee break into an operational meeting. "Tell me," he cut in to Zosia, sipping his coffee then nodding approval, "when you remember, do you remember technical? Procesal? Or story only?"

    Carol watched Zosia's posture straighten as she looked back to Manny, the naval authority resurfacing. It reminded her of Raban, or rather, Raban's stance had always been an imitation of this. Carol had written the shift as haughty, Raban slowly squaring up. Zosia just relocated, one room of herself to another in under a second and didn't seem to know she'd done it.

    "I remember skills," Zosia said, and then—before Carol could brace—she switched into Spanish, testing it. "Todo lo que hice con el cuerpo, lo recuerdo. Antes no sabía español, ahora sí."

    Carol stared at her, then at Manousos, and his face brightened, the bastard.

    He nodded like Zosia had just solved a problem for him. "Excelente."—she knew that one—"Avísame cuando estés lista. Mientras tanto, cuida de nuestro… amiga."

    Now they really were talking a language she didn't speak, or fluent enough, at least. "We're doing this now?" Carol said. "You're both just going to, what—run away together in Spanish?"

    Zosia's head turned toward Manny, and her tone changed to an edge that made it clear she wasn't asking. "Pero hablemos inglés delante de Carol, para que ella pueda entender."

    Carol wasn't happy about being left out, and worse, the sound of it coming from Zosia, and the shift in her cadence again—she narrowed her eyes at Manousos. "Yeah, gracias, Zosia," she said, staring him down and heating up for no reason that had anything to do with him.

    He frowned. "She spoke first."

    "You encouraged it. Why do you always have to look so fucking pleased about everything?"

    Zosia looked at Carol then, and the spark softened and her whole bearing loosened. "Sorry, Carol," she said, and her voice had lost the officer's edge. "I didn't mean to exclude you." Carol's mug paused halfway to her mouth. She didn't know what to do with Zosia snapping to attention and then standing down, but only when she turned Carol's way. She probably just felt sorry for the monolingual idiot in the room. "It's just strange, I open my mouth and it's there." Zosia said, unable to hide her excitement.

    Carol's indignation went out of her like air from a punctured raft and she fought the urge to shake her head at herself. "No, it's—" She waved her hand uselessly— "Do your thing," she muttered into her mug.

    Manny hefted his backpack to leave. 

    "Manousos," Zosia said, "I should tell you something else."

    Manny paused, alert. "Say it."

    Carol hovered by the counter, trying to look like she wasn't listening, even though they were speaking English now only for her benefit.

    "I'm Navy," Zosia said. "I worked for a decade in navigational watch."

    Manny's face changed immediately. "Navigation," he echoed, awed.

    "Radar, signals," Zosia corrected. "If the key to this is radio transmissions, interference—I can lend my expertise. I'll review what you've found." She didn't add no offense.

    Carol watched in horror as his expression brightened into delight. "Yes," he said, too enthusiastic for him. "That is… excellent." He nodded once, stoic again, "I'll give you everything. You read."

    Zosia nodded once, sharp.

    Carol watched the exchange—Manny allowed to respond to Zosia like a plant turning toward sun—and her blood was boiling again. She told herself it was just because Manousos was an insufferable dick. She took a loud slurp of heavenly coffee she didn't deserve.

    He turned his attention briefly to Carol, his gaze flicking over her. "Good," he said, as though Carol had contributed by existing uselessly.

    "I've been relegated now she's here, hm?" she said, with humor, but also, not.

    Manny blinked. "Relegated."

    Carol lifted her eyebrows. "Demoted. Downgraded." She pointed vaguely at herself and shrugged. "Not that I was ever in your good books in the first place, probably."

    He shouldered his bag, ignoring her tone. "You are the only person in the world in my—" he made finger quotes— "good books." Carol felt the fight deflate out of her again and resented him for that too. 

    Manousos looked back at Zosia as he walked to the door and said, "You also now. We work. I will go to the library. I will return with more. You look. You tell me if you find signal logic."

    Zosia nodded, posture still. "Bring everything," she said, "even if it seems irrelevant." Not a request. Raban giving orders on the Revenant. The reflex to compare was getting very fucking annoying, mostly because it had stopped being about craft and Raban had never made Carol jealous that someone else was receiving a command.

    Manny stopped long enough to meet Zosia's eyes with a rare flicker of genuine respect. "Do not exert over," he told Zosia, and then, to Carol, "And you—cope." 

    Carol nodded, folding her lips in. "Thanks for the pep talk."  

    He left the house without another word.

    For a second the two of them stood there in the kitchen doorway with nothing to do, the steam from the mugs curling up between them. Zosia stood there level, even while uncertain, and now how she'd held herself when she first came downstairs made sense. Feet apart, like the floor might tilt: legs learned to be on deck and couldn't switch off on land. 

    "Okay, so." Carol jerked her chin toward the dining table off of the kitchen, putting furniture between them as a safety precaution. "Let's… sit." Zosia nodded, looking grateful for the suggestion. Yesterday she'd told Carol where to shove it. 

    Carol set her mug down harder than she meant, and pulled out a wonky rattan chair that squeaked. Zosia sat opposite. 

    "So, what's his story?" Zosia asked.

    Carol looked up, surprised. Zosia was watching her, not the door he had left through. "Manousos?"

    "He's not military?"

    "Nope. I think he just—he's like that. Very 'we deal with the problem in front of us.'" She turned her mug. "Why? Are you, uh, scared of him?"

    "No," Zosia said, in a tone that meant she didn't get scared of people. "I'm assessing him. He looked at me like I was a repaired piece of equipment," she said, not hurt.

    Carol almost laughed. "Yep." She paused. "He drove for weeks from Paraguay to find me, which… I don't know if that's reassuring or not." She thought about it. "He's not going to hurt you. He's just—he has very strong opinions about what's right and wrong, and doesn't take a lot of detours getting there."

    "How does he feel about them? The hivemind?"

    "He wanted to kill them all," Carol said bluntly. "Originally."

    Zosia's expression didn't change. "And now?"

    "Now he wants to undo it, like we did with you, which is progress." Carol turned her mug. "What else do I know… He didn't have a good mom, but who does?" She thought for a second. "He welled up at Guardians of the Galaxy." Zosia tilted her head. "The movie. We watched it—he said it was the desert air. He was very firm about that."

    Zosia stared at her for a moment, then she looked back down at her coffee, "Okay," she said, and Carol saw the corner of her mouth rising before she controlled it.

    The smallest possible concession and Carol's whole miserable morning rearranged itself around it.  She'd told herself last night she was done reaching.  "Uh, he has too much integrity for his own good, makes everything into a goddamn principle. He didn't talk to any of them, for weeks. Just—refused. He had a whole position about not engaging with them as if they were people. I—" Carol stalled. "Well. You know now. I had a similar approach, to start with." Zosia looked at her, just waiting. "I know the—hivemind, you're calling it?—I know they're not evil," Carol said. "Manny doesn't really have room for nuance, for him it's pretty binary."

    "He thinks they're wrong," Zosia also turned her mug, considering. "Morally wrong. Like it's settled."

    "Isn't it?"

    Zosia's mouth pressed together, not quite agreement. She looked out the window at the late morning light, and her expression went distant. "What they did was wrong," Zosia said. "Taking people without asking. That's wrong. But what it felt like—" She shook her head. "The feeling wasn't wrong. It was the best I've ever felt."

    "But—but that's how it works," Carol said, and a feeling much older than this conversation put the edge in her voice. "The good feeling is the trap. It only comes if you're not yourself."

    Zosia didn't push, but her eyes stayed on Carol with patience that felt dangerously close to seeing through her. "Before," Zosia said carefully, like she was handling something she hadn't taken out in a while, "I'd been managing myself for years, and just… didn't think about it much. I got used to it. Then they dissolved all of it—the pain, yes, but also everything I'd put up to survive it." Her jaw worked, like she was trying to find exact language for something that didn't seem to have it. "Yesterday, everything flooded in and I could only register the bad coming back, but the—" She searched. "The calluses didn't. I can feel things again I haven't felt since I was—" She cut herself off. "More myself. Before I learned to stop."

    Carol studied her across the table. She'd spent three days telling herself the real Zosia would hate her, be nothing like the one she'd lost. Yesterday had confirmed it, she'd been so sure she'd spat the word screensaver.

    Zosia continued, "What I'm trying to say is just because its good feelings doesn't make them fake. You can condemn how it was given and still…want everyone to feel that. No fear, because everyone's got your back, and no shame, because everyone knows everything." Then Zosia added, "You might think I'd feel invaded, but I didn't. I felt held."

    "Yeah," Carol said. Zosia glanced up, surprised by the lack of judgment. "I felt some version of that, from the outside." She stayed purposefully vague. "They're very convincing." She didn't agree, exactly, but she didn't correct it either.

    "I understand why it was wrong not letting people choose, but in it, I felt—everyone. No one carrying anything alone." Zosia kept turning her mug like it was a dial she could tune to the right frequency. "They do want that for good reasons."

    Yeah, so did every religion. Every ideology. "The road to hell…" Carol said, and left it there.

    Zosia nodded, looked like she wanted to say more and didn't.

    She was presumably holding back because she was fluent in Carol's bruises again now, sourced from everyone who'd ever seen her be a mess, and was politely not pushing. Only twenty-four hours from being ripped out of a global consciousness, already handling the whole thing with no drama. Carol, meanwhile, had spent the last ten minutes sublimating her horny shit into being a bitch to Manousos.

    "Manny didn't cry, by the way," Carol said. "To be clear. His eyes were just—adversely affected by the CGI."

    Zosia's posture broke. It was only a breath and duck of her head, but Carol was pathetically pleased with herself again. Before, the smiles had come easy and often. This Zosia was harder to crack, and the difficulty made each one feel like she'd earned it. Rarer was better. Better was worse.

    "Alright," Carol said, "The dreaming. Do you want to talk about that?"

    Zosia's posture came back again and her face was intent, a little proud. "Yes. It's… strange," she hesitated, placing each word like a boot on wet rock. "I don't know if the thoughts in my head are mine now, while I'm reliving it, or mine then, or we were all thinking it. Last night it ended with Koumba asking if I could go with him. You—" She paused, eyes glancing away. "You looked at me like you wanted me to say something."

    Carol remembered that look. She'd needed an answer out of Zosia so badly it'd made her angry. "No," she said, too fast. "I mean, yes. But—you said I let you go." Carol's pulse thudded. This was where she tried to fix things, where she tried to keep a future Zosia from waking up angry at a story Carol hadn't told correctly. "I didn't let you go," she said, and the words came less steady than she intended. Her hand moved across the table before she could stop it, palm down. "I didn't just…hand you over. I stopped Air Force One, on the tarmac."

    "Carol. No spoilers."

    Carol stared at her blankly. "What?"

    "No spoilers," Zosia repeated, as if this was the most normal rule in the world. "You can't tell me the ending of my own dreams."

    Carol's mouth opened and closed. She felt genuinely confused. "Zosia," she said slowly, "this is not one of my books. This is your life."

    "Yes," Zosia said, utterly unbothered. She took another sip of coffee like she was excited for chapter two. She watched her with open curiosity, like she didn't understand why Carol was so tense and couldn't yet guess why. Then, seeing Carol's expression, she added, "I'm serious. I want to see it the way I saw it. I don't want your version in my head while I'm trying to find mine."

    Carol forced herself to try again. She owed it to Zosia to correct the record. She owed it to herself to stop being a coward. "It matters," Carol said, quieter. "How you relive it. I don't want you to think I didn't care." The words came out before she could vet them and she heard how wide they were, Zosia's face flushed warmer and Carol leapt for the nearest safe ledge. "I mean—the Koumba thing."

    "That's nice of you," Zosia said. "But I really don't want you to tell me anything."

    Carol stared. "Why not?"

    Zosia set her mug down carefully. "Because I can't trust it," she said, and the excitement dimmed. "The dream, the thoughts, the feelings." Her fingers tapped against the ceramic. "If you tell me what happened, I'll start expecting it, fitting it into your version, and then I won't know."

    Carol had to look away. The logic made sense.

    Zosia sighed. "I want to see it firsthand and be as present as I can." She sipped her coffee and continued, "Besides, I already know I have a happy ending."

    "What—you do?"

    "Right now. I'm fully myself." Zosia said, ticking it off like a list. "I'm drinking great coffee, and I'm sitting across from my favorite author."

    Carol froze. "Favorite."

    Zosia looked like she hadn't meant to say it out loud.

    Carol should've had a joke ready to deflect, but yesterday she'd knelt on the mattress whispering that word into Zosia's hair like a prayer. And here she was, alive and free, using it to describe Carol. She didn't know. She couldn't know. Carol leaned back and assembled her face. "Favorite author," she repeated, and her voice only cracked a little.

    Zosia lifted her coffee like a shield and took a gulp too fast. Carol scrambled for a joke. "I don't know if that makes me like you more, or less." The blush had spread to Zosia's collarbones, visible above the neckline, and her thumb pressed white against the ceramic. Carol's fingers flexed against the table before she caught them.

    "Anyway," Zosia said, to the coffee. "I can feel all of that again. Three months ago I couldn't. So how bad can the middle be?"

    Carol kept her palm flat to the wood and made herself speak like an adult. "Just to be clear. It won't be all…sunshine and rainbows," Carol said, waving her other hand in an arc.

    Zosia's eyebrows rose. "I was picking up children's corpses last night."

    Christ. Zosia knew how to be present, that was the thing. She was already on the other side of it, not trying to get sympathy points. Carol had been pre-suffering this conversation for three days, anticipating the worst, as if that was the same as being brave. Zosia was sitting right there, plain as daylight, refusing to decorate the horror or borrow trouble from the future. 

    Carol immediately punished herself for admiring it. "No," Carol insisted, "I mean, I don't come out looking great."

    Zosia waited patiently. Normal human patient, which meant she could still walk away if she didn't like what she heard. Carol's fingers dug into the wood. She wanted to reach across the table and take Zosia's hand to make her understand. She wanted it so badly it scared her.

    Carol met her gaze and let some truth show. "I'm scared," she admitted, "of what you'll think about it. You'll be angry with me." Zosia's lips pressed together. "So when you wake up and you hate me—"

    "I won't," Zosia said, too fast. She looked irritated with herself. "I mean, I don't know, but I'm not planning to." She said it like she'd said everything today, like the present was solid ground and the rest was weather she'd sail through when it blew in.

    Carol let out a shaky breath. Her gaze flicked up. "And you really want it with no warning."

    Zosia nodded. "Yes." She hesitated, then repeated, precise again, "Because if you tell me, your tone will become part of the memory, and I can't afford that. I need to know what I felt, not what you think I should feel."

    Carol nodded slowly, chewing her lips.  "Okay," she said, and meant it. "Okay. No spoilers."

    "Thank you."

    She didn't deserve gratitude, her restraint now didn't erase anything. She took a breath and a leaf out of Zosia's book and tried to stay in the present. "So where did it end exactly?" she asked, making her tone casual with effort. "The dream."

    "You and Koumba arguing, you looking at me. And then…" She frowned. "And then it blurred. Like the tape cut out."

    Carol's brain supplied the missing footage anyway: deciding, at the last second, to stop Koumba from taking Zosia away because she couldn't stand the thought of losing the only person she had left; who had been assigned to her, and she'd be damned if Zosia ended up somebody's sex doll. At least Carol would leave her alone. She'd meant it at the time, and then she'd broken it, and that was what no amount of context could make okay. Carol wanted to say something—any of it—and couldn't. No spoilers.

    Carol dragged some words out. "If you wake up upset," she said, "you can—" She paused. She didn't know what she was allowed to offer. Space? A blanket? "You can tell me. Okay? Or leave. If you want."

    "Okay, and if I wake up and I'm fine, you don't get to act like I'm a fragile flower."

    Carol looked at her. This Zosia was cute, to put it mildly, but her humor wasn't cutesy. Without the psychic glue smoothing her out, she was unpredictable. Carol couldn't pin her down. She was strict one second, sweet the next, complicated like a real human. Calluses, Zosia had said. Carol had been given a version of Zosia without all the rough that makes a person, everything that comes from any bad feeling, even the good things that come out of it—blushing from embarrassment, pride from surviving pain—that had all been absent. The hive hadn't invented Zosia's happiness, it had just removed everything that made it brave.

    Carol thought she'd made her peace last night: puppet, character, scraps. Alone on the couch, staring at the ceiling until the feeling could be folded up and put somewhere out of reach, end of chapter. Turned out it had the shelf life of wet paper. Hours later, the peace was in pieces, and Carol couldn't even say what replaced it, only that she felt less safe than yesterday, when the distance had felt like a closed door she could lean on. Today every goddamn thing Zosia did had opened it a crack and Carol could feel the light coming through and couldn't stop it, and what Carol had lost was beginning to look like a first draft of who was sitting in front of her.

    Zosia reached for her mug again and Carol's eyes tracked the movement helplessly. The line of her wrist. She looked away fast but Zosia noticed anyway, of course.

    "I noticed, you've been acting like I'm handling a live grenade every time I move." Zosia gestured toward Carol's own hands on the table. "And look at you, you want to fidget. You keep giving me an exaggerated amount of space. You can stand down. I'm not going to break."

    The room was suddenly too bright. Zosia's gaze was patient and dark and not letting her off. Carol looked down at her hands like they belonged to someone else. "I'm trying to be respectful."

    Zosia studied her. "Okay," she said slowly. "Just, don't punish yourself with it."

    Carol laughed once, sharp. "Too late."

    Zosia's eyes softened then, and the gravity pulled—that awful, familiar drag toward being seen. She kept her hands still, and kept her distance. She'd let Zosia keep her story unspoiled, even though everything in her wanted to reach across the table and rewrite it.

    Later, Manousos came back with his pack full of notebooks and textbooks, and Zosia told it all from the beginning, while he took notes of anything he deemed relevant.  

    Carol looked at the table and kept looking. She did not add, correct, offer, or explain. She breathed through her nose and let Zosia's version exist untouched. She kept her mouth shut. It was the most disciplined she'd been in years, and she wouldn't have been able to do it if she hadn't been excruciatingly stone-cold sober.

    When her stomach grumbled, she went to the kitchen and heated three of the last few frozen meals stockpiled from Sprouts, and set them at the table without ceremony. Zosia thanked her and Manny only prayed his thanks, asshole.

    He asked questions Carol would never think to ask and Zosia answered what she could. He did not ask how it felt, Carol noticed, and couldn't tell if it was tact or limitation, but watching Manny lean forward, she realized that he had never heard any of this. She'd told him stuff relevant to unjoining, but the rest she'd never said, and he'd never asked, and it occurred to her now that she hadn't spent enough time with him for it. She had come back spiteful and with a mission and they'd been running ever since. 

    Afterward, Manny gathered the notes he'd taken. "Good," he said, which from him meant closer to great. He looked at Zosia. "Sleep well."

    "That's the plan," she replied. It had been Zosia's idea; early night, as much dreaming as possible, seemingly determined to treat this like a challenge she could win. 

    At the front door he turned back to Carol, "You too," he said, "New record. One hour, no opinions. Well done." He was out of the house before she could respond, which was probably strategic.

    Carol sighed and got up to wash the plates, and Zosia came to dry them without asking. She picked up the dish towel and stood close enough that Carol could feel the warmth off her arm. 

    Helen had done the cooking and the washing-up both, and after, Carol had stopped plating meals altogether. Paper and plastic for weeks, disposable as the days, nothing that needed to be cleaned by a person who was no longer there or no longer functioning. She'd only graduated back when Zosia moved in, drying each dish with the same serene competence, and it had felt like enough. Now the same woman stood in the same place with a towel only she had chosen to pick up, and Carol scrubbed the plate harder than necessary.

    "Tonight," Zosia said, "I'm going to remember more. And tomorrow, I'll tell you."

    Carol nodded, trying to look steady. "Alright."

    Zosia looked at her sideways, a quick glance down at Carol's hands, still gripping the plate too hard. "Try not to pace outside my door all night."

    Carol scoffed. "Me? Never."

    One side of Zosia's mouth curved up at her and Carol felt a weakness in her knees that had nothing to do with the exhaustion she felt. She hated herself for it, and for agreeing so quickly to no spoilers, but she also couldn't stop being glad Zosia was here to have the choice about it at all.

    Zosia dried the second plate and set it in the rack with careful precision. Carol was rinsing the last one, sleeves shoved past her elbows, and the silence between them was almost comfortable. The house lacked every sound a ship supplied—no engine thrum, no bells down the corridor—and the light through the window had gone copper.

    The debrief with Manousos had felt like confession, absurdly. The thought had been in Polish, in her mother's voice. Him sitting where the priest would, attentive and withholding judgment, and Carol with her hands jammed under herself doing penance for a mysterious sin. Zosia had been walking him through the mechanics, how it didn't feel like compulsion but agreement, and he'd said they took the will, flat with conviction. She heard the catechism underneath. God's most dangerous and sacred gift. She knew this man. She'd grown up surrounded by them, the absolute confidence that the rules existed because God loved you enough to draw a line. She'd loved the rules too, until she'd understood she was on the wrong side of one.

    She glanced down at Carol to her right and away again. The day had not gone to plan. She'd meant to be useful—the skills, the dreaming, the no-spoilers rule—that was the briefing she'd prepared. Instead Carol had been funny and graceless and kept looking at her with that guilty attention, and Zosia kept answering it with more than she'd budgeted for. She hadn't planned to tell a near-stranger about her calluses and how she hadn't felt happy for years or say favorite author out loud. She could feel the embarrassment of the overspend now in the quiet and had no idea how to settle it.

    It made what she'd said last night worse. She'd told Carol Sturka, whose books had kept her sane across two decades, that the physics was melodramatic. Carol had taken it well, or taken it Carol-ishly, but that didn't excuse it. She'd sounded like the worst kind of pedant.

    She glanced back down at Carol. The slight curl of hair at her nape, her forearms tensing when she scrubbed. The steaming water ran over Carol's hands and Zosia looked, and then wished she hadn't, because her mind produced what she could only call a daydream: a feeling of those hands wet and warm on the back of her thigh, fingers gripping, and—

    No, she told herself. She felt heat flood her face, stared at the dish rack and willed it back to neutral. She was going to need a serious conversation with herself about what counted as appropriate material to intrusively imagine about a grieving wife, which was nothing.

    "I was rude last night," she said. 

    Carol paused, sponge in hand. "Huh?"

    "When I said the windward chase was impossible."

    Carol turned, putting the last plate down, a crease between her brows. "You don't have to apologize for having an opinion about my fantasy bullshit."

    "For giving you a note when you gave me your book," Zosia said, and her tone was more honest than she'd intended again. She felt her ears burning. 

    Carol stared at her for a second, then looked away first, busying herself with the dish towel Zosia was about to pick up again. "You were right though," Carol said. "The tacking was a bunch of crap." Carol folded the towel, unfolded it, folded it again. "I've got the original routes, I drew them, they're in my office, I could—" She refolded the towel a third time. "Never mind. You don't want to see my sad little maps."

    "I do."

    Carol looked up and the embarrassment was plain on her face. Zosia had accepted before she could seal the exit. Carol tossed the towel onto the counter with a decisiveness that was clearly compensating. "Alright," Carol said. 

    Carol was already halfway to the stairs when Zosia reached back and rehung the dish towel square along the seam. She led Zosia upstairs. The office door was open, the desk lamp already on. She went inside and it felt like stepping behind a theater curtain. 

    Zosia's heartbeat went very embarrassing. She was standing in the room where the books had been written. A career of kit bags and port-city bookshops from the Baltic to the Atlantic to the Mediterranean and back, and the whole time, the room they came from was this. She had imagined, not consciously but somewhere in the back of her mind, a wooden captain's quarters, a place that looked like the prose. The reality was plainer and more human. 

    "It's a mess," Carol said. She pulled a stack of books off of the floor and dumped them on the armchair.

    Among the unstable book towers were little offerings to the nautical world: a brass telescope that looked too heavy to be decorative; a model Mercator; a compass in a glass case lay on the shelf beside a row of foreign-language editions of Wycaro; and on the desk, a hand-drawn map on paper, its edges curling with age. 

    "It's perfect," Zosia said, and then immediately wished she'd said literally anything else. She turned fully to the map so Carol couldn't see her face. Carol's handwriting ran along the borders, but there were extra islands and channels that didn't exist in the published one. Labels penciled in, then crossed out, then rewritten, then crossed out again.

    Carol came to the desk and reached for the laptop to close it, making room. "You found that fast."

    "It's different from the books."

    "Yeah." Carol came to stand beside her, arms crossed, studying her own map with a fond critical eye.

    Zosia looked around the room. "What's that?" she asked, pointing at the little corroded ship's wheel on the desk.

    Carol's eyes followed. "Oh. It's from the Drowning Market, yeah, it's not a thing you'd know. That paperweight made me think it up."

    Zosia's eyebrows lifted. "Tell me."

    Carol hesitated, then smiled a little, pleased to be asked. "It's a place I cut from Bloodsong. A trading post built on old pilings and everyone pretends it isn't sinking into the slipsand, so their currency is whatever keeps the floor from dropping—nails, clamps, chocks. Prices literally rise with the tide. A little wheel like that would be worth more than gold because it's round but spiky, so it could be rolled to wedge a beam."

    Zosia's gaze stayed on Carol as she spoke. Her voice steadied when she talked about Wycaro, the brittleness gone. Zosia looked at the paperweight. All of that imagined from such an ordinary thing. She thought how romantic Carol's mind was. Oh no. "Why do you keep all this?" she said too sharply instead, pointing to the objects.

    Carol's eyes flicked over the room. "I guess it reminds me I'm… not making it all up from scratch," she said. "It's easier when it's outside, not only in my head." 

    Carol pulled a battered stack of papers from under another stack and opened it to a yellow page dense with handwriting and diagrams. "Alright, so, these are the original sailing routes." Her finger tapped a line. "The chase goes through the Straits, I had the current running against her as a metaphor, which, yeah, would make it impossible to tack windward too. You were right."

    Carol was already flipping pages, her energy shifting. The stack fell open to a section with annotations, arrows, small angry crosses. "This—oh my god, this was so fucking annoying. In Winds, you know the sequence where the ship's becalmed for three days? I had six goddamn pages, how the crew turns on each other, Raban climbing the mast every morning and just sitting up there alone, watching the horizon." Carol's hands were alive, her shoulders had dropped. She'd found the current she needed and the self-consciousness was dropping away. "And Lucasia watches her...him… from the deck, and that's when she realizes she loves him, he's the only person on the ship not falling apart."

    Carol started pacing now as she complained, the paper rolled in her hand like a baton, voice climbing. "Well, as you know, the editor cut four freaking pages. He kept the moment Lucasia realized, but cut everything that earned it. All the crew tension, the sense the world had stopped. He said—" Carol pitched her voice into a parody of editorial patience— "'The reader already knows they're in love, Carol.' God, he was a fucking asshole." 

    Zosia watched her and felt the room get warmer, or smaller, or both. The defensive hunch, the constant readiness for rejection, all gone. This was Carol in her element, complaining—earnest and intermittently profane.

    "Alright, I'll stop," Carol said, which Zosia already knew was a lie and didn't want to be true. Carol had pulled out book two and flipped to a dog-eared page. "You know in Sands, when O'Riordan goes below deck during the mutiny and he finds Moggy guarding the rum stores? He wanted to cut her."

    "Cut the cat?"

    "She was doing thematic work!" Carol jabbed a finger at an open page. "Everyone's choosing sides, and she's where the rats are. That's the whole fucking thesis of the chapter. Loyalty versus appetite."

    "But she made it in..."

    Carol shrugged one shoulder. "You know how it went. Goddamn Greg cut the best lines I've ever written about rum, but the cat stayed..."

    Carol kept talking, gesturing with the book. She'd called Wycaro a soap opera and fantasy bullshit, but nobody who hated their own work kept this many copies of it, this much memorabilia. The self-deprecation was a lock on a door Carol opened only when she was alone, or like right now, when the guard dropped. Carol's contempt was aimed inward and off-center, and Zosia recognized the angle—the gap between what you wanted and what you let it become, and the refusal to forgive yourself for the distance.

    "...and that's why he laughs when he finds her among the barrels, it's the first honest thing he's seen all day." Zosia had the deeply embarrassing thought she could listen to these behind-the-scenes anecdotes all day. She went to look at the compass to hide her face. Carol's posture contracted. "Sorry, I know you know this stuff now. I talked for like ten minutes about a fictional cat."

    "Well, I love Moggy."

    Carol smiled, tentative and crooked, and turned back to the shelf.

    I know you know this stuff now. Zosia frowned at the phrasing. She almost asked, but Carol was already pulling out a foreign edition paperback. She thrust the front cover towards Zosia, enthusiastic again. 

    "Look at this shit," Carol said. "The Swedish publisher commissioned their own cover art and they made Raban blond. Blond!" Carol's outrage was completely genuine. Zosia huffed a small laugh and it surprised her, it came up so easily again. "I emailed and they said the artist had 'creative license'. Dark hair is on the goddamn page, it's like yours, it's in the text a million fucking times!"

    Carol said it without flinching, like the comparison was obvious, her blue eyes bright with indignation, and Zosia watched her not hear what she'd just said. Seeing herself in Raban had carried Zosia through so much hope and loneliness, and now here was Carol drawing the line back the other way, the circle closed, and neither of them had drawn it on purpose. She looked at Carol still pacing and ranting, and wanted to say: you made something, and I wish you knew how much it mattered. Instead she kept her mouth shut and looked at the compass again.

    "That's not a compass," Zosia said. 

    "What?"

    "This." Zosia leaned over the case to examine it. The instrument inside was a polished brass arc with a spirit level and degree markings mounted on a mahogany base. "It's a clinometer. It measures heel angle, how far a vessel is listing."

    Carol stared at her, still holding up the Swedish book. "We got it at an estate sale," she said. "The guy told me it was a compass."

    "He was wrong."

    Carol made a sound that was somehow both annoyed and pleased as her hand dropped.

    "It could still be Lucasia's," Zosia said. A compass was navigation, technically Peregrina's role. A clinometer read what the ship was doing under you, what the sea was doing to it. "Actually, I like it better now. Lucasia would want to know if the deck was level before she trusted the horizon."

    "That's exactly—yeah. That's her."

    Zosia looked at it and felt the fond pull of Wycaro, the nostalgia of reading each book for the first time; turning pages gone soft from the damp air, the diesel-lit lamp she'd read under until her bunkmate threw a boot. Then, close behind, she thought about what had just ruined that: she already knew how it ended.

    "I never finished Bloodsong," Zosia said, her mouth pressed thin. "I know the twist, the betrayal, how it ends." Carol's face went still. Zosia heard the flatness in her own voice and didn't correct it, she hadn't meant to sound annoyed, but she was. "I'll never get to read it for the first time." She'd been robbed, and the worst part was that she had no-one to blame. It was simply how it must work; some bits of knowledge as residue. She sighed.

    Carol was watching Zosia with a stricken expression, and she pushed off the desk, turned away, fussed with a jar of sand. Her back was rigid. Carol had gone from a twenty-minute sprint through Wycaro lore to this, and the pivot was too sharp.

    "Are you okay?" Zosia asked.

    Carol turned around, and whatever had been on her face was already being folded away behind a half-smile. "Yeah. I just—I hate that they did that."

    Zosia frowned. Carol knew she didn't like spoilers, but this apology didn't fit. "You didn't do anything wrong." Carol was circling the drain again of something Zosia couldn't know yet.

    Carol cleared her throat. "Anyway. Enough of my—" She gestured vaguely at the room, herself. "You've seen Greg's war crimes. What's your verdict?"

    Zosia looked at the hand-drawn map, then at Carol, who was already bracing for dismissal.

    "Verdict," Zosia said, "is that I'd like to see the rest of the charts tomorrow."

    Carol chewed on her lips, nodding. "Alright," she said. "Tomorrow."

    Zosia said goodnight and went to the guest room. She dressed for bed and had to shutter the window it was still so early in the evening. She lay down and stared at the ceiling. 

    In the hive, rest had been the signal softening without ever going fully quiet, company always humming underneath. Here and now, she could hear her own breathing, and nothing else. She kept reaching for something that was no longer there, like a nightstand that had been moved in the dark.

    Instead of counting sheep, Zosia thought about the sound of Carol's voice, unguarded and unrepentant, and none of it pitched towards her. Carol was rude when she was uncomfortable and loud when she wasn't, and whatever she felt came out without the pretension Zosia had spent years perfecting, the calibration that had moved her up and hollowed her out at the same time. It made the unexplained weight of her apology harder to dismiss.

    She fell asleep still thinking about it, directly into the dream.

    Chapter 4

    Zosia was driving through the city, past empty storefronts and silent intersections. The grenade sat in her lap, and the weight of it was absurdly light and absurdly heavy.

    Carol asked, we'll provide. She'll feel better.

    And through it, a thought Zosia wanted to claim as hers and couldn't: She was being sarcastic. The door opened on Carol's face, irritable and exhausted.

    Zosia felt a chuckle leave her mouth. She was already turning to leave, the visit a failure, the grenade dangling from her hand, when Carol's voice caught her.

    "Do you maniacs drink?"

    The door was more open and Carol was standing in it. We're being invited in, they thought, and the reverence flooded every node at once. She should stop, stow the grenade at minimum, but Zosia stepped through and the warmth that moved through her was indistinguishable from theirs. She wanted to be here. They wanted to be here. The wanting was the same, felt in the same body, at the same threshold.

    Carol's house smelled of sesame oil and something faintly burnt, and Zosia breathed it in with seven billion brains and one pair of lungs and couldn't tell the difference.

    The dream painted it with hazy detail. Zosia's dream-self took in Carol's shaking hands, her sleepless eyes, the brittle energy vibrating through her. Carol poured two drinks and started talking. She was the one who reached first, asking questions with a combativeness that was also curious. She wanted to know.

    She's suffering. She needs companionship.

    Zosia answered, and she heard herself offering facts with a brightness that startled her. She had every fact in the world now, available the instant she reached for it, and she kept reaching. She could hear the delight of knowing something worth sharing, and it sounded like—it sounded like someone she used to be—pleased with herself for knowing things. Now she knew everything, and Carol had asked, and sharing it lit her up and they wouldn't dilute it. Joy ran free, encouraged, passed hand to hand until the happiness belonged to everyone.

    Carol's mood shifted without warning. "How long do I have left before you turn me into a worker bee?"

    The hive answered Carol's resistance with tenderness, with a bottomless conviction that she'd understand eventually. "You just don't know it." She said it as fact. In the dream she could feel how true it had been, love and coercion the same breath, and the breath was hers.

    She needs to understand. Carol rose from the chair. She needs to see how good it is. 

    Carol was talking, hands moving, and she was describing paradise. Her voice was mocking, dismissive, calling it postcard bullshit, and underneath the mockery every image was a memory and Zosia's mind reached for context, for a better model of what Carol needed. The dream widened, and she felt the hive's attention scatter across a thousand inputs simultaneously, rifling through memories of Carol on vacation, from Helen, from hotel staff, from strangers on beaches, the irrelevant impressions decaying even as they appeared. Her mind couldn't grip it. Everything dissolved, leaving only knowledge that it had been there and was now lost to her.

    Carol's cadence slowed. "Or you're in Norway…" she said, and her voice lost its performance.

    Zosia could only follow what they gave her to speak, rendered as scene without sensation: the crisp sterile cold of the hotel room, the stale-sweet smell of fur warmed by skin. Zosia's stomach knotted hot. 

    "In a hotel made of ice," Zosia heard herself say. "Under a pile of furs." They offered it back like a gift, using Carol's grief as a sales pitch, and they meant it with all their hearts. Remember how happy you were. That's what we can give you.

    Carol's expression didn't soften.

    The pin slipped. A small sound, metal on wood, almost delicate, and then the count began.

    Their attention collapsed and Zosia felt the calculus running and underneath it, calm and absolute: she hasn't given permission.

    Carol stared at her own hand and the delay stretched, wrong, unbearable to Zosia dreaming it, the instinct to snatch it hitting her mind with the force of a drill but she stayed still. They couldn't take what hadn't been offered, even this. Carol could choose to die holding it and they would let her, would stand in this body and burn alongside her, one expendable cell in a skin that covered the world. "Carol, if we may?"

    Zosia's hand closed over the grenade, finally, the metal warm from Carol's grip, and she threw it through the window and her body to the ground over Carol in one motion. The pain hit her back like a wave to hull—total, percussive and white. Shrapnel pierced, and it was so intense that for one full second it belonged only to her before it drained.

    She was outside and falling, the bright blaze dulled to a throb her nerves kept insisting on. She felt Carol's frantic hands press at her wounds with clumsy urgency.

    "Shit. Fuck! I'm gonna get some help, okay?" She felt the hive react with unified concern as her worsening condition was signaled as information. "Oh my God—Zosia—" She said my name.

    Her vision went black. It felt like the ocean closing over her head, and when she surfaced, down was up. Hospital lights on the ceiling, burning a second before she understood what they were. 

    The blast had rattled something loose behind her eyes. The memories came thin here, half-dissolved, her concussed brain too porous to keep what was fed it. Carol was pacing like a trapped thing, vibrating with guilt. Zosia's stomach turned over, slow and heavy. Brain swelling. It will pass. They dampened it, pressed warmth over the nausea.

    Zosia picked up the carton, knew its ingredients. Carol hovered, helped. That's sweet. Take away her guilt. The directive followed so close behind the feeling that Zosia couldn't tell which had come first or from where. She drew on the straw and winced, and whether it was her back's torn muscles or what was going down her throat, the discomfort siphoned off before she'd finished feeling it regardless.

    Then Zosia's voice hit a wall. There were things she couldn't say. She'll understand soon.

    "Tell me about Camp fucking Freedom Falls."

    An older memory was needed. The hive reached out again through every mind that had ever had a piece of Carol. A wide searchlight turned, indiscriminate except Helen's kept in shadow, an attempt to respect her wishes when they could afford to. Thousands of impressions of Carol lit at once: strangers, teachers, bar patrons, coworkers, cashiers, family, classmates, neighbors. None of it held. They scrolled and scrolled, then stopped, the others discarded like photographs already fading.

    A cramped room with institutional carpet. A young Carol sitting too rigid in a folding chair, hands clenched, eyes bright with the effort of not crying. The counselor thought calmly, piously, that Carol was selfish and dramatic and required correction.

    Zosia felt sick again, and then the dream softened.

    She slept and woke and slept. The concussion kept its undertow—each time she surfaced, thoughts rolled thick, lagging behind sensation. They bore the headache and the dizziness, and still she felt muffled, wrapped in gauze that wouldn't thin.

    Carol's voice was close. Zosia opened her eyes. She came back.

    "Hey. You look, uh—yeah. Got a lot more color in your face."

    Zosia's face looked back at her from a mirror across the room as she sat up. It swam. Doubled. Her vision pulled itself together. "We feel much better today."

    "How about some fresh air?"

    She wanted to go wherever Carol was going. She nodded.

    Carol wheeled her outside to the courtyard. What came through felt waterlogged, already loosening the edges of everything: her mouth, her purchase on the scene, the dream itself. Carol was demanding answers. Her own mouth was moving.

    Her voice was getting closer to the answer, and they could feel the drug fraying her hold. Bodies gathered in the courtyard in clusters. Please, Carol—said all of them, through every mouth, a chorus to fill the air until there was no room left in it for Carol's demands.

    Zosia wanted two things at once and the drug was pulling a tangled knot apart in her. Make her happy fired first, a fraction ahead of don't say it, one pulling toward Carol's face while the other pulled away. In the blur, she thought she felt the difference, for the first time, between her want and theirs—but it was so slight it must've been the same signal, her drug-laced concussed neurons making it stutter, and one part had felt, for a second, like it belonged to her.

    In the last flicker before everything cut, when she was about to answer Carol, make her eyes soften—her heart stopped.

    She woke up.

    Her heart in the present was beating like it had never stopped, like she'd just sprinted a mile. Her skin felt damp along her spine. 

    Zosia stared at the ceiling and counted breaths. On the nightstand, Carol had left a glass of water and painkillers. Zosia sat up slowly. The movement pulled at her mid-back and she hissed.

    She'd carried the pain since the container and blamed the extraction. The pills went down and the understanding came with them: this was older, and the hive had been swallowing the hurt. She set the glass down silently, listening for the house. Quiet.

    Her mind reached for the time and found nothing, obviously. In the hive she'd have known it to the second. Now she had the hue of light through the curtains and a guess. That was all.

    She crossed to the guest bathroom and the shower took a long moment to warm. The steady drum of water on tile filled the bathroom with white noise, and for the first time since extraction the inside of her skull wasn't cavernous. The ship had never been quiet—the pitch of the engine felt through the deck in her feet, the hull when she pressed her palm flat to feel the sea state. The hive had hummed louder and closer, from inside rather than underneath. Both gone now.

    Zosia stripped and the privacy of a locked bathroom all to herself was strange. Modesty was a luxury that didn't survive shared quarters, you made your body impersonal and got on with it. What she'd guarded was internal. The hive had dissolved even that boundary; she'd been seen by everyone, known at the cellular level, her body an open channel.

    Zosia stood, tested her shoulder with a cautious roll, and felt a dull complaint radiate down. She did not like it. They had turned her body into a shield and the gratitude they'd felt doing it had felt indistinguishable from her own. She'd have thrown herself over Carol without being told—but they hadn't given her the chance to choose, and the difference between sacrifice and deployment was the same as between a locked door and an open channel, noise earned and noise she'd been given.

    She knew the aloneness was freedom, and still couldn't stop it from feeling like loss too.

    Zosia tested her hand under the stream and the waste calculation came before she could stop it: liters per minute, tank capacity, someone else's ration running cold. Four minutes deck to dry on a good day, she used to tell cadets, and they'd laugh because they thought she was joking. The water would come cold or barely tepid, you took what the pipes offered and you were quick about it. 

    Zosia stepped under the shower, and the heat loosened her muscles, eased the clamp around her spine. She leaned forward and braced both hands on the tile, head lowered, letting the water run down her back. She watched the steam thicken and didn't move. She was getting comfortable here. That was the problem, or one of them—the towels were thick, the hot water was endless, and she was treating Carol's house like a shore leave hotel. 

    Something about the thought produced an image of Carol's face in low light, her mouth open around something that wasn't quite speech, her voice at a register Zosia had never heard—lower, fraying. Zosia clenched her jaw, pressed her forehead against the cool tile and killed it. It had only been two days, and she was standing naked in Carol Sturka's bathroom inventing scenarios that would mortify them both. 

    She washed quickly like she was making a point to herself, but the heat felt good. On a ship this would've been over three minutes ago. She should turn it off and get dressed and go downstairs and be professional. She closed her eyes. The image came back gentler, like it had been waiting: Carol's mouth again, but at the curve of her neck now, and hands on her hips with no grip in them, just resting, thumbs brushing. Zosia let it stay. The steaming water ran over her shoulders and she stood in the heat of both and felt the pull low in her stomach and gave herself the length of a slow breath, until she couldn't separate one indulgence from the other.

    Then she turned the tap off because she was someone who turned taps off.

    The cold air hit her wet skin and her shoulder complained about it, radiating down through the blade. She sucked a breath through her teeth and looked at her back in the mirror. Two pale and pink puckered marks, the remnants of shrapnel and burns. She hadn't known to look for them. The skin around them was faintly raised, still healing.

    Zosia stared at them, irritated. So that was Carol's guilt. She understood it now: the stricken face in the office, Carol saying you'll be angry with me like she was reading her own sentence. Of course. Carol had been careless enough to play with a grenade and reckless enough to drug her, and both times her body had paid the price.

    Zosia let the annoyance sharpen. Good. This was useful. It burned clean where everything else burned complicated, and she needed clean right now. She would go downstairs irritated and the irritation would be a guardrail and it would keep her hands steady and her face neutral.

    She dried herself carefully, mindful of the scars now. Clothes could wait. Her skin still held heat from the shower, and she allowed herself the small relief. She wrapped the towel around her torso and twisted her damp hair up into a messy bun that immediately began collapsing.

    It's like yours. Carol's voice, warm and indignant, bright-eyed over a book cover, furious at a Swedish illustrator, oblivious. Zosia felt the same shy heat she'd felt then—the private, ridiculous pleasure of being compared to something Carol loved. The bun unravelled further.

    She reached up again and her fingers caught on something. The small clasps close to her scalp where the extensions were bonded, because Raban had longer hair and the resemblance was the contrived point. She hadn't been consulted about any of it. Her fingers closed around a clasp and pulled, testing. It held. She'd need pliers, a steady hand, and a shoulder that wasn't on fire, and she had none of those. She twisted the hair tighter, and opened the bathroom door.

    And nearly ran straight into Carol.

    She was outside like she'd been standing watch in the hallway and jumped back half a step, caught. Carol's eyes moved, more startled than leering, taking in Zosia's bare shoulders, the towel pulled tight, the damp skin along her collarbone.

    Zosia felt heat rise up her neck, suddenly too conscious of the unfairness of the towel's edge pressed under her arm, the air cooling her skin, while Carol was fully dressed, in jeans and a white tank top that did nothing to obscure the definition in her shoulder, the line of muscle down her arm. 

    Carol's gaze jerked away to a point somewhere over Zosia's shoulder. "Sorry," Carol said, too fast. "I—uh. I didn't know if you'd—" She stopped, clearly deciding not to finish that sentence.

    "It's fine," Zosia said flatly.

    Carol's mouth bent toward a smile, and she held out a bundle of clothes, still not looking. Zosia shifted her weight to accept them, and the towel tightened across her chest. Carol's eyes flicked down and up again. Her jaw was set like she was physically restraining herself.

    Zosia forced her voice out. "I remembered more." 

    Carol's posture stiffened. "Yeah?"

    Zosia nodded once. "Grenade. Hospital." 

    Their eyes finally met. "Are you okay?"

    Zosia considered the shrapnel burns, the counselor's sneer over Carol's fear, the crushing pain of cardiac arrest, and the fact that she was standing here half-naked blushing like an idiot.

    "I'm alive," Zosia said. Carol winced, like she recognized the jab. "We can talk downstairs," she added, "after I'm… dry."

    Carol's gaze went down to the towel again, then away. Her face was red, which at least made Zosia feel less alone in her embarrassment.

    "Right," Carol said. "Yeah. I pulled out some stuff." She gestured awkwardly to the clothes and moved past her quickly down the hall, already leaving, going downstairs.

    Zosia stepped into the guest room and shut the door carefully. Only then did she let herself exhale. Zosia had been looked at enough times to know it was nothing more than reflex, she'd learned to recognize it young and dismiss it faster. What she couldn't ignore was her own reaction.

    She had no explanation for it beyond the frightening fact that she wanted Carol to look. She'd spent her whole life refusing to be seen and she'd been wide open like she'd somehow been waiting for it.

    What flustered her, once she was safely alone, was that Carol could no more fake her own indifference than she could carry a tray without cursing. Carol had been standing there, eyes moving and arms bare, and Zosia had felt it go straight through her—past the checkpoint she'd built, past decades of expert containment—which was, given the circumstances, frankly absurd. She'd just remembered shrapnel scars. She'd just re-lived cardiac arrest. She was very angry about both. She was still wet, and had been since the shower.

    That was the embarrassing truth of it, standing here behind the closed door, indifferent to the fact that she'd decided it should stop minutes ago. Carol had been reckless with her body and her body didn't seem to care. Zosia put it under post-unjoining, everything heightened, and made herself sort through the bundle of clothes.

    The dark overshirt she recognised. Carol had been wearing it in the hospital, in the dream that was a memory. Now here it was, washed and folded, and it looked a little like a naval utility shirt—the color, the pockets, the placket. Carol couldn't have known that. She'd just handed over what was clean, or what was nearest, or—Zosia looked at the bundle again. The navy blue and white shirts. The canvas belt. Each ordinary alone. Together, a near-familiarity Carol had built without being told to, and Zosia couldn't tell if the gesture was practical or caring and suspected it was both, which was worse than either. Zosia pulled the cuffs straight but the sleeves were still too short and she didn't examine what was tightening in her chest because she was supposed to be irritated right now.

    She dressed slowly, mindful of her shoulder. She rolled it, evaluating, trying to separate discomfort from damage, temporary from permanent. She couldn't afford a weakness long-term, not if she ever wanted to sail alone. If the shoulder failed her, then what Carol had broken wasn't just tissue but Zosia's only credible plan for after. If this affects my range… she made the thought stop there, unfinished, because the alternative was needing someone, and she'd lived a life making sure she didn't.

    Zosia perched on the edge of the bed to pull on socks and the ache when she reached remained. Her mind went to the hospital again as she buttoned the overshirt. Carol had treated her like a problem to be solved rather than a person with a body that could break, and the fact that she clearly felt terrible about it didn't undo that. Annoyingly, her plan had nearly worked.

    Before leaving the room, she paused, thinking abstractly about Helen's memory. Carol, there's something I should— Her mouth rehearsed the words and her stomach shut it down.

    She knew what it cost to be known without choosing it. She'd spent a career making sure she wasn't.

    The first day kept surfacing underneath the rest. Carol red-faced and shaking, hostile with grief, and through Zosia's body a celebration so vast it had no edges—the greatest day in the history of humanity, pouring through her while she smiled, her mouth saying those words while Carol's hands shook. 

    I don't mind, Carol had said later, about the residue, that you know things. Her voice had been steady and generous and Zosia hadn't believed a syllable of it. The fury on the first day was proof enough that Carol would surely hear 'I saw you and your dead wife' as violation, and Zosia wasn't sure she could endure it when she already felt guilty enough about that and everything else too.

    She would tell her later, when the memory had decayed into something less vivid, when Zosia could speak about it without sounding like she'd lingered. When it could be framed as 'the hivemind rifled through your vacations' rather than 'I saw something'.

    She paused with her hand still on the doorknob. She had hardly deliberated avoiding the difficult confession, and the relief that came with the decision felt so good it scared her. She'd forgotten how effortless it was, how the silence was default, like a door swinging shut on its own weight. She'd done it on the first day too—husband, technically—and the lie had come out greased and easy. She'd thought that armor was gone with everything else the extraction had stripped away, and had accidentally said as much to Carol yesterday. It had been hanging in the dark the whole time, oiled and waiting.

    She went downstairs.

    The den was dim. Overcast light came through the window flat, hitting the gray sofa where Carol sat, mercifully in a blue plaid shirt over the tank top now, elbows on her knees, hands clasped tightly as if she were restraining herself from pacing. She looked up at Zosia immediately.

    "Better?" Carol asked.

    Zosia moved to the couch and sat carefully, testing her shoulder against the cushion. "Painkillers are doing their job," she said, "I'll get used to it." She straightened and let her eyes rest on Carol for a moment, taking in the tension and the guilt. The only way out was through. She did what she'd learned to do at sea: a brief, factual report. "Okay. You said you wanted a grenade."

    Carol's face tightened immediately, "I was being sarcastic."

    Zosia watched her for a second, because this was where she could choose cruelty or clarity. "I got it," Zosia said. "You didn't slam the door. You didn't call me an idiot—with words at least." She held Carol's eyes. "You invited me in."

    Carol's mouth opened, then closed.

    "You drank," Zosia said. "We talked. You tried to pick a fight with me. Then you made the pin come out."

    Carol's head jerked up. "I—"

    Zosia held up one hand, not harsh, just stopping the reflex. "In the dream," she said. "I'm telling you what happened. What you meant is a different conversation." Carol's jaw worked, and it looked like she wanted to argue. Zosia let the silence sit for a moment. Her back ached when she breathed too deeply. "I took it," Zosia said. "I threw it out the window. I… covered you. You were fine. I wasn't."

    Carol's face went pale. She started shaking her head immediately, like the denial could rewind time. "I'm sorry," she said, hoarse. "Fuck."

    Zosia wanted to protest kindly, the way she had in the dream, but the truth was Carol had made choices. The scars were hers to be angry about and she was, but she looked at Carol's white face and the familiar swerve began—involuntary the first day, deliberate now, and she understood it less for being able to feel herself choosing it.

    "I'm not telling you this so you can flay yourself," Zosia said. "I'm telling you because it happened."

    Carol's face reddened. She looked angry, then she looked hurt, then she looked, finally, like she recognized herself in the description. "Okay."

    "Then the hospital," Zosia said. "You're—" She searched for a word. "You're you." Zosia kept her voice steady, kept the report moving. "I drink the HDP. It tastes like nothing."

    Carol was startled. "You didn't want to puke?"

    "I don't think so, and if I did, that was probably me reading into it. It's like… think about dream logic. You're you, but you can't control what you do, and most of it is not as concerning as it should be."

    Carol's shoulders hunched.

    "It's hard to explain. They would direct me," Zosia said, "Prompt speech, action, attention. I didn't experience that as force, because they weren't forcing me. I was…" Her mouth tilted. "Extremely content."

    Carol gave a short humorless laugh. "Yeah. I noticed."

    "Nothing was a conscious decision in the ordinary sense. More like… the intention moved through me without resistance. The fun facts are a good example." Zosia shrugged one shoulder, self-conscious. "I had all that knowledge. We'd want to make conversation. It came out sounding like me, because it was coming through me, but it didn't feel like a choice I was making." Carol just looked confused and uncomfortable. Zosia watched her fidget—hands clasping, unclasping, then clasping again. She cleared her throat. "Anyway. You were kind, in small ways. But then you asked how to undo it."

    Carol's eyes sharpened. "And?"
