    "And I can't tell you," Zosia said simply, then added, "Then you do something I'm not thrilled about." Zosia kept her tone calm and vague. "You decide you need answers badly enough to… change my condition." Carol's eyes darted up and she opened her mouth and Zosia held up a hand again. "No spoilers," she said.

    "Okay," Carol said, voice tight.

    Zosia's shoulder was throbbing. "The end of the dream was… medical," she said. "My heart—" She paused. She didn't like saying it. She didn't like how she could see Carol clinging to it like it was proof she was monstrous."My heart stops." Carol leaned forward a bit, as if proximity could change the outcome retroactively. "Cardiac arrest," Zosia said, precise. "That's where it cuts out."

    "Zosia—"

    "Listen, it already happened, and I'm alive. So don't spiral."

    Carol looked down at her own hands. "I didn't—" she started, and the rest didn't come out.

    Zosia could guess what she meant. I didn't mean to. I didn't want that. I didn't know. 

    "I know," Zosia said, simple.

    Carol stared at her like she'd been punched. "Why are you telling me this like it's—like it's nothing."

    "It's not nothing," Zosia said, and for a second she couldn't keep the irritation out of her voice. "I'm not going to tell you everything's fine. I know I said that then, but I'm not going to be as easy as I was." Did she mean it as a warning? A complaint? An apology? She didn't fully know why she said it. "You put something into my body without asking."

    Carol went very still. Her hands pressed flat against her thighs. "I know," she said. Too fast, too quiet.

    Zosia could stop there. She didn't. "They made me bring live ordnance into your house, and let you handle it. I would never have done that." Something underneath the composure gave way and heat flooded through. "They walked me off my ship, made me pick up bodies, flew me across the world, changed me, went through your private memories, made me cover you with my body." She wasn't asking for sympathy. "I found the scars this morning. I didn't know I had them. Eighty days of using me and I wasn't asked once. They kept me useful, kept me—" 

    She'd learned years ago to make her case before the feeling reached her voice, because once it did the feeling was all anyone heard, but she could hear herself accelerating and couldn't stop. They would have dampened this, she'd never have felt it, and instead the feelings came with no buffer, and her voice was climbing and her face was hot. "And then you decided—you, on your own—what went into my body, because you needed the answer badly enough to—"

    "I know," Carol said. Her voice had gone flat, drained of everything except endurance. "I know I did."

    "Stop saying you know." Zosia's hands were white-knuckled on her knees. "You keep jumping ahead to the guilt so I can't finish a sentence. I'm not telling you this so you can feel bad. I'm telling you what happened to me."

    "What the fuck do you want me to do? I can't just sit here hunky-dory while you tell me I nearly killed you."

    "I want five minutes where I'm the subject of the sentence and not your conscience!" Zosia's breath was audible. Her back was screaming now, the tension pulling at every healing seam.

    Carol's eyes were bright. She pressed her lips together and then her voice was low. "I drugged you. That's mine. You're right about that and I'm not going to argue it, but you left that behind three sentences ago." Zosia's teeth clenched. "You want to be angry about eighty days being kept a prisoner, be angry, God knows you should be. But I drugged you because I was the only person on the goddamn planet trying to get you out. I had no-one else. No other ideas." Her chin came up. "What I did was the opposite of trying to keep you, and if you can't see the difference right now then whatever, but I'm not going to sit here and nod like I'm one of them."

    Zosia's fingers had gone slack on her knees without noticing. 

    They both looked at the coffee table. Neither spoke. 

    Sasha had ducked fights, he was too easy-going, and colleagues always deferred or escalated to a useless meeting. Carol had stood in the blast radius and taken the fair hit without ducking, stayed on the sofa and argued like Zosia's words mattered more than her anger, like they were worth the trouble of contradicting, and the effect of being taken seriously was alarming. Zosia wasn't even angry at Carol anymore, she found. More that her own remembered past had been stolen and turned into a series of not-exactly-nightmares. 

    "You're right. I went too far." She paused on how to say it. "But you go too far too, you keep running ahead to the worst." Her breath was still uneven. "Just—stay in the room with me." Carol looked faintly defiant, like she'd held her ground and wasn't sure yet whether to be proud, and Zosia resolved to let her have it. "Your plan almost worked," she said. It felt like climbing down a ladder she'd kicked over. "You wanted the answer, to force a limit." She held Carol's gaze. "You were close."

    "That's not—" Carol's voice cracked on the second word and she visibly shut the rest up.

    "It's not a moral thing," Zosia corrected, and she couldn't stop an embarrassing edge of pride in her tone then, "but you built an angle of attack from almost nothing and executed under pressure. That's… impressive. Resourceful."

    Carol just stared at her like she'd said something incomprehensible.

    "Before my heart gave out, I was about to say 'radio signal.'"

    "You were?"

    "Yes," Zosia said. "I don't know if it would've been the whole key, but… that's where it was going. It was working." Carol's shoulders dropped a fraction. Zosia watched her carefully. "You're not stupid. You're just dangerous when you're cornered."

    Carol's laugh was shaky. "Like a feral dog. That's the nicest thing anyone's said to me all week."

    Zosia gave her a small wry smile. "You're welcome."

    Carol was still tense, but her eyes had come up from the floor and stayed up. Zosia couldn't take full credit for that. She'd lost the course and they'd still arrived, somehow, where she'd been heading—if anything, Carol had steered them out of the worst of it while Zosia was still spinning.

    Carol stared ahead. "Manny will lose his mind," she muttered.

    As if summoned by the word radio, three sharp raps hit the front door. They looked at each other and Carol's eyebrows lifted, incredulous.

    "Good timing," Zosia sighed, and stood stiffly. She needed caffeine badly and still, absurdly, wanted to stay on the sofa a little longer. Usually after conflict she wanted the deck, a cigarette she wouldn't have, and an hour alone. The house had already begun to acquire a ridiculous dependency: it felt complete when Carol was in the room and expensively underfurnished when she wasn't. She sighed again. "Do you want coffee?"

    Carol looked up from her hands. "I've still got—" she started, then remembered that her mug was empty now and she'd been too busy ruminating to refill it. "Yeah," she said instead. "Sure." Zosia crossed the hallway, and Carol let herself breathe.

    Zosia had never raised her voice before. She'd never needed to. She'd been warm without friction, soothed her like a drug. Today, Zosia wasn't soothing anything. She didn't pretend any of it was fine—she'd said look and kept making coffee anyway.

    Zosia had shouted at her for the first time ever and Carol felt, bizarrely, better than she had in days. 

    They'd had the worst conversation yet and somehow she'd come out of it being called impressive. She could still hear the grudging pitch that Zosia hadn't tried to disguise, and she'd been furious with Carol thirty seconds earlier, so Carol couldn't even call bullshit. It had sounded more of a field evaluation than flattery.

    She turned it over, waiting for the catch, and it didn't come. Morning sun had broken through the overcast and it found the back of Carol's neck through the window and warmed it.

    She answered the door and Manousos didn't bother with hello. His gaze went past Carol's shoulder into the house as if he expected to see Zosia standing at attention to deliver another report. Carol blocked the doorway, territorial. 

    "You're early," she said.

    "Update."

    Carol exhaled. "Nothing new, except—" She hesitated, because saying it aloud made it feel like she was handing him a gift. "Radio signal. Zosia says she was about to say 'radio signal' when I… drugged her."

    Manny's expression barely changed, he just nodded once. "Yes." 

    "That's it? You're not going to—I dunno—jump for joy?"

    "No. We already knew signals, but it is confirmation." He shifted his weight, already half moving again. "I am going back," he said. "I am returning your books."

    Carol's eyes narrowed. "My books. Like, my books? Or—"

    "Technical books," he said, as if Carol was slow. 

    Oh. Right. "Uh, do you want coffee?"

    Manny's stare moved to the kitchen as if he could smell it from here, but then he shook his head. "No. I do not want to be relaxed." He reached into his bag to produce a stack of notebooks and shoved them at Carol. She caught them against her chest with a grunt. "These," Manny said, "Zosia reads. She will find what I miss."

    "You're giving her your actual notebooks."

    "Yes," he said, "Do not spill coffee on them."

    Carol glanced down at the pile, then back up. "You know she's not—"

    "She is capable," he cut in. "She wants to help. Good. Let her."

    Carol's mouth tightened. Manousos took a step back, already turning. "Alright," she said automatically, and then, because she couldn't resist, added, "Try not to get killed by an avalanche of text books."

    Manousos didn't even look back. "I am not you," he said, and then he was walking down the driveway, purposeful.

    Carol shut the door and turned back to the kitchen. Zosia was there with Shrek, and held it out to her, a garish green the color of a booger or something you'd find in a wet drain.

    "He's so ugly," Carol said, to fill the air. 

    Zosia paused in front of her. Her eyes narrowed over Carol's face, concern disguised as irritation. "I'm trying," Zosia said, "to make us both less a mess."

    Carol huffed a laugh. "Thanks," she muttered, and took the mug. She searched around the room for something to say. "He left those for you," she said, gesturing at the notebooks she'd put on the island. "If you want to read them." 

    "He already trusts me with his notebooks?"

    "I think he trusts you with everything now that you said 'radio.'" She shoved the notes another inch closer to Zosia, as if sliding them across a line. Carol shrugged, too casual. "I'm just the courier." 

    Zosia pulled the notebooks toward her and was already deep in them within seconds, pen in hand. Carol stood with her coffee and picked up one of the loose pages. Waveform diagrams. Numbers with too many decimal places. She turned it the right way up and it didn't help. Zosia's shoulders dropped by degrees as her pen moved. Carol watched her flip back three pages to cross-reference something, then forward again, then scribble a note. 

    Manousos had his signal theory. Zosia had the navy. Carol had a couple of liberal arts degrees and strong opinions about semicolons, and she'd sailed those ships through four novels, but they wouldn't carry her here.

    "Carol." She looked up. Zosia had stopped writing. "Do you want me to walk you through what we've got?"

    I'm fine. The words were right there, fully formed. She'd used them on Helen, on Val, on every therapist she'd fired after the first session—which was all of them—but Zosia had called her resourceful, and resourceful people didn't bluff, they asked.

    "Yeah," she said instead. "Actually. No idea what any of this means beyond one frequency."

    Zosia's face didn't change. "Get something to write on," she said.

    Carol went upstairs. Her office door was ajar, the desk lamp still on from last night. Zosia had asked follow-up questions about the routes, stayed through the cat rant, seeming to want more. Carol could've gone until dawn, she thought, rummaging through the drawer, caught herself smiling about it and stopped when she remembered she'd accidentally said it's like yours about the hair, out loud, mid-complaint.

    She pulled a notebook from a drawer and flipped it open to find clean pages.

    Only the first few were full. Messier than usual, from what she guessed was four or five years ago. Along the top of one page: Luc's route thru Ashfall—needs three days not two, pacing wrong. Below it, a rough sketch of a coastline with arrows indicating wind direction, a dashed line for a ship's course, and in the margin, a small detailed drawing of Lucasia's dagger, labeled with dimensions she'd never used.

    She should rip these out. Zosia was waiting. Carol flipped past them to the blank pages and went downstairs.

    Zosia had cleared space on the dining table and the notebooks were arranged in a row. "Okay," Zosia said. "Start here." She turned a notebook to face Carol and pointed. "This is the signal he's been tracking."

    Carol sat next to her. She wrote the date at the top of her page and underlined it squiggly. Zosia started explaining, and Carol wrote things down, most of which she half-knew already from a week of his scrawled diagrams and her own panicked research.

    She kept checking Carol's face. Carol noticed because she was trying not to look, and every time she did Zosia was already gauging something, whether Carol was following, whether she needed to back up. When Carol's pen slowed, Zosia slowed. When Carol frowned, Zosia rephrased without being asked. As Zosia explained carrier frequencies, her eyes were radiant with it, a kind of pride with no arrogance to it. 

    Zosia continued, "With radio the atmosphere matters," she said. "Temperature, humidity, it can bend waves, refract them, so what you think is a straight line isn't always straight. Signals can travel further than they should, or not as far. You would—" Zosia saw her face and stopped mid-sentence, suddenly serious. "Am I being condescending?"

    "What? No."

    Zosia didn't look convinced. "I'm not trying to—I teach as part of my job but my usual audience has five years of training, and I'm... recalibrating." Her mouth went wry. "Am I explaining this like you're five?"

    Carol snorted, a little too fond. She hooked her feet around the chair legs. "No, you're not condescending. You're doing great."

    Zosia gave her a dark look. "Don't encourage me. You'll be here all day." 

    Carol's throat bobbed. Jesus. Zosia could probably explain paint drying and Carol would sit here nodding like an idiot. 

    She had a brief flash of Zosia on a ship somewhere, this same earnest intensity turned on some dumb cadet who would've developed an immediate and career-ruining crush on teacher and Carol felt a sudden kinship with this imaginary ensign.

    She tried to actually participate instead of gawking. "Can I ask a dumb question?" Zosia's eyes came up. "We keep saying electromagnetic." Carol tapped her pen against the paper. "What does that actually mean? Like, it's a force? But also a wave? I still don't know."

    "That's not a dumb question," Zosia said. "That is the question." She sat forward slightly, pushing up the sleeves that were too short on her anyway, and Carol realized she'd accidentally found fifth gear. "Light, electricity, radio, it's all electromagnetic. It's all the same force at different frequencies. It holds your atoms together. Every chemical bond, every nerve impulse in your body, every signal in your brain."

    Carol wrote same force, diff freq on her paper.

    "It's what you feel when you touch something," Zosia said, and Carol's pen stopped. Zosia pressed her fingertip to the table. "You think there's contact, but there's not." She slid her long finger across the surface slowly and Carol felt it in her spine. She shifted in her chair and disguised it as adjusting her notebook. "The electrons in your skin repel the electrons in the table. Your nerves are sensing it. They don't have the strength to overcome it." She flattened her hand on the table and looked at it with genuine wonder. "At the atomic level, there's always a gap. You've never truly touched anything."

    Carol stared at Zosia's hand, on the table. She was thinking about the inch of air between her knee and Zosia's, under it. 

    "What you feel," Zosia continued, completely oblivious, "isn't contact. It's the sensation of getting as close as the force allows." She turned her own forearm over, ran one finger along the inside of her wrist, tracing the vein there. "Your body pressing against something else, and your nerve endings—" her finger followed the vein up past her inner elbow, slowly— "interpreting that as feeling."

    Carol moved her knee away to clench her thighs together. "Great," she gulped. "Good to know."

    Her face must have been doing something because Zosia's head tilted—quickly overridden by the next thought. "Anyway," Zosia said, and Carol exhaled. "Same principle at every scale." Zosia leaned over to point at something in the notebook. 

    "This band, here—" Zosia said, and Carol could not see the page because Zosia's bare forearm was right there, the vein, the one she'd just— "Radar sends an electromagnetic pulse across kilometers and reads what comes back." Zosia said, inches from Carol's ear. She felt Zosia's breath shift her hair. Carol was sure she was vibrating at a frequency only dogs could hear. 

    "Your skin does it across nanometers." Carol could smell her—salt and sun-warmed wood, the scent of her skin and her clothes and in the sheets she'd stripped and buried her face in last week before she could stop herself. She'd thought of Raban, her fictional sailor, her made-up sea. It had always been real, and it had always been hers, and Carol breathed it in because she needed more air suddenly. "Both are just—reacting to what's on the other side of a gap." 

    Zosia sat back, satisfied with the lesson.

    Carol let out a wobbly breath. She made a mark on her page that wasn't a word. She was going to need a minute.

    "Should I keep going?" Zosia asked.

    "Yep yep," Carol managed. "Keep going." She drew a careful line under the non-word, and gave herself the length of it to reassemble.

    "I should warn you," Zosia said, one side of her mouth pulling against the other, "I was about to say fun fact." Carol smiled weakly as her pulse settled. Zosia had said earlier that had always been hers too, peeking through.

    What else—

    Something opened under Carol's feet and she shut it, fast, because what difference would it make, picking through the rubble for scraps? As if it mattered. She couldn't go back to pretending she'd lost nothing, but she couldn't have what she'd lost, anyway.

    Her eyes went where they were going to go regardless, helplessly, and Carol watched the self-satisfaction in her face as Zosia said something about radar. The first time, she'd sniped at it. By the tenth, she was expecting it. She couldn't say when she'd started loving it, and loving it changed nothing.

    "...so you're seeing things that are geometrically below where you are. You're seeing past the edge of the world. Isn't that cool?" 

    Carol looked down at her notebook before her face could give anything away. She kept her pen moving and thought keep this for book five, because what else was there to do but be a magpie stealing from a wreck. She was writing a tiny enchanted crystal bends light? in the margin when Zosia stopped mid-sentence again. "—what's that?"

    Zosia was looking at her notebook. The binding had just relaxed and the book had fallen open to the earlier section, the coastline sketch and the dagger drawing visible.

    "Nothing," Carol said, "Just old stuff."

    "Is that Lucasia's dagger?"

    "It's just a doodle."

    Zosia's voice had done a one-eighty from instructor. "The handle has her family sigil on it."

    Carol's hand paused on the page. She'd forgotten she'd put that in. "Yeah. Except, well, it's not actually their sigil. Nobody knows that." She said it casually, but nobody knew. That had only ever lived inside her head. "It's from the Tyreline," Carol explained, at Zosia's raised eyebrows. Helen knew the broad strokes of why she'd started writing Wycaro, but by the time they met, the inciting incident was the volcano eruption. Carol had never found a reason to excavate the original lore for someone who loved her but read the drafts out of loyalty rather than hunger.

    "The monks who can read the old maps?"

    "Yeah. Or that's what they became. There was something I never—" She waved it off. "Originally they had this whole thing, this church doctrine. You had to turn in your compass to the elders before every voyage. And if you wanted it back, you had to tell them where you'd been and where you were going." She looked up. Zosia had stopped looking at the notebook and was looking at Carol. Carol kept her eyes on the dagger drawing. "Lucasia leaving her compass was supposed to be the inciting incident, the refusal to confess. So she steals their sigil instead, puts a line through it and wears it anyway. Like a middle finger."

    "A middle finger to the church," Zosia repeated. 

    Carol's mouth twisted. "Yeah."

    Zosia was eating this up. Before, they'd listened to Carol like this, and honestly, they'd been more engaged then—never distracted, never checking the clock. Now Zosia kept glancing at Manny's notebooks and then back at Carol, like she was guilty about enjoying this more, and each time she chose Carol, her attention was more keen. 

    Carol hadn't planned to say the next part, but she did anyway. "That was the first part I ever wrote, in the library at UNM. Grad school. It was five years since Freedom Falls and I still couldn't—" She made a vague gesture at her own head. "I sat in the reading room and wrote a page about a sailor who'd rather go out blind without a compass than tell anyone. From the most landlocked college ever." Carol snorted. "And then I found the diner when I started temping, and the desert had got into everything by then, all the goddamn sand, so that's where Wycaro started forming, and you know the rest."

    Zosia had tucked one leg under herself on the chair and she was looking at Carol with those dark eyes and Carol thought, for the millionth time, that Zosia was the most beautiful person she had ever seen in her life and she was probably irreversibly fucked. She forced her eyes back down to the sigil and kept talking.

    She'd written a love interest she was too scared to keep, the hive had found the real one and sent her to Carol's door, and the real one had already been loving Wycaro before Carol existed as anything but a name on a spine. The circularity of it should have been funny. It wasn't funny. It was the most romantic thing that had ever happened to her. She couldn't even be angry about it. Those fuckers had known her down to the studs, and hadn't even known the half of it.

    She looked back up. Zosia's chin was resting on her hand. Zosia liked this, liked her, when she was like this, and that was embarrassing to feel and impossible to ignore. She was performing for a beautiful straight woman's attention over a dead subplot. Pathetic. She was absolutely going to keep her hat with bells on and continue juggling.

    "There's more," Carol said, flipping back through the notebook. "I had this system for the tides in the Ashfall where the coastline changes every twelve hours. I drew charts." She found the page—a grid of small diagrams, twin lunar cycles mapped to shifting shorelines, her handwriting getting smaller as she'd run out of space. "Nobody saw these either. They were just for me, so I could keep the continuity."

    Zosia leaned in to look. "This is proper cartography," she said, almost to herself.

    Carol scoffed. "It's chickenscratch."

    "The methodology's sound. You imagined all this from your office." Zosia looked up from the page, and her face was very close, and she was smiling, and Carol's vision went white for half a second. "You should've been a navigator."

    Carol leaned back in her chair, putting twelve more inches between them, and scratched the back of her head. "Don't think I have your brains for that," she said, and meant it as a joke but it came out sincere.

    Something shifted in Zosia's expression, and she looked away first. She stood, collecting both mugs. "More coffee," she said, already moving toward the kitchen, and Carol felt the loss of her attention like the light in the room left with her.

    Carol watched Zosia go through the drill at the counter; kettle, grinder, that weird pour. The shirt shifted between her shoulder blades. All afternoon Carol had tried to keep herself leashed because she refused to be the creep at the table, but now Zosia's back was turned and she felt every minute of restraint crumble. Carol's gaze tracked down the back of her, starved and free, and her memory of that morning supplied what her eyes couldn't reach: bare skin, warm from the shower, steam still clinging, the soft edge where the towel had been. Below it, two welts. 

    She was ogling a back she'd blown open. 

    She looked down at the table and stayed looking at it.

    Zosia came back with Carol's mug, her fingers around the handle. Carol's closed over it too, a fingertip brushing a knuckle.

    Zosia's whole body jolted and the mug tilted a fraction and hot coffee sloshed near the rim. Zosia caught it, but her hand still yanked back as if Carol had burned her instead.

    Carol froze. "I'm—sorry. Didn't mean to—" Zosia wasn't even looking at her. Oh great. Great. Of course this was what touching did, now that Zosia knew she'd almost killed her. Twice. 

    Zosia's eyes snapped to Carol's face and held and Carol had the uneasy feeling of being looked at and looked past. Zosia's lip curled, a flash of fury—almost revolted—and then every part of her expression clamped shut at once. Carol looked down at her own hands. She felt contaminated.

    She'd sat there for an hour feeling warm and seen while Zosia was one brushed knuckle away from flinching. She'd been preening like an idiot. Juggling her little balls. Meanwhile Zosia's body had tagged Carol under threat, and you couldn't argue with a reflex.

    Carol pushed her chair back. "Listen. I've got chores to do."

    Zosia exhaled a long breath, her expression blank. "Chores," Zosia repeated.

    "Yeah," Carol said quickly. "Laundry and whatnot. You don't need me. You've got your own reading."

    Then she turned and left. She did everything except be in the same room.

    She did two loads of laundry. She reorganized the freezer by expiration date though that had stopped meaning much. She swept floors that were already clean. She moved through the house in tight circuits, never landing anywhere long enough to stop. Her feet kept drifting to the dining room anyway, and Carol kept overriding them.

    You put something into my body without asking. Zosia had meant the drug and Carol had heard the rest. She'd told Zosia she wasn't the hive and meant it, but she was full of fucking shit. She knew where the scars were because she knew every inch of her body, learned it with her hands and her mouth over weeks when no had never been a possibility. She knew all of it without asking and none of it by right, and the hive had done the same thing.

    She'd thought the worst case scenario was being hated. That had been the easy case. The actual worst was having her back but better than the invention, realer, still close enough to smell and straight—every fragment Carol had loved now welded to a woman who had earned every piece of it; every hour Zosia spent more interesting than the last a fuse burning toward the night she'd learn what Carol had done, and then it would just be Carol and the empty house again, both condemned.

    Flinching should have been a clean kill. Instead, by late afternoon, Carol had run out of chores and she was circling the sound of Zosia's pen on paper like a thing with a broken wing. 

    She'd passed the doorway five times and glanced in on three of them, and on the fifth Zosia was still at the table, angled into the work, hair slipping down in loose strands. Carol saw her roll her shoulder, wince, and keep reading.

    The painkillers were on the nightstand where Carol had left them that morning. She'd spent the whole afternoon being cowardly careful while Zosia's shoulder burned eight hours past a pill she was too proud to mention.

    She came up behind Zosia to set the pill bottle on the table in her periphery, and Zosia flinched again. Full-bodied, pen scoring a dark line across the paper. Carol's stomach dropped. She should've known better. She did know better.

    "Sorry, I should've—"

    "It's not—" Zosia was already smoothing the page, posture reassembled. "On a ship, if someone comes up behind you near the rail..." She trailed off as if the rest were obvious.

    "Yeah. I'll remember," Carol said, and she turned and left before her face could say the rest.

    She hid in her office until evening, then scraped canned soup into a bowl and ate it hunched at the sink, quick and furtive, while Zosia debriefed Manousos.

    Carol went upstairs to leave Zosia's laundered clothes in the guest room, and from below, her voice reached faintly, Spanish she couldn't follow. Carol's hands were still warm from the dryer, and she stood at the threshold until they weren't, looking at the perfectly made bed with its sharp corners, the pillows squared carefully. She pulled the door shut behind her.

    Chapter 5

    Zosia was in a hospital bed that wasn't even near Albuquerque. The air was too humid. The ceiling tiles were stained in one corner. She could feel electrodes on her skin, the sticky pull when she shifted. The handcuff was still there—chain snipped, the other half on Carol. The metal had gone warm against her pulse.

    She hurt distantly, like pain remembered through a layer of gauze. Rest now. We have you. In the dream she watched herself recover with dutiful obedience. She walked the hallway with a patient nurse at her elbow, in silence except for linoleum that squeaked under her stagger.

    Then the dream widened.

    Zosia felt Carol arrive in the feed before she saw her—a resistant signal moving through the empty city, rattling padlocks, peering through warehouse windows. The perspective in fragments: drone-eye views; rooftop angles tracked the police car; a street camera showed her climbing a dumpster. Zosia shifted in the hospital bed and the electrodes pulled at her chest, and Carol ducked through a doorway, and something tugged too, a tether she couldn't peel off or press flat, tauten or slacken.

    Between locations, the feed showed Carol leaning against the car, drinking water, the cuff glinting on her wrist. She turned it, traced the cut edge. Zosia watched through a window Carol didn't know existed, and for the duration of the gesture—three slow turns—her hands forgot the carton they were holding, and pressed against the glass of the feed, uselessly. 

    In the videos, Carol sat in front of the camera auditioning a posture that didn't belong to her—back too straight, voice measured. Offering facts, theories, connections. Zosia watched Carol arrange herself into someone palatable and the rejection was immediate. You don't have to do that—like a cross slashed in the dream's margin.

    We love her, every version. 

    Carol got in her car and drove. The feed showed her cutting through daylight toward Las Vegas, flipping off a speed camera, the road long and empty. Koumba's voice entered the collective space, quietly: She's lonely. 

    Zosia's grip dented the waxed carton, then her fingers loosened and her breathing levelled and the feeling—she couldn't hold it, and the hive tracked it before she could've named it: dipping serotonin, elevated norepinephrine. They logged it with affection: she missed her, and they felt it too. It won't hurt forever. It had been happening then, in her body—the missing had been hers before it was theirs, and they'd caught it and redistributed it before she'd finished feeling it. Somewhere in Las Vegas, they would mention it to Koumba, because it was true, and because true things timed well could be useful.

    Koumba kept talking. He told them she knew about the other immune, scattered and meeting over intermittent connections. Carol had been shut out. Zosia, dreaming, surely, felt a flare of anger, and underneath it, recognition sinking through her like cold water. The empty chairs in the circle at camp, the same verdict—too loud, too much. We'll bring them together where everyone belongs. To the hive, the concept of exclusion came malformed, as a system fault in each immune. Bugs fixed as soon as they joined.

    Days passed in the dream without the courtesy of being counted. At some point they had done something unprecedented: tracked Carol's vehicle to the edge of the nearest relay, and then—let go. Let her position dissolve to unknown. The decision seemed to precede consensus, as though the feeling had outpaced the thought. Zosia felt it moving through the signal strangely: a pleasure no language they'd indexed could name, because none had ever needed the word. 

    Then, as soon as her body could hold itself upright without support, the dream cut her loose.

    She was in a car crossing open desert. The landscape was high and lunar, a broad basin bleached and winter-stripped of shadow, stretching to a horizon that had no shore. Each breath she drew searched for moisture and found dust, the dryness of New Mexico again.

    Dishes. Enormous, pale structures planted in a vast spread like mechanical flowers: The Very Large Array. Twenty-seven of them aimed at the same silence. 

    Individuals moved among each other, frictionless, each smooth face a surface no gaze caught on. Zosia took her place among them without hesitation. The work was maintenance and repurposing. Receiving turned to transmitting, one dish at a time—ladders, feed horns, cabling runs, the satisfying click of components seated correctly. 

    And through all of it, under the task and consensus, like a second heartbeat, was Carol. 

    One day, Carol started singing to herself, a few bars of something. They heard it and catalogued it: Self-soothing. Good. Zosia, soldering wires three stories up, heard the melody wander off-key and her mouth pulled sideways and her hands went still on the iron. The heat brought her back—she'd kept it too long, the connection overcooked—and pulled it away. Below her the desert was enormous and empty and Carol was singing to herself in a car a hundred miles north.

    The days blurred on. Carol's isolation deepened. Her coping got stranger: talking to the golf clubs; narrating her own driving sarcastically; laughing at her own jokes with the brittle edge of proving she hadn't gone fully off the rails. Her loops around the neighborhood got wider, more reckless, treating the city like a playground with no rules and no witnesses.

    Zosia climbed the third ladder of the evening with a toolbelt she hadn't packed. She re-seated a panel and felt the desert wind push her sideways and held. Below her the dish held too, aimed at one distant point, rooted to a concrete pad, free to turn but never to leave.

    Carol set up fireworks on the cul-de-sac, chair dragged to center-stage, beers already half-demolished. Colors broke across the rooftops of empty houses as they watched from above. The last rocket listed and dropped to be aimed at Carol's head, and she looked right at it, chin and beer half-raised. The love lurched. Every linked mind swung toward the cul-de-sac at once and Zosia's hand slipped off the rung and her stomach dropped and she caught herself, gripped the cold metal with both hands and her pulse in her palms. No—theirs and hers and indistinguishable and it didn't matter.

    The firework tore past Carol's ear and buried itself in the neighbor's garage roof as flames caught the eaves. Carol finished her beer, stood up loose-limbed to find a hose, and put it out with all the urgency of watering a houseplant.

    Zosia was gripping the rung of the ladder, a hundred miles away, watching Carol decide in real time to let fate flip a coin and call heads while it was pointed at hers. The tremor in Zosia's hands wouldn't stop and it was the cold and they smoothed it before she could discover whether that was all it was. 

    The feed cut to painted letters at the end of the cul-de-sac, huge and blunt on the asphalt like a command. Zosia felt it in her bones: reassignment. Back to her. The relief was unanimous and enormous and she couldn't find the edges of her own inside it. She wanted to go, they wanted to go, they were sending her, trying to separate hers from theirs like trying to cup one current in a river. 

    Her lungs opened. The air smelled different here, closer to Carol's house; sun-baked concrete, sage gone to seed, and underneath it something Zosia recognised from the pillow she was sleeping on. 

    The hive's pleasure ran through and Zosia felt herself smile and the smile was simple and belonged to everyone and she didn't care. She had spent her life in love with going, crossed oceans for the next horizon, loved the long blue nothing between ports, and this distance felt longer than any of them, and for the first time she could remember, the want wasn't to go—it was to arrive.

    Carol reached her and collapsed forward into her shoulder and her senses answered before the mind could sort it. She smelled of paint and soap. Zosia's arms closed around her and Carol's ribs shuddering against her own. The ragged heat of breath at her collarbone. 

    Her hand rose and—brief as a skipped heartbeat, her fingers were climbing toward the back of Carol's head—then her palm was on Carol's shoulder instead and her thumb was moving without instruction and the transition happened so smoothly she couldn't find the change. The shoulder was right. Her thumb pressed its slow rhythm and everything in her converged on a single imperative—make her okay—and whether that belonged to one mind or every mind, she couldn't cut the line that fine, not in that light, Carol breathing hard against her, alive. 

    Zosia knew now, holding her, what Carol's weight felt like against her body, the temperature of her skin through cotton, the smell of her hair. Arms they moved for her held an answer delivered by a moment she hadn't chosen, and what she felt was real and was also second hand and she could feel both at once without being able to separate them, and the dream moved on before she could, turning softly at the edges, into a card game. 

    Everyone loved it, loved being near her, loved how Carol's mood steadied under her attention. Zosia's mouth offered Henry, two hours east, and happy to drive if Carol wanted another face she'd known before. 

    "It would be just like talking to you, right? Then nah." She discarded a card.

    The hive took in the refusal with fond bafflement. Carol had asked them all to come back, Henry would have served both ends, and she had turned him down for just one. Zosia looked back at her again and felt herself warming, at being kept, held in her hand when she could have drawn another. She picked me. The thought surfaced in first person. Whether she had been the one holding it then, or was holding it now, the dealing went on either way.

    Carol won the first round and gloated. The hive didn't care who won; the game was contact, proximity, Carol's mood lifting. Zosia cared. She had not been beaten at cards by anyone since a petty officer in Świnoujście in 2014—a defeat she still considered fraudulent—and didn't want to watch a clumsy novelist with a no poker face end the streak, no matter how cute she looked winning or who was steering the ship.

    She watched her hands shuffle the cards expertly. 

    "Why do they call it spit?" 

    Zosia answered, because she and they loved being asked things, and also tracked the cards, because they could hold a billion attention streams simultaneously. Carol's misdirection was flattering but required only two. She slapped her winning hand flat on the table, hard enough to rattle the lemonade. 

    Ha. 

    She felt a smugness so pointless the hive could hardly find a hook to hang it on. They let her keep it.

    She invited Carol to see where they slept and Carol followed with a wary gait. The air carried the faint, comforting hum of shared consciousness as she showed her the blankets calmly arranged, the people resting in proximity. Zosia watched Carol's face twisting, fascination fighting revulsion, longing fighting fear. She was inside their space. Breathing their air. Standing among them without running. Almost like she's joined, they thought, ecstatic and greedy, billions of minds savoring the almost, the closeness, the tantalising nearly. 

    She offered, gently, "Would you like to stay with us tonight?" An open palm, nothing more. 

    Carol's head turned toward her, eyes wide for half a second before turning her down. They could see the want in her anyway, clear as daylight. To not be alone. Zosia didn't push, they didn't push in ways that looked like pushing, and Carol stayed, of course.

    The dream blurred, softened, let the hours dissolve—

    —and Zosia surfaced to Carol's arm around her, slid there in sleep, the body's blind reach for heat. See, she needs us, she's already closer than she knows, and Zosia felt the joy of that and felt the truth of that and also felt, beneath both, something she thought the consensus couldn't reach.

    She matched her breathing to Carol's and her blood slowed and warmed and she felt it everywhere. Eyes closed, she could almost believe they were just two people sharing a bed because they wanted to—but the almost might have been then, buried and breathing, or it might have been now, the dream reshaping the memory, inventing it because she wanted it. 

    The dream softened. The collective murmur deepened, a lullaby, and the world darkened again…

    As Zosia woke in the present, she half-expected to feel Carol's arm around her still. She stared at the ceiling and waited for the feeling to fade. She turned her head and saw the pale strip of light under her bedroom door. Carol was already up. She'd been avoiding her. Zosia had felt it all yesterday, Carol moving around corners so she didn't have to look her in the eye.

    Zosia tried not to take it personally.

    Still, her mind offered a theory she didn't enjoy as she sat up. Zosia had come back from the hivemind more porous, her feelings pulled forward to the surface and left there, so her crush was shamefully obvious. It could probably be seen from space. Carol was maintaining distance out of kindness or discomfort or both, or worse, maybe she felt it was too close to what the hive did, another version of someone wanting her without permission—

    She stopped the thought where it was going. Through the window the sky was still gray, and she sat there and went over the dream instead.

    The immune had been quietly cooperating to keep them alive, and Carol had been excluded. She'd heard worse judgments in her life, but aimed at Carol, Zosia felt herself reacting like it was personal, and she had a clue why.

    The day before, their fingers touching on the mug handle. Her instant recoil, not from Carol, but from a flood of memories. 

    The world had split into a handful of angles at once, film strips scattered on a light table, no warning, the full sensorium of someone else's memory of Carol, projected without her consent.

    A microphone under hot stage lights—moderator's laugh—mom porn—a male voice talking over her while Carol smiled blankly. Then a corridor outside the green room: Carol cornering her, a younger author, with a kind of brutal kindness—You were good. They were fucking rude. Next time don't let him cut you off—

    A small wrist in a hard grip—kitchen tiles—her mother's voice sharp as a slap: selfish, selfish—the cousin watching from the hall too scared to move. Then playground gravel, sun on metal swings: kid-Carol pushing half a smashed candy bar into a crying boy's hand, eyes darting—Don't tell anyone I did that—

    A college party, a cruel joke aimed at someone smaller; Carol drunkenly stepping between it and the target with flat contempt—Wow. That's embarrassing. For you.—turning laughter into awkward silence. Sirens, later—the frat guy who didn't deserve help turning blue on the lawn—Carol's hands over his chest while she swore at him: Breathe, fucking asshole—

    A high school storage closet, dusty heat, the thrill of secrecy; a hallway later under judging eyes, the same girl laughing too loud and spitting dyke—Carol's face blank by spite. Bunk bed springs in a camp dorm, a kid's hissed irritation—can you stop crying?—and Carol rolling over—

    Neon light illuminated Carol at a dive bar, and Zosia was a wasted fan demanding a hug, phone already up to record; Carol saying no, and the woman turning it into theater—ungrateful, selfish— Outside by the curb the same memory pivoted: Carol in the rain, jaw tight, voice low—I'm not hugging you. But don't be an idiot. Cash in a palm, taxi headlights.

    A dozen memories hit and then collapsed on contact, already decaying into impressions. 

    Feelings had risen in Zosia with humiliating speed, too fast to sort. Cold anger on Carol's behalf, for every person who'd pushed and punished and tried to diminish her. Underneath that impulse, not cold at all: the world had tried to take pieces, and Carol had stayed herself anyway. Zosia had spent decades paring herself down to survive and Carol had done nothing of the kind; remained loud, reactive, inconveniently principled—none of it considered.

    Zosia pressed her fingers to her sternum, which did nothing useful. The knowledge made the protectiveness worse, and the protectiveness had made the feeling worse, and it was accelerating past anything she could attribute to circumstance. She'd known her four days. Four days and three dreams.

    She could only assume these flashes were because the hive had been rifling through memories in the dream hours earlier, and some were thawing in a new way.

    She crossed to the bathroom, ran the shower cold enough to be helpful, and washed quickly while she triaged the situation. The neatness would steady her.

    The procedural skills from the dreams were easy to accept. Her body had done the work; the knowledge was a leftover, and it didn't cost her anything. In fact, it was pretty cool. 

    The dreams were hers. The hive had been steering, but the record was her life, it was her eyes seeing and her senses sensing. Even pulling up vacation memories, the camp counselor's judgment—those had passed through Zosia. She'd been present for them. 

    What the touch had delivered was different. It was general knowledge of Carol, harvested from every person who'd ever noticed her. She hadn't been there, hadn't lived it, hadn't asked. These memories were pure trespass, triggered by an action in the present. 

    If she told Carol she'd seen those things—people insulting her, rejecting her—Carol wouldn't hear it as the world was cruel to you, she'd hear that Zosia had been inside her worst memories, again uninvited, and that would surely curdle every conversation they could have. The hive had already stripped her bare without asking; Zosia refused to do it twice. The generosity Carol had offered over somehow knowing her favorite mug would collapse under the weight of what Zosia had seen, and she owed Carol the dignity of not having to perform that forgiveness again. 

    Zosia had decided in that moment, without deciding, against telling. The scenes stuffed next to Norway. The old callus for keeping things back thickening when things got hard, and her fingers had found it again without being told. The first time they'd touched, in the container, she'd known Carol's name before she had any right to it too, and she'd said nothing of the strange feeling then either.

    She dried off and crossed back to the bedroom, picked up the folded clothes from the chair. The bedroom was cool as she dressed quickly, pulling on the dark slim pants and white shirt from the first day, freshly laundered. She gulped down the painkillers and checked her shoulder's range in the mirror—much better. She moved to the bed and started making it, and the routine required nothing from her, which left too much room to think.

    Zosia felt the absurdity of her situation crest close to panic.

    She didn't know if she'd developed feelings in eighty hours, which was mortifying, or eighty days and had woken up with a hole in her head where those missing chapters should be. Those days were coming back, re-lived at a density her waking hours couldn't match. Her conscious mind was having trouble processing, perhaps, and her feelings were running ahead of the true calendar.

    Or it was leftover, she told herself. That's all it could be. The hive loved Carol. Seven billion minds adoring one woman—of course it clung. Just another withdrawal symptom that would fade. The comforting thought was there for a second before the obvious flaw ate through it. They had loved Manousos with the same devotion. Zosia liked him well enough. She didn't lie awake thinking about his eyes.

    She didn't know, and she wasn't going to figure it out making up stories.

    She paused at the top of the stairs, one hand on the banister, listening. She could hear clicking faintly down the stairs. A chair creaked. 

    Zosia should've been thinking about the notebooks, signal carriers, arrays. Instead, she thought about touch, and how her body had woken up hungry for it, and how the only person who could answer it was exactly the person she couldn't touch and also shouldn't be wanting. A grieving woman. She'd lived with inconvenient feelings before, and she'd been good at living with them, but this new complication felt like a cosmic joke.

    She needed to know what these flashes were. A one-time glitch or a permanent curse.

    If it was permanent, she'd have to learn how to live with it. If it was a one-time thing, she needed to know too, because that would be its own problem. It was practical, she told herself, and made a decision that felt treacherous but inevitable: she would test it once, intentionally, and this time she'd be ready. She would take whatever the touch gave her, if anything, and swallow her reaction.

    She set her shoulders and walked downstairs. 

    Carol was at the dining table and Zosia saw with dismay that she was in another tank top that would be far too distracting. She'd spent most of the dream at a hundred miles, watching from above, and the distance must have hurt even then because the hive had noted it somehow. Now the gap was ten feet of tile and the pull was still absurd.

    She was clicking the pen, metronomically, involuntary, and Zosia's mind produced without permission: Carol's thumb sweeping slowly over her knuckles, slowly, the same idle rhythm, back and forth over the bone, Carol not even looking at their hands. Zosia's hand closed into a fist at her side and the sensation broke, worse than anything explicit had been. She was not going to walk into the dining room shaking because her imagination had invented a Carol who touched her absently, like it was ordinary.

    Carol dragged her hand through her hair to push it back as she bent over the notes on the table, elbow out, bicep flexing. Zosia's eyes stuck there. She already knew what that arm felt like across her, the careless claim of it in sleep—only now it hit her harder and hotter, because Carol was awake and right there. Zosia gulped and forced her eyes away like she wasn't imagining being held on purpose instead of by accident.

    She stalled at the doorway and her fingers tapped the wall, much harder than the habit called for, while she breathed. She had equations to review. A mission that mattered.  Her imagination could continue producing whatever it liked; she was not required to entertain it, especially not while the woman was ten feet away trying to save the human race. 

    The notebooks were open in front of Carol and she was reading and trying to take notes, stubborn and still trying to solve it by herself, and the feeling pressed behind her ribs, unwelcome and warm. There was something wrong with her. The hive had held her mind by psychic glue and this felt almost as involuntary. Carol had acquired the ability to alter her internal weather simply by being there in a room looking pleased or ashamed or tired. 

    Carol turned a page and didn't look up, and the awareness that she was going into the second day of strategic distance sharpened into decision. She felt the sudden need to be clear, maybe not directly, but clear enough that Carol's past was not a thing to be erased or avoided. Zosia needed her to understand that she wasn't here to diminish what Helen had been. She could show respect. That, at least, she could offer.

    And she also, finally, had some new intelligence relevant to the mission. Carol still didn't look up. The tension was palpable, but Zosia wasn't going to let that stop her. She moved into the room, standing for a moment at the threshold, as her fingers tapped twice on the doorframe for luck.

    Carol had been keeping her distance like a crime scene she'd left prints at. 

    The flinches had been bad, and what she'd done with the night was worse—lying awake turning it over until the sharp edge faced forward. Yesterday, Zosia's reflex had recoiled, and the dreams would finish the job.

    But there was also the mission to save the goddamn world that she'd nearly forgotten about, and Zosia's recovered memories were useful to it, whatever else they were. Manny's notes were open in front of her making a little more sense than they had yesterday before the lesson. If Carol wanted any chance of keeping Zosia fully herself—and keeping them out of her own head—they would still need to work as a team, like adults. So Carol sat at the table pretending she understood the waveforms and her feelings. 

    The morning light shone white through the sheer curtains, showing every crack in the wood and smudge on the page. Her eyes moved across the lines. Anyone walking by would assume she was participating. In reality she was reading the same page for the fifth time and absorbing none of it because her brain kept circling:

    She's going to remember.

    Last night, tonight, tomorrow. Zosia's dreams were marching forward, and Carol heard her upstairs—soft footsteps, a door opening. Thin sounds she could only hear because her nerves were already skinned. Carol kept her eyes on the notebook as if staring hard enough would make the words turn into a plan she could use as an excuse to be around her.

    Zosia came to the doorway without fanfare, hand resting on the frame as if she'd bolt back out of the room. Carol didn't look up immediately, because turning too fast would look guilty.

    "Morning," Carol said, eventually, to the page.

    "Morning." Her tone was… serious. Carol's stomach did an unpleasant roll. Zosia moved closer and didn't bother with small talk. "We need to talk about my dream," she said, firmly.

    Carol's heart dropped out of her ass. Here it was. The moment of truth. She felt herself go cold from the inside out and her brain urgently pulled up the usual menu—deflect, deny, joke, get angry first—but Zosia deserved none of them. None of them would save Carol from what was coming.

    Carol's fingers tightened around the pen so hard it creaked. She forced herself to keep her face neutral, to not flinch like a guilty dog. Zosia didn't sit down.

    "Yeah?" Carol managed, and her fraying voice betrayed her. She braced for hatred. For Zosia to spit out what she deserved, finally look at Carol and see exactly what she had done—used her, then had the nerve to pretend it didn't happen. Carol was ready for a punch, or worse, a disgust so complete there wouldn't even be a raised voice. 

    She couldn't make herself swallow, but she forced her eyes up, because if she was going to be condemned, she was going to take it like she deserved.

    "After the hospital," Zosia said, "they moved me to a different state, and then when I was stable, I got sent to an observatory. The Very Large Array, back here in New Mexico..."

    Carol's mind registered the words as background noise, technically meaningful, but not currently making contact with her brain. She was listening. She wasn't. She went light-headed with relief. Zosia wasn't yelling or looking at her like filth, wasn't saying I remember what you did to me. Not yet. Carol let the reprieve flood through her, guilty as it was, and wanted to hate herself for it—add it to the long list—but her body didn't care about moral bookkeeping. It heard not today, and her shoulders sagged. 

    Zosia was still talking. "They're re-purposing the dishes," Zosia said, moving further into the room. "From receiving to transmitting. They need it to maintain the global signal."

    Carol nodded, trying to focus. This was what Zosia had been doing while Carol was without them: being deployed to the machinery. The next part was where Carol's isolation turned into contact again.

    So it was coming soon. Tonight, probably. 

    She made a decision in the space of a heartbeat. She was going to take today, like a gift and a hit. This last day where Zosia looked at her without hatred, she was going to stop fucking avoiding her like a coward and let herself have it before she lost it forever.

    Zosia's voice pulled her back in. "Manousos was on the right track," Zosia said, tapping an open notebook on the table with a long finger. "The signal isn't random. It's a carrier. And the frequency—"

    Zosia leaned in slightly. Carol's eyes stayed on Zosia's mouth as she spoke, on the contour of the words, trying to focus. Zosia's hair was slightly damp around the edges from showering. The collar of her shirt sat crooked where she must have tugged it on too fast.

    "The band is the same one used for ship-to-shore communication," Zosia said. "I knew it wasn't just…" 

    Carol nodded, taking in maybe a third. Ship-to-shore. Fine. Important. Useful. Zosia deserved better. She was giving them a key, information Carol had nearly killed her for, but Carol couldn't help it. Her attention slid to the way Zosia's shoulders shifted under the collar, the line of her neck when she tilted her head. Carol looked at her ridiculous profile and committed it to memory, because that was all she was going to get. 

    Zosia kept going, "If his notes are right," she said, flipping a page, "then the carrier isn't just a beacon. It also holds the network together..."

    Carol nodded again, eyes fixed on Zosia's hands as they moved over the page. She wanted to reach out and touch them, trace the line of knuckle and tendon. Her own hands ached with it. She didn't, wouldn't, couldn't. 

    Zosia turned to the next page. Carol left her hands where they were and let the lesson wash over her.

    Somewhere between wave propagation and how submarines hide, Zosia mentioned, in passing, her first posting: a frigate in the Baltic. A frigate. Carol didn't even know what a frigate looked like, and Zosia had lived on one, had a rank and a routine and years of cold water before Carol was anything but a name. Carol had missed the details, too busy staring, and Zosia had slipped a whole life through the gap. 

    Carol looked down at her page and her pen had been doing a convincing impression of being busy while her brain did nothing of the sort. She could keep nodding, keep simulating studious attention, or she could just—stop. 

    In the container she'd run dry of material in five minutes. She'd pressed Zosia's hand to her face and said she wanted to know everything, meant it like a deathbed confession, and then Zosia had come back and Carol had spent the days just looking—inventorying a burning house—saving the wrong things. She'd promised herself, in the dark, that if she got another chance she'd ask. Here was the last chance, and it was already slipping by. 

    She closed the notebook and pushed it aside, and it made Zosia pause.

    "I'm not going to pretend I followed that," Carol said.

    Zosia's mouth pulled sideways, more amused at Carol's honesty than put off by it. "Which part?"

    "The submarine thing. Can I ask you something that has nothing to do with antennas?"

    Zosia's eyebrows rose. "Sure."

    "What was your rank? At the end."

    "Commander," Zosia said. "The one below Captain. That's where I was, eventually."

    "How long did eventually take?"

    "Not as long as some," Zosia said it without arrogance. "You put in your time. I was good at it. You say the right things to the right people."

    "Tell me about life at sea." 

    Zosia eased, the lecture posture gone. "What do you want to know?"

    "Anything. What did you do when you weren't working?"

    "Read, mostly. I'd pick things up in port cities."

    Carol asked where. Zosia told her, sketching out a Baltic patrol route with a finger like she was drawing a map. 

    Carol asked about the cold. She knew Zosia liked cold.

    "Around freezing, surface temperature. Colder with wind chill."

    "And what—you swam in that?"

    "Required. Winter fitness assessment, every year."

    Jesus. Carol hooked her feet around the chair legs. "Walk me through it."

    Zosia glanced at her like the request was unusual, then leaned back. "You stand on the platform in your suit and the air is already bad enough. Then you go in, and for the first ten seconds your body doesn't believe it. Everything locks."

    Carol was listening too carefully and felt herself imagining the platform, the gray chop slapping Zosia's shoulders.

    "The first assessment at the academy, everyone blacks out. It's about who lasts longest." She said it like a sport, which, for Zosia, it clearly was. "I wanted to beat everyone, and I was sure I would. I'd been swimming in cold water since I was twelve."

    "Where did you place?"

    "Sixty eight seconds. I lost vision at sixty." She frowned, as if the memory still irritated her. "I was the fourth last to lose consciousness."

    "Out of how many?"

    "Thirty."

    "Fourth is fucking good."

    "Fourth is fourth. The three who lasted longer were all bigger than me." Her mouth thinned. "I would've needed to gain twenty kilos to match their thermal mass." Carol watched her face. Zosia was annoyed, still, decades later, at physics and her own body's mutiny.

    "And you have to do that every year?"

    "You get used to it."

    "You say that about everything."

    Zosia's mouth twitched. "Because it's true about everything. There's a moment where something releases. Your body stops fighting and just works. The cold is still there but you're moving through it instead of against it." She paused. "That part is good."

    "Good?"

    "Everything unnecessary falls away. You're just—present."

    Carol couldn't remember the last time she'd been that. She was usually either behind or ahead of herself, regretting or bracing.

    “Was that your coldest posting?" she asked, and that opened the routes back up, in the Atlantic and the Mediterranean on her next ship, a training vessel. Carol had noticed Zosia's resting position was reticence, but if you got her started on something she cared about she would go for fifteen minutes without breathing. 

    They'd both been through the Strait of Gibraltar. Carol had seen it from a cruise ship, sunburned and hungover against Helen's shoulder—the photo was upstairs. Zosia had navigated it at night. "The current runs east on the surface and west underneath," Zosia said. "So you can feel the hull disagree with itself and you have to hold the line between them." She said it like it was a technical fact. Carol heard it like a sentence she wished she'd written. Hold the line. She'd spent her career trying to grab them.

    Carol ransacked her own travel history for an offering back—and Helen was in every scene. She needed somewhere coastal, somewhere she'd been alone…

    Lisbon. They'd been to Lisbon and Helen had got food poisoning on the second day, vomited into a hotel toilet, waved Carol away—go, I'm disgusting, go see the city. Carol had wandered alone that afternoon, climbed hills, eaten pastéis de nata on a bench overlooking the ocean, and she'd never told Helen the details, because how do you say I loved the day you were sick.

    She gave Zosia that—just her, the hills, the light—and felt relief at the edit. Zosia's face lit up. Had she been to the fish market, any miradouros? Carol had, and she could talk about those without touching the dim hotel room, the wet flannel she'd pressed to Helen's forehead when she got back, how Helen had mumbled you smell like sunshine into the pillow, falling asleep holding Carol's hand.

    She'd stay on safe ground.

    She told herself it was practical—Zosia already knew, there was nothing Carol could add—except that wasn't why she was doing it, and she knew it. The good memories were bad, what she'd had and lost, and if she let herself feel that, she'd crumble in front of a woman she was idiotically still trying to impress. 

    They compared the overlaps. Zosia had navigated three north Atlantic routes by traditional instruments, but got comprehensively lost in the streets of Bruges trying to find a bookstore, spent ten minutes following a duck back to water because it'd seemed certain of something. 

    Carol laughed and started curating, selecting funny stories where Helen wasn't in the frame, and the frame kept shrinking.

    Dubrovnik, their anniversary trip. The organ meat disaster was tellable because Helen was in the restroom and Carol had sent the plates back quickly. She trimmed it, kept the main punchline, but kept back what came after: Helen returning oblivious, parking her appetizer fork on the plate at four o'clock, every time, never aware she did it—because you had to eat across from her for a lifetime for fork-at-four to be what told Carol she'd got away with it.

    She didn't know why she was avoiding that; whether it would be too much to feel too, or if she wanted to keep it only hers, or something else. There was a Helen the hive had every angle of, inside and out, and a Helen only Carol had—when she'd been half-asleep or unaware. Carol was the only mind the second one existed in, and that place felt suddenly thin, like her Helen was in there all alone. Something about holding it back felt like infidelity, which was insane. She'd already done worse on that scale and this was a story about a goddamn meat pastry. 

    Zosia recounted getting trapped behind the counter in a Copenhagen bakery during a protest march, with six dozen cinnamon rolls and a furious owner. Carol laughed again, and it slid the editor's pen out of her hand. She gave one about her mangled attempt to order coffee in Dutch while Helen had been smoking outside, and the slip of saying her name out loud was a smaller grief than she'd braced for. Light kept on the table. Zosia smiled at her. Helen's name went out into the air and didn't take anything with it. They kept talking.

    When she mentioned pizza in Naples, Carol's stomach growled and they both stopped, looked at each other, then at the high sun out of the window.

    "Holy crap," Carol said. "What time is it?" Hours had passed. She hadn't noticed. "We should eat."

    Zosia seemed surprised by the angle of the light too. "That's the longest I've talked in years," she said, almost to herself. Then, as if the accuracy mattered, "to one person." She pressed her lips together as though she'd caught a classified secret on its way out.

    Three knocks on the door came sharp. Manousos.

    "I'll get it," Carol said, standing. Zosia was already up, moving toward the kitchen. 

    Carol let her go and opened the front door. Manousos stood on the porch, his shirt wrinkled, holding a stack of papers that looked ready to slide out of his grip at any moment. She sighed.

    "Come in," she said, in a tone that meant the opposite. "She's got a lot to tell you."

    They stopped in the kitchen doorway. Zosia was at the counter, measuring coffee grounds. "I'll walk you through it, Manousos," Zosia said, without turning around. She moved around the kitchen as if she'd been there for years, not days. She didn't hesitate now.

    Zosia turned to face them while the coffee brewed, leaning back against the counter with her arms crossed. "You were right," she said to Manousos. "The signal is a carrier. And they're converting an array from receiving to transmitting to maintain a global coordination signal. The frequency kept us synchronized."

    Manousos was already taking notes. Zosia poured three mugs, all the while reporting what she remembered of the observatory in a way he could ingest quickly and copy down.

    She described what she could of the location: "Desert, obviously. Remote. Clear line of sight." She paused, eyes distant. “Perfect stargazing. You can see the Milky Way like it's been poured across the sky," she said, then seemed to realize she'd offered poetry, and corrected. "High altitude."

    Carol's stomach rolled. They'd gone stargazing together. In the dreams that Zosia would have, probably tonight, she'd remember. Carol looked down at her coffee, took a sip. She had to stop herself from making a noise at the flavor, despite the faint nausea.

    Manousos was writing frantically as Zosia sat down with them. "How far from here?" he asked.

    "Around two hours. It'll be on maps."

    "Power source? Grid, or independent?"

    Zosia's face shifted. Carol had seen her field his questions without hesitation for the last ten minutes and this was different. A stall, a tightening around the eyes and mouth that looked like irritation aimed inward. "I can't get that anymore," Zosia said.

    "Materials?" Manousos asked instead, pen ready. "What are they built from?"

    Zosia described what she could—crystalline arrays, parabolic dishes—and the technical details slid off Carol's attention. She tried to listen anyway, because it was important and because her brain needed somewhere safe to be. But it wouldn't stick. She kept  slipping to the morning instead. It had been good. She wasn't going to throw it back over her shoulder by spending the afternoon staring uselessly, but underneath that was what she'd been refusing to look at, and her mind had nowhere left to go but in.

    Whatever she was feeling wasn't just leftover from before. It was growing, or it was new, or it was the same thing finally allowed to be honest, and she wasn't going to examine it. She wasn't brave enough to try, not with Zosia three feet away explaining signal propagation with both hands, animated and oblivious. She knew the word. She'd said it once, to the same face, a second before she'd torn her apart. The word and the act had left her mouth in the same breath, and she still didn't know which one had made the other possible. 

    It had still ended with Carol on her knees, and before that, loving Helen had ended with her in the yard with a shovel and every version of a life she'd ever imagined gone forever. Even Carol wasn't stupid enough to line up for more, from a straight woman who was guaranteed to leave, no less. She was two for two and too chickenshit for three.

    "I need maps," Manousos said suddenly, standing. His coffee was half-finished, forgotten. He was already moving toward the door, papers clutched. "When I find the location—"

    "Wait," Carol said. "Don't you want to—"

    But Manousos was already at the door. "I'll be back in few hours. Maybe tomorrow."

    The door opened and clapped shut and he left them in the quiet. They both took a sip of coffee.

    "He gets excited," Zosia said, "When he has a new angle to work."

    "Yeah."

    "You okay?" Zosia asked. "You've been quiet."

    "I'm fine. Just thinking."

    "About the antenna?"

    "Among other things."

    Zosia studied her face for a moment. "We should probably eat," she said finally. "It's been hours." Neither of them moved immediately. 

    The light caught Zosia's hair, and Carol thought about how strange it had been to sit across from someone again and feel hours vanish rather than drag. She'd spent months counting minutes. 

    She took Shrek to the sink, rinsing him, and looked out of the window. The glass was smudged in one corner where Helen used to press her forehead when she watched the weather. Carol should've cleaned it, couldn't bring herself to. 

    She looked at the grave. The light was pulling longer across the yard as the cloud cover moved, and the wind had picked up, pushing the shrubs sideways. The slabs were still, gone bone-pale in the sun, and the bindweed was back, pushing through a crack. Helen would've been out there with gloves and a trowel.

    Behind her, she heard Zosia's footsteps and she stopped beside her. Carol's body leaned a fraction. Zosia followed her line of sight and Carol saw it happen in the reflection: Zosia's eyes narrowing as she understood what she was looking at, and then a small shift in her posture, like she'd stumbled onto sacred ground.

    Zosia spoke first. "Do you…want to talk about it?"

    Carol's reflexive answer was no, but she didn't say it. She didn't know why. Maybe because Zosia's tone made it feel like an option rather than an intrusion. Zosia added, as if offering context instead of pressure, "I remember that day," she said. "Standing out there with you." 

    Carol's stomach turned. She set the mug down on the counter. "Yeah," she said, rough. "I was a real treat." 

    Zosia's gaze stayed on the grave. "You were grieving," she said, as if correcting an inaccuracy. 

    Carol's jaw set. That was one way to put it. She'd been feral. She remembered the day with ugly clarity—how the world had narrowed to one impossible fact: Helen was dead, and the thing wearing Zosia's face had been there to witness it.

    Zosia shifted her mug an inch on the counter, and said, very carefully, "Carol. Can I say something about Helen?"

    Carol's fingers clenched. She didn't look away from the window. "Sure," she said, because the alternative was saying no and having to admit she was scared of whatever came next.

    Zosia's voice stayed gentle and matter-of-fact. "In that first dream," she said, "the one where I was assigned to you, I remembered something else." Carol turned her head slowly to look at her. "It wasn't random," Zosia said. "Me, as your chaperone."

    Carol's skin went cold. Zosia kept going. "We knew Helen was going to die, in the truck, on the way to the hospital." She paused, saying it out loud a cruelty she couldn't avoid. "She was already joined. She loved you best. They consulted her, and agreed."

    Carol stared at Zosia like she'd stopped understanding English. "What."

    "Helen chose me. For you."

    The kitchen went thin around them. Carol could hear the tap drip and the faint tick of the water tank refilling, and none of it felt real. The floorboards had lifted and shown her the roots underneath, every assumption pulled up by the foundations.

    "You're—" You're lying didn't fit Zosia's reluctant face. The hive lied to Zosia felt more plausible, and that was impossible. She knew they'd mined only Helen's memories to select Zosia, she'd made a kind of peace with that, but Zosia wasn't describing mining.

    Zosia's eyes didn't waver. "It was the kindest thing they could do with one decision, and they're all about that. Helen got peace, you got a chance at company, and I got to meet you."

    She was describing consensus—Helen wanted it and the hive agreed because her wanting was already the most efficient kindness. Carol couldn't even be angry. There was no violation to point to. Just Helen, still managing her, one hand on the wheel and the other already gone.

    Carol's eyes stung. "That's…" Her mouth worked around nothing. 

    Zosia waited like she knew Carol needed a second.

    "She knew you would be alone with it," Zosia said. "So she picked someone she knew you'd like."

    Carol's scoff came out ugly. "Because I'm a picky little monster," she said, voice cracking on the end, and she brought her hands up to press against her face then dropped them. "So, she chose you…what, like a dying wish?" and immediately regretted the flippancy.

    Zosia looked like she understood exactly what Carol was doing: trying to make it small so it wouldn't crush her. "Yes," she said simply.

    Carol chewed her lips. Saying it felt comforting felt like betrayal, like she was letting them win by using Helen as leverage.

    Zosia seemed to anticipate the thought. "I'm not telling you this to defend them, or to make you grateful for it. But you deserve to know." She paused. "I didn't bring it up before because—" Zosia's jaw tightened. "We tried to tell you and you were so angry that day. And I understand, completely, but—" She stopped, chose a different route. "I'm not them anymore, I can say it differently."

    Carol took a shaky breath. Her fingers found the smudge on the glass where Helen's forehead had been. She held them there.

    Of course Helen sent her a… Polish Sailor Supermodel Raban, and it sounded ridiculous enough that a proper laugh came, then. For a second Carol could see it so clearly: Helen, one foot out the door, assessing the situation with the same no-nonsense she'd brought to every crisis, deciding to nag Carol one last time. You're going to make Raban a woman, Helen would've said, like it was a household chore. Stop pretending you don't want what you want.

    Carol's laugh cracked. "Of course you did," she breathed. And it had worked. The morning after, she'd written it. The most honest thing she'd put on a page since the first draft thirty years ago. Carol huffed another laugh, half-bitter half-fond. She couldn't argue. Helen was dead and still had the last word, and when Carol looked up, Zosia was watching her, and Helen's last word had been I love you, you stubborn idiot, now do the brave thing. 

    Carol pressed her fingers to her eyes and let another sound come out of her, ugly and grateful.

    She forced herself to look at Zosia again. Helen always saw jealousy as a waste of energy—never once begrudged another woman a glance—and Carol had been jealous of that, too. She would hate seeing Carol with all her dogged devotion and no one to open the door for, no one to guard, circling the backyard like it would bring her back.

    "So she wanted me happy," Carol said, "And I…I tried to hurt you the first day."

    "Carol. I called the day your wife died the greatest day in history. I said that to your face. I felt it." Her voice had been even through all of it—but here it wobbled. "You had every right."
