    Carol had expected judgment and what she got was worse. Zosia's own guilt, evidently heavier than Carol's, and she couldn't pick hers back up now. She wanted to say that wasn't you—but Zosia's face made it clear she wouldn't accept that any more than Carol would've accepted it's okay from her.

    Carol's eyes went back to the grave. The quiet. Her chest ached. She stared at the slabs and her vision blurred and she let it. Helen had never stopped. Even from inside the thing that killed her, even through a woman whose voice had shook with the guilt of being its instrument. She'd always been better at knowing what Carol needed than Carol was.

    Carol pulled air past the tightness in her throat and spoke before she couldn't. "Thank you. For telling me." 

    Zosia nodded, accepting it without making Carol conjure more. She took a breath that sounded like she was bracing herself. "I keep thinking… maybe I've been… pushing. Just by being here. When she can't be here herself. I thought that might be why you've been—" She didn't finish, but her eyes moved briefly to the distance between them. “I want you to know I would never try to take up that space."

    Carol blinked hard. That wasn't what it was, at all. It was nearly funny how much kinder Zosia's interpretation was than the truth.

    She'd spent weeks with Zosia and underneath it they were quietly working on her stem cells, lying by omission about something Carol hadn't consented to and didn't know about. Carol was standing here now doing the same thing; feeling everything she felt for her, all of it genuine, and not telling Zosia what she'd done. She didn't know if that made her feel better or worse. It meant the happiness before hadn't been a lie, it had been real, and she understood now: how easy it was to hold something real and something damaging in the same hands because the feeling was true.

    Carol's distance had had nothing to do with Helen, or her grief. It was her own dirt under her nails, but she couldn't say that while Zosia was looking at her like she was still salvageable.

    "I know," Carol said instead.

    Zosia watched her, still cautious. "Okay," she said, like she was accepting the answer but not convinced by it. "Good."

    Carol pressed her palms flat on the counter and breathed through the heels of her hands. In the silence she could hear her own breath, ragged, and Zosia's, steady. She stared at the grave again, and felt, for the first time, like she could talk about it. Zosia had just carried Helen's name with care, had said she loved you best like it was fact and not consolation, and her mouth opened before the rest of her caught up.

    "I didn't… talk about her with you," she said. "Not with—" Carol's mouth caught on the phrasing. "Not with you before. Sorry if that's a spoiler."

    Zosia didn't protest.

    Carol rubbed her thumb along the chip of her rinsed mug. "I couldn't," she said. 

    Zosia's gaze stayed on Carol's profile. Carol could feel it without looking. She was doing it again. Leaning into the only one who had made the weight liveable. The difference was she couldn't write this Zosia off as a con, call herself a victim. She was just standing there, and Carol was walking right up to the same edge sober.

    She exhaled through her nose. She stared again at the grave until the world blurred at the edges. "And the fucked up part is you helped anyway."

    Carol's mouth opened. You made it easier to exist. The words were right there, fully formed and not coming out of her mouth. She thought of the firework aimed at her face, three outcomes, and not giving a shit which occurred. Dead, fine, or hurt enough that they'd come back without her having to beg. "When I let myself be happy, I could feel some of it—quieting down.”

    She could hear herself talking and couldn't believe it was happening on purpose. Maybe it was the grave doing it, or the fact that Helen had just been invoked and Carol's guard was still on the floor. Her jaw clenched. "I hated that. It felt like if I stopped hurting all the time, it meant Helen mattered less." She swallowed hard. "But I did… need a goddamn break."

    Zosia had filled the space where the bottle went and Carol had called herself a fool for falling for it. Now she'd had nothing for four days, and Zosia hadn't smoothed the edges or numbed the grief. She'd just let Carol feel it, and somehow it was doing more than three weeks of engineered paradise, which meant the fool part had never been about the con. It had just been her. 

    Zosia nodded once, small. "It doesn't mean she mattered less."

    Carol's huff was sharp. "You say that like it's obvious."

    "It is obvious," Zosia replied, dry, "and it's still hard to believe in the moment."

    Carol looked at her. There was no artifice in what she said, or therapeutic face. Only the honesty from burying her own person and surviving. That was the difference—Carol had known, without naming it, that the kindness before would've been real and the understanding wouldn't be, couldn't be, from inside it, and her gut had refused the trade.  

    Carol cleared her throat. "What about your husband?" she asked, needing to change the subject. "Do you…want to talk about him?"

    Zosia looked surprised. "Not much to say," she said. "It was a long time ago."

    "Still."

    Zosia's mouth pulled wryly tight, almost a smile. "Still dead, yes," she agreed. Carol winced and Zosia shrugged at her. "That's the truth. It won't make him less dead." 

    A snort escaped before Carol could catch it. Zosia had a way of saying things that were bleak and somehow not self-pitying. She turned it over. She'd been so sure that feeling anything good was proof she was already forgetting, but Helen had felt more real just now, Carol laughing about her nagging, than any time at the grave or crying in the dark. 

    Zosia watched her, then looked away at the window. When she spoke again, her voice was quieter. "I should tell you something." Carol's stomach did another unpleasant flip. Zosia nodded once. "About who he was. What he was." She paused, then added, as if laying down a card carefully on a table, "I've been… letting you assume things."

    Carol didn't move.

    "He was my best friend," Zosia said, "and he needed a wife on paper, so people wouldn't ask questions, and I didn't mind being useful."

    Carol stared at her. "A beard," she said, before she could stop herself. 

    Zosia gave a small, amused exhale that didn't reach her eyes as they flicked to Carol's face, then a tiny nod. "We made people stop asking. It was easier." Zosia's gaze dropped to her mug. "I told you 'husband' because it's what I say," she said, "but you asked."

    Carol felt a pang of guilt at being trusted, which of course made her want to ruin it immediately by not shutting the fuck up. She went to the obvious: So what does that make you, then? It would be easier if Zosia was straight, it would be safer if Zosia said a word to shut that door again.

    "Okay," Carol said, was all she could manage. She stopped the self-destructive part of herself that wanted to know whether there was any universe in which this wouldn't have been doomed if Zosia hadn't remembered.

    Zosia nodded once, like it was enough. "He died. He was the only person I had. That's still true. I'd made peace that he was...that that was it, for me. The closest thing. That it was enough." Carol watched Zosia's reflection in the window, speaking about it like it was a logistical problem rather than an emotional one. "It made me… flat," Zosia added, after a pause. "As a person. Less alive." She glanced sideways at Carol. "So I understand what you said."

    Carol nodded.

    "Not in the exact way," Zosia said, correcting herself. She was quiet for a moment. Her thumb ran along the mug handle. "It still—he was worth every bit of it."

    Carol looked at the grave. "Yeah." 

    "But—you just keep moving. Do your job. I stopped imagining anything different for myself."

    Carol wanted to comfort and couldn't find anything without sounding fake. "Well," she said, "the end of the world happened, so maybe you were right not to be optimistic."

    The side of Zosia's mouth pulled up again. "Vindication." 

    Carol blew a laugh out and felt the urge to step closer. She didn't. She looked out at the grave again and accepted the fact that she was still here, and being here meant she had to keep doing this—living—whether she felt ready or not. Here they were, trying to be alive with all the pain that came with, in a new fucked up world where everyone else kept trying to convince her otherwise.

    Zosia's fingers moved near the edge of the counter—close to Carol's, close enough that Carol's hand almost shifted toward them on instinct. Zosia didn't seem to notice, which didn't seem like her. Zosia's gaze was still lingering on Carol's face. Carol kept her hands still. The proximity made her skin feel too tight. She still didn't move. After a moment, Zosia drew her hand back and the withdrawal was so subtle it could've been nothing. 

    Carol stood with the knowledge that tomorrow Zosia would remember, and whatever this was would shatter. She knew how it would go. She'd been writing the scene in her head for days, drafting and revising it with the same compulsive attention she gave her worst chapters. Zosia had stopped imagining a different life, and Carol had the opposite habit: she could only live ahead in the worst, instead of being present and feeling whatever happiness she felt she hadn't earned.

    Carol shifted. She wanted to actually be here, in the room, and not as just a last-ditch grab before it got taken away. This was what Zosia had been doing the whole time she'd been free—being in the fact of it, letting it be without trying to survive it in advance. Carol wanted to try.

    Zosia was still a few inches away, present, her face still faintly pink. Carol cleared her throat. "Since we're being brave today. I should remind you. I usually take my coffee with sugar."

    Zosia's eyes narrowed.

    Carol let out another small laugh that scraped its way out, and Zosia watched her with a satisfied look, like she'd set out to get that reaction. Carol turned back to the faucet to run it, because she needed something to do with her hands besides reach for Zosia, and to buy herself a job before she said more stupid shit. 

    Now some air was being cleared, she could feel an apology coming.

    "I—" she started, and then Zosia moved in close enough to reach past her for the knife block. Carol's pulse picked up and she shook water off her hands in the sink as water slid down her wrist, cold. Carol tried again. "About yesterday—"

    Zosia reached and caught the bead of water with her thumb, brisk and automatic, as if any mess no matter how small offended her. One clean swipe, more fussy than intimate, and Carol's whole body locked. Yesterday Zosia had recoiled from a brush. Now her thumb was on the thin skin of Carol's inner wrist where her pulse was being humiliating, and she looked—fine.

    Zosia exhaled slowly through her nose, and kept her hand a little longer than necessary, like she was steadying herself as much as Carol. Then she took it away and picked up the knife as if that had been the only reason she'd reached over. 

    Carol didn't move, didn't speak. She stood very still with the faucet running and every nerve in that strip of wrist singing and no idea what to do with the fact Zosia had touched her. It didn't mean anything. Obviously. She was wiping up a spill. She'd done it everyday she was here. Straight women touched people. She was desperate and stupid and her wrist was still warm.

    "We're making dinner," Zosia said. "You're not allowed to apologize the whole time."

    Carol exhaled, shaky, and let herself nod.

    "This morning." Zosia was already moving, pulling a pan from the rack, setting it on the burner. "When I came downstairs. I thought you were upset—" 

    "I wasn't angry at you, that's what I was going to—"

    "I know." Zosia said quickly, a door closed before Carol could walk through it. "You've been kind, even when you don't have to be." It sounded like a field report finding more than a compliment.

    Carol's chest hurt. She didn't know what to say to that, it was so opposite of the truth. She almost argued and opened her mouth to—

    "Anyway," Zosia said, "Thanks for letting me be weird about all this." She pulled her hair forward over one pinking ear. “The memories. How I've…been." 

    Carol shrugged. "You're handling the dreams better than I would," she said, which was true. 

    Zosia tilted her head and her mouth pulled at a corner. "You'd be terrible at it." 

    "Disastrous," Carol agreed, and was rewarded with a fuller smile, eyes crinkling. God. She was so fucked. 

    Carol turned her head back to the counter and tried to remember what she'd been about to do. Cutting board. Something involving the vegetables they had left, all past their best.

    "Do you cook?" she asked. The question came out before she'd decided to ask it, like most of her questions today.

    Zosia was already sorting through the cupboard. "The conditions were not—" She paused, choosing. "You're at sea. Everything moves. You can't use open flame. Mostly I ate what the cook made and was grateful." She produced a can of tomatoes from the back, examined the label, set it on the counter. "Before then, my father worked two jobs and my mother cooked all day. She believed a woman who couldn't cook was only half a woman."

    "Charming."

    "She was, occasionally."

    "So you've never learned?"

    "On Iskra, in winter when it was late, sometimes the galley was the warmest room." She was quiet for a moment. "Sasha used to find me there. He would eat whatever I made and tell me it was terrible." Zosia had found a box of pasta and was reading the label. "He would've liked you."

    Most people didn't—Carol had evidence going back to the first grade—but the certainty with which Zosia said it had her almost believing anyway.

    Helen liked you too. She picked you. Her eyes watered instantly as she cut the last of the onions, grateful for the excuse. Instead, she thought about Helen's cooking and considered. "So between the two of us we have your occasional and my—" She paused. "Helen was—it was her thing. I stayed out of her way."

    "You don't cook either."

    "I mean, I can. Kind of." Zosia hadn't said it like a question, because she already knew all of this. Carol didn't know why she wanted to narrate it back, as if saying it out loud might make it known to just them instead of all of them. Carol took the can opener from the drawer and handed it to her. "We ordered in most nights, or we went out, or she made something while I wrote. It was a system." She was aware after she'd spoken of how it sounded: the money in it, the married in it. 

    Zosia turned one of the remaining cans over in her hand. "My mother made everything herself," she said. "Bigos. Gołąbki. Everyone in the block cooked the same meals from the same rations. She'd queue before her factory shift and everyone knew each other." Zosia opened the can with the competence that made everything she touched look simple. "Nobody had anything, but it was the same nothing. We never thought of it as struggling. Just living." 

    Zosia said it like she said plainly, without asking for anything back. She handed the can to Carol, who tipped the tomatoes into the pan. Carol thought about her own mother's condensed milk and how poverty in America always came with a sermon attached, some bullshit about bootstraps or blessings, as if being broke required a moral. "And then?" 

    "Then the wall came down and choices came in and we couldn't afford any of them. Half the block lost their jobs. Suddenly time was the only ingredient she had plenty of. Then it was a lot of cabbage, mostly. It stunk up the apartment and took forever." Zosia aligned the empty can with the others on the counter. “After that, her life was in the kitchen. I didn't want that." 

    Carol thought about her wife's cooking and their hefty take-out and dine-out budget and the easy assumption of availability—the only question being how much to tip. She poked the tomatoes and stayed silent because there was nothing to say that wouldn't sound like tourism. 

    The pans were simmering. The kitchen smelled like garlic.

    Zosia didn't seem to mind, she was re-folding the dish towels into exact squares and started humming absently. Carol stood still by the stove and listened. It was strange, though she couldn't have said why it felt that way. Not a melody she recognized. Carol was no virtuoso but it moved in a direction she kept expecting to resolve and didn't, like a sentence stopping before its verb, the meaning suspended.

    Carol let it go for another moment. "What is that?"

    Zosia looked up and registered that she'd been humming. A faint confusion crossed her face. "I don't know," she said, then, easily: "It must be from them." 

    Zosia's hands were still folding, still precise. The woman had been body-snatched, force-fed memories, woken up in the desert—and just filed a psychic parasite's leftover playlist under miscellaneous, and Carol was apparently the only one in the room who thought that was a bigger problem than a wrinkled dish towel. 

    Zosia added, drily, "At least I can hold a note."

    Carol's hands stopped on the pan. "You—what?"

    "We could hear you sing," Zosia said. Her face was composed, reporting a finding, but her eyes had that sparkle they got when she was enjoying herself. "Badly."

    Carol pointed the spatula at her. "I was alone in the apocalypse, not performing at Caesar's Palace." 

    "I know," Zosia said. "That's—" Her mouth clamped shut. She turned to wipe down the counter. "Anyway. You were monitored. Just so you know." She picked up another towel that didn't need folding. 

    Carol nodded, still thinking about Zosia being braver about the present moment than anyone Carol could imagine being. She didn't even seem to know it. Recovering from a heart attack Carol had given her, then put to work immediately, and still forced to listen to Carol's tuneless garbage, unable to do anything about any of it. Carol couldn't do anything about it either, but she could make a plate of pasta. 

    "Sit," Carol said, coming out rougher than she meant. Zosia looked uncertain in a way that was endearing on someone who'd navigated warships. "You've made coffee every morning. Let me do this." 

    Several minutes later Carol plated it and set them down at the table. "It smells good," Zosia said, with slight surprise, which Carol decided to take as a win. She asked more questions through dinner, about Poland, about what she read besides Wycaro. That opened into an hour about books Zosia had opinions on, genuine and occasionally blunt ones, which Carol argued with even when she agreed, to keep her talking. 

    "What did you read as a kid?" Carol asked.

    "Pippi Longstocking," Zosia said. "My uncle brought them on the ferry from Malmö. He worked the crossing for a few years. Every week he'd come back with whatever he could carry in his coat. Another Pippi, a tin of Danish butter, once a pair of jeans three sizes too big for anyone."

    "A smuggler?"

    "A romantic. He thought he was saving us from cultural deprivation."

    Carol thought about Raban running cargo through a blockade. How every pirate story is about someone bringing something someone else needs from a place they can't reach themselves.

    "Why Pippi?"

    "She was literally the strongest girl in the world. She beat every boy. She lived alone and didn't need anyone." Zosia shrugged. "I was a kid."

    Carol could see the through-line so clearly it was almost comic: Pippi lifting a horse, Zosia in ice water at nineteen trying to outlast every man in her unit through sheer will. The same girl, the same refusal to accept a limit she hadn't tested herself. And Carol at twenty two writing a pirate who was stubborn and brave and solitary. They'd made the same person from opposite ends of the world, Zosia from the inside, Carol on the page, both of them too proud to admit what they'd made was a way of surviving.

    Carol looked at her. "Her father was a sea captain, right?"

    "Yes."

    "And then you joined the navy."

    "Those are unrelated."

    "I'm calling bullshit on that one."

    "Mostly unrelated." Zosia's mouth pulled, enjoying being caught. She collected their plates and carried them to the sink. 

    Carol stayed at the table a moment, watching her move through the kitchen with a proficiency that would make Pippi proud, and then stood and went to the counter. 

    In a few hours they'd run out of evening, and Zosia would go upstairs, and the dreams would do what Carol couldn't bring herself to. She pictured the vodka behind the cabinet door where she'd shoved it the day Zosia woke up. She knew exactly how much was left, and she could taste it—the cold bite, the heat that followed. A simple answer to a simple question: do you want to feel this or not. It would numb everything—take tomorrow's dread and tonight's kitchen and make them both the same nothing.

    Behind her, Zosia was humming.

    Carol opened the cabinet above instead and found the instant decaf, filled the kettle. She had to keep choosing it for as long as the water took to boil, every second sober and here. She spooned it into two mugs, too much sugar in hers, and carried them to the sofa. 

    Zosia came to accept hers, took a sip, and her face went through a very small struggle. She took another sip anyway, and set it down without comment.

    "You don't have to drink it," Carol said.

    "You made it," Zosia said, as if that closed the matter, and picked it up again.

    Carol had run out of ways to make her questions sound casual, and kept asking anyway. At some point she noticed it wasn't because she was hoarding facts like a thief, grabbing anything before the alarm came—she wasn't casing the place at all. She was just in it.

    Carol looked at the darkening windows. "What was it like at night?" she asked. "At sea."

    "Depends on the watch. Second watch, midnight to four, was the darkest." Zosia considered. "Sometimes the best. Once we were in the Finnish archipelago, on the training schooner, second year. Sasha came below and just said come with me. I went, because when he said that there was usually something worth seeing or something on fire." She paused, smiling at the memory. "And the whole bay was glowing. Blue-green bioluminescence, everywhere the water moved. He threw a boot in and it exploded into light."

    "A boot?"

    "His boot. He wanted to see what would happen." Zosia's voice went fond. "Then he dared me to put my hand in."

    "Did you do it?"

    "Of course I did." Zosia glanced at Carol like the question was ridiculous. "The water must have been two degrees. My hand went numb in seconds. But when I moved my fingers, each one left a trail of light like a comet." She looked at her own hand as if she could still see it. "I kept reaching further in. The cold stopped registering because the light was—I'd never seen anything respond to me like that. Every part of me that touched the water became visible." She paused. "Sasha had to grab the back of my coat and haul me up. It was stupid, I could've lost my hand. He sat with me and held it between both of his until the feeling came back. Said I had the survival instinct of a moth."

    Carol laughed and it caught on the way out. Zosia said it wryly, quoting, and Carol heard the space around it where a living person should've been. She could imagine them, feel it as a paragraph already: two kids on a dark deck, Zosia's arm submerged in freezing light, so absorbed she'd forgotten the cold, the numb fingers trailing fire; Sasha pulling her out, calling her a moth, Sasha dead at thirty three and Zosia still carrying his exact words, lending him to Carol one sentence at a time. She made it look easy. Or not easy, but possible. 

    Carol felt that strange new impulse of wanting to do the same: hand Helen to Zosia like Zosia was handing her Sasha, say here, she was real, she insulted me lovingly too. But Zosia had most of it in her head anyway. She swallowed a mouthful of terrible decaf and kept her own Helen where she kept her.

    "Sounds like he was right," Carol said instead.

    Zosia shrugged, conceding nothing, still looking at her own hand. The tendons moving under tanned skin. "When something is that beautiful and that close, you reach for it."

    Carol stayed very still and did not apply that sentence to herself. The windows had gone fully dark, the only light was the kitchen behind them, spilling yellow across the tile between the sofa and the hall. The room had contracted to a small bright island and the rest of the house had gone. They were close enough now that Carol could have reached out. Zosia's knee was an inch from hers and Carol could feel the radiance without contact, a strip of heat along her thigh that she was pretending not to track. She did not reach out. She was thinking about it, which was bad enough. 

    "Have you ever been scared?" Carol asked. "At sea."

    Zosia's expression shifted. "There was a waterspout," she said, "Near Crete, summer exercise. You see them from a distance and they look like nothing, a thread hanging from a cloud. Then the pressure dropped so fast the instruments lagged. It was closing on us, enough to heel the ship, and the thread was suddenly thirty meters wide and the sound—everything below the cloud was roaring. Continuous thunder. The wind and water being torn upward."

    "But were you scared?"

    "I was responsible for seventeen souls. I was giving orders."

    "That's not an answer."

    Zosia's jaw tightened, amused at being caught again, bringing out the line of her cheekbone. “There was no evasive maneuver. I was aware that something much larger than me was deciding where to go, and I was irrelevant. But that's the sea." 

    Well, that explained a lot. She'd been practising for the hive her whole career. Carol imagined the waterspout. A thread hanging from a cloud. Zosia said it like nothing and it was better than half the lines she'd fussed over.

    "What?"

    "Nothing." Carol took a sip of decaf to stop herself saying something stupid. "A thread hanging from a cloud."

    "That's what it looked like."

    "That's a line." Zosia frowned, uncertain whether she was being teased. Carol wasn't teasing. "Have you ever tried writing?"

    Zosia's fingers tapped against her mug. "I write in books," she said, partway through thinking something else, like she'd just remembered she should warn Carol.

    "What, marginalia?"

    "Margins, underlines. My books look very used. I lent my copy of Winds to Sasha once. He gave it back and asked if I could get him a clean one. Said he didn't want my opinions in his head while he was reading." Zosia's mouth had curved. “If I disagree, I have to cross near it. If I love it, I underline it."

    Carol smiled, small and crooked. "Man, I wish I could see your copy."

    Zosia tipped her head. "You'd hate it. I've underlined you a lot."

    Zosia hadn't said it like flirtation. It didn't help. Carol's skin went hot from her chest up. Zosia at sea somewhere, alone in a bunk, pulling a line under one of Carol's sentences and meaning it. Zosia's pen on her words. It was an intimacy Carol had not been prepared to picture and now couldn't stop picturing. Zosia had been out there—every strait and swell Carol sweated over, guesswork from a desk in the desert, Zosia had crossed, every underline drawn by a hand that gripped actual rigging.

    Carol gulped. "But have you ever tried writing properly?"

    "Once."

    Carol waited.

    "After he died," Zosia said, "They gave me leave. I thought I might write about him, because I didn't know what else to do."

    "And?"

    "I read it back and it was terrible. I could hear his voice in my head and couldn't make it come out. So I stopped. Went back to work."

    Carol knew that exact failure, the gap between the living person and the dead sentence. She wanted to tell Zosia that was the whole struggle: you spend your life trying to get it right and never do, just get close enough that you hate it slightly less each time. Decades of marriage, and Carol still couldn't get Helen on the page.

    She didn't say any of that. She looked at Zosia's profile in the lamp light, the line where her jaw met her throat, and thought of Raban—her Raban, the one she'd only written thirty years ago and thirty days ago. I've already spent a lifetime trying to get you right too. 

    Zosia shrugged and went back to her mug. "Some people have that. I don't." 

    "That what?"

    "You knew what you needed to say since you were a kid. That's why you write. I knew what I needed to do. I've always been better at doing than saying."

    She'd said that's why you write, as if whether she was any good was beside the point, which it was. Fans said gift and talent and Carol signed books and smiled and never corrected them, because what was she going to say? Actually, I write because I'd die if I didn't, and the purple sand is just how it comes out. It wasn't about a knack she knew she did and didn't have. Zosia said need, like she saw teenage Carol alone under a flashlight with feelings that were too big and putting them down was the only way to survive—as necessary as eating, breathing, as getting out of the town that was killing her.

    Carol noticed the splay of Zosia's fingers around her mug. Her thumb dragged slow circles on the rim. Her other fingers slipped through the handle's opening, then out, then in again. Carol looked away and forced her eyes to stay up. 

    "What did you know you needed to do?" Carol asked.

    "Leave," Zosia said. "I used to sit on the breakwater and watch the ships go out and dream of anywhere else."

    Carol could imagine it so clearly by now it hurt. She'd grown up in a concrete block that smelled of boiled cabbage, and wanted out badly enough to climb her way to a career at sea. Carol looked at her and felt the distance—between this home and that one. Harbor to frigate to grief to hive to here, and the sum of it made Carol feel hollow with the staggering improbability that every thing that had happened to Zosia, good and catastrophic, had pointed here, to her. Remove one and she'd be someone else, so somewhere else.

    "I'm glad you left."

    The blurted words hit the air and Carol wanted to die. It was too naked. She could hear Helen laughing at her: smooth, babe. The heat was climbing her neck and she couldn't look away because that would confirm that she'd meant what it sounded like: I'm glad the whole awful journey brought you to me. Selfish and true.

    "Gdansk," Carol grabbed, "I'm glad you—you got on the ship."

    Zosia looked down at her mug. A faint line appeared between her brows. "Me too," she said, simply. Carol couldn't tell if she hadn't heard the rest, or if she was pretending she hadn't. Both possibilities unbearable.

    "Did it work?" Carol asked, voice lighter, to cover it. "Leaving." It had worked for Carol.

    "No, but it was still worth it. Most dreams are like that. I got very good at departure. Every port, every posting…" Carol stretched for her mug on the table and heard Zosia trail off. She looked up and caught Zosia in the middle of her gaze dropped on Carol's bare shoulder, traveling down her arm to the inside of her wrist, where she'd wiped the water hours ago, where Zosia's thumb had been. The gaze lasted a second past deniable and then Zosia's chin lifted, her face pinking, reaching for the sentence she'd dropped. "It's—it was the staying I never learned," she said, to the middle of the room.

    Carol sat back slowly without the mug she'd been reaching for. She could feel her own skin everywhere it was exposed even as she told herself she'd misread it. Obviously. She was projecting, her pathetic ass dressing evidence up for something it wanted. But. That had happened. Carol had seen it. 

    Zosia's jaw tightened. She set her mug down on the table and it clinked against the wood. "It's getting late," she said.

    The evening snapped down the center. Carol felt it split, suddenly aware again of the countdown she'd actually forgotten about—the hours she'd ambled through behind her and the cliff edge ahead, and her body flooded with panic. It had gone too quickly.

    Zosia would remember and Carol would have sat here all night within arm's reach and done nothing, said nothing, because she was scared, because she was always scared. Neither of them moved.

    She could tell her. Break the rule, pre-empt the dream. This was the last time Carol could say something honest about it and have it received as true. 

    Zosia was close enough that Carol could feel the warmth along her side, the almost-touch of a shoulder, a thigh. Carol's hands were gripping her own knees and she could just—she could put her hand on Zosia's arm, or her knee, something small, something Zosia could brush off, and if she flinched like yesterday Carol would apologize and survive it. She could say: I know you said no spoilers but I need you to know—

    Whatever Carol felt, she knew it wasn't just leftover feeling from something easier. She had no idea what face she'd be looking at in the morning, if Zosia would even be here at all. Carol's blood was loud in her ears. She should say something. She should just say it. 

    She could feel herself running out of seconds, a wave gathering before it broke, and her mouth was dry and her palms were damp and she was going to do it, she was going to reach over and—

    Zosia stood, and the space came back, air that felt punishingly cold, and the wave broke without her on it.

    "Good night," Zosia said. 

    Zosia crossed to the hallway and her hand found the doorframe, tapping, and she looked back at Carol. The look lasted longer than a goodnight needed, and it wasn't dread, like Carol was feeling, exactly. Maybe closer to reluctance, probably for what was waiting upstairs, the next instalment of a life she hadn't chosen to live or re-live, and Zosia didn't know it but the look was goodbye to the last ordinary day before everything changed.

    "Night," Carol managed. Zosia's fingers lifted from the frame. She went. Carol stayed on the sofa and listened to the footsteps on the stairs, and said nothing. Her wrist was still hot from hours ago. Her whole left side was cold from seconds ago. She pressed her palms flat and sat in the silence and the want and had done nothing about either of them.

     

    Chapter 6

    Chapter Notes

    Zosia's body was in the driver's seat, legs too long for the space, the road too empty. Carol's neighborhood slid by in dark shapes. The dawn lit Carol's profile, made her look younger and more exhausted at once. One hand restless, tapping her thumb against the seam of her paint splattered jeans.
