    "Yes, they're planning a build," she said, and kept her words technical. "The VLA coordinates the hivemind here on Earth, but this is expansion. A huge transmission array to push a signal with the RNA sequence encoded off-world." 

    When he handed her the mug she took it, heat against her palms, as a reason to lower her eyes. 

    Manousos nodded. "Yes, they're building it to infect space, Carol told me."

    Zosia felt an involuntary kick in her chest at Carol's name. She saw Manousos notice it, but he didn't comment. She took a sip of coffee as cover. Ethiopian. Not bad.

    "That would be one way to say it. They call it sharing the gift," Zosia said.

    Manousos's eyes sharpened. "Do you?"

    In the back of her mind, she thought of stargazing with Carol and how the plan, then, had sounded like a vow instead of a threat. Carol's shoulder warm beside her. The night sky above them like a cathedral ceiling. Their voice—her voice—echoing and reverent, explaining it as if it were romance: We want no one to be alone ever again. In the dream, Carol had listened intently, face turned up to the constellations, torn between horror and fascination. Zosia had felt the pull of it then—how seductive it was.

    Zosia looked at Manousos. The question was not sentimental. He was checking whether she was compromised. Zosia's temper rose again, pride first. The urge to snap at him was immediate.

    Carol had slept with a version of her who never snapped, who'd done things without storming out of houses or saying a cutting thing she didn't mean or lying awake furious at her own transparency. She had never made Carol manage her feelings on top of Carol's own considerable pile of feelings. She had been patient, and warm, and reliably easy to be around.

    "I've heard it in that voice. It sounds beautiful." She forced the next sentence out like a correction. "But it's not."

    Manousos nodded once, satisfied. "Is this imminent?"

    "They're moving fast," she said. "Continuous work. Their timelines don't look like ours did, they don't sleep or debate."

    Manousos exhaled through his nose. "Where?"

    Zosia moved to the coffee table where he'd already laid out maps like an altar. "They need a place that can take heavy equipment. Remote. They considered a ridge of the Antarctic Plateau, the Atacama desert, the Australian outback, everywhere viable… but they wanted established infrastructure nearby for power." Her finger pointed to the Mojave Desert. "So, here."

    Manousos nodded, almost to himself, and then his eyes came back to her.

    "Why did you come to me," he said, "instead of waiting?"

    Zosia's pulse thudded. She kept her face still and failed to keep her voice perfectly level. "I'm here because I want to be useful."

    Manousos stared at her for a long moment. "That is not an answer."

    "I have new intelligence." She kept eyes on the map. One finger stayed planted on the Mojave. If she looked up, he would see the instability. "You said you wanted to know anything right away."

    "I did." Manousos took a sip of his coffee and sat down. "But this information, while valuable, doesn't change our immediate timeline. Our countdown is still based on the stem cell treatment, how long before they can cure our immunity. This antenna project sounds like a longer-term goal."

    Zosia said nothing.

    "So I'll ask again. Why are you here, Zosia?"

    She met his eyes. His expression didn't change, but his focus narrowed as he looked up at her. The same look you would give a loose bolt on a critical rig. He already knew, or guessed, and he wasn't going to let her hide behind mission logistics. 

    In the hive, there had been no disclosure to manage. Everything she was had been available, her sexuality as unremarkable as her blood type. Now she was back in the narrow corridor of one brain, no one else to turn to, and it was humiliating how vulnerable she felt again. The only person she'd ever come out to was Sasha, and he had high-fived her and that had been the end of the conversation. She couldn't believe she was going to say this to a man she barely knew.

    "I remembered something else," Zosia said, to the table. "Something personal."

    Manousos waited.

    She sat down and set the mug down before it cracked in her grip and clasped her hands together to keep them still. This was insane. Absurd. She didn't talk about this, not to anyone.

    "Carol and I... when I was joined. We—" The words locked.

    "I know."

    "You know?"

    "You told me. Weeks ago." He leaned back, his expression carefully neutral. "I won't say more. No spoilers."

    Zosia felt heat rise up her neck. "She kept it from me—"

    "Yes," Manousos agreed, "because you asked her to. You have every right to be angry, but before you decide Carol is a villain, I ask you to consider the context."

    Zosia's jaw clenched. She didn't think Carol was a villain.

    "They manipulated her," Manousos said. "Isolated her. Gave her exactly what she needed and then used that to keep her compliant. Carol didn't initiate the relationship. Do you really think she had the clarity to recognize what was happening? I don't believe she didn't care about you. I know she did."

    Zosia wanted to argue. It would be easier if it was that black and white, but she knew otherwise. She knew they didn't leave Carol to manipulate her, and either way Carol should've known better, and she had. She'd seen through it—the offer of closeness that loneliness had made irresistible—and surrendered to it anyway.

    Her hands were shaking. She pressed them flat against her thighs. She wanted to say that it made her feel sick and wanted at once, protective and predatory, and she didn't know how to untangle it all. "I don't know how to—" She breathed. "I wanted it to be my choice. I'm angry I didn't get to choose. They took that from me."

    Manousos nodded. "Both of you were wronged. They used you, and they used her loneliness. Your anger is justified, but direct it where it belongs. At them."

    They weren't malicious, which was what Manousos would never accept and she couldn't explain. They didn't know how to be. They had seen Carol's need for connection and simply responded. The imperative to lessen her suffering, finding the path of least resistance through Zosia. She knew there was nowhere to aim, and the anger that should have been simple kept refusing to be.

    "For what it's worth," Manousos said, "It's eating her alive." 

    Zosia pressed her palms harder. She would not cry in front of Manousos. She would not cry at all.  

    "She worked to get you out, because she knew you deserved for it to be your choice," Manousos said. "I watched it cost her. Now that you're back, she's walking on glass. She asks before she breathes. She's trying to do it right."

    Zosia thought about last night. Carol apologizing, over and over. She dropped her hands. "She thinks I hate her," Zosia said, quietly.

    "Do you?"

    "Of course not." It was the easiest words she'd said all morning. She took her mug back for another sip, determined to change the subject. "We need to stop it. The signal. The antenna. All of it."

    Manousos nodded, accepting the pivot with a small smile. "We will."

    Zosia pulled the notebook closer. "Let's get to work." 

    Her handwriting filled the margins—coordinates she half-remembered, construction timelines, array specifications—and somewhere between the third page and the fourth she noticed the anger had already thinned. 

    She'd already forgiven Carol. Of course she had. She'd probably forgiven her somewhere in the middle of Manny's defense. Maybe before that—the second Carol's voice had cracked on I'm sorry last night. 

    The hive had orchestrated this and they could claim the choreography, but they didn't get to have the meaning. She knew they didn't manufacture everything she felt right now. They didn't manufacture what Carol felt either, only the conditions, and Carol had been alone in it without even knowing what she was standing inside.

    Her own harm kept folding in on itself, contaminated by complicity and amnesia and the impossibility of proving what she'd felt. Carol's was visible from the outside. Carol alone for months, grieving, and they had caused the loneliness. They couldn't intend cruelty, but the result had been cruel regardless, and Zosia could be angry about that like she couldn't be about herself. 

    She pressed harder on the pen. She was still furious, she just wasn't furious at Carol anymore, which meant she had to figure out how to talk about last night.

    It was many hours and empanadas later by the time she left Manousos to his reading. Zosia stood outside the front door of Carol's house for a full minute before she made herself go in. It was incredibly stupid. She'd already been living here. She'd slept here. She'd had breakfast here. She'd fucked herself in Carol's bed while Carol watched.

    Heat crept up her collar. She opened the door.

    Carol was at the dining table, exactly where Zosia had left her hours ago, like she'd been frozen there. Her head snapped up. Her laptop was open beside her now, and Carol's fingers went to the lid and clicked it closed when she saw her.

    Zosia stopped in the doorway. "Hey."

    "Hey," Carol said, her voice cracking.

    Zosia couldn't get a good breath of air in. She made herself walk into the dining room, though every instinct told her to turn around and go back to Manousos where things were simpler and no one looked at her like that.

    "I talked to Manousos," Zosia said. She crossed her arms, uncrossed them, didn't know what to do with her hands, put them in her pockets.

    "Yeah?" Carol's voice was careful. This morning Carol had pushed—demanded rules, a lane—and Zosia had walked out, and Zosia could see the lesson she'd taught her: be careful, or I'll leave.

    "He—" What could she say? He made me realize I'd already forgiven you? "He helped with some things."

    Carol just nodded. Waited.

    "I don't hate you," Zosia said, too loud and abrupt.

    Carol's face collapsed for just a second before she got control of it. "Okay."

    Zosia pressed on. "I'm not—I'm still processing. A lot. But I never hated you."

    Carol nodded and swallowed hard. "Okay."

    "There's more, isn't there?"

    "Yeah." Carol's expression shuttered. "Sorry, that's—shit, that's a spoiler. I shouldn't have—"

    "It's okay," Zosia cut her off. "I'd rather know." She moved further into the room, held the back of a chair. "I forgave you. He made me see—" She made herself say it. "It wasn't your fault. They manipulated both of us." Carol's eyes were shining. She pressed her lips together.

    The silence was unbearable. Zosia had faced down maydays at sea, kept her composure through storm drills and firefights, and now she couldn't figure out how to stand in a room with a woman who'd seen her come last night. And lots of other nights to come, apparently. Her skin was too hot.

    Zosia shifted her weight. She'd come here to say this, to clear some air, and now she had she didn't know what to do next. Leaving felt wrong. Staying felt impossible.

    Carol's gaze kept flicking to her face and then away. 

    Zosia had never been in love before. The thought came from nowhere. 

    She'd had sex, obviously—short encounters in port cities, women whose names she sometimes remembered and sometimes didn't. She had come out to only one person in her entire life, and kept it all carefully compartmentalized. Sex was one thing. Whatever this was, was entirely another, and she had no idea what it was or what to do.

    Carol cleared her throat. Zosia's attention came back.

    "Do you want to—" Carol's shoulders lifted. "We could—I don't know. Do something normal. Later, I mean. Not right now. I know you need—but later. Maybe. There's a community garden, behind the helicopter. We could, if you wanted—or just you—could take a walk? Or not. You haven't been outside much, the air might be—I don't know if that's—"

    "A walk sounds good."

    Carol stared. "Yeah?"

    "Yes." Zosia's heart was pounding. "Later. After I—after we've had some time. Manousos reminded me you watched that movie last week. We could do that instead, or something. If you want. He could join us too. If that—if that would make you more comfortable." Zosia's insides twisted. She didn't want Manousos with them. But the thought of sitting on the couch with Carol right there, pretending everything was normal—

    Well, she wanted it. Wanted to sit with Carol again, to see what it felt like without the anger of this morning, without the drama of last night, but that was terrifying. That was too much.

    "That might be good," Zosia heard herself say. She could hear the lie in her own voice. "Having Manousos there."

    "Sure," Carol said. "I'll—I can ask him."

    "He really did help today," Zosia added, and didn't know why she was saying it. "He's... he had a good perspective on things."

    "Zosia," Carol said carefully. "If you don't want to do any of it, you don't have to. You can just... do whatever you need."

    "I don't want to hide in my room," Zosia said. "I've been avoiding you and it's silly."

    "It's not."

    "It is. I'm not angry anymore. At least, not at you," Zosia said, and her hands gripped the chair like a helm in a gale now. "Which should make this easier, but it doesn't, because now I don't know what this is."

    "What what is?" Carol's voice was barely audible.

    Zosia gestured between them. "This. Us. Last night. Any of it."

    Last night. Zosia could still feel it—Carol's gaze had felt on her skin. Carol's voice when she'd begged. Both of them falling apart, separately but together, and how it had felt like the most honest thing she'd ever done. Her face was burning again.

    She'd told Carol it was nothing, walked out rather than finish a sentence. She'd been less honest than the version of herself she resented, and the proof was sitting across the room with wary eyes, tiptoeing around her and still braver than Zosia had been about any of it. 

    Carol pressed her lips together but her mouth was pulling into something that wanted to be a smile. "Join the club." Zosia huffed a laugh but it came out shaky. Carol's mouth curved quickly then it fell away. "I know what it's not, though," she said firmly. "It's not me wishing you were them." 

    Zosia's fingers on the chair relaxed. Her pulse was doing something she hadn't authorized, softening when it should have stayed guarded. The anger that had been holding the distance between them was gone, and the air between them was shifting, molten replacing the hard edge.

    "You asked for me," Zosia said. "At the door." 

    "Yeah." 

    Carol was looking at her with that same expression from last night. The one that had made her feel stripped bare and powerful all at once. 

    She could be brave. She could do this. "I've never—" She took a breath. "I don't know if I liked you when I was them, or if they liked you through me, or if it's happening now because of—because of everything, because I've never—" She still couldn't push it past, couldn't finish the sentence. She couldn't say because I've never felt like this even though I'm forty-fucking-four and I don't know what it is. 

    She didn't know if she could trust any feeling. 

    Carol exhaled like she'd been holding it for hours. "It's—okay. You don't have to know." Then she inhaled like she was steeling herself. "And, uh—no spoilers, whatever, but—" She wasn't looking at Zosia. "You already know sometimes they'd let you talk about… yourself. I don't know if you would've liked me—" Her shoulders hunched— "But I liked you. The real you. Even then." She shrugged badly. "So, there's that." 

    Zosia stared at her. She was hyper-aware the space between them was full of something she hadn't earned and couldn't navigate and every second she stood in it made her feel more exposed than she had kneeling above Carol with nothing on. 

    "I still want Manousos here," Zosia said quietly. "For the movie. If that's okay." The disappointment on Carol's face was unmistakable this time, but she nodded. Zosia looked away. "It's not that I don't—I just need..."

    "It's okay. We'll—we'll watch a movie. All three of us. Very normal."

    Zosia's mouth twitched. "Right."

    She should leave now. Should go back to her room or anywhere that wasn't here, standing in the same room as Carol with the memory of last night burning between them. But she didn't want to.

    She'd been leaving her entire life—bays, berths, the occasional bed—and it had always been easy, the momentum of needing no one carrying her through every exit. She didn't know how to be someone who wanted to stay. She wouldn't move toward the door because she didn't want to, and she had no precedent for this, no muscle memory, no protocol for the feeling.

    She looked at the notebooks on the table, and Carol's laptop reminded her of the zoom calls. The memory from the dream. Carol sitting alone in this house while the rest of the immune gathered, excluding her. Leaving her out because she made them uncomfortable, because it was easier to pretend she didn't exist—and then Zosia had come back with warmth Carol couldn't refuse because she'd been starving for it. 

    Zosia's jaw set. It felt like the first solid ground she'd stood on since four AM. 

    "The antenna to broadcast to space," Zosia said. "They're diverting resources to it. Power, materials. Out of Las Vegas."

    Carol blinked hard at the change of subject. "Uh. Koumba lives there."

    "I know," Zosia said. "I remembered. Your videos. Vegas. The zoom calls." 

    Carol's mouth tightened. She glanced at the closed laptop like it had tattled on her. "Yeah."

    Zosia's eyes narrowed. "They kept you out for no good reason." 

    Carol shrugged. "They were trying to keep the peace."

    "Bullshit. They were being comfortable." Her fingers flexed on the chair back. "There's a difference." 

    Zosia exhaled through her nose. This was a feeling she could name, a sentence she could actually complete. She'd felt this ever since seeing those flashes of memories; Carol being a kid who never got picked, who got humiliated. The thought of Carol sitting alone in this house, excluded and isolated…

    Carol leaned forward. "Hey," she said. "It's okay, really. I'm used to it."

    "You shouldn't be."

    Carol was quiet. "I could call Koumba," she said eventually, and immediately looked uncertain. "He might have seen something, or at least heard things." Zosia watched Carol's face do the internal calculus. "If you guys think it's worth it. I don't know if he'd—I don't know if he'd want to hear from me. And," Carol added, almost as an afterthought, "I don't know what he'd tell them."

    Zosia watched Carol's curved posture, how she wouldn't quite meet Zosia's eyes. She'd internalized the idea that they wouldn't want anything to do with her. She was sitting here second-guessing whether she was allowed to ask for basic human decency and it was making Zosia want to throw every chair back from every table Carol had ever been turned away from.

    "We'll call him," Zosia decided.

    Carol's eyes widened. "Yeah?"

    "Yes." She could hear how it sounded like an order, so she added, "If he doesn't care, that's information too. If he does, we don't give anything that can bounce back to them." Carol nodded, but she still looked wary. Her insecurity was plainly there, and Zosia was tired of watching other people punish Carol for being lonely. "If they didn't want to hear from you," Zosia said, firmly, "that says more about them than you."

    Carol was staring at her like Zosia had just said something incomprehensible. "You're… really mad about the calls."

    Zosia didn't deny it. "I'm angry they left you alone. Everyone. Including me."

    Zosia turned to get the phone from the console before Carol could see her.

    "Wait—" Carol started. "They listen to phone calls, right? They must—"

    "No." Zosia picked up the phone. "Not between immune. They need permission."

    Zosia dialed zero and put it on speaker. They both stared at it on the table.

    "Hi, Carol." The woman's voice was friendly, everything that had happened notwithstanding. "What can—"

    Zosia spoke first. "Get Koumba on the phone." Her voice came out harder than she planned, and she let it.

    A pause. When the voice came back it was the same kindness, recalibrated. "Zosia, we're so glad—"

    "Koumba."

    "Of course."

    There was silence.

    Carol shook her head. "He's not going to—"

    "Hello?" Koumba's voice came through. "Carol?"

    Zosia raised her eyebrows at her. 

    "Uh, hey," Carol managed. "Hi. It's—yeah. It's me."

    "How are you?" Koumba asked warmly. "You never called to check-in." 

    Carol looked at her helplessly. 

    Zosia made a gesture that meant keep going, but before Carol could say anything Koumba continued, "I was thinking of you at Christmas. They told me you were on a romantic getaway with Zosia, you must tell me about it, I am not at all jealous."

    Carol's face crumpled into a wince. Zosia tried not to react. She didn't remember it, not yet.

    "Listen, I need to tell you something," Carol said, forcing the words out, her face red. "About how they might be using you."

    Koumba's timbre shifted. "I'm listening."

    Carol started pacing. Zosia stayed by the table, watching her. "They said they'd have to get our stem cells from our bone marrow, right? But turns out they've got mine from my frozen eggs, from storage, and they're using them to work on a way to convert me, without consent."

    "Ah. This is very troubling to hear. I'm sorry, Carol."

    "Yeah sure, but—its genetic, reproductive material, whatever, and you've been dicking around like you're in a music video. They might be harvesting yours without you knowing."

    A long pause. Then Koumba started laughing.

    "It's not funny," Carol said, defensively.

    "It is a little funny, you call to tell me they might be stealing my sperm."

    "Ugh—" Carol covered her face.

    "Carol," Koumba said, still chuckling. "I appreciate the concern. Really. I am pretty sure they already have enough of my genetic material to clone an army, if they wish, and they'll do what they think they have to. I have always understood this." 

    He'd made his peace with it. Zosia wondered if that was acceptance or delusion.

    "Just—ask them," Carol said, pinching the bridge of her nose.

    "I will," Koumba said. "Thank you, for thinking of me. Is there anything else? Or did you just call to discuss my…creative resources."

    Zosia made a give me the phone gesture. Carol looked at her, surprised, and slid it across the table.

    "Koumba. It's Zosia. I'm not one of them any more."

    "What?" Koumba's tone changed completely. "How? They did not tell me—Carol, how did you do it? That is incredible. You actually reversed it?" Carol seemingly couldn't speak, she just nodded, though he couldn't see her. "How did you—"

    Zosia cut him off sharply. "It's not something we can discuss."

    "Okay, okay. And you are safe? You are really yourself? You're not—"

    "I'm myself," Zosia said firmly.

    "Are they safe? I cannot imagine they—"

    "We're not going to hurt them," Zosia said, choosing her words.

    "You are cutting me off," Koumba said, teasing. "Perhaps I liked the other you better." 

    Zosia's mouth pressed shut. Carol folded her arms and stiffly cut in, "Hey. She's been through a lot. Don't be an asshole."

    "I am just kidding. And you two are…working together?"

    "Yes," Zosia said carefully, not looking at Carol.

    "Ah."

    Carol and Zosia's eyes met across the table then looked away quickly. Carol was still red. "We're—it's not—" Carol started, and Zosia could hear Carol trying to defend herself against an accusation Koumba hadn't even made.

    Zosia cleared her throat. "We need your help with something."

    "Anything," Koumba said immediately. "What do you need?"

    "You're still at the Westgate? Have you noticed anything unusual?" Zosia asked. 

    "Define unusual," Koumba said slowly.

    Carol hovered over the phone like it might float away. She glanced at Zosia questioningly. They would have to dance around the truth together. Zosia nodded slightly. 

    Carol paced once more, then stopped near the table, "We need you to keep an eye on… a construction project."

    "One that requires unusual power draw." 

    "And big deliveries," Carol said. She caught Zosia's eye and Zosia nodded again.

    Koumba made a pleased sound, as if he'd just solved a puzzle. "You're asking about the antenna."

    Carol froze mid-step. "You know about it?"

    "I know they're building it," Koumba said. "I don't care to ask for details."

    Zosia leaned over the phone. "If you were to hypothetically keep an eye on it. Would you be willing to share that information?"

    "Hypothetically," Koumba said, "Are you planning something?"

    "We're asking you to observe," Carol corrected. "And to remember what you observe, in case we need the information later."

    Koumba chuckled. "How long have you been planning this spy routine?"

    "Will you help?" Zosia asked.

    "Of course. I will be your eyes and ears," he said theatrically, "and I will pretend I am clueless. Just call me James Bond, and you are my Judie Dench."

    Zosia's voice turned brisk again. "If anything changes, you call Carol."

    Koumba made a small approving sound. "Yes, ma'am. Will you permit me to tell everyone about you in our Zoom call on Friday?"

    Zosia heard the word everyone and felt the anger rise—like they hadn't purposefully excluded Carol, someone who'd actually done something useful. She glanced at Carol and caught the change before she could cover it, her shoulders drawing in, gaze dropping.

    Zosia wanted to say no. She really wanted to. But if they knew joining could be reversed, it could shake them up. It could bring help. She exhaled once, controlled. "You can," she said, voice tight. "But don't call it 'everyone.' I can't say I'm interested in being discussed in a room Carol wasn't allowed into."

    Carol's head lifted.

    Koumba sighed. "Okay. I take your point. I apologize for hitting a nerve." Then, more pointedly, "For what it's worth, it wasn't my decision."

    Carol stepped in before Zosia could sharpen again. "It's fine. The immune guy from Paraguay is our neighbor now, by the way," Carol added quickly. "He's helping."

    "Ah, the mysterious Manousos," Koumba said. Someone called his name from a distance, melodic and insistent, and his breath shifted away from the receiver. "Listen, I must go." He lowered his voice conspiratorially, "I was in the middle of dinner and I'm about to lose my seat at a table full of extremely forgiving women." He chuckled. "But you should visit me, both of you. I want to hear the whole story. I will ask for a Cirque du Soleil—there are aerial silks. Don't pretend you are not tempted."

    Carol made a face. "Uh, yeah, we'll see."

    "Take care of each other. Okay? Whatever you are doing."

    "Okay," Carol said absently.

    "Call me anytime."

    The line went dead. They stood there in silence, the phone still on speaker between them. Zosia was close enough that she could see Carol's pulse jumping in her throat.

    "That went well," Zosia said finally.

    "He knows," Carol said.

    "That we're planning something? Yes."

    "No," Carol said. "He knows about—" She gestured between them awkwardly—"about us." Carol was staring at the phone like it might start talking again.

    "Carol—"

    "You should tell Manny about the call." Carol still wasn't looking. Her hands had found a piece of paper on the table and started folding it unnecessarily.

    Zosia felt the urge to tell Carol it was okay—but her hands were still folding, and she knew what Carol looked like when compassion would be seen as pity and make it worse. She just needed Zosia to look somewhere else for thirty seconds.

    "Okay," Zosia said instead, to the wall. "I'll ask about the movie too."

    She turned and walked toward the door, then stopped to look back. She caught Carol watching her through the doorway with an expression that looked hopeful and resigned at once.

    Zosia wanted to cross the room, wanted to stay, but turned and left through the front door before she could do something stupid like walk back and—and what? Touching Carol was impossible, explaining why was worse. Kissing her, reaching for her, closing the twelve feet of floor between them or the larger distance she didn't have words for yet—none of it available. 

    Zosia's hands were shaking. She needed a cigarette. Her brain supplied the old protocol as though it didn't know she hadn't smoked in a decade. Maybe it would treat the tightness in her chest, exhale the burn. Anything to give this feeling somewhere to go. She walked toward 1204 and slowed without deciding to.

    The light was coming in at an angle. She'd been with them when they had experienced sunsets. Billions of them, simultaneously, processed and distributed. She could have known, at any given moment, exactly what the light looked like over the South China Sea or the Siberian steppe. She had been able to reach into it at any moment and find the answer to anything.

    It was nothing like this—a yard of gravel going gold and the knowledge that was just there, not accessed, that Carol was inside the house behind her, already trying to find something else to do with her fidgeting hands.

    She could read Carol too easily now, and when that had happened she couldn't say, a threshold crossed without her noticing. She knew her, in ways she hadn't chosen and ways she had. It felt like knowing someone like she knew the sea—never fully, but enough to recognize its tells and respect its moods, enough to see the truth under the surface.

    It gave the feeling she kept trying to make small an alarming specificity. Infatuation was supposed to be vague, half-imagined, but Zosia could feel how detailed this was, how much of Carol it accounted for, and she didn't trust it because she had no idea whether something that skipped the ordinary steps could be—or whether it was just what happened when you poured a person into someone who'd spent her life keeping the door shut: it flooded, and the flooding felt like falling, and she didn't have enough experience to tell the difference. 

    She didn't know if she'd been conscious underneath the hive, her own wanting indistinguishable from theirs because it ran in the same direction—and if that was true then the water hadn't come up fast at all. It'd been waiting. 

    She knocked on 1204's door and tried to breathe.

    Maybe it didn't matter if the feeling was new or old. She was swimming in it regardless.

    Manousos answered on the first knock, which meant he'd heard her coming. He was still holding a pen.

    "Movie, tonight," Zosia said, in Spanish. "Our house. Are you coming?"

    He stepped back from the door to let her in. The living room had acquired three more stacks of paper since she left. "Yes," he said, "What film?"

    "I don't know." She looked around the room. "Can I borrow your phone?"

    His eyes went to her face, trying to read her. "Why?"

    Zosia held out her hand. Manny looked at it for a long moment, then handed over the handset on the side table without a word.

    Zosia dialed zero. Manousos had gone to the window. It picked up on the second ring. 

    "Hola Manousos."

    "It's me," Zosia said.

    "Zosia, may we ask—"

    "No," she said. "I'm not calling to talk. I'm calling to tell you fucking skurwysyny something. Stay away from Carol."

    The command was absurd; it meant nothing they weren't already doing, she was ordering them to do what she hated them for, and Zosia was saying it anyway because the anger needed somewhere to go and she felt better for it. She'd been Carol's unwitting jailer and was now compulsively auditioning as her guard as penance and she couldn't untangle it.

    "No surveillance. Let it all go." A pause on the line, the kind she knew meant consensus-forming, and she talked straight through it. "And bring cigarettes and a lighter to this address. And popcorn." She looked at Manousos. "What movie do you want?"

    He turned. "I—" He looked briefly at the ceiling. "Tootsie?"

    Zosia turned to the phone. "Tootsie," she said. "On DVD. You have thirty minutes. Don't make me call again." She hung up. Manousos had turned his back, but she could see from the set of his jaw that he was smiling. "They'll send it," Zosia said, because she needed something to say.

    "I know," he said. "You and Carol." He kept his eyes on the wall. "You made peace."

    "Kind of." 

    He nodded again, slower, still not looking at her. "Good."

    He went back to reading. She waited in the entryway and caught sight of herself in the hallway mirror. The orange knit she'd pulled on that morning, she'd done it automatically, not wanting to wear anything of Carol's, but it was wrong. Something they had chosen to make Carol comfortable, to look approachable. Zosia had never worn orange in her life.

    She looked down at her hands, that had done what they were told for weeks. Her nails were trimmed short as they'd always been, but her hair—she reached up and touched the ends. They'd added extensions because Raban had longer hair. She'd noticed before and been too tired and pained to do anything about it then. She looked at Manousos. "Do you have pliers?"

    Upstairs, in the bathroom, she took off the orange thing and studied her reflection. The extensions fell glossy and obedient. 

    She braced her elbow against the wall and found the first crimp near her neck. She worked methodically, the tiny metal clasps releasing with each pull of the pliers, until she gathered the last of it into her fist and threw it in the trash. 

    She felt lighter, now her hair skimmed her shoulders, not her back. She combed her fingers through it and changed the part from center to looser. The front fell across her forehead in a way that made her feel faintly rebellious. Good. She picked up the top from the floor, stared at it, and felt her jaw set. 

    The Wilson's master closet was larger than her quarters had been. The wife's side was full of bright colors, patterns, things that looked expensive. Zosia's mind reached for her name reflexively and found nothing, obviously. She only knew Martin's, and pulled from his side.

    She grabbed an empty rucksack from under the rack and packed a bunch of t-shirts that would sit baggy on her shoulders. On a hanger, a mens flannel in slate blue and black caught her eye, faded at the elbows until the pattern barely showed. She'd always liked plaid on other people, never had a life that included it. She decided to pull it on. Then she added to the bag a few of the wife's tank tops, and a leather jacket that smelled good.

    She stood at the mirror and looked back wearing hair and clothes arranged by her own taste, not uniform code, just because she liked it. It looked pretty good. 

    Back downstairs, Manny's eyes tracked her. "Better?" he asked.

    "Better," Zosia said. He nodded and turned back to his textbook.

    Zosia stood with the front door open and watched the street in the fading light. Carol's bedroom light turned on and off. Three minutes later the drone came in over the roofline, deposited a paper bag on the driveway, and left.

    She went out to get it. Cigarettes, lighter, popcorn, DVD case. She turned it over. Dustin Hoffman in a wig. 

    When she came back in, Manny was pulling his jacket off the hook. She handed the popcorn and movie to him and they walked up the street.

    Zosia stopped beside the shipping container to light a cigarette while Manousos went straight inside. She tapped one out, lit it, and stood in the early evening air with the container at her back and the house in front of her, lights on in the front room. Through the window she saw him starting to peel newspaper off the glass in long strips, then opening and shutting the blinds.

    Zosia smoked and let it settle in her chest. She couldn't deny it felt good. She stood with it and tried not to think about the phone calls to them. She'd spoken and they'd done what she asked and that ease was vaguely like what it had felt like, all the time, from inside. She'd spent the last four days telling herself she didn't miss that. 

    She took a long drag. She missed it. Today she'd woken up furious and stayed furious for hours and aimed it at the wrong thing twice and had to cross the street twice to get her head right and still hadn't quite managed it. She had no idea what she felt about Carol, or she had too many ideas, all colliding.

    Inside, none of this would have been allowed. Anger would have dissolved before she'd finished feeling it; confusion smoothed over, answered, redistributed across a billion calmer minds. There had always been somewhere for it to go. 

    She took another drag and accepted that this was the deal. Could she miss the peace without wanting it back?

    If she could feel it again—the communion, the absence of doubt—would she take it? The answer came before the cigarette reached her lips again, blunt as a hatch slamming shut. 

    She would rather see Carol with eyes that were only hers—stand here confused and aching for the rest of her life—than watch her through a window that never opened. 

    She'd rather have the mess. Every fumbled morning, every argument, every humiliating misunderstanding of wanting one difficult woman for reasons she could not yet sort—because those were hers, and the looking was hers, and Carol could see her back.

    She looked at the horizon, and let the feeling exist without trying to steer it, which was more than she'd ever allowed and less than she needed and all that she could do.

    The front door opened. Carol came out in a bomber jacket, hands shoved in the pockets, and stopped on the step when she saw Zosia. Her eyes went to the cigarette, then up to Zosia's face, then back to the cigarette, and she leaned against the doorframe with an expression that wasn't as subtle as she thought it was.

    Zosia looked at the middle distance. Her ears were warm.

    "Didn't know you smoked," Carol said.

    "I don't," Zosia said. She took a drag. "Used to. Navy. Everyone smokes. Something to do."

    "When did you stop?"

    Zosia exhaled slowly, watching the smoke dissipate. "Sasha's funeral. I smoked half a pack on the promenade deck. Then I quit." She paused. "Until today." 

    Carol was quiet for a moment. "I didn't drink as much before. I mean I wasn't falling down drunk, or anything, like you've remembered. A bottle could last a week. And then everything happened."

    Zosia took another drag, mostly to fill the silence. "When did you stop?"

    Carol's mouth twitched ruefully. "When I decided to get you out. Figured I could keep drinking myself stupid or I could try to be here for whatever this was going to be."

    "This," Zosia repeated.

    "The whole fucked up thing." Carol's hand went back in her jacket pocket. "I haven't had a drink since. Five days. Which isn't—I know that's not impressive—"

    "It's more than zero." Zosia frowned at the curb. 

    "Yeah, we'll see if I make it to six," Carol joked.

    Inside, the window blind moved. Zosia clocked it without looking directly: Manousos, spying in a completely unsubtle way. 

    Carol was looking at the side of her face, Zosia could feel it. She looked at the pack in her hand. "I told myself it would make me feel better."

    "Do you?"

    "No." 

    They stood in the silence. The streetlight flickered on, casting everything in amber. She looked at the pack again and thought about Sasha's funeral. Standing at attention in the rain, watching the sea take him. Chain-smoking while her fingers shook. It hadn't helped. Nothing had, except time.

    "I'm going to stop," Zosia said.

    "Right now?"

    Zosia started walking. There was a drain. She crouched over it, pack in hand. Flicked the stub into it.

    Carol called, "You don't have to—" 

    Zosia dropped the pack through the grate then stared at it. Her hands felt empty. She wanted to reach down and fish it back out.

    "Okay," she said instead. "Done."

    Carol was watching her. "Just like that?"

    Zosia walked back up the driveway and shoved her hands in her pockets. "If you can go five days, I can go—however long. And I'll want a smoke, and you'll want a drink."

    "Yep." 

    "But we won't," Zosia said. "Right?"

    Carol didn't answer immediately. "Right." She sighed and looked at the drain grate for a long moment. "I really wanted one yesterday. I just—the decaf helped more."

    Zosia turned to her incredulously. "The instant decaf."

    Carol made a face. "Not the coffee itself, obviously. Jesus." Her neck was going red. "I meant—drinking it with you." Zosia's heart kicked against her ribs. "Uh, that sounds—"

    "No," Zosia interrupted. "It's—yes. It's better. Talking."

    Carol was looking at Zosia, hopeful and wary at once, like she was stepping onto ice. "Yeah?" Her voice climbed half a register. "We'll just—we'll want each other instead, I mean—as support. As—I meant like—"

    "I know what you meant." Zosia finally looked at her. "I want that too. Better than numbing it." 

    Zosia's hands were still in her pockets. She could feel the phantom weight of the cigarette pack, but stronger than the craving, was the feeling of Carol standing next to her in the cooling air, close enough to touch. Zosia returned her eyes to the front yard. Her hands stayed in her pockets. She didn't reach for cigarettes that weren't there. Didn't reach for Carol even though she wanted to.

    The silence was easier than it had been. 

    "Are you okay?" Carol asked, finally.

    Zosia shrugged. "I'm fine," she said, which was partially true. "I'm angry," she said, which was more true. "Maybe I'll be better when I've had popcorn."

    Carol huffed a laugh and looked down at the ground. The porchlight threw her shadow long across the driveway. She tucked her chin further into the collar of the jacket.

    "Manny picked Tootsie," Zosia said. "Is it good?"

    "Dustin in drag kissing Jessica Lange?" Carol said. "You tell me."

    Zosia fought a smile.

    The couch could usually have seated three adults comfortably, and there were three of them, yet somehow through a combination of Manousos lowering himself in the middle and Carol and Zosia independently gravitating to respective ends, it had become a problem. 

    "Why is this sofa so goddamn small?" The DVD menu was looping its ten-second jingle for the fourth time. "Someone press play," Carol grumbled to the room at large.

    The jingle started again. Manousos pressed play.

    "It's going to fucking loop again," Carol said, and it did.

    Manousos stabbed play. 

    The film mercifully opened. Manousos immediately sat forward, perched on the sofa, elbows on knees, popcorn bowl balanced between his palms, wholly absorbed. 

    Zosia watched the film. She was watching the film. Carol had pulled her socked feet up onto the cushion, arms around her knees, over the jacket she'd taken off to drape over her legs. Zosia took a handful of popcorn, arranged herself more casually, and told herself to watch the film.

    Dustin Hoffman put on a dress. Manousos made a short sound of appreciation. "He did his own makeup," he said. "For weeks to practice."

    "Great," Carol said. 

    "Also he was—" Manny made a so-so gesture—"not easy on set. But the result."

    "Hm." Carol pulled the jacket up to her chin. "How long is this?"

    "One hundred and sixteen minutes," Manny said, without looking.

    Carol let out a groan and dropped her head back to the sofa. Zosia felt the sound travel through the couch frame and her body like an earthquake.

    She uncrossed her legs, dropped both feet flat, sat straight, and had reset to the posture she'd started in. She watched the screen. She watched the screen and registered nothing. Her mind was running a secondary track, mapping the topography of the couch in granular detail: the sag of the middle cushion, the exact distance between her left thigh and Carol's right knee, the temperature differential between her Carol-facing side and her armrest-facing side. A thermal survey of the sofa.

    Her eyes felt like they'd been filled with sand. She reached for more popcorn and sensed Carol's hand already in the bowl.

    They both withdrew. Manousos didn't notice. On screen, Dustin was having a complicated conversation. "This part," Manousos said, with satisfaction, as though he had made the film himself.

    Carol tucked her hand back into her lap and Zosia somehow knew the exact moment Carol glanced at her without needing to see it. The back of her neck was warm and she blamed the lamp and her inch shorter hair. Her pulse was erratic.

    Carol shifted her legs behind Manny's back and her socked foot bumped Zosia's knee and then moved away again. "Sorry," Carol said, to the television.

    "It's fine," Zosia said, to the television. Her leg stayed hot. She didn't move her knee, didn't look down at it either. She was trying very hard not to think about kneeling above Carol, the distance she'd had to hold between them, Carol begging please and Zosia saying no, and still wanting so much to—

    Manny laughed. A single bark of delight. They both looked at him in shock. He didn't acknowledge it and reached into the bowl. "Why are you so quiet?" he said, still watching the film.

    "We're watching," Carol said, in a tone that dared him to push it. She looked at the popcorn. "Why is the bowl so small?"

    "You are not watching," Manny said. "You are—" He made a gesture with his free hand that seemed to indicate the general atmosphere— "something else."

    Neither of them said anything.

    Carol's foot slipped off the cushion and her heel found the floor. She tucked it back. 

    Carol's cotton-socked foot against her denim-covered knee had been fine. Her bare hand grabbing in panic and then the—the other thing through the polyester blanket had mercifully passed safely. Maybe gloves would work. She caught herself wondering whether a touch through the jacket on her knee might slip past whatever cruel mechanism governed this, and her ears burned at the squalor of the thought. She had a sample size of two in her internal ledger like a deprived adolescent and was already cataloguing textile conductivity to supernatural memory recall. 

    It would have been less embarrassing if it was just lust. That at least had the decency to be crude. This was worse; wanting to lean, to rest her head briefly against Carol's shoulder or to take hold of her hand for one stupid second and keep hold of it. Humiliating. And she had agreed to this torture, had in fact orchestrated it, conscripted Manousos specifically because she didn't trust herself to sit alone with Carol in a dark room for two hours.

    Was this it, then? Until they saved the world, broke whatever biochemical farce had reduced her existence to this, was this how she would live? Three people doing anything useful on the planet and she was brainstorming fabric barriers.

    By an hour in, Zosia had arranged herself against the armrest, committed to the fiction of relaxation, because her shoulder ached and the position was better, and if it pointed her toward Carol that was incidental. Carol had migrated slightly toward the middle of the couch. She was probably cold. The house ran cool in the evenings and she wasn't wearing—

    Zosia's eyes drilled through the television. She was trying very hard not to think of how Carol had looked under her, that idiotic Garfield shirt rucked up and Carol's hand moving—and she had—and they had—

    "He is very committed," Manny said. "You see how he moves? He studied for months."

    "You said," Carol said, and readjusted the jacket, which had slid off her knees. "Why is it always freezing in here," she said, not a question.

    On screen, Dustin-as-Dorothy fell for Jessica Lange, or Hoffman-as-himself fell for her, or both at once. 

    The movie limped on. Zosia retained none of it, aware of Carol through blurred peripheral vision only, and she was fighting sleep. Zosia was tracking the war in slow drops and sharp corrections, then Carol's eyes too wide on the screen.

    Outside, she could hear the wind, and somewhere down the street, metal clanged loose against metal. The drone on the streetlight. The world remained broken beyond the windows. Somewhere far beyond the dark houses and empty roads, they all still existed. And here she was, stranded on a couch, with secrets she was keeping from Carol, secrets she was keeping about Carol, and each hour of nothing added another layer between what she felt and what she showed.

    Inside the room, the television painted their faces in shifting light. On screen, Dorothy was laughing at Jessica's joke, and the laugh was Dustin's, and Jessica didn't know the difference.

    Her eyes were heavy. She blinked and the room came back into focus and Dustin was in a different dress now. She had missed something. She wasn't entirely sure how long she'd been—she hadn't been asleep, she had been resting her eyes.

    Carol made a sound, small and barely there, and Zosia chanced a glance over.

    Carol's head had dropped forward again and caught itself, and now she was sitting with rigid posture, one hand gripping her tilted neck. Her eyelids were drooping.

    On screen, Dustin was confessing, the gap between the performance and the person underneath collapsing. 

    Carol's other hand slipped off the jacket and fell on the cushion between them loosely, palm half-open. Zosia barely saw it in her peripheral vision and her lungs locked. Carol surrendering one outpost at a time to sleep...probably...Her hand seven inches from Zosia's thigh. She imagined reaching over. Lacing their fingers together in the dark while Manny watched the film and Zosia would feel—

    Everything. She'd feel everything. Every sense from the hive's stolen inventory, tens of memories pouring in; Zosia would know things she'd never been told, see rooms she'd never been invited into. The violation of it closed her fist and she couldn't hold Carol's hand even if she'd been brave enough to.

    Zosia had told her the hive's memories were gone, and it had been true, and then a touch had made it a lie, and the silence had swung shut behind her before she'd even felt it close. She wouldn't sit Carol down and say I've seen your worst moments and watch her learn she'd been read without permission once again. Carol's face on the first day, red and shaking at the thought of it, was evidence enough of what that would do. 

    After a while the hand curled and drifted back to her lap. Zosia exhaled through her nose, silently, and felt her chest release and tighten simultaneously—a hull flexing in a cross-sea, yielding in one direction, bracing in another.

    "The ending," Manousos declared, with deep satisfaction, when it eventually came. "Every time."

    No one answered. He turned. Carol was fully asleep, head tipped against the armrest, hand curled beneath her chin, mouth slightly open. Her breathing had the deep evenness of total capitulation, the fight abandoned.

    Zosia looked at him. She was not asleep. She'd been awake for every minute of Dustin's disguise and Carol's slow dissolution and the popcorn she'd eventually stopped reaching for because the bowl required crossing the border of Carol's gravitational pull and she was already too close to the event horizon.

    "Good movie," he said. 

    Zosia nodded.

    "He got the girl," Manousos said. "After everything." 

    "I missed most of the middle, I think." 

    "That's okay. The ending is good." He nodded, picked up the popcorn bowl, and carried it to the kitchen. 

    Zosia heard the tap run and the clink against the counter. He came back to retrieve his jacket and paused at the edge of the room. "Goodnight," he said, to both, or possibly to the room. He let himself out, and the latch clicked, and the house contracted around the two of them. 

    Carol was asleep inches away from her. The screen had gone blue and lit the room in a wash that made everything look submerged.

    Zosia looked at Carol openly for the first time all day and the relief of it was immediate. She stayed there longer than she should have. On each exhale Carol made a sound, almost a snore but not quite, a low soft catch at the back of her breathing. Then her mouth moved, "Ridiculous…" Carol murmured with conviction, to no one, and went under again.

    Zosia's mouth pulled sideways before she could stop it. Unconscious and she still had complaints to lodge. Zosia smiled fully. Carol couldn't see her. Nobody could, and her face could do whatever it wanted finally.

    The shadows under Carol's eyes were violet, mouth slack, hand curled beneath her chin. Carol had not slept well either, Zosia knew why, but there was more to her exhaustion than that: the things Zosia had said and hadn't meant and the things she'd meant and hadn't said.

    The crease between Carol's brows had finally let go. It had been there all day, through the fight and the forgiveness and the careful distance on the couch, and now it was gone. Carol had worn herself out trying to be fine today, and she'd done it for her, and Zosia should have told her she didn't have to. Should have told her a lot of things. 

    A strand of hair had fallen across Carol's lips, lifting with each exhale. Zosia's hand moved toward it reflexively and stopped. She could have tucked the hair behind Carol's ear, cupped her jaw like she had in the dream, smoothed the jacket collar twisted against Carol's neck. Small things anyone would do for someone they—for someone asleep on a couch.

    Zosia had been robbed of months of time and every choice, every unshared first, the whole unremembered history of knowing her, and none of it stung like this did. A strand of hair she couldn't tuck. She could want and be wanted, be free and still be sealed inside herself.

    Her eyes burned and she let them.

    She watched Carol in the TV light, and the loss pressed against the fact of her being right here, not through glass and not close enough, and Zosia had to hold both at once. She'd made the trade already, on the driveway with a cigarette burning down. Her own two hands, useless. Her own heart, uncharted. 

    So she held still, looked at Carol, and let looking be enough. 

    One tear spilled down her cheek and she was too tired to wipe it and too alone to need to. The room was blue and quiet and the glow made Carol look cold. 

    She looked at the blanket folded over the back of the couch, got up carefully, retrieved it, shook it open, and draped it over Carol with care she'd perfected on a thousand night watches.

    Carol woke up anyway, in a single blink. Zosia pressed the heel of her hand to her cheek before Carol's eyes found her face, and she had nowhere to go. She stood where she was.

    Carol's eyes went to the blanket, the blank television, then up to Zosia and stayed there, wide, for just a moment. She brought both hands up and rubbed her eyes. "Was it good?" 

    "The ending especially, he told us."

    Carol huffed a laugh into her palms. 

    Zosia stood there, aware of one of the feelings she'd been carrying all evening that she hadn't looked at directly: knowing that when she closed her eyes tonight the dreams would keep coming and she had a good guess about some of it.

    Carol was sitting with the blanket around her shoulders looking at the middle distance and seemed to arrive at the same subject from a different direction. She looked at Zosia, and her face was trying not to show that she was worried and not doing a good job. 

    "I'm fine," Zosia said. It was approximately true. She was hollowed out and her shoulder ached and she couldn't touch Carol and the hive had spoiled any part where she got to know her slowly and she was—fine. She would be fine. 

    Carol pressed her lips together. Nodded at the blanket, or the floor, or some middle point between them. She unfolded herself from the couch, slow and stiff, and stood. 

    Neither of them moved for a moment that went slightly longer than normal. Then Carol said, "Sleep well," in a voice that indicated she was aware of how stupid that sounded given everything.

    "You too," Zosia said, equally stupid.

    Carol left. The room still smelled of popcorn. She could feel the faint heat where Carol had been sitting, radiating off the cushion like an afterimage, and she pressed her palm flat against it briefly.

    She turned the TV off and went upstairs in the dark. She tapped twice on her doorframe and lay down on the spare bed and looked at the ceiling and felt the ordeal of the day come to rest on her.

    She'd hid her face and lied once and gone silent more times than she could count, and every time it was the same blankness, no precedent—she didn't know when this started, if it was all hers, had never felt it before and couldn't compare it to anything that would let her be certain or even feel less vulnerable.

    Whatever was coming in the dream was coming regardless. She couldn't prepare for an unknown memory, and she'd never been afraid of knowing things. The question was only whether she'd recognize an answer. Zosia could feel her pulse slow now, patient, as if her body had finally forgiven her brain for the day it had put them both through.

    Carol was also lying awake, she was certain of it, through twenty feet of plaster and timber she couldn't know but she knew it anyway, and Zosia had never been in love before and was beginning to understand that this was not going to get easier.

    Chapter 7

    Chapter Notes

    a relatively short one this week bc touching grass happened. we'll call it [linka voice] dream work.

    She came to herself in a warm bed.

    Warm and soft and the moonlight coming through the window was wrong—too still for a ship's cabin. Zosia's eyes opened slowly and the ceiling above her had beams, not metalwork. A house. Carol's house.

    One arm slung over Zosia's waist, a leg wedged between hers from behind, her breath coming in slow tides against the nape of Zosia's neck. Carol made a small sound in her sleep and shifted. Her hand fumbled, found Zosia's thigh under the sheet, held for a second then relaxed.

    This happened. 

    She blinked and the room changed by a degree, like the camera in her mind deciding a different angle.She was on her front, the space at her back cold where Carol had been. A beam of golden light behind her. Zosia turned her head. The other side of the bed was empty, sheets pushed back. The faint clack of keys.

    Zosia sat up, the sheet sliding down her hips, her skin cooling where the air touched it. Carol was at her desk through the window, deep in concentration, luminous by the screen's light. She didn't notice Zosia. The dream offered a chorus of affectionate feelings, and one fact stayed clear: Carol was writing again.

    Carol paused, frowned at the screen, deleted a line, typed again, laughed once like she couldn't believe herself, and kept going. The lid of the laptop came down—

    and Zosia wasn't looking into the office anymore. She was in it, as present-day Carol's palm flattened the laptop lid on the desk four days ago. Zosia's mind tried to separate them. She stood in both times at once and neither one would yield. Zosia blinked and she was back in the bed and the screen was still open. The dream was… doing something weird.

    Zosia got out of bed without thinking, put on Carol's cardigan, and moved quietly. The dream had that familiar undertow: her feet moved with purpose before her mind had finished choosing.

    She stepped inside Carol's office. The air was warm and smelled of paper.

    Somewhere at the edge of her hearing, the hive made an appreciative sound. This is where it was made, a thought came, and Zosia knew it belonged to them all, because she'd once had the same thought too. The hive stared through Zosia's eyes with endless curiosity.

    "Morning," she said, because the hive had counseled restraint against fanaticism and she was grateful for it, vibrating as she was. She could feel their fascinations pressing forward, eager for anything they didn't know. "How long have you been up?"

    Carol's mouth twitched. "Uh, long enough," she said, neatening a pile of papers, shoulders still bare in her tank top, eyes too bright for this early. Carol held out the stack, nervous and proud at once—an expression they knew she rarely wore. "Do you want to read chapter one?"

    Zosia suddenly had the sense of millions of minds snapping to attention like a flock turning in midair. She took the printed pages, still warm at the edges, and stared at them, caught off guard. New words, new canon, and she would be the first to read it. A human-made thing they hadn't already catalogued. The hive leaned in, a greedy pressure at the back of her skull. We'd be honored to.

    Carol spoke too fast. "I'm uh, gonna go downstairs, so you can read it without me staring at you."

    Zosia glanced up. "Go," she said, amused. "I'll come down when I'm done."

    Carol backed out of the doorway like she was retreating from a cliff edge. "Okay," she said, and then, quickly, "Tell me what you like."

    Carol disappeared down the hall before she could respond. Zosia stood there with the chapter and began to read, too excited to sit down. 

    It opened cold. No slow reveal. Just Raban, on the page, and she was a woman.

    Millions of Wycaro readers reacted in a storm of feeling, like a wave running through a crowd, and everyone else was interested purely because it was something new. They remembered surprise, and understood it: the prediction error signal, the dopamine response to the gap. They had almost no experience of it. A thought arising in Sydney could arrive in São Paulo before it had finished forming.

    Zosia felt her breath stall. She did it, Zosia thought—hers, it must have been, not theirs, except the hive echoed it immediately, adoringly.

    She read carefully, and they read with her, through her, and somewhere inside or outside that attention, Zosia also felt something: annoyance. She didn't want to share this with a million invisible onlookers. The feeling was fleeting and she didn't know if that was her own distraction or their dissolution.

    Zosia could see Carol's mind behind the words: defensive and bold, as if the world had corrected itself and anyone who complained was behind. There were rough edges—a transition that skipped a beat, a passage where Carol tried for a device and didn't quite land it on the way through—and the hive sailed past, but Zosia noticed. Carol had rushed the opening. The first pages had the breathlessness of running downhill.

    Then the prose changed on the third page. The lush vocabulary fell away. Carol had stopped writing ornamentally for an audience from muscle memory and started writing for herself. Lucasia touched Raban's face and called her beautiful, and the prose around it was so simple it was almost clumsy.

    The description of Raban stopped her. One eye darker than the other—nearly black, the iris fixed wide from an old wound—and Carol had written it as beautiful. Had given Raban her eyes. Zosia sat down in Carol's chair. They processed it all with curious appreciation. Zosia processed it with her hands warm on the pages and her face would surely be hot if they'd let it be and a feeling in her chest she didn't want to share, if she'd had it then.

    Mid-chapter was a love scene. The description wasn't identical to the last dream, but it didn't need to be. Carol had written them, and the scene was good. The scene was actually good. The books tended to spend themselves on the action sequences and go light through the intimacy. Here it was the set piece. Carol had been unafraid where she usually fled.

    Zosia read on. Carol got the sails wrong again—she always had the rigging wrong—and Zosia felt her mouth pull sideways and they didn't need to correct the feeling. 

    She got to the end, then sat still in Carol's chair. She felt a bloom of pride so sharp it startled her. 

    Before she could wonder the origin, she thought for the first time that maybe the time of it didn't even matter. Maybe the only truth was there on paper, black on white: Carol had written something she wouldn't have before, and Zosia was part of the reason.

    She gathered the pages into a neat stack and stood, cardigan hanging off her shoulders, and felt herself hold the chapter to her chest for a moment longer than necessary.

    On the stairs, Carol pretended she hadn't been waiting, foot bouncing. 

    Zosia made a short sound that was half joy and half disbelief, and then they were talking over each other and she felt herself cycle through canonical possibilities with the speed of the hive's processing power and also from having spent night after night in a narrow bunk turning this world over in her hands. The Font of Truth—no. No, it wouldn't work, the Font required to ask for help and Raban's pride would never allow that. Carol was watching her think.

    "The Shapeshifters of Gollinbray," Zosia heard herself say.

    Carol tilted her head. "I was thinking of the Caverns—"

    "The Caverns of Aevalor! But weren't those lost to time?" 

    "Well sure, but what is time to someone like Raban?" Carol moved closer, smiling now, conspiratorial, and Zosia felt a thrill that was unmistakably hers at a line that reframed a character she'd loved. Of course. They existed outside time, outside the rules of the world, and Raban had always been drawn to a beyond—every book had her standing at some liminal edge, even the plank, refusing to cross or be crossed. This was the threshold Raban had been circling for four novels without knowing it.

    "They just have to get their hands on Captain Virgil's—"

    "Temporal compass!" Zosia said reverently enough to make Carol smile. The compass in Winds had been a minor plot device, and Zosia had always suspected it would return to be significant later. She'd been right. She'd been right for years, arguing with no one, in a language she could read but barely speak yet.

    The delight was everywhere at once, the hive's and surely her own, because here was Carol Sturka on a staircase talking about her own lore with the enthusiasm of someone who'd been waiting for the right audience. 

    Zosia watched from inside the dream, and from after, and what she felt was tangled beyond sorting—theirs and hers, the communal awe and her pride, a reader who'd believed in this story longer than she'd believed almost anything, who'd borrowed Raban's hope to find her own. All of them wanting the same thing: for Carol to know this mattered, to know she was seen.

    "So," Carol said, and the bravado thinned. "You like it so far?"

    "Carol..."

    The hive surged forward, warm and ready—they had so much to say, all of it admiring and generous, and they were gathering the words. Her mouth said the simple thing instead. Low and precise, like she was stating a fact.

    "I love it."

    Carol looked away, as if her own reaction would be embarrassing. "Coffee," she said, briskly, and stood up from the stair.

    The dream softened and blurred. Heat seeped into her palms. Zosia took a sip. Good, not great. 

    Carol looked at her over the rim and her eyes were on Zosia's lips. Zosia felt a pulse of want and they offered no relief from it. 

    "It's amazing." 

    Zosia felt the pride bloom through again, "Yeah?"  

    Wait—wait—this happened four days ago, not then. The dream was doing something strange again.

    The kitchen light went too bright. The edge of the counter was digging into Zosia's hip. Carol's gaze was hopeful and wary and hungry, all at once. "Fuck you, again," Carol said, but she was smiling. 

    "Later?" Zosia said, and watched her stutter, Carol's pulse jumping under her thumb. 

    The dream was about to shift, she could sense it now. Time was folding. It wasn't chronological.

    Then instead, Zosia's hand was on her wrist, but she was driving in a car at night, the touch a question. Carol turned her palm to answer.

    No—Zosia's hand was on her wrist in the kitchen, wicking up a drop of cold water, Carol startling still.

    The same touch, different. The dream didn't care. It shifted again. Zosia pinning her against bookshelves. The library that wasn't a library. Time was folding. No—not a library. Carol was against the bedroom door.

    Carol pushed her down onto the bed and Zosia went, let herself be moved, and Carol was kissing her neck, pulling her hair, then working her way down. Carol's hand slid between her legs and Zosia was already wet, had been wet since Carol kissed her, since she'd read the chapter, since she'd woken up in Carol's bed.

    "What do you want?" Carol said against her mouth. 

    At the same moment, Zosia heard her own voice, "Tell me what you want," from last night, kneeling on Carol's bed in the dark, furious and hot. The phrases overlapped, indistinguishable, a loop, echoing between their mouths mid-breath. Time kept collapsing and re-forming.

    The dream reached the part that was less narration and more sensation again. Zosia under Carol, Carol's hands pulling off her clothes, spreading her palms flat against Zosia's bare stomach. Carol's hair falls across both their faces. Zosia breathes the word—inside—and Carol's fingers push in, and the slick drag of it wrenches a sound from both of them. Carol whimpers something against her throat, knuckles flush, already curling, and Zosia is so full of her she can't think in sentences. 

    Then—Zosia above Carol last night, Carol watching her with desperate eyes. The ache of not touching and the power of being watched. The frustration of her own hand when she wanted Carol's.

    "More." (Which me? When?) "Please." (Which Carol? Where?)

    "Tell me what you like," Carol says, breathless. At the edge of it, words surface, like lungs breaking through water:

    I—

    The pronoun stays. "I like when you curse." 

    This must be me. A real preference, blunt and ridiculous, working loose, as the heat of sensation softens the hive's grip, warmth unknotting a muscle.

    The words keep coming, each thrust of Carol's fingers pulling another sentence up from wherever they've been buried, embarrassing and unmistakably hers. Zosia clings to Carol and the pleasure rolls through her in waves that collapse time; the same bed as last night—her own fingers, Carol watching her.

    "I like how you look at me." This is me. This is me.

    Each I hammers loose and then words blur into moaning, into the clench and pulse of her whole body bearing down—and everything whites out. For one bright obliterating instant she is nothing but body. No one else inside her except Carol. 

    Then her pulse was coming down, and in the aftermath her hand found Carol's neck, her frantic heartbeat under Zosia's fingertips, and she tried to fight the dream's next jump. 

    The darkness of the bedroom turned to bright light, sun coming in too hard, and the edges of things shimmered as the world rendered: bright pavement, blue sky, a faint exhaust smell in the air. SPROUTS, the green sign said, but the word kept sliding around, half dissolving. Fluorescent lights, a polished floor that reflected their feet in pieces. 

    The store had been prepared, the parking lot swept for their arrival, the muzak overhead Carol had asked for once in a hospital elevator. All staged for an audience of one who no longer noticed. 

    Carol pushed the cart with one hand. The other rested on the side of the handle, fingers tapping an impatient rhythm. Zosia watched her own hand move toward a mound of oranges and then stall, suspended above the fruit. Minimize waste, they thought. Choose those with soft spots. Zosia looked for tiny bruises, the matte one at the bottom would turn in five days, not seven.

    "Don't tell me you can't even pick fruit from the produce aisle," Carol said, and her voice made it a joke even as her jaw tightened. Carol's hands darted in and grabbed oranges with decisive force, like she was rescuing them from an argument she didn't want to have.

    Zosia laughed agreeably. In the dream she listened for any line, any fissure, and heard only one sound. 

    Mangoes were stacked in a neat pyramid on Carol's side of the cart, green-yellow skins waxy under the lights. Carol picked one up and turned it over, "Are you going to make mangoes weird too?"

    A thought slipped through—Mango is my favorite—and she knew, she knew that was then, now. They answered before Zosia could have.

    Fun fact: mango skin contains urushiol-like compounds, people allergic to poison ivy react to mango peel.

    Carol snorted. "What the—well, that's kind of useful. I'll give you that."

    Zosia watched Carol's face in the fluorescent light: eyebrows lifted, mouth half open, reluctant amusement. They were pleased. Carol's face when she learned something was one of the few expressions that looked exactly the same whether she was guarded or open.

    Carol blew a laugh. "You and your facts."

    Zosia felt their satisfaction at the tone. Carol shook her head as she dropped the mango into the cart and they moved on, aisle after aisle stitched together in sensory jumps: the cold air plume from a cooler, the clang of cans thrown into the cart. Then Carol was mid-sentence, her hand on a packet of crackers, and Zosia had lost the beginning. The floor felt briefly like it was moving, a gentle roll beneath her feet, and then it was there again.

    They were further into the store, the cart fuller. They passed a box of dinner candles and Carol slowed, her hand hovering over them, and she made her voice casual. "Power might go out," she said too quickly. "Better to have backup." 

    They knew Carol knew they controlled every light in every building in every city on the planet. The power would not go out unless they wanted it to, and they didn't want it to, because Carol didn't want it to. 

    They knew she knew this was an excuse, because she wanted them for the dinner table. She wanted the soft light and the excuse to look at Zosia as if she'd arranged the atmosphere herself, as if all the days weren't already arranged around her.

    Carol dropped the candles into the cart without meeting her eyes and Zosia wanted... she didn't know if it was what she wanted. She wanted Carol to allow herself to want things. She wanted Carol not to be alone. She wanted Carol to look back at her.

    Carol stopped at a display of berries, "Okay," she said, turning toward Zosia, "Tell me something only you would know."

    Only you. Carol's tone was casual, and Zosia felt a jolt of wanting, wanting to answer. They searched, instant and infinite. 

    Only we would know: the global raspberry windfall yield is disproportionately affected by—

    Carol squinted. "No, not 'we.' Not a Wikipedia answer. Something only you would know. Lowercase you."

    They recalibrated. Only you now interpreted as: knowledge possessed by this individual. The surfacing she was waiting for, the loosening, didn't come. 

    Only Zosia would know: there's a smell of diesel exhaust in the entry air this morning. It's from a delivery truck that left eleven—

    Carol exhaled sharply through her nose. "Jesus Christ." She looked away, then looked back, quieter. "I mean about you. About Zosia." 

    They paused again, and Zosia felt them search not outward this time, but in, and there was an answer. Zosia's preferred resting heart rate is—No. Still wrong. They searched again, deeper, and Zosia waited for the surge she'd felt before, when she'd come through in a rush with a preference, her mind to the surface with the "I", but nothing happened. They hit on something that was small and true and cost nothing strategically to release.

    "I don't like being surprised from behind," her mouth said. Zosia waited for a tug of memory, someone behind her at a railing, a sudden hand on her shoulder. Nothing. They'd offered the fact without the feeling.

    Carol's expression softened with immediate relief, as if that one fact had given her a whole person. "Oh. Yeah. Okay. Makes sense," she said, nodding at nothing. She gripped the cart with both hands. 

    Zosia couldn't find the ground again. Then it was there, and it was different, and the direction she'd come from no longer existed.

    They were on a hike. She knew that much and little else with any discipline for a second. Zosia felt a stab of annoyance that the dreams were not being minutes dutifully replayed in real-time. They seemed to only catch when something tore or gleamed long enough.

    A narrow trail cut through scrub and rock, dry grass whispering at the edges. A long slope fell away on one side to a far-off blue that must've been the sky, not the ocean. Their steps made the same rhythm for a while, then not, then did again. 

    Carol was beside her, then a little ahead of her, then beside her again, as if the dream couldn't decide whether it wanted to watch her profile or her back.

    "What is your accent, anyway?"

    Zosia turned to look at her. Carol was studying the horizon.

    The answer rose at once. "Polish," Zosia heard herself say. 

    "Yeah, I got that far, Einstein." Carol took a sip from her bottle. "I mean where from."

    Gdańsk came the thought, the fact, and for a moment she hesitated. Knowing and owning weren't together now.

    "Gdańsk," Zosia said. "On the coast." 

    Carol glanced at her then, quick and curious, like she had been rewarded for persistence. "The coast. Huh." 

    Zosia had the sense that Carol was fitting the fact into some little cabinet in her mind marked things that might explain her, as if the sea might account for a posture or a way of looking at distance.

    They loved that about her, they thought. Approaching this like a crab on a beach, circling sideways toward the thing she wanted. Zosia felt herself smile, or a smile trying to begin, at Carol fishing for scraps of a person she couldn't quite reach.

    They kept walking. 

    "So how do I say something in Polish?" Carol asked, too casual to be casual. "Something, I dunno, practical."

    The breeze moved Carol's hair across her forehead. A phrase presented itself that was simple and harmless. "You can say: Gdzie jest łazienka?" 

    That felt more like hers. As if Polish ran through older channels in her, ones the hive had filled but not built. The syllables traced some outline of the person she'd been before becoming easy to enter, easy to share.

    "Are you kidding?"

    "It means, 'Where is the bathroom?'"

    "That can't possibly be the easy version."

    Zosia repeated it slowly. 

    Carol listened with furious concentration, lips parting slightly as she tried to assemble the sounds. "Gjeh—"

    "Not quite."

    "Zuh—"

    "Nope."

    Carol narrowed her eyes. "You're enjoying this."
