    "A little," Zosia said and the words came out smiling. She couldn't place it. She only knew that when she spoke Polish again, correcting Carol around the sounds, it felt closer to being alone with her, like hearing her own footsteps underneath the marching of a crowd.

    Carol tried her best and the full phrase emerged wearing her accent like an ugly borrowed hat.

    Zosia laughed, or maybe they lifted the laugh through her, or both things happened so close together the distinction no longer mattered. In the dream the sound startled her with its brightness. Was that hers? It was different from their pleased echo at Carol being ridiculous. 

    She was still trying to parse it when Carol looked at her with unmistakable satisfaction, and immediately did it again on purpose.

    "Glersh yest wah-zonk-a?" Carol asked.

    Zosia laughed harder. That one felt even less sortable. Carol grinned then, so pleased with herself it bordered on idiotic. 

    Such a dork, Zosia thought, unsure exactly whose fondness she was feeling. Her cheeks ached from smiling.  "Hopeless," Zosia told her. 

    Carol shrugged and took another sip, looking smug now. She took Zosia's hand and kept her eyes on the trail as she did it, the path turning under their feet, the sun on Carol's neck, walking beside her in some bright place beyond the house, terrible at Polish, pocketing pieces of Zosia and pretending not to be.

    The dream lurched again, and the light became a different light, and time was folding rapidly.

    Carol reading to her on a beach somewhere—Thailand? This must be that getaway, a thought that could only have been hers, now. The sensation of sand under her back, sun on her skin, Carol's voice soft. But also: Carol's voice yesterday, stammering softly, offering to take a walk outside. Then: that library again. Zosia pulling Winds of Wycaro from the shelf, pleased, "Look who's here." But also: Carol closing the laptop on her desk four days ago. The new chapter inside, already written, already a gift Zosia hadn't remembered receiving. Then: Zosia's hair against Carol's shoulder, the bed again, sheets tangled. Zosia falling asleep in the dream, thinking about the chapter on the kitchen island with stunned reverence.

    The dream stacked that and more, layered, collapsing, until the feeling she couldn't name remained even when chronology didn't. Zosia couldn't tell whether it belonged to the woman falling asleep, or the woman waking up. Time was folding and it didn't matter, the dream seemed to answer, and she woke.

    Zosia turned her head and saw the line of the guest room door in the pre-dawn darkness. It didn't matter. That didn't feel like a revelation.

    She sat up. Her mouth was dry. The rest of her was not. 

    Then, with humiliating clarity: Of course. Of course this was how she found out she had existed. There were surely less embarrassing proofs of personhood than orgasm. Descartes had his cogito, Zosia had apparently required a more thorough demonstration. Her inner-self had never once missed an opportunity to be mortifying. 

    She pressed the heels of her hands into her eyes and almost laughed, but underneath the absurdity of the delivery was the thing itself: she had been there. The glass had not been opaque, and had enough of a crack in it for Zosia at some points to break through. That was the revelation she'd been looking for.

    She'd suspected already. The feelings had been too immediate to be wholly new. Something in her had known Carol before the dream supplied context and now she knew why. The feeling had been there first, waiting for her to catch up—less like falling twice than waking up already halfway down.

    The hive didn't have preferences, they loved the totality of Carol and ranked every thing about her as indifferently as the next, never choosing one part over another, keeping private proclivities. What had risen in the dream hadn't been collective, it had been unmistakably hers, and was still hers. Continuous.

    She hadn't been some sealed-off prisoner without language or will. Some of the thoughts in the earlier dreams that had struck her as too private, now seemed less mysterious. She'd been underneath the whole time since the first day, she thought, with wonder.

    She tried to imagine telling Carol any of this and nearly laughed again. Carol would hear one sentence and make a suffering out of it before Zosia even got to the second. I was there all along would become I should've known, I'm a piece of shit. No, Zosia thought, she would need to be careful. 

    She could already feel the next dream waiting, like weather beyond the horizon. Her pulse felt bright in her fingertips. She was up too early for anything useful, but this wasn't the sort of revelation that improved with ruminating in circles.

    Zosia pulled on the cardigan—from the pile of laundry Carol had left on the third day—that she knew now she'd borrowed and never returned, and walked to use the bathroom. Cold water on her face. Her reflection looked tired and faintly stunned.

    On her way back, the door to Carol's office stood open. She paused. The hallway was dim, but in the office a desk lamp was on, casting a warm circle. Carol wasn't there, the chair was pushed back at an angle, and the laptop was closed. 

    Zosia should've kept walking, she knew she was tired enough to get back to more dreaming, to more answers. She could close her eyes and unpeel another hour of a Carol she could actually touch, a dream that would be dense and sweet and slightly rotten—a fruit she wanted anyway. All it would cost was the admission that she was looking forward to it. 

    She stepped inside instead. 

    The room was the same. Days ago she had stood here for the first time, awed, a fan granted access to the workshop; then in the dream, they'd stared through her eyes with cataloguing fascination, and Zosia had felt the awe again, shared across millions of curious minds. Now here alone, it was all hers once more, and she felt a possessiveness that embarrassed her.

    On the book tower on the windowsill was a framed photo of a crowd at a book signing. Carol younger, with Helen at her side. She looked closer. Carol was smiling warily. Helen had known what Carol needed before Carol did. Zosia felt a rush of gratitude for Helen, for loving her first, for her steady insistence that Carol deserved to be seen and loved at all.

    And for choosing me, Zosia thought, and felt the vertigo of it. 

    A world away, a Polish naval officer in a bunk that smelled of petrol had been reading herself into a pirate and dreaming of a life less metaphorically landlocked. Carol had been here, building that world without knowing who was living in it. They'd existed on opposite ends of the same thread and Helen, in her final act of love, had looked across that distance and pulled it taut. One decision, and Zosia's life had pivoted.

    She wanted to laugh, or cry, or both. If someone had told her that one day she'd be standing in Carol Sturka's office wearing Carol Sturka's cardigan, she would've requested they be evaluated for heatstroke. She wanted to tell the young version of herself in that bunk: it gets stranger than you think, and better, and worse, and you won't believe any of it.

    That girl had read the published version, felt the tug of something she couldn't name, built a private world out of Carol's imagined one. Zosia had loved that part of Carol since she was twenty-five, and that feeling, too, had been continuous all along. 

    She had read the lie and recognized the truth under it anyway, and the years before felt less like ignorance and more like patience. Carol had written Raban as a woman again. Zosia had read it in that chair weeks ago, and it didn't read like a correction. It read like the story had been holding its breath and could finally breathe freely—the true thing surfacing that had been waiting to be seen. 

    The loop was closed and Zosia was inside it: Raban had inspired her and now she'd inspired Raban, and the circularity of it made her dizzy. 

    The pride she'd felt reading it was tangled up with the hive's reverence for new art, but Zosia remembered the bloom of it in her chest, how sharp and startling it had been, and wondered again.

    It was mine, she decided firmly, because it was still here. She could feel it now, standing in the lamplight, alone with Carol's work all around her. 

    She let her gaze travel the room—the brass telescope, the foreign editions, a painting above the side table she hadn't paused at the first time: a barque trying to out-sail a storm. Outside the windows, the glass was black and gave nothing back except her own reflection, half-transparent.

    She turned to look closer at the map on the desk. Zosia touched the corner of it, lightly, and remembered Carol's voice from that first evening—how her guard had dropped so completely.

    "That's a newer draft." 

    Zosia straightened so fast her shoulder twinged. Carol stood in the doorway holding a mug, damp hair pushed behind one ear, wearing a teal sweater. It brought out the blue in her eyes. She looked like she'd been up for a while, and she also looked sheepish. "Sorry, I know—I figured my voice was better than a knock." Her eyes flicked over Zosia's posture, hands clenched at her sides like she'd been caught stealing. Carol smiled a bit. "You're up early." 

    "The door was open," Zosia said quickly. "I wasn't—"

    "Wasn't what? Snooping?" Carol came in and set the mug on the desk, not remotely concerned. "Why would I give a crap?"

    It was so plainly genuine that Zosia's apology stalled. She'd expected at least a sensible boundary. Carol dropped into the desk chair and pulled one foot up, elbow on her knee. The chair creaked. She looked up at Zosia with an expression that was almost amused at how stiff she was being.

    "And you live here too," Carol added, with a shrug.

    Zosia heard the sentence and the dream she'd just woken from rose to meet it.

    Carol taking her hand in the sun, after asking unsubtle questions aimed at Zosia underneath, thrown like a pebble into a well to listen for the depth. Zosia in bed, opening her eyes to find Carol propped on one elbow, studying her with an expression she rearranged too slowly. Carol deliberating in Sprouts, unwilling to let go of Zosia's hand, so holding two avocados in one palm, demanding Zosia choose a favorite.

    She'd never woken up beside a woman. She'd never held one's hand in public. Not in any port, where she'd have to leave before dawn for morning muster, and definitely not in Gdańsk, where the parish priest knew her family. 

    The dream had handed her a strange new world where none of that applied. She'd been given the experience of something nearly ordinary, and in the face of all her grand plans and ambitions, ordinary was the thing she wanted most. She wanted every boring thing with Carol she'd spent her life assuming she could live without.

    Zosia's mind treacherously offered her an impossible future: years from now, this same lamplight, coming in with coffee in the morning.

    "You can have it." Carol nodded at the mug. "It's the instant though, so don't judge me."

    "Too late," Zosia said, and took it. Her face was hot. It was terrible. She drank it anyway.

    Carol watched her, amused. "You always make that face."

    "Every time, I hope it will be different." Zosia looked at the mug. "Every time, I'm disappointed."

    Carol's mouth pulled sideways. "Bold talk from someone drinking it."

    Last week Zosia had stood in this room for the first time and Carol had paced and complained, and the crush had been so new it still felt like a condition she might recover from. She was not going to recover from this. She knew that now. The room was the same and she was not.

    "You okay?"

    "Fine," Zosia said. "The dream was long." 

    She wasn't fine. Her ribs felt too narrow for whatever was in there. Her pulse was heavy and she could feel it everywhere, in her wrists, throat, the crease of her elbows. Her discipline had dissolved somewhere between the dream and here, and what remained was just herself alone in a room with Carol, too warm.

    She looked at the desk where the Swedish edition still was. Below the blond impostor: CAROL STURKA, and the warmth loosened her lips. "Sturka is Polish," Zosia said fondly, and the alarm came too late. 

    The only reason she knew was from the kitchen sink two days ago, her thumb catching a bead on Carol's bare skin—a genealogist fan explaining the etymology at a book signing. Strugać: to whittle. Carol awkward and pleased, and the memory invading Zosia's skull like a chord struck on every sensing nerve at once.

    Carol reached to put the book back where it belonged. "Yeah, a fan told me once my ancestors were carpenters or something." She snorted. "Ironic, given I can't hang a shelf."

    Carol hadn't even paused, had probably assumed what anyone would: that a Pole recognised a Polish surname. The vowels were right, the suffix was common enough. Zosia could've been guessing, but she hadn't. She'd been stupidly pleased about the coincidence and it had made her stupid again.

    Zosia put the mug down on the desk and breathed through her nose. Her eye caught a sticky note half-hidden under the laptop, Carol's handwriting, small and hurried: R — won't ask for help. 

    "What were you looking at before I came in?" Carol asked.

    "This painting," Zosia said, turning to it again on the wall. "It's before the Battle at the Threshold?"

    "Here's what nobody knows." Carol came to stand beside her. "In my notes, it happened at dawn. The sequence was written around the light changing as the sun came up. Lucasia has this moment where it catches the enemy sails and she can't tell if it's beautiful or terrifying, and that's the emotional hinge."

    "What happened?"

    "Fucking Greg suggested the climax for book three should be a battle at dusk, before he even knew. Said sunset battles were romantic. I caved because the advance had already been spent on the down payment." Carol crossed her arms, chin lifted. "I'm still mad about it. The point was that she couldn't tell if it was beginning or ending. Sunset makes it obvious."

    "Yes, I would've preferred dawn," Zosia said. "It's when watch changes. One ending, one beginning."

    Carol stared at her. Then she exhaled and looked away, shaking her head. "Nobody's ever said that," Carol said, sulky. "Helen thought dusk was fine. Greg thought it was better. You just—" Carol turned to the desk and unnecessarily shuffled paper, not looking at her.

    Outside the window, the sky was still uniformly black. Hours from dawn. The lamp's reflection floated in the glass like a small fire suspended in nothing.

    Carol dropped into the chair, pulled her knee up, and tucked her chin behind it, mouth set in a line that meant she'd retreated behind the barricade. Zosia let her have the moment, turned back to the painting instead.

    The barque stayed on course. Whatever was off-frame was still coming. The storm was well done, that sick yellow-green every sailor dreaded, but there was something missing...

    "The helm's unattended," Zosia said, almost to herself. "In that sea state, with that canvas, you'd need someone on the wheel constantly. She'd round up in seconds without a hand on it." She tapped a finger toward the empty cockpit. "The painter left out the most important thing. She won't hold the heading alone."

    Behind her, the chair creaked. When she glanced back, Carol's chin had lifted onto her knee. Carol nodded towards the model ship on the shelf. "Is there anything to correct on the Mercator?" she asked, her voice warming.

    Zosia moved to it. The model was detailed work—someone who knew their rigging had built it—and the damage on the mainmast was exactly where it would be after the Battle of Nepenthe, when Lucasia had lashed herself to the lines with a shard of the yardarm in her shoulder. "There's nothing wrong. Did you buy this?"

    "Helen got it made for me, for finishing Stormshadow," Carol said softly. "The burn is from when Lucasia sets fire to the powder." 

    Zosia took it carefully. Up close, the damage was everywhere; burns and scratches and chips layered over each other, years of storied battles scored into the wood, and the result was a vessel that looked battered and beautiful and stubbornly afloat. "It's good work." Carol had been doing this for years, alone in this room, building her world one scar at a time, and Helen had given her the vessel to do it in. "She had good taste."

    "She did," Carol said, and for the first time that morning Carol's eyes didn't skitter away from her.

    Zosia set it back on the shelf with both hands. "It's the best thing in the room."

    "Don't tell the clinometer."

    Zosia huffed a laugh.

    "You remembered the chapter," Carol said.

    Zosia's back straightened. "What makes you say that?"

    Carol shrugged. "It was the next thing. And you're… less murderous."

    Zosia was still smiling and hadn't managed to rein it in. She kept her eyes on the model. "Raban. When did you decide?"

    "I'd been thinking how to do it," she said, scratching her head. "Different approaches. And then when—it just felt right." She brought her hand down. "Does it feel right to you?"

    Zosia turned to look at her again. Carol had pulled both feet up onto the chair, arms loose around her knees, expression open in a careful way. Zosia turned back.

    Did it feel right. Zosia thought about the dream, Carol's hand in hers in daylight, about Poland, every woman she'd touched behind closed doors and left before sunrise. She thought about Carol's fictional church that called love a compass and then confiscated it, Carol at sixteen, told what she felt was sin and forced to agree. Herself at twenty, in uniform, learning to make her face a wall. The answer had been yes since before Zosia understood the question. It had always been right and only the world had been wrong.

    "You know it does."

    She sensed Carol holding very still. "Okay," she said, and her voice cracked on the second syllable.

    She'd loved a character who'd been carrying the same secret she was, written by a woman carrying it too, and all three of them had held it for years, and now Carol had finally put it down. The chapter read with a joy and freedom that hadn't existed before. She was writing what she'd always meant to write, for herself again.

    Zosia stayed looking at the painting because her face was going to be humiliating. Her throat was full and hot.

    Carol's hand went to the back of her neck, thumb pressing in like she could work something out of the muscle. "I didn't mean to—Raban's eye—it's just—just a good detail for a pirate, but I can—"

    "Carol."

    "Yeah?"

    "The chapter is amazing."

    Carol's jaw shifted. "It's a start."

    Zosia turned to face her. "It's better than anything in the books and you did it in a few hours." She watched Carol absorb this, but the tightening around her eyes meant she was refusing to let herself have it fully. Zosia decided then to give up her dignity to give her the embarrassing truth. "I'm proud of you."

    Carol looked at the floor. Her knuckles tightened on her own arms. "Thanks," she said quietly, and Zosia wanted to say it again, louder, until Carol believed it wasn't going to be taken back.

    She crossed to the desk and perched on the edge of it, one foot on the floor, close enough that their knees were near. The lamplight circled them both now—the only lit room in the cul-de-sac, in the city, while the desert slept around them in its miles of cold dark.

    After a pause, Carol exhaled and tipped her head back against the chair to look up at Zosia, and the expression had been packed away. 

    "The boom was backwards on the last page," Zosia said before she could catch it. It simply fell out, how it always had, alone in her bunk, explaining to no one. "They'd sail into the dock."

    Carol stared at her, then laughed. "I'll fix it."

    "No, don't." Zosia meant it. "Keep the mistakes. They're part of why I loved them."

    Carol's hand rested on her own arm, close enough to reach. Her hangnails were bitten. Zosia thought she'd noticed before, but maybe she couldn't tell the difference between noticing and remembering.

    Zosia could have covered it with hers, like she had in the dream, felt the warmth for just herself instead of with seven billion others. Every first had been shared and any ahead wouldn't be much different, because even now it would mean seeing things that didn't belong to either of them. 

    The secret sloshed in her gut like saltwater, impossible to keep and impossible to bring up.

    Protecting Carol's dignity over her own need to be honest, she could call it—and it was that, partly, but underneath was a reason less noble. She'd armored selfishness with principle and the fit was too good to be accidental. If Zosia told her the truth—that she had seen parts of her existence from angles Carol herself had never seen—Carol would look at her with horror again, like she had on that very first day.

    "You look tired," Carol said. Then, with no shift in register, "I mean, you're perfect, obviously, but you could get more sleep."

    Zosia felt her face go warm. Carol said it how she might observe that the sky was blue, like it was so settled it didn't even qualify as a compliment. Zosia remembered her saying the same thing the night before, You're perfect, breathless in the dark. Carol, who complained about everything, for whom nothing was ever quite right.

    "You look—" Zosia started, and Carol was already waving a hand.

    "Like shit, I know."

    "I was going to say you look like someone who's been up writing."

    Carol's hand dropped. "How do you know?"

    "The lamp was on." Zosia reached for the mug and took another abominable sip of coffee. "You look good when you've been working. More awake."

    Carol looked away, pulling at the cuff of her sweater. "That's..." she said to the shelf. "That's more the cold shower, probably." Carol's tone was aggressively casual. "Woke me right up."

    Carol, who'd grumbled non-stop through the movie about the chill and liked to run the kitchen tap until it steamed, had voluntarily stood under cold water at five in the morning. Zosia finished the terrible coffee and kept her face neutral, as she looked at Carol's damp hair, ruddy face, her refusal to hold eye contact again.

    Something had shifted in her overnight. The question that had dogged her was answering itself; every dream the knowledge deepened, and every morning the feeling had too, with the inevitability of a tide coming in.

    She had survived absorption into a consciousness that contained the memory of every feeling ever felt and had apparently processed the sum total of human longing simultaneously without breaking stride. She had none of that now. She had her own single stupidity and an all-consuming feeling she still couldn't compare to anything. The moment she tried to force it into a sentence, it sounded small, insignificant—but this feeling was the entire sea, there weren't any other words she knew big enough for it, to hold the swell.

    It was getting too much to be contained in one body. A body with only two hands that could hold two lines—why she couldn't touch her and the feeling she couldn't name yet. Everything else—the careful pretense—she'd have to let slack, because she physically couldn't hold it all anymore.

    "I used the bathroom sink," Zosia said. 

    Carol's eyes narrowed. Zosia met them and watched the calculation happen, Carol deciding whether that sentence meant what Carol thought it meant, and Zosia letting her decide without confirmation or denial. A flush darkened the skin at her throat, and Zosia looked at it and then made herself stop because that was the opposite of cooling down.

    "Right," Carol said. She picked up the mug, seemed to remember it was Zosia's now and empty, and set it back down. "Great. We're both—"

    "Colder," Zosia nodded. Carol made a sound that was mostly air. "What are you working on?"

    Carol shrugged. "Getting thoughts down," she said. "Nothing organized yet."

    Zosia nodded again. She didn't ask further. She was loathe to leave the room but she needed to get back to sleep before the caffeine hit. "I'll make proper coffee later." 

    The dream didn't start with a beginning. Zosia's hands had already cracked eggs against a bowl, shells splitting cleanly, yolks sliding out. The motion practiced and not quite hers. Carol was washing tomatoes.

    "You like omelets, right?"

    Zosia heard herself answer without thinking. We do. The pronoun as automatic as breathing, the consensus came from everyone: we love all breakfast food.

    Carol made a sound and she was smiling. "Sure. But lowercase you." She gestured at her, a little clumsy, trying to be casual about it. "Does Zosia like omelets?"

    The larger chorus thinned around the question, and they could process the distinction now: Carol was asking for something that belonged only to Zosia once.

    Zosia likes… "I like omelets," Zosia said, and heard the 'I' but didn't feel it. "Never had many chances to try them."

    "What is your favorite food?"

    Zosia's whisk paused mid-circle and the eggs remained half-beaten, waiting. The dream hinged around the stillness, she could feel herself surface as a pressure shift, a sensation like coming up from underwater. The hive didn't resist, they let the happy memory come through vivid and hers, and Zosia felt like a wave was lifting her.

    Time folded how it did in these dreams: the countertop under her hands became rougher concrete, pitted and cold; the light shifted from warm to Baltic gray; the smell of butter and coffee dissolved into salt and diesel and the mineral tang of harbor air.

    "Mango ice cream." The delight of it caught her off guard. "I love mango ice cream." She hadn't thought about this in ages, had flattened herself long before the hive ever came, starved out everything that wasn't useful for survival or forward momentum disguised as purpose. Carol had asked for lowercase-Zosia, and here she was surfacing, young with sticky fingers, blinking in the light and thrilled to be remembered. Still alive in there, whole.

    She could taste it. Cold and sweet. Almost too sweet, the synthetic edge of the flavor tasted for the first time by a girl who'd never eaten the real fruit. Her tongue knew it before her mind had finished organizing the image. 

    The shipyard visible from the end of her street, cranes against the sky like enormous metal birds. Cobblestones under her shoes, and she was maybe ten, and the kitchen in the desert was layered over it, both places at once. Carol had stopped cutting oranges.

    "There was an old man in my neighborhood," Zosia said, and the kitchen blurred at the edges. A cart, metal wheels rattling, with a bell. Children turning their heads as one. Sometimes he handed out ice cream bars, when the day was hot and the children were too poor and it was better to be generous than to watch them melt. 

    Carol's eyes were bright and present, the knife forgotten on the board, stepped fully into this moment and staying with her. 

    Zosia's voice went warm, a register the hive couldn't have produced because it required having been one little girl on one street corner squinting at hulls so vast they blocked the sun. Big ships, new paint, and she felt the awe like it was fresh, before the decades had dulled the shine.

    Who built them? Why? Where were they going? The questions came with her child-self's curiosity, leaning forward on the metal railing. The world had just opened. Proof that somewhere else existed and could reach all the way to her street corner. 

    And now I know, Zosia thought, and it hurt in a good way she couldn't explain. She had wanted the world so badly, and she'd got it. The ships, the sunrises, the ports, the politics of everything those cranes were building—she knew all of it now, the beauty and the ugly too, and she wouldn't go back, and still.

    Carol's eyes hadn't left her face, she was looking at Zosia like she'd never seen her before. 

    "Suddenly he had new flavors; mint, coffee, peach." She could see the wrappers in her mind, colorful and foreign. Gdańsk was grey and poor and smelled like grease and coal smoke, and suddenly these ships were going places, there were new things in kiosks, new words she couldn't read. The smallness of her life had become unbearable almost overnight because she could finally imagine beyond it.

    "But…" Zosia looked down, somewhere that wasn't Carol's face, and her mouth curved into a shy smile; her cheeks were warm, she could feel it. "Mango was my favorite." The memory sharpened again around the taste. Tropical in a way that didn't belong to Gdańsk. It was perfect. It tasted like elsewhere.

    Carol's expression had gone past charmed into enchanted, chin lifted, lips parted around a breath she'd forgotten to finish when Zosia said favorite—and looking at her like she recognized something from the inside out. The hive identified the precursor to a deeper attachment forming. Zosia couldn't have named it that clinically. She only knew that Carol's face made her heart beat, that this had come only from her, and Carol was looking at her like it mattered.

    "Thank you for sharing that," Carol said, taking her hand, and there was roughness in it Zosia already knew now, from this distance. The flush deepened—she could feel even in the dream—and Zosia didn't know what to do with being thanked for a memory. Carol's thumb moved once across her knuckles, and for one more second Zosia stayed. Herself. The girl who had watched ships leave and wanted to go with them. 

    Before she could respond, the dream trembled. Manousos, arriving in two hours; timed to release at the moment it would be most useful and the salt air vanished. Carol's voice came from somewhere close and far at once.

    You're going to have a visitor, her mouth said, and her voice was full of everyone again.

    The hive's feelings toward him were simple. Love with an orderly caution, not unlike how they'd felt about Carol not long ago. After breakfast Zosia showed her the drone footage, the ambulance small as an insect from that height before zooming in, sealed away and coming toward them. 

    Carol stood, arms folded, her face gone set, something mean turned inward. The dream Carol had been living inside thinned and showed its seams: her past principles that had been exchanged for an exception.

    The hive and Zosia wanted to comfort her and the feelings rose together, instinctive as hands reaching for a falling glass. It's alright, the feeling said, though no one spoke. You'll both be with us soon anyway. 

    The comfort had been genuine—the warmth was real and the threat lived inside it, a blanket and a net, and from the other side of sleep Zosia could separate the two, but maybe she hadn't then. Their wants and hers had fallen into alignment so often that obedience hardly felt separate from want.

    The dream didn't linger on the leaving. It jumped.

    She was outside and then inside again, at a different threshold, in a borrowed room with Manousos and no Carol. He asked questions. Not the ones Carol asked. Carol worried at a thing until it turned warm. Manousos asked like he was stripping wire. Where exactly. When exactly. Who exactly. His face was doing nothing, and by now she knew that look for what it was: work. Right now in the dream she was only a problem to be solved.

    In the dream she answered him, or half-answered, and at some point her mouth said, in Spanish, that she and Carol were sleeping together. They had no embarrassment. Zosia felt it for herself now, on its behalf; the flatness of the delivery, offered with no particular significance. Outwardly, she remained serene.

    Then Carol was there again, quick and annoyed, guarding Zosia but also something newly exposed in herself, made worse by being witnessed by someone who belonged to the version of her life that would've called this betrayal.

    Carol didn't know what to do with the fact that they loved him the same.

    "You're my—You are..." 

    The confusion in her was almost painful to watch, a hand moving in the dark and finding no wall. "You're my chaperone. Mine."

    No trace of it reached the surface, but mine sang through her, possessive and delicious, a reaction to being seen as individual she could recognize immediately now as embarrassingly her own.

    Carol sounded angry and proprietary in spite of herself. She was baffled by their love that didn't narrow, that could hold Manousos and Carol in the same colossal palm and call neither diminished.

    "That's true," she said, and the thought vanished beneath the next command as every body that belonged to them received the same instruction in the same instant.

    The room stayed level as she lay down and reassured Carol, and the next moment the world knotted. Zosia felt the seizure take the body from the inside, a violent wrongness in the pattern.

    When she woke up, Zosia heard herself say, "I'll be fine," and knew why the singular had come from them: for Carol, as comfort, and as a small reward for the devotion in her face.

    Carol's hand found hers and Zosia felt it stay there, grounding, her thumb brushing. Underneath her smooth surface and the hive's translation of it as reassurance, Zosia knew better, and felt herself go soft. Carol had already done the useful things, and this was what remained when she still wanted to keep hold of her anyway.

    The larger feeling toward Manousos shifted and sharpened. He would hurt them to know them, to reach the mechanism underneath. They started to withdraw from the city, a school of fish changing direction because the water had become poisoned again. They moved in coordinated streams.

    Carol was behind her and then with her. She chose us. Soon, they thought with serene certainty, this choice would stop needing to be made; soon she would be with them how she was meant to be, all the time, no doors left between one moment and the next. 

    She chose me, Zosia thought in the dream, with a stubborn correction. Not exactly, she corrected herself—but my face, my body, my voice that had become for Carol the least frightening and most comforting form of the end of the world. Maybe the thought should have hurt, but in the dream it couldn't and didn't. It felt like purpose.

    Below them, the city unscrolled in grids and sodium lights. Beside her, Carol sat taut with adrenaline and denial and something giddy she would never name if asked. Manousos remained behind. Small now, a fixed point shrinking. Their attention split equally, one cherished and one threat, both loved with the same impossible fullness. Zosia still looked at Carol.

    The dream jumped to a library with all the lights on, Carol took one look at it and said "you guys are such freaks," another form of being moved that she'd never admit to. Zosia smiled at it and felt the collective's warmth around that, the satisfaction of watching her walk through a door they'd kept open.

    The dream hinged and changed around the feeling rather than away from it, and suddenly they were on a plane: sealed hush, recycled air already dry against her lips. Carol came into focus in the aisle, squaring up to the luxury cubicle with skepticism. The feeling that was still there moved around them, broad and warm; the satisfaction of having Carol, who had treated every comfort they offered like a trap, cross an invisible threshold to somewhere cushioned and contained.

    "Well, my knees are fucked, and I'm not doing ten hours folded like a receipt," she said, shoving her bag onto another seat. "If you're going to waste this on me, I may as well commit to the bit."

    Her knees were fine. They had her full medical profile, and this was understood with total patience. Carol prodded a button with one suspicious finger and the seat lurched with expensive obedience. "Jesus."

    Beneath their benevolence, Zosia felt something much less dignified. She'd watched Carol sit in the last row of coach with her jaw tight, refusing any upgrade on principle, and here she was now, spreading the quilted blanket. Carol wrinkled her nose before pulling it up anyway, still muttering, tucking herself in. Zosia kept watching. The indignation, the surrender, the effort to make it look temporary. Disastrously endearing.

    At some point the foiled butter was already soft in her hand and she didn't remember opening it. Carol had stopped glaring at the little lamp and acting as though the tablecloth and metal cutlery ought to apologize to her. After dinner, Carol took the book Zosia had picked for the plane, excerpts from Paradiso, and opened it. She read half a page, lashes low, then looked over the top of it.

    "Read me the first canto, you've got the Euro accent for it," she said, already settling deeper into the seat, as if this was scholarship and not something so transparent it may as well have subtitles.

    They received it as another domestic ritual to keep her happy, but she wanted Zosia's voice. Something that was only hers. It wasn't a useful thought, but the hive allowed through her own smile, as it allowed most things that ran in a helpful direction. There was no friction anywhere in her about making Carol happy.

    Her hands opened the book and her mouth moved through the poetry with tranquil fluency. The reason she was glad to do it was her own.

    The seatbelt sign was off, though Zosia knew when any turbulence was approaching anyway. The dream had shifted again. Carol was making a token effort to remain upright, lost, and listed toward Zosia by increments so cautious it may have passed for accident to the few left in the world who didn't know her. Her shoulder touched Zosia's first. Then her head drifted there, the soft weight of it warm through her shirt, and a minute later, after a patch of turbulence, her hand found Zosia's sleeve and stayed.

    What moved in Zosia did so singularly at first, as she sat very still and let Carol have all the room she wanted, careful with her own breathing. Something about being chosen like this in passing, with Carol holding her by instinct rather than invitation, without a bed or darkness to excuse it, pierced her more completely than anything deliberate.

    Carol, half asleep, mouth askew against Zosia's collarbone, said, "Sorry if I drool on you."

    "We'll risk it," they said.

    Carol made a sleepy sound that might've been a laugh and tucked in closer with the unembarrassed selfishness of the nearly unconscious.

    The thought rose from somewhere more deep and private than their great calm: I'd hold still for ten hours. She could have the blanket, the armrest, my shoulder, my sleep, anything, if it kept her like this. The stubborn line between her brows finally gone.

    Carol's breathing evened. The hive took this as a tender conclusion: Carol was falling asleep somewhere she had once refused to sit, and the ease of it was proof that something fundamental had shifted—progress toward the larger welcome waiting for her.

    Zosia thought: no, that's not what's happening, though no trace of the feeling touched the face they wore. She glanced down at the bent gold of Carol's head pressed into her, asleep with a half-eaten bread roll balanced on her sternum, the blanket she'd denounced pulled up to her chin, and felt the distinction matter in a way they might understand but couldn't feel.

    They loved Carol and wanted her permanent contentment. The complaints and reflexive resistance, the same muscles that had held ground through fifty years of being told she was too much, all to be lovingly removed.

    Zosia, underneath, wanted something more difficult: a future in which Carol kept saying yes to bread rolls and luxurious seats she didn't shrink from, and sleep that came without her needing exhaustion or alcohol. Tomorrow, and after that, Zosia wanted to be present for all of it; to hand over the bread basket, hear every muttering about the butter, and watch Carol allow her own happiness, because she remained, against every pressure the world had ever brought to bear on her, still herself each time she chose.

    At thirty-seven thousand feet, with Carol sleeping through it and the hive mistaking this for a prelude to surrender—Zosia knew she was in love with her. It settled in her like nothing in her life had ever matched, surer than her own name, it had been true in the cabin and was true now, undimmed for all the days between. The dream hadn't invented it, only given it back, all with the knowledge that the future she wanted for Carol was not one the greater mind Zosia was inside of intended to allow.

    Chapter 8

    Carol had been awake since four-thirty, which would have been annoying enough without the reason. By five she'd required emergency decontamination in the shower, after a sex dream so vivid it would've barely felt like fiction if it hadn't been an anatomically improbable and unsanitary scenario involving the dining table. 

    Since then, she'd made coffee, then more coffee, and was now caffeinated and carbonated from the collarbones down, fizzing under the skin. Her hands were shaking and it was seven in the morning.

    Carol opened a cabinet to reach for sugar and the kitchen vodka was right there, pushed to the back but visible. Four fingers left in it, and for one second she considered. Just enough to take the edge off the jitter and her brain replaying I'm proud of you on loop.

    She thought about the deal they'd struck on the driveway last night. She'd stuttered like a fucking idiot and Zosia had understood too quickly, without making a production of it, which was its own problem. 

    The morning light caught the bottle and laid a warm stripe across her wrist. The deal and the praise were Zosia's, but the cabinet was Carol's to close.

    She shut it and got the coffee beans out instead, and felt how light the can was. Great. One more minor emergency to lay over the major one.

    She went to the sink and rinsed out a mug that was already clean. Does it feel right to you, she'd asked earlier, like a coward from behind her knees, about Raban and not the other thing. And then when she was only just recovering from that answer Zosia had said she was proud of her. Proud of you. Just like that. No hook in it.

    Her hands wouldn't stop. She wrung the dishrag until it squeaked, folded it into quarters, unfolded it, folded it again. The six coffees had nowhere to go and neither did she, but by eight she couldn't stand the kitchen. She'd wiped down every surface twice and reorganized the spice rack by height, then by color, then back to height.

    The dumbbells were in the bedroom closet, on top of an ancient Buns of Steel VHS tape of unclear provenance. Pairs of fifteens and tens, dusty and accusatory. 

    She did bicep curls, sitting on the edge of the bed, creaking, counting reps because it gave her mouth a job. 

    Yesterday had been a shitshow.

    She'd pushed too hard, Zosia had bolted, and for hours Carol had been left with that old surety that she had finally ruined the thing by saying the obvious out loud. 

    Then Zosia had come back and said there was something there after all, which should have been a relief, except she'd also made it sound confusing, provisional, maybe tainted by everything that had happened. Enough to keep Carol alive, not enough to let her rest. 

    I don't know what this is, Zosia had said, white-knuckled on the back of the chair. Carol had watched her try to get the sentence out—I've never—and Carol had no clue what the end could be. Never been with a woman?

    She'd asked Zosia to take a walk in the garden with her, stammering it out like she was asking her to prom or something, Jesus Christ, the terror so total she'd offered three separate exits before finishing, for fuck's sake. She'd pulled this sappy shit constantly when Zosia was joined—walks, sunsets, reading poetry, let's eat by candlelight, look at the moon—she could propose anything, all to land in a cushion of collective warmth that couldn't bruise her, when what it had actually been was a padded cell. 

    That trap had snapped but now she couldn't even look at Zosia without remembering what letting go felt like. She'd spluttered through the same moves and couldn't even blame the ease this time because God knows she had none now. Every nerve she had was exposed and she was still being pathetic. Worse, Zosia had said it sounded good.

    Her muscles began to burn and she kept going because it was better than the loop.

    Shoulder press and she thought of Tootsie. Hoffman doing whatever the fuck he was doing on screen while Carol kept circling back, unwillingly, to Zosia on her knees in the dark, Carol begging outright by the end of it, dignity dead in a ditch. Which, fine. Whatever. That horse had already left the barn and cleared the county line.

    What she could not get comfortable with was how Zosia still went strange around touch. Carol had read the flinches as the obvious thing—but then it seemed to have turned into a weird choreography of almost-touching that made her pull up short or go careful. Zosia wanted to, and she couldn't, or wouldn't, and Carol wasn't going to ask or push for clarity again after everything she'd done already.

    She switched arms. Tricep kickbacks, one knee on the mattress, muscles she hadn't used since before everything. Her body remembered the form. Her brain supplied you look good when you've been working, and Carol had fumbled the receive so badly she'd brought up her cold shower. Zosia had looked at her with those dark eyes and let her flounder.Same principle, less commitment. What the fuck.

    As if that weren't enough, how fucking unfair was it that Zosia had chosen now to get hotter, which Carol hadn't thought was possible. Sweat gathered at her hairline and she didn't wipe it. 

    It was only a side parting and a men's shirt, for Christ's sake. She needed to get a fucking grip. These were not immense alterations. Except Zosia had chosen it herself, and wore it with a carelessness that her curated wardrobe had never managed, more at home than someone still deciding whether to stay.

    The caffeine was thinning, finally, metabolizing into lactic acid and lucidity, as she caught herself in the mirror—hair plastered flat to her temple, a vein visible at her throat—and stared herself down for a mean second. She knew what this was. The last time she'd thought this hard about being looked at, she'd been a temp picking fights with Helen in a law firm break room. She put the weights down and sat there with her forearms on her thighs, breathing hard. 

    Carol pressed a finger into the bone under her eye. She was so far past fucked it was embarrassing. On a better Earth she could've had a normal Tuesday to panic about this in peace—as it was, she had all of it stacked on top of a planet to unfuck first, where the odds were not what anyone would call encouraging and Carol didn't know if she'd get a normal Tuesday ever again. So the feeling was just there, overwhelming and unprocessed.

    She'd thought, at various dumb points over the last few days and weeks, that she'd already felt the worst of it. The glimpses of her from scraps, or the relief of being accepted unconditionally by something wearing her face. Turns out that had been the kiddie pool. Beginner shit. 

    This was the fucking deep end. Carol had no idea where she stood.

    The shower ran hot this time and she shaved her legs, which she hadn't done in—since a hotel bathroom. Her second shower before nine. She dressed in one of her nicer pairs of jeans and a light blue button-up and did not examine any of these choices. 

    As she went downstairs the guest bathroom door was closed and the shower was running and she did not picture anything. She went straight to the kitchen. She could have breakfast ready. That was a thing she could do.

    The supplies were bleak. Oatmeal packets. A quarter jar of peanut butter. A sleeve of tortillas she sniffed and declared survivable. A can of peaches. The fruit bowl held a rubber band and a penny. 

    She made the oatmeal in the microwave. Warmed two tortillas in the dry pan and spread peanut butter on them and rolled them tight, and she listened to water run through pipes overhead and did not picture anything. 

    Carol sliced the peaches into a bowl and licked the syrup off her thumb and heard the shower shut off and did not imagine anything at all.

    She mimicked the motions of a functional person, set two mugs out and arranged herself against the counter to hopefully communicate relaxed person drinking a normal amount of coffee and not woman who has been wide awake for five hours in crisis about being told she's good at her job, among other things. 

    When Zosia came around the corner, still in the cardigan Carol had stopped pretending she wanted back, open over a white t-shirt, the sight of her was the same goddamn problem it had always been. But her second thought was that something had changed.

    She couldn't have said what. The first morning free—only days ago, but it felt seismic—Zosia had come down cautious and stiff, hands in her pockets, moving like she was trying to take up less room. Every day since had been a variation on it, as though each required a renegotiation. 

    That was gone. Her shoulders were lower than Carol had seen them all week and her face was... clear. More rested, maybe, but it was more than sleep. 

    Her bright eyes moved to Carol's and stayed. Carol's pulse picked up and she tried to ignore it. "I made the coffee," she said, and gestured at the plates clumsily, "And whatever this is. The pantry's not exactly thriving." 

    Zosia looked at the counter. "You didn't have to do that."

    Carol busied herself with pouring coffee. "Eat. You needed the sleep, so I'll let you off the hook for the coffee, but I'm keeping a tab." 

    Zosia took a sip and her face was about to do the thing.

    "Don't," Carol warned.

    Zosia smiled instead. She set the mug down and wrapped both hands around it, and her eyes came up to Carol's again, and this time it was unmistakable: she'd figured something out and was about to deliver news she'd rehearsed. Carol recognized it from the first morning; her eyes sparkling and saying I have a report.

    "Should I sit down for this?" Carol asked.

    "Maybe."

    Carol folded her arms instead. "Okay. Hit me." 

    "The dreams were long," Zosia said. "Covered a lot. Living here."

    Carol nodded.

    "The day Manousos arrived. My ice cream memory." Carol remembered that morning. She'd felt, for the first time, that the woman in front of her had a past that belonged to her, and it had somehow reached Carol through them. Carol nodded again. "And then up to us leaving, on the plane."

    The geography of their shared history shifted under her. She'd known, logically, that everyone was there. But Zosia had come back blank and Carol had grown used to being the only one in the room who remembered that week. She'd filed every memory as hers alone, and now they had a second witness.

    "I need to tell you something," Zosia said.

    Carol's hand tightened on the mug. "Okay."

    "I've worked it out. I was there." Zosia said it plainly, the same register as proud of you and you know it does. "My own thoughts, my own consciousness."

    Carol uncrossed her arms because she couldn't breathe with them crossed.

    "Not intermittently," Zosia continued. She was watching Carol with an attention that felt almost medical. "Continuously. Sometimes very close to the surface, sometimes further back."

    "When you say there," Carol said, and her voice sounded very far away and controlled. "You mean aware."

    "Aware. Thinking." Zosia paused. "Feeling."

    Carol nodded. She was nodding. She was a person, nodding.

    She'd solved it, the hours of self-recrimination, into something she could live with. Precariously balanced on the cornice of the premise that Zosia wasn't sure either, that there might have been no one home to hurt. 

    "You could hear what I said, at the time."

    "Yes."

    "You could see—" Her mind was racing through a catalog of everything she'd done in front of what she'd believed was, functionally, a global surveillance system with a face that made her stupid.

    Zosia had been in there. A real person. Unable to respond as herself?

    Carol touched her neck. Her fingers were cold. "So when they—when we—" She didn't finish the sentence because finishing it would mean saying it aloud, and if she said it aloud it would be real, and if it was real then she'd fucked someone who was being operated like a puppet while the actual person had been inside, and that was—

    "Carol." Zosia's voice stayed warm. "I need you to hear the rest before you go where you're going."

    "I'm not going anywhere," Carol said, so transparent they both ignored it. "I mean, that's—that is—" Carol put a hand to her pounding temple. "I knew it was complicated, and I tried to ask—and then I kept doing it anyway, and you were—"

    "There was no magic question. You saw fragments. That's not the same as understanding. You spoke to me as if I was there before you had any reason to believe I could hear it. You kept looking for me when it would've been easier not to." 

    "No." She shook her head. "No. I should've pressed more. I should've—" Her mouth tightened. "I don't know. Done something less chickenshit. If I'd kept going—I should've tried—"

    "You tried something better." Zosia's voice was factual. "When there was something to do, you did it. You pulled me out."

    Carol scoffed. "This is not the time to start rewriting me as some kind of hero."

    "I'm not rewriting you." Zosia's tone never rose. "You saved me."

    Carol's hand was still pressed against her temple. She could feel her pulse in her palm. 

    "You're about to make this about your guilt," Zosia said patiently, "and I need you to not do that. You're already running ahead to the version where you should've known." Zosia held her gaze. "I know you. I knew you before I had the words for it. Please don't take what I say and turn it into your fault. Even I, from inside, wasn't sure until this morning."

    Carol's teeth clenched. She wanted to argue. God, she wanted to argue, but Zosia met her with only patience, no pity. Carol looked away and huffed. "Fuck." 

    "It wasn't like being locked in a cage," Zosia said firmly, and Carol could see her searching for precision. "It's hard to explain. I was happy. More than happy. We all were and I agreed with them."

    Carol stared at her. Happy. She'd been braced for trapped, or suffering, for something she could feel guilty about.

    Zosia went on, "Sometimes I surfaced as only myself, briefly, in moments of strong feeling, and then the current would take me back."

    "Feeling," Carol repeated.

    "Yes. Remember when we talked about the fun facts? And I told you we wanted to make conversation, so I did. I wasn't at the surface, that was unconscious. Me coming through in how I followed what we wanted. They wanted something, I wanted the same thing. I was happy there."

    Carol still didn't get it, but Zosia was saying she wasn't a puppet or a prisoner, which meant Carol couldn't even frame this as a rescue she'd failed at. She frowned.

    When she'd had the guts to take her hand, Zosia had been behind there, content and aware. When Carol fell asleep on her, Zosia had been present for that. Every time Carol had reached for her, Zosia had felt it. 

    Carol couldn't make that mean what she wanted it to mean. Someone could be present and happy and still not feel anything specific about the person in front of her. Zosia had been swept along by euphoria and Carol had been part of the scenery. She didn't get to claim more than she knew.

    What she knew was she had no idea what any of it meant for what she'd felt and what she'd done and what any of it was.

    "I need a minute," Carol said. Zosia didn't move, didn't fill the silence. She let Carol have the minute, and her patience was different from anything Carol had felt from her, from before. She could see the effort of it now. Tension in her shoulders, her hands too deliberately placed still on the mug.

    "So you didn't feel trapped."

    "No."

    "Did you ever have any control at all?"

    "No. Not enough to change what was happening, even if I wanted to."

    Carol set down the mug because her hands were unsteady. She started where she could.

    "In Sprouts," Carol said. "When I asked you to tell me something only you knew. Were you there for that?"

    "I was there. Behind it." Zosia's voice stayed level, reportorial. "I wanted to answer you. I remember wanting to."

    Carol rubbed her face and remembered the frustration of that conversation, narrowing the question again and again and the clinical flatness of the answers. "And my next attempt. When I butchered your language."

    Zosia's face warmed. "Maybe. The feeling was—" She paused. "More than before. Enough to…enough to have my own sense of myself while it was happening. More than Sprouts. Less than mango ice cream."

    "Mango ice cream." 

    "Yes," Zosia said, and there was no hesitation in it at all. "That was me. Entirely me, for that stretch of it. The memory was mine and the feeling was mine and they let me through."

    Carol's throat bobbed. Of course it had been then. The first time she knew she was gone, had been the first time Zosia was fully there. Her heart, in all its pathetic lack of discipline, had apparently taken one look at the real woman and said yes, that one, we're fucked now. 

    Zosia watched her carefully. "You already knew."

    She'd said it in the container, kneeling on a mattress in the dark, holding Zosia's hand and gambling everything on a kitchen anecdote: I saw you. And then, in the silence after: maybe it was wishful thinking. Maybe she'd loved a trick of the light, a ghost, a glitch, a global consciousness, her own loneliness projected back—the doubt sewn into the feeling, inseparable. It wasn't wishful thinking. She'd seen her. 

    She wanted to tell Zosia, wanted to say: the moment you showed up I knew, and I've been pretending I didn't. Carol picked up her mug and put it down again instead. "I didn't know it was—"

    "It was me," Zosia said.

    So they'd already met. That was what this meant. Carol had been talking to her then, in the same room they were standing in now. 

    Carol looked at her. "And the rest of it? How about before?" 

    Zosia considered. "After everyone left and came back, those days were clearer than before them. I don't know if it was the distance, or missing something, even without knowing—" She frowned, dissatisfied with her own articulation. "I had thoughts of my own from the beginning, but I wasn't separate enough to examine them properly, and I don't know why. But I could feel when…I was being drawn to you."

    Carol's grip tightened on the counter.

    "I don't mean consensus," Zosia said, quietly. "Not only that."

    The room tipped. It was right there and Zosia was almost handing it to her—confirmation that Zosia had wanted to be with Carol, for reasons that belonged to her alone. She could ask. Drawn how. By them or by you. Her nerve gave out at the edge and she stepped back from the drop. 

    Carol cleared her throat. "So when I thought I was getting… you." Her hands did a hopeless little gesture. "I sort of was."

    "Yes."

    "And sometimes wasn't."

    "Yes."

    Carol nodded, then immediately regretted where her mind went next. Her mouth almost outran her. What about when you came— She stopped thinking, mouth clamping shut around the question.

    Zosia's expression changed by half a degree. "There's something else," she said. "About how I know I was present." She paused. "The first confirmation was during—when we—"

    Carol watched Zosia's ears turn red in real time. The blush fell down her neck and kept going. 

    "In bed," Carol supplied.

    "Yes."

    Carol's hands were flat. She could feel the grain under her fingers. "When you—"

    "Yes," Zosia said, before she finished.

    Another silence. Zosia was looking at the wall with fixed determination. "Certain things surfaced," Zosia said, carefully, to the wall. "That couldn't have been—they didn't have—" She searched for a clinical enough word and visibly failed. "Individual responses. To specific—" She gave up and sighed. "You know what I mean."

    Carol did know what she meant. Carol remembered with a clarity that made her own face hot. If the hive couldn't touch that, the feeling was Zosia's. Just hers. The real woman wanting her.

    "I thought about if that was you," Carol said roughly. "Or if I was just...I decided I was projecting." Carol's laugh was humorless. "That I was an idiot who wanted it to be real." Her voice cracked. "But it was you. And I let it go." 

    Zosia was quiet.

    Carol stared at the counter. She picked up the coffee can and wrapped both hands around it and squeezed until the cold metal went hard into her fingers, sharp enough to crowd everything else out. "I'm not going to spiral," she said, more to herself than to Zosia. "Not making this about me." Carol glanced up. "I did, for a sec."

    Zosia's mouth had the faintest pull at one corner. "You don't have to ask everything today."

    Carol had imagined the worst reading so many times: the real Zosia, buried with no voice and no vote, hating every second Carol had soaked up. But she'd wanted to be there. It didn't fix it, but Carol could breathe around that.

    She made herself let go of the can and exhale. "Good," she said briskly, "because we've got a more immediate crisis. We're out of beans." She pushed the can across to Zosia. "There's maybe one cup left, which you should have, because I've had—" She counted. "Six? An amount that explains my current state."

    Zosia took the can, her fingers where Carol's had been, where the metal was warm now. Carol watched her carry it to the counter with both hands, careful with it for no reason, and her heart gave a painful turn. 

    Then there was three knocks down the hall and the front door opened anyway. A dry breeze came through with Manousos.

    Carol didn't even turn around. "I've got to find my keys," she said. "Or at least make a sign."

    "Morning, Manousos," Zosia said. "Please, come in."

    "I am in," he said, blankly. 

    Carol turned to look at him. "You know doors have a middle stage, right? There's supposed to be a gap between the knock and entering. The part where people decide whether they want a man in their house."

    "I always knock," he said, baffled. "Any new information?"

    Zosia's face went still. "Nothing pertinent." 

    The word was doing a lot of work and his eyes narrowed. Carol could see his follow-up forming, and she cut across it. "Christ, Manny, she just woke up." She moved to the counter beside Zosia. "She said nothing. Sit down or don't." 

    Carol drank her relatively bad coffee and dared him with her eyes. 

    Manny exhaled through his nose, but he sat. "Eat," she said, and pushed her plate toward him.

    Manny picked up the tortilla, inspecting it.

    "She made it," Zosia said.

    "I see that," he said.

    Carol felt her face heat. "It's not the Ritz." She turned to busy herself wiping the counter that was already wiped.

    "Where are you in Winds of Wycaro?" Zosia asked him. 

    Carol's hand stopped. 

    "Chapter fourteen," Manny said, finishing the tortilla in two bites.

    Carol whirled around. "You're reading my book?"

    "He had it on the table yesterday," Zosia said to Carol. "From the library."

    "Since I had spare time." Manny picked up a peach slice with his fingers. "Which is now always. Zosia said read it before sleep."

    Carol almost laughed. "You're—that's like three hundred pages."

    Manousos wiped his fingers on his knee. "I know how long it is. That is part of why I respect it."

    "Yeah, it took four years," Carol said, before she could stop herself. She didn't know why she'd said that. It usually felt like a confession of slowness, and she'd trained herself to shrug and say a while. "You like it?"

    "When I finish," he said, ignoring her question, "is there another?"

    "Three more."

    He nodded. "That takes dedication to yourself. Most people do not finish things."

    Carol turned to the sink and ran the water for no reason. To yourself. She'd never framed it that way, after all the concessions, and she hadn't thought of the new chapter as proof of anything except no consequences…but she had also sat down most mornings for thirty years and got the damn things done. Maybe both could be true. 

    "The captain," Manny said to Zosia behind her. "She reminds me of someone."

    "Who?"

    "Me." He folded his arms. 

    Zosia wanted to smile—Carol watched in the window's reflection, the pull at the corner. 

    "Raban, though," Manny continued. "He doesn't make it easy. They both know. Neither say. Very tiring to read."

    "That's the genre," Zosia said, "Give it due time."

    "They are on a ship in a desert full of monsters." He looked between them. "When is it time?"

    Carol turned around. "Are you two running a book club? In an alien apocalypse? About my books?"

    "When we survive it," Manny said, and unfolded the map under his arm onto the counter, changing the subject. "Today. VLA site. I will do reconnaissance. Fast." He lifted the ambulance keys, metal flashing in the morning sun.

    "Fast," Zosia repeated. She set her coffee down. "Why fast?" 

    "Because they watch," he said, like it was obvious. 

    Zosia shook her head. "You're assuming surveillance that wasn't always there." Carol could see Manousos resisting the urge to distrust her on principle. "They miss things on purpose. I saw them withdraw a drone watching Carol's car, mid-feed." 

    "Why?" Manny asked, and the contempt for them was audible.

    "I think we wanted to be surprised."

    Carol tilted her head. "Huh. They must be bored shitless." Manny's expression didn't improve so she attempted to rally. "There. You heard her. They're only regular terrifying."

    He glanced at her without interest. "I do one pass. No heroics."

    "Good," Carol said, "because we're fresh out."

    They talked over the map for a few minutes and Carol stood to the side eating her oatmeal. She watched Zosia's hand trace the paper, her index finger following the interstate. The word happy kept circling back, like a dog she refused to feed but couldn't shut out.

    She didn't know how much this changed what came next, or exactly what Zosia wanted now or then, and was still too afraid to ask. She only knew that she'd already done two things differently today because Zosia was here, and Carol wanted, for once, not to answer that with self-hatred. She'd wanted the vodka and not poured it. She had felt the second spiral open and stopped on purpose. The bar was in hell, but she'd cleared it.

    When Manny was satisfied, he tucked the map under his arm. "I go now. Back later." 

    "Later?" Carol said, following him down the hall.

    "Four hours if I don't stop." He strode through the door and down the driveway like dawdling might kill him.

    Carol watched him thunk the ambulance door shut, then the engine turned over with that ugly diesel complaint she'd hated, and since made a grudging peace with. The ambulance backed out, gravel cracking under the tires like knuckles, and then he peeled away, the dust cloud settling into silence.

    The morning light was already harsh. Carol rubbed her eyes against it and padded back to the kitchen. She let out a breath she had not been planning to admit to. She looked at her mug. "We still need coffee." 

    Zosia was finishing her breakfast and looked forlornly at the jar of instant decaf on the counter. "Badly."

    "There's Sprouts. It's five, six miles? And someone just drove away in our only vehicle." She drummed her fingers on the counter. "We could call them. They'd deliver." Zosia's face went carefully neutral. "Or," Carol said, pivoting, "we walk…through the desert..."

    "It's too far," Zosia said, which must be her way of saying that's insane.

    "What about the helicopter?" Carol had grown used to it in the open ground beyond 1202, another piece of apocalyptic street furniture like the atom bomb or the ambulance. 

    Carol could see her turning it over genuinely. "I have some hours from the Navy," Zosia said. "Familiarization flights. Enough to get one off of the ground." She paused. "Not enough to feel good with you in it."

    Carol's heart did something she refused to acknowledge. "So…that's a no."

    "It's a not yet. I'm assuming it's a skill I haven't dreamed. Once that comes through, I'll have enough."

    Carol nodded. "There are bikes in the garage?"

    Zosia straightened at that. "Wait here."

    "Huh?"

    "Give me five minutes."

    Zosia was already heading for the stairs, taking two at a time with those long legs. Carol was left holding an empty Shrek. She heard the guest room door open and close. She poured out the dregs and rinsed the plates and set it all on the rack and stood in her own kitchen feeling mildly abandoned.

    She heard the front door open and close. Carol went out to the porch. 

    Then, from somewhere in the cul-de-sac, an engine she didn't recognize, deeper than the ambulance, tighter, turning over with a low reluctance before catching and steadying into a contained growl that made every nerve in Carol's body snap up.

    The garage door of 1204 lifted and Zosia rode out on a matte-black motorcycle, the engine running at a murmur. Carol stared at her for another second, then muttered, "You're freaking kidding me." Zosia turned onto the street, and came toward the house. 

    Leather jacket half zipped, collar standing against her jaw, fingers on the grips with the same authority she brought to everything she touched. Carol's hand found the door frame. She had no reference for motorcycles except cinema, and maybe the Top Gun theme would be playing in her head if she could remember what the fuck it was.

    Raban's entrance in chapter six had taken Carol three days. Arriving at the port on horseback, the salt-stiffened coat, dismounting without looking down—Zosia pulled up to the curb and swung one long leg over in a single motion that Carol followed from hip to boot—and here it was, and the reason she'd known what she wanted to write for it had never occurred to her until now. 

    Carol was, in fact, gawking, and had been since the garage door opened. Zosia lifted one hand from the handlebars and made a small come-on gesture.  

    "Martin had a Bonneville in his garage," Zosia said, as Carol approached, as if she was supposed to know what that meant. Zosia killed the engine. The sudden quiet was strangely intimate.

    "Is there anything you can't do?"

    The corner of Zosia's mouth pulled down and her eyes went to her hands on the tank and she turned away, staring at nothing. Then she opened the saddlebag and pulled out a pair of enormous leather gloves. "Bikes are useful for getting around base quickly." 

    Not a hive skill. Carol dragged her eyes away from Zosia in the leather and up close the motorbike looked alien to her. She had never been on one. She'd never wanted to be on one. Motorcycles occupied the same category as skydiving and raw oysters: placed mentally under not for me.

    Zosia held out a helmet. One helmet. "What about you?" Carol said, but before she could organize more of a protest Zosia pushed it onto her head carefully. The world narrowed.

    "There's no one else on the road," Zosia said, her voice muffled by the ear pads, "and I know I won't crash." No bravado in it, then softer, "But I'd rather you wore it."

    Carol chose not to argue. She buckled the chin strap while Zosia watched. The padding pressed her cheeks up and made her feel like a hamster wearing a bucket. 

    "I look ridiculous," Carol said.

    Zosia smiled fully, color high in her cheeks, eyes sparkling and almost shut with it. Carol's hands stalled on her chin. She'd seen Zosia's face do a lot of new things lately and this smile was older but rare enough now to feel like an event, and Carol stood below in her glow like an idiot. 

    "Gloves," Zosia said.

    "They're enormous."

    "Tighten the wrist."

    Carol pulled them on. The fingers were a full inch too long. She held up both hands and waggled the empty tips. "Mitts."

    "Don't flap them around or we might take off."

    "You know how to fucking fly a plane anyway, so won't be a problem."

    Zosia smiled again—smaller this time—and turned back to the bike. She swung on. Carol watched her easy transfer of weight, hands finding the grips without searching. 

    Carol stood there clueless and for one bewildering instant she was seventeen again and someone had just pulled up for a date in a sports car. And she was wearing oven mitts.

    "Can you get on?" Zosia asked, over her shoulder.

    Carol looked at the bike again. "I honestly don't know." 

    "Left foot on the peg. Swing your right leg over. Hold on to me."

    Carol walked around the side of the thing and wondered if it was anything like a horse. If that was her saddle, it was small.

    Her right leg barely cleared, and there was a full second of graceless spatial confusion during which she was draped over the back of it at an awkward angle. She caught Zosia in the wing mirror watching her clambering and her feet found the pegs only after an embarrassing amount of shuffling. Then she was on. Her legs bracketed Zosia's. She gulped. Her hands had only one place to go.

    She put them on Zosia's waist. Through the layers, the contact was insulated, practical, the minimum grip for staying alive. Carol's palms pressed against Zosia's sides and her fingers curled against the leather and she felt the expansion with each breath.

    Zosia didn't react. Turned the key. The engine came up under both of them, shaking through the frame, through the seat, through Carol's insides. Zosia checked over her shoulder once, her outrageously gorgeous face in profile, jaw set and focused.

    "Ready?"

    "Nope."

    Zosia pulled away from the curb.

    The first acceleration was a shove. Carol pitched backwards and she tightened her grip, body jolting closer along the line of Zosia's back. She felt Zosia register it—her abdomen tighten, absorbing the weight shift, and then they were moving, the cul-de-sac opening into the access road and the desert spreading wide on both sides. Zosia steered through the turns toward town with utter steadiness, without any visible enjoyment of being good at it, which made it significantly worse than if she'd been showing off.

    She was acutely and unhelpfully aware of every point of contact. Her forearms against Zosia's stomach, her chest against her back, her inner thighs clamped around Zosia's hips, and the engine vibration was doing obscene things and she was wet. She'd had Zosia above her and begged for the weight and heat of her and been refused, and now she had it through three layers of cowhide and a pair of comedy gloves.

    "Left," Carol said. She had to lean in to be heard, because the helmet and the wind allowed no alternative. "Left at the junction, then straight until the highway." The words left her mouth and went into the warm hollow between Zosia's hair and the collar, and she could smell the leather, feel her own breath come back to her off Zosia's jaw. 

    Zosia leaned into the turn. Carol leaned with her, because there was no alternative except dying, and for one tilted second their centers of gravity aligned and the road was beneath them at a heart-pounding angle. Carol's arms tightened, and under them, Zosia's body moved as a single integrated thing, committing to the turn, rolling the throttle through rather than braking.

    Then the road straightened and the highway was empty, obviously, and the desert was streaming past, scrub and sand and the occasional bleached fencepost. 

    Zosia breathed under her palms, a steady expansion that meant she was calm, the road was good, that Carol was safe, and she believed her. She'd been bracing for a crash and now, the speedometer reading a number Carol chose to ignore, she actually felt her shoulders drop and her heartbeat slow. 

    Sprouts appeared on the right and they pulled into the lot and Zosia parked with neat efficiency, engine cutting off into the dry morning. For a second neither of them moved. The engine ticked and every square inch where Carol's body met Zosia's was hot and about to end. 

    Carol peeled herself off. She swung her leg over, staggered slightly, and pulled the helmet off as soon as possible. Static launched her hair toward the sky in several independent directions and she flattened it with one oven mitt, which did nothing. She stripped the gloves off and flexed her fingers, red-lined at the knuckles from the loose leather.

    Zosia put the kickstand down and looked at her.

    "What?"

    Zosia shook her head. "Nothing." She was smiling and wasn't hiding it. Zosia took the helmet from her and hung it on the mirror.

    They walked to Sprouts together and Carol knew this store as well as her own kitchen. Produce right, bakery back, canned goods in the middle aisles. They'd moved the beans to aisle six eight months ago and she still resented it.

    The automatic doors slid open and the blast of air conditioning felt almost indecent on her neck, still flushed from the ride, enough to raise goosebumps. Carol pulled a cart free from the row—the one with the sticky front-left wheel, because she knew—and went in.

    The store was too quiet, no muzak, only the lights buzzing and the hiss of misters spraying nothing. Produce section: empty. Dairy fridge: bare. Meat counter: no trays.

    The place looked like a bunker dressed in cheerful signage. Behind the checkout, a laminated sign said SMILE! YOU'RE THE REASON THEY COME BACK. Someone had given the smiley face fangs. 

    Zosia looked at the empty produce bins with pity. "They were thorough."

    "They took the bananas but left the Froot Loops. Don't know what that says about their priorities."

    "Froot Loops don't decompose." They turned the corner into canned goods. "The roof trusses are undersized for the span," Zosia said then, to no one.

    Carol followed her gaze. She'd been shopping here for fifteen years and had never once looked up. "What?"

    "The lateral bracing. For this width of building, you'd want—" Her mouth closed. "It's fine. It's stood this long."

    "Were you just doubting my Sprouts's structural integrity?"

    Zosia's ears went faintly pink. "On a ship you notice load paths. It transfers."

    Carol studied the ceiling again. It looked like a ceiling. "I'm going to think about the roof collapsing every time I'm in here now."
