    "You're welcome," Zosia said, and she sounded genuinely pleased with herself. Carol grabbed three cans of diced tomatoes and stacked them in the cart. Zosia picked up a can of chickpeas, read the label, turned it over, and put it back. She selected a different brand. "Everything has too much sodium here." She picked up the replacement and checked it. "The ingredients is a paragraph."

    "God bless America. We put corn syrup in bread."

    Zosia set two cans in the cart. "Bread should be dark. Dense. Razowy—" The word came out before the English caught up. "Wholemeal. You should taste the grain." Carol bit down on a smile and Zosia noticed. "I'm serious."

    "I'll add that to the list. Coffee is serious. Bread is serious. What else?"

    "Butter," Zosia said immediately. "Yours is too pale," she said with conviction, chin lifting. 

    "Too pale."

    "Butter should be yellow. Dark yellow." Her voice didn't waver. If anything she stood straighter. "Yours is—" She finally checked herself.

    "Go on. Drag my butter."

    "Anemic," Zosia said, diplomatically.

    Carol pointed at her. "So that's what you were doing under there. Last time we were here, you in the hive, me asking my little questions—you were having independent thoughts about pale butter."

    The pink in her ears spread to her cheeks, fast and visible, and she looked down at the olive oil in her hand. "Among other things," Zosia said, and she put the olive oil in the cart and moved past Carol toward the next shelf.

    Carol waited. Zosia didn't look at her. Carol stood there. Among other things. Her eyes narrowed. She gripped the cart handle and followed. 

    She watched Zosia reach for something on the top shelf—tahini—and retrieved it one-handed, flat-footed, without tip toes or straining or any of the indignities Carol would've needed.

    "Show-off," Carol griped.

    Zosia smiled before she even said it. "Am I? Maybe you're just short." She held out the tahini, eyebrow raised. 

    "I can—I'm nearly five five."

    "Sure."

    Carol scowled at Zosia obviously relishing her indignation about it. She took the jar and their fingers didn't touch because they never did. Zosia gave her things at arm's length, stood close enough to reach but never close enough to graze and it was maddening. 

    Zosia had been arranging the cart. Cans grouped by type, labels facing forward, weight distributed evenly. The chickpeas were nested beside the white beans. The tomatoes formed their own orderly rank. It looked like a supply locker that expected inspection.

    Carol set the tahini on top of the tomatoes, crooked. Zosia looked at it, looked at Carol, reached down and moved it to its correct position. Carol did it again. Zosia stopped, took a slow breath, fixed the can. "Are we doing this all morning?" 

    "If you call me short again." 

    Zosia pushed the cart forward without a word. 

    The coffee aisle was where things got heated. Carol reached for the medium roast, pre-ground, the same one she'd been buying for ten years. Zosia was already shaking her head.

    "I can't watch you buy that."

    "It's free now and it's my coffee."

    "Za darmo to uczciwa cena." Carol watched Zosia's mouth move around the Polish, her jaw unlocked, the word in the middle crackled contemptuously through three consonants Carol couldn't have produced with a gun to her head. "Free is a fair price for this dust in a bag." Zosia picked it up, read the roast date, and set it back on the shelf with finality. "Carol. This was roasted nine months ago."

    "So it's aged. Like wine."

    "That's not how coffee works. After nine months you're drinking cardboard," she said haughtily. 

    Zosia pulled a bag of whole beans from two shelves up and ran her thumb across the roast date on the label as tenderly as handling a first edition. "This was roasted four months ago. Single origin. The elevation matters—slower growth, denser bean, more complexity." She turned the bag so Carol could see the label. "You can taste the altitude."

    "Taste the altitude," Carol repeated.

    "You will when I make it." 

    Zosia was not remotely embarrassed. This was hers—her own accumulated snobbery that predated Carol completely—and the pride on her face was so undisguised it bordered on smug. Carol felt a rush of affection so large and so stupid she turned to the shelf. "Fine. Both bags. I'm not abandoning my coffee just because you have opinions now."

    Zosia dropped them in the cart side by side, a detente, and they moved on.

    The canned soups took longer than Carol expected because Zosia read every label like she was reviewing a legal contract, turning each can to study the ingredients, the sodium content, the suggested serving temperature. She asked Carol what half of them tasted like, and Carol realized that she was being consulted as an authority. 

    "You've never had tomato bisque?"

    "I've never had most of these." Zosia's eyes were bright with curiosity. She turned another can over and looked at the illustration. "What's chowder?"

    "Thick soup. Creamy. That one's clam."

    Zosia looked skeptical. "Creamy clam."

    "Don't make it sound like that." Carol put the bisque in the cart. "We'll add it to the curriculum of whatever else you haven't tried."

    "I'd like that," Zosia said, and her voice had gone from wary to warm. Carol gripped the cart handle with both hands. She'd offered something without thinking—we'll—and Zosia had said yes as if time together in the future was a given. Carol pushed forward and her pulse was loud in her ears and she wanted to make Zosia canned clam chowder, God help her.

    Zosia turned the can once more and set it down with the label out, joining the rank. She was already onto the soups, weighing minestrone in one hand and cream of mushroom in the other, frowning. Carol watched her too long. Zosia ran a finger along the shelf as she walked, scanning brands, as the aisle continued into dried beans and pasta. 

    Carol had to reach for turtle beans and her sleeve brushed Zosia's arm, close to the wrist, and Zosia flinched sharply away.

    Carol's hand froze. She pulled it off the shelf and stepped back. "Sorry."

    "It's fine." Zosia's voice was steady, her hand found the shelf edge and she was reading a bag of lentils with an intensity lentils didn't warrant.

    So that had been another flinch. This morning Zosia had gone red to her collarbones admitting she'd surfaced during sex—her own responses, nobody else's—and Carol still didn't know what to do with that, but now a sleeve was apparently too much. 

    Carol pushed the cart forward and the sticky wheel squeaked. She gave Zosia an extra foot of clearance rounding the next corner and hated that she'd measured it. 

    Carol picked up a box of ravioli and Zosia made a face. "You're going to tell me about superior Italian pasta now."

    "Polish pasta is better."

    "Really?"

    "Pierogi."

    "Aren't those dumplings?"

    Zosia picked up a bag of flour. "I could make you pierogi."

    "You told me you can't cook."

    "It's isn't cooking. It's—" Zosia's hand moved, a folding motion. "My mother would let me do the edges. You just press." The motion repeated, and Carol saw the muscle memory in it, a child's hands on a kitchen counter. "That much I can do."

    "Your mom taught you?"

    "Only the edges. She didn't trust me with the filling. She had a system."

    "Sounds familiar."

    "I come by it honestly." Zosia set the flour in the cart, aligned with the label facing out. 

    "Were you close? You and your mom?"

    Zosia considered, her hands pausing on the cart. "She loved me, but she also had a clear idea of who I was supposed to be." Her thumb traced the edge of the handle. "A husband, children, a kitchen of my own. The life she'd already chosen for me. I left for naval college and she cried for a week. Told her friends I was going through a phase." Her mouth pulled up. "It's been twenty-five years." She picked up a bag of rice, checked the weight, and her smile faded. "She made pierogi for my wedding too. I think it was the best day of her life. She didn't know what it was."

    "And you never told her."

    "Now she knows." Zosia's voice was even. "She knows her daughter lied to her for twenty years and she feels...content. Happy for me at last."

    Carol didn't know if that was mercy or one more theft. "I'm sorry."

    "Don't be. She's not suffering. That's more than I could've given her."

    Carol wanted to ask what she meant by that. She wanted to ask a lot of things, and instead she dropped a bottle of soy sauce in the cart. The sticky wheel squeaked. 

    "What was your family like?" Zosia asked.

    Carol almost said you already know, but caught herself. She was asking like she'd asked Carol not to spoil her own dreams—wanting Carol's tell of it, maybe, not the version she'd already been given.

    Carol shrugged. "Small. Just me and my mom." Who had died believing Carol's life was a series of choices made specifically to wound her, to shame her, who'd sent a card when she got married—no congratulations, just a barbed Bible verse. 

    She was not, historically, a person who volunteered her own damage. Helen had excavated it over years with patience and wine and the refusal to accept Carol's first answer. Zosia hadn't asked a follow up, probably because she knew most of it, but Carol found she minded less when she wasn't being prodded.

    Carol held up a can of condensed milk. "My mom used to buy these. She'd make fudge for church fundraisers. Boil the can for three hours." She put it back. "Her life was that church. It's how she knew about the camp." 

    Zosia nodded. Carol caught it and kept going, grateful that it saved the exhausting preamble of everything she'd never have been good at providing anyway.

    "One of her Bible study friends sent me a card when the second book was a bestseller. Something with a D...Dorothy, Diane?" Carol frowned. "I can't remember. She wrote 'your mother would be so proud,' which was such a goddamned lie." Carol pushed her tongue into the inside of her cheek. "What was her name? The D lady. You'd have her."

    Zosia stopped walking. "I don't," she said.

    "She died? You don't have that?" 

    Carol turned back to look at Zosia and the ease had gone out of her shoulders. "No. I don't have anyone."

    "What?" Carol stared at her. "What the fuck? But you—I thought you had everything. The—" She gestured vaguely at herself. "The all-access pass."

    "No," Zosia said, too flat.

    "You don't know everything about me?"

    Zosia looked at the shelf. "No." Her jaw was set. "I have the camp because it came through me in the dream."

    Carol blinked rapidly. That was… not what she'd thought. At all. Every conversation where Carol had assumed comprehension and Zosia had—what? Nodded? Let it pass? She'd been scrambling for new stories to tell her and anything would've been fine. 

    The confusion curdled into dread. Zosia could hear something new now and decide she wanted less. The flinch Carol had been trying not to think about sharpened instantly. It had been a relief, perversely, to believe the floor was already set as low as it was going to go. 

    She'd said things thinking she was repeating herself. Zosia had been listening, and Carol had read it as recognition, but it had been something else. Curiosity, maybe. 

    A new kind of relief surprised her, then. Her life was her own again, to hand over like a normal person. Carol could decide what to share and Zosia could decide what to ask, and the thing between them would be real and more equal. This was… better… probably…or just different from what she'd thought. She'd have to live in it a minute before she knew. 

    Carol put a jar back. "Huh. That is weirdly good to know."

    Zosia nodded once, too quickly, and reached for another jar with forced attention, obviously braced for a follow-up.

    Was Zosia that much of a nerd that not-knowing embarrassed her this much? Carol wanted to ask why she hadn't said something sooner, but knew that would make her embarrassment worse. Instead, she picked up a bottle with a label completely in Spanish. Bright red, a chilli on the front. "What does this say?"

    Zosia took it and the shift was immediate. She turned the bottle. "Salsa de habanero. Artisanal. From Oaxaca." She checked the back. "Ingredients are clean, actually. Habanero, garlic, lime, salt. That's it."

    Carol picked up another bottle. "And this one?"

    Zosia read it. "Much milder. You'd prefer this one."

    Carol kept her voice light. "And how do you know what I'd prefer, hm? Now everything's gone?"

    Zosia's cheeks went pink. "You put sugar in your coffee," she said, as if that explained everything.

    Carol took both bottles and put them in the cart. Zosia watched one tilt crooked against the aligned cans and reached in to correct it, and Carol let her, and the worst of whatever had locked Zosia's shoulders for the last minute was gone.

    Carol led them toward pantry staples. Zosia followed in silence, and then, halfway down the aisle, her hand drifted to the other side of the cart handle. She gradually began making suggestions again, quieter at first—a brand preference offered sideways, a label read aloud. By the time they hit canned goods again they were speaking in whole sentences.

    They moved through the rest of the store efficiently, making decisions jointly and quickly—canned tuna, no; canned chili, sure; the bizarre powdered cheese, no chance.

    Zosia picked up a box of Lucky Charms, turned it over, and her expression deteriorated. "Trisodium phosphate," she read aloud. "That's a cleaning agent."

    "And delicious."

    "There are over forty ingredients. Razowy has four."

    "Yeah, your bread doesn't have tasty marshmallows in it."

    Zosia put it in the cart with a sigh.

    By the checkout, Carol held the re-usable plastic bags open while Zosia loaded them, heavy items first, building a base, then lighter things on top, cans nested so they wouldn't roll, and then a knot at the top. "You're good at this," Carol said.

    "It's just weight distribution."

    "You say that about everything. At some point you have to admit you're a control freak."

    "I prefer organized." Zosia placed the two coffee bags side by side in their own bag, separated from the cans. She'd put them together, Carol noticed. Hers and Carol's. Dark roast and terrible dust, sharing a bag.

    Zosia straightened, frowned, reached into one, and rearranged something Carol couldn't see—a can turned, a jar shifted—and then nodded.

    Carol picked up the two heaviest bags before Zosia could reach them.

    "Those should be mine," Zosia said.

    "I got there first."

    "The bike needs to balance. You're the passenger, you—"

    "I'm carrying them. You can have them back at the bike."

    Carol made for the exit. The automatic doors slid open, but beside them was a manual door, and Carol hip-checked it wide and stood holding it with her shoulder, bags in both hands, nodding Zosia through.

    Zosia stopped.

    "Go," Carol ordered, and shifted a bag to make more room for Zosia to pass.

    Zosia raised her eyebrows. "The automatic one is right there."

    "I'm—" Carol sighed. "Let me have this." 

    Outside on the lot, the sun hit them again all at once and she squinted through it.

    Zosia loaded the heavier bags. "These go on the rack, the light one in the backpack. You carry the pack because you're the passenger."

    "So there's a reason."

    "There's always a reason." Zosia looked at her, and her voice dropped without seeming to intend to. "I'd rather the weight was on me than on you."

    There it was again. The sentence was practical, about motorcycle load distribution. It was also, transparently, not only about that, and Zosia had said it, without looking away, as she handed her the light pack. 

    Their hands didn't touch—Zosia held it at arm's length—and the contradiction widened again, and Carol just stood there in it, confused and out-chivalried. She picked up the helmet from the handlebar. "I despise this thing," she said, and put it on anyway.

    Zosia was already swinging the heavy pack onto the rack. The leather shifted across her back. She pulled a length of cord from the saddlebag and Carol made the mistake of watching her hands move through it with insane fluidity as she strapped the bags down one-handed with a knot that was fast and foreign. 

    Carol had spent an afternoon with Lots of Knots for a passage in book two, and been privately proud of an economy-of-motion line: 'hands that knew the rope before the mind named the knot'. Here, in a Sprouts parking lot, it was like magic. She was a plagiarist, a forgerer. 

    "What knot is that?" she asked, before she could stop herself. The closest her hands had come to a rope was the drawstring on a hoodie.

    Zosia glanced up then looked at the cord, as if she'd not even noticed what she was doing. "Rolling hitch," she said, and tugged the cord once, demonstrating. She tested the second. "Groceries are less dramatic than cargo in a force eight. The bags won't shift." Carol filed rolling hitch away for book five and the rest somewhere she was not going to think about in daylight. 

    The gloves went on. Too large, still ridiculous. Zosia's mouth did that almost-smile again as she sat on the bike, and Carol clambered on, and her body against Zosia's back had become less avoidable than ever. The groceries shifted the balance. 

    "The weight's different," Zosia said over her shoulder.

    "Yep."

    "Hold tighter."

    Zosia's tone didn't sound like physics, and now Carol's whole upper body was pressed against her and Zosia hadn't flinched, and Carol still didn't understand, but didn't need to be told twice. Her helmet bumped the back of Zosia's shoulder.

    The desert opened around them again as they pulled out, but differently now that she could no longer pretend the first time had been a shock-induced hallucination. The sun had climbed while they'd been inside and the landscape was blown wide with light, every color saturated past bearing.

    "Okay?" Zosia called.

    "Yep." Carol's arms were locked around her. "Go."

    Carol leaned into Zosia's back and this time didn't invent a reason. They'd been somewhere semi-ordinary together, she thought. She hadn't been surviving in a delusional bubble. They'd just been two normal-ish people. They'd gone somewhere to not-buy coffee and canned tomatoes. 

    The leather jacket held the sun's heat and Zosia's, indistinguishable, and Carol's face rested between her shoulder blades where the jacket creased up and stayed warm.

    She probably didn't even know Carol's birthday anymore. 

    Zosia had spent the last hour choosing between chickpeas and critiquing ceilings and blushing saying among other things like a door open one inch that Carol was too cowardly too open, and she had done all of it better than the version of her that knew the full picture, that had her whole, without friction.

    Mixed signals and yesterday's fight and all, she should've been worse at this now, by every metric, and was still so much better that Carol wanted to laugh. And she'd done it knowing almost nothing. 

    Three weeks ago Zosia would never have been pissy about pale butter, for Christ's sake. She would've provided Carol's preferred butter, and Carol would've felt tended to, and never known what she was missing.

    Carol's arms tightened around Zosia, shifting against the leather, finding a more secure hold that had nothing to do with balance and everything to do with not letting go of the feeling.

    What she'd been missing was the argument. That was the whole ordinary thing.

    They'd been to a grocery store and bickered. It was the most normal hour she'd had since Helen died. Carol pressed closer and grief arrived on the back of something that wasn't grief at all, the two feelings drafting off of each other impossibly.

    The last time she'd felt this ordinary had been the Sunday before the book tour, Helen driving, Carol complaining about the parking. They'd argued about hummus. Helen had bought the wrong yogurt on purpose because she thought Carol's brand loyalty was absurd, and Carol had sulked, and Helen had laughed, and it had been nothing. An ordinary Sunday that meant nothing. Carol hadn't known it was the last one. There was no placard, no countdown, no change in the light. They'd driven home with the windows down and Carol had not once, at any point, thought: remember this. Pay attention to this ordinary hour because you won't get another one.

    The hive knew every memory she'd ever had, including all of Carol. Helen rolling her eyes at Carol's yogurt loyalty. Helen reading the camp letters. Helen's hands shaking at the start of their vows, the word always, or had it been from the beginning. The hive had all of it, uncorrupted. If the plan worked and they unjoined everyone, the glue would dissolve and the memories would go with it. Every last one.

    What would remain was stored in a fifty-three-year-old head that was already slipping: the exact shade of Helen's eyes, the sound of her voice on an ordinary Sunday, which ear Helen held the phone to. Carol knew the answer was left. She was almost sure. She was less sure than she'd been three months ago, and in a year she'd be even less sure, and the slow erosion was happening right now in the space between one heartbeat and the next.

    But she could tell Zosia. She could say: Helen held the phone to her left ear and bought the wrong yogurt to annoy me and put her fork at four o'clock and her vows started with I loved you from the first morning. She could hand those over now, one by one, and Zosia would hold them, because she held things carefully, with both hands, labels facing forward. 

    It wouldn't be the whole Helen. It would be Carol's Helen. Given and chosen, not archived and absorbed.

    Her throat burned and she pressed her face hard against the leather between Zosia's shoulder blades and felt the tears come, pushed sideways by the wind before they could fall. Zosia adjusted and Carol felt a deliberate smoothing of the ride, the bike leaning less, the throttle steadier—and knew that Zosia was responding without turning around or asking, making the road easier to bear.

    Carol held on and let the grief and the other thing move through her together, because stopping either was impossible.

    The desert blurred. The mountains bled together. She couldn't tell how long it lasted—a minute, maybe two—and then the tears passed, receding like a wave pulling back, leaving her scraped. Her breathing evened. 

    The cul-de-sac reappeared and Zosia slowed, the engine note dropping, and turned in, asphalt under tires. They stopped beside the curb. 

    Carol's arms were still around her. For a held second she didn't move, and then she had to force her hands to loosen. The distance came back—Zosia already shifting her weight forward to make room for Carol to dismount—and it was worse this time, worse than the parking lot, worse than the store, because something on the highway had come loose that she couldn't put back and she could feel it moving in her, unsecured. 

    She got down badly, plucked the gloves off and wrenched the chin strap before Zosia could offer to help, which she wouldn't have, Carol realized. Carol had assumed politeness. She was reconsidering. 

    She'd gotten somewhere on the ride back and it didn't help. Knowing what she wanted to give only made it worse not knowing what Zosia wanted to take.

    The helmet came off and the dry air hit her face, exposing everything, the wind-raw skin, the red around her eyes, the mess of damp hair clinging to her temples. The street was merciless with light, no shade anywhere, every surface reflecting—the chrome on the bike, the windows of the empty houses, the gravel throwing heat back at her. 

    She wiped her eyes with the heel of her hand and set the helmet on the seat hard enough that it rocked.

    Zosia killed the engine and the bike ticked as it cooled in the silence. She didn't dismount, just sat there with her hands on the grips, her brows drawn, her eyes tracking the red around Carol's. 

    "The air," Carol said.

    Zosia dismounted. "It wasn't the air."

    Carol started pulling grocery bags off the rack and the jars of hot sauce clinked dangerously and she didn't slow down. "Whatever. Are we going inside?"

    Zosia reached for the other bag, lifting it clear in one motion, and Carol grabbed for the same handle at the same time and their knuckles nearly grazed and Zosia's whole arm jerked back.

    Carol stood with her hand still extended into the space Zosia had vacated. The bag swung and something inside shifted.

    "Fine." She picked up the other bag herself. "I've got it."

    "Carol—"

    "I said I've got it."

    She hauled the bags toward the house and the tears were threatening again, fucking infuriating, because the quota for a Tuesday morning should have a goddamn ceiling. Behind her, Zosia said her name again, but Carol was past listening. Zosia stayed at her usual careful distance—three feet, four, the calibrated gap Carol had been measuring without admitting she was counting.

    Carol dropped the bags and turned around. "What is this?" 

    Zosia stopped. The sun was behind her, catching the hair that had blown free during the ride. "What is what?" 

    "This." Carol gestured a motion that encompassed the distance, the bags, the bike. "The weight should be on you, you're proud of—" She stopped. Couldn't say it back and survive being told it was nothing. "You can say those things. So you can just say it." 

    Zosia looked startled, her lips parting, color climbing. "Say…?"

    Carol watched the blush rise and her stomach sank, because that was obviously someone caught avoiding confessing. "That I make you flinch. I get it. You don't owe me anything. You spent three months inside a body you couldn't control, people touching you, deciding for you. I get it. I'd flinch too." 

    The wind pushed grit across the pavement between them.

    "That's what you think?" Zosia's voice came out thin. 

    "Then what is it? Tell me what I'm supposed to do, because for ten minutes I had my arms around you and now we're back and the two-foot rule is in effect again and I can't—" She pressed her mouth shut. She'd told herself she'd wait, and she was doing this instead, doing it ugly and unfair with canned soup rolling down the driveway and her face a mess. 

    Zosia's gaze dropped to the reddened eyes, the salt tracks at her temples, the evidence Carol had been hoping the wind had erased.

    "You were crying," Zosia said.

    "I was doing a lot of things. Don't change the subject."

    "I'm not—"

    "You are, and I'm telling you it's not going to work right now because I've had a fucked up morning emotionally and I need you to either come closer or go further away. This—" she gestured at the gap again— "is killing me."

    She could feel herself veering, the tears fusing everything into one unbearable mass and she couldn't separate what hurt from what scared her from what she wanted, but the words were already coming.  "You left me thinking I was known. I spent a week talking around Helen because I thought you already had every angle and were just being gracious about it, and you didn't say anything. You just let me."

    "I told you." Zosia's voice was tight. "The first day. I said I only had what came through me directly. I thought that was clear."

    Carol stared at her. "Clear? And instead of checking, you just—assumed I'd decoded it. You do that. You assume and let people assume and then carry it yourself, like it's noble." Zosia's nostrils flared and Carol knew she was being a nightmare but the frustration was older than today. "I can't read your mind. Stop smoothing all the road for me and fucking tell me when you hit a bump."

    Zosia's chin dipped. "If I tell you why I flinch, it changes things."

    "Things are already changed! You told me this morning you were there, happy, wanting—" The word caught and the heat rose in her face and she barrelled on, aware this was the same freight train that had sent Zosia out the door yesterday and still unable to find the brake. "You came into my room and that was you, they weren't making decisions anymore and you still—" She looked at the desert instead. "And then you say things that sound like—and I can't tell if you mean it or you'd load anyone's groceries with that voice—"

    "I wouldn't."

    "Then tell me what this is! Because you never explained what you wanted." Carol knew she was being unfair, she had no right to say it, because most of their proximity hadn't been optional. "And I've told myself it's not my business, but I can't keep doing that. I can't be this close to you. It's killing me."

    Zosia's lip trembled hard, her teeth pressed down against the quiver, and it was an arrow, straight through Carol's heart. Her anger deflated instantly. There was the real thing, trying to surface again, and Zosia catching it between her teeth. 

    Zosia turned her face half away, toward the bike, one hand reaching for the seat, her first instinct to find a task, adjust a mirror. Her fingers found the knot on the rack and stopped there, holding it, doing nothing with it. Her feet were still planted in the same place they'd been when Carol started. 

    She'd been so braced for Zosia's stride to carry her across the yard like it had yesterday, she hadn't prepared for Zosia to stand there in the sun, hearing her through all the noise.

    "You're...still here," Carol said, no fight left in her. "Last time I did this you left."

    "I know," she said. "I shouldn't have." Her profile was rigid: the set line of her jaw, the cords in her neck pulled taut, her nostrils flaring on each exhale with a controlled rhythm. "I'll tell you, and when I'm finished you can decide whether you want me here."

    What a stupid fucking thing to say. Carol sat down on the curb because her shaky legs had made the decision for her.

    "When I touch you…when my skin touches yours," Zosia corrected, testing each word for precision before releasing it, "I recall memories. From when I was joined. Other people's memories of you."

    Carol heard it, understood it. "So that's why you flinch."

    "Yes." 

    Carol was sat on the curb with her elbows on her knees, the sun on the back of her neck. Her eyes went to the sky, which was enormous and blue and unhelpful. "Walk me through it," she said. "What do you have of me?"

    Zosia's brow creased. She had clearly prepared for a dozen reactions, and Carol calmly connecting the dots had not been among them. "What do you mean?"

    "I mean, there's what you dreamed, and what came through the touch." Carol counted two with her fingers. "Those aren't the same."

    Zosia looked at her for a long moment. Then her posture shifted—the rigidity easing into something more like a briefing.

    "The dream ones came first," Zosia said. "When I brought the grenade, you were talking about vacations. They pulled up memories of you, Helen's mostly, and ran them." She paused. "Most of those dissolved. I couldn't remember them. They went through me but I kept almost nothing."

    "Almost."

    "Only what I used. The ice hotel." Zosia's gaze dropped. "Helen was—it was intimate. I shouldn't have that."

    Carol looked up at her. "You saw us."

    Zosia nodded once, jaw tight.

    Carol rubbed the back of her neck. "What else?"

    "Freedom Falls," Zosia said this carefully, watching Carol's face. "Those were pulled through me when you asked me to, in the hospital."

    Carol knew this. "And then the touch?"

    Zosia's jaw tightened. "Those weren't in the dreams. They're from everyone, none from Helen, just random people. Your cousin, college, a girl in a storage closet, fans. Across your whole life."

    Carol heard an inventory that was more than the nothing she'd assumed for an hour but a lot less than everything, and any panic simply wasn't coming.

    At sixteen, anyone knowing any of it would have crumbled her. Even the Carol who married Helen had kept most of it locked in a room she only opened on purpose, when the audience was one person, the only person, she trusted. Her life had taught her that being known was the first step to being rejected, and Carol had believed Helen's argument in the daylight and doubted it before dawn. 

    The hive had blown the door off. Proven it unintentionally and at scale: total exposure, every ugly thing she'd ever done or had done to her, absorbed into the collective that loved her anyway.

    A few fragments in Zosia's head barely registered.

    "I thought you already knew all of that. I've been assuming, since you woke up after the first dream, that you had everything." Carol rubbed her jaw with her thumb and shrugged. "This touch thing is different how?"

    "I thought—" Zosia faltered. She had clearly prepared this moment to withstand anger, not a shrug. "You don't mind?"

    "Mind is a strong word. I'm not thrilled about my trauma being available at a fingertip, no. But I was being surveilled by a half-alien consciousness that knew my gynecologist's point of view and my childhood fear of garbage disposals. I've had zero privacy for three months. This is what you've been agonizing over?"

    Zosia looked winded. "I didn't want to—You thought I had everything but I've been operating on the opposite. I thought you understood I had almost nothing, and this would cross a line that hadn't existed before."

    "So I was performing for nothing, and you were saving me from something I didn't care about. We are…impressively shit at this."

    Zosia's exhale was audible. Her hand was still on the cord but her grip had loosened. She glanced at Carol then away again. "I told myself I was protecting you." Zosia's thumb ran along the cord, a small repetitive motion that looked involuntary. "But I was afraid."

    "Afraid of what?"

    Zosia took a breath that shuddered visibly through her chest. "That you'd be angry that I knew, or that I kept it from you. That it would—" Her hand released the cord and gripped the edge of the seat instead. "That you'd look at me like the first day, before I seized, and I'd deserve it."

    Zosia's jaw was clenched so hard Carol could see the muscle jumping, and her eyes, still turned away, were glassy with tears held at the rim by what looked like sheer will, and the effort of holding it in was visible in every tendon. Carol had never seen her like this. The joined Zosia had been immaculate, even at the end, every feeling smoothed before it could accumulate enough to spill. Then she'd seen fury, and the fights on the sofa and yesterday had been sharp enough to cut glass, but through all of it Zosia's composure had bent without breaking.

    Carol had been yelling for the real Zosia and here she was—more honest than any version Carol had known—and the breath she'd been holding left her in a rush that hurt. "Zosia," Carol heard it come out of her mouth softer than she'd ever said it, softer than she'd known she could make it. "Hey." 

    Carol pressed her palms hard against her own knees because the alternative was reaching for her. Zosia had asked her not to, and now she knew why, and the very fucking least she could do, after everything, was that.

    The sun was in Zosia's eyes and Carol wanted to block every harsh thing in the world from reaching that face, which was melodramatic and exactly the sort of impulse she used to mock, and she stayed where she was because she wouldn't be tall enough to block the light anyway. Goddamnit. 

    Zosia's nostrils flared on a breath that came in too fast and went out uneven, and Carol saw the tears spilling before Zosia could catch them. Her jaw clenched and the muscle jumped and she turned her face away toward the empty street, one hand coming up to press against her mouth, and the effort of keeping silent was visible in every line of her. Carol watched her fight it, undone by the absence of anger, crying because Carol hadn't recoiled, and felt the thing she'd been refusing to name shift, becoming weight rather than motion.

    "It's alright," Carol said, and her voice came out low and nothing like the woman who'd been shouting two minutes ago. "Zosia. It's okay."

    Zosia's chin turned. Her eyes were wet and furious about it. "I thought you'd feel violated again, and you'd already been through—" She gestured vaguely at the air, meaning everything. "I saw things you never chose to share. Things that made me angry. For you." Her voice cracked on the last word, and Carol had never heard her voice do that before either.

    Carol looked at Zosia standing in the sun with tears on her face, angry on behalf of a child she'd never met, and thought: you gorgeous, principled, infuriating idiot. Keeping this inside for days because you thought I'd be ashamed, and the whole time I was thinking you flinched because my hands reminded you of awful shit.

    Carol's heart was hammering and she didn't know why because nothing bad was happening. Something good was happening, probably, if she could get her body to stop treating all strong feelings as incoming fire.

    If Zosia could stay there and say the hard thing, Carol could give her the stupid thing back. "I thought you were afraid of me," Carol said. "The flinch. I thought your reflex had, I dunno, filed me under danger. Because of what I did to you. The grenade, the drugs, the— " she waved a hand uselessly so she wouldn't have to say it.  "I thought touching reminded you of all that."

    Zosia pressed her hands against her eyes, and her shoulders shook once with either a laugh or a sob, and the sound she made split the difference. "No, Carol," Zosia said, muffled behind her hands. "That wasn't it. Not at all."

    The corner of Carol's mouth pulled sideways before she could stop it. She huffed a laugh, and Zosia dropped her hands and looked at her with an expression of helpless incredulity. 

    "We're so dumb," Carol said. "I swept clean floors. I organized the freezer alphabetically."

    Zosia exhaled hard. She wiped her eyes with her thumb and forefinger, pinching the bridge of her nose, and sniffed once—a sharp, pragmatic sound that was trying very hard to be the last word on the subject. Her jaw unclenched. She took a step forward and sat criss-cross next to Carol.

    A roadrunner appeared out of a bush, and crossed the cul-de-sac, indifferent to the emotional rollercoaster occuring on the curb.

    Carol turned to her. "So what happens when it triggers? Does it hurt?"

    "No." Zosia tipped her head back. "It's disorienting. Lots of angles at once, with temperature and sound and feeling, and I can't choose what comes." She paused. "And then it stops, and I'm standing in your kitchen, and I know things about you that you didn't tell me."

    "Does it only happen with me?"

    "I don't know. Manousos and I haven't tested it."

    "You don't want to hold Manny's hand. Understandable."

    Zosia's mouth twitched and trembled. 

    Carol found the grocery bag behind her and grabbed a bottled water. The seal cracked loud in the quiet street. Carol couldn't touch her. She could do this. She set it on the curb beside Zosia's knee, and returned her own hands to her own legs.

    Zosia didn't pick it up immediately. Her breathing changed—one ragged inhale, then a slower exhale—and after a moment Zosia's fingers closed around it and she drank, and Carol watched her throat move and looked away. 

    "Alright," Carol said. "Here's where I am. I don't care that you've seen me and Helen, and I wish you hadn't seen the camp, for your sake, because it was a shitty fucking place and nobody needs that. But the idea that you've been torturing yourself while I thought you were scared of me—" she sighed. "I could've just asked. We could've had this conversation days ago."

    Zosia finished the bottle. "I could have told you."

    "You could've told me."

    "I thought I was protecting you."

    Carol didn't hold it against her, because she understood now how good it felt to call the cowardice kindness when you genuinely cared.

    "I know," Carol said, "but for the record, I don't need to be protected from my own past. You can't show me a room I haven't already slept in." She rubbed under her eye again. "Next time something's making you miserable, just tell me. You still know like ten languages. Use one."

    Zosia huffed a laugh. The rigid set of her shoulders had loosened. 

    "Any other hivemind secrets you've been white-knuckling?" Carol asked. "Clearance sale. Everything must go."

    Zosia considered. Then she shook her head. 

    "Good." Carol exhaled. Something eased in the street, or in her, or both. The confession had spent itself, and she'd absorbed it, because they were facts about her own life and she'd already survived all of them.

    She stood up and crossed to the grocery bags. She picked them up and held them against her hip and looked down at Zosia, who was still sitting with her eyes red and her hair falling loose and the leather jacket hanging open, looking like she'd just put down something enormously heavy. 

    Carol could feel the last lock loosening, and felt both wildly unsure and unwaveringly certain. She had no idea what she was doing, but at the same time, knew exactly why she was.

    "The girl in the gym closet," Carol said. "Her name was Becky Markham. We had sex in there in ninth grade, and she told everyone I assaulted her. I went to Freedom Falls the next Friday." She looked at the bag in her hands. "She married a woman in Scottsdale, the last I heard, so she can go fuck herself." 

    Zosia looked up at her. Carol shrugged. "Figured you should have my version." She felt the full weight of her own stupidity and something else she was not going to name while standing on the curb holding bags of beans. "I want to tell you," Carol said. "The stuff you haven't seen. I'd rather you hear it from me than from a handshake."

    Zosia smiled small, and crooked. "I'd like that."

    "Alright. Now get off of the ground. You're going to ruin your—" Carol looked at the leather jacket, the dusty denim, the boots. "Actually, you're fine. But get up anyway." Zosia stood. Carol had taken the heavier bags before Zosia could. "I've got these."

    Zosia looked at her, softer than amusement. "You don't have to—"

    "I know, that's the point." Carol hoisted them and went up the driveway, nudged the door open with her hip and held it with her shoulder for Zosia to pass through. They set everything on the kitchen counter, high noon sunlight blaring through the window. Carol ran a hand through her hair again, but it was officially beyond help.

    Zosia looked at her for a second. "Your hair."

    "Yeah," Carol said. "I've accepted defeat."

    "It suits you." 

    Carol's hand stopped. She hadn't been fishing. Zosia had already turned away, opening the cabinet as if she hadn't just said it. Zosia found the Shrek mug and set it on the counter and pulled down the plain white one for herself. 

    Carol picked up hers and held it out above the counter, "Here." Zosia looked at it then looked at Carol. Her hand reached for it and hesitated an inch from Carol's fingers. "Take the mug, Zosia."

    Zosia's fingers closed around the ceramic, and Carol pulled her own hand away, no contact. The distance between their knuckles had been a coin's width. Carol felt it in her whole arm. She pressed her hand flat against the counter and left it there, giving the feeling somewhere to drain. 

    Zosia looked at the mug in her hand and her face eased.

    "Nothing?" Carol asked.

    "Nothing."

    "Good. That's good. Decaf for me, please," Carol managed. "Or I won't sleep for a week." Zosia held up the jar between her thumb and forefinger at distance, as though it might be contagious, and her nose twisted up. "Try not to look so visibly pained."

    "The pain is mine to manage." Zosia set the kettle on with a sigh. "You'll have your decaf."

    Carol stood in the too-bright kitchen. The noon light hit every surface Helen had chosen—the tile, the counter, the backsplash. The woman at the kettle, too—Helen's parting gift, her last hunch, picking beans like she was defusing a bomb, two beans put back for reasons nobody else on Earth could audit. 

    The house had held years of marriage, then a week of contraband peace, and now this, weirder than grief or imitation: Zosia fully herself, spooning Carol's decaf like she planned to be appalled by it again tomorrow.

    Three months ago she'd lost everything at once—Helen, the world, the future, the ordinary assumption that tomorrow would resemble today—and Carol had spent the weeks after expecting nothing except to keep going until she didn't, kept upright by the grim spite of being the last difficult woman standing. She'd spent months enduring time.

    The three weeks with joined Zosia were the only ones that hadn't felt like a sentence to serve. Happier than she had any right to be, and she'd known it, and couldn't stop picking at it. Happy, and still killing time, waiting for the catch that had eventually come.

    That Zosia had never once raised her voice, or left the room, or said something she didn't mean or failed to say something she did. This Zosia fought and ran away and came back, knelt on Carol's bed shaking with anger, said those plain things and then flinched at a sleeve, and the gap between all the signals had gone unexplained, because Carol hadn't asked properly and Zosia hadn't offered. They'd fought over it twice already. Somehow one whole person was no less complicated than seven billion of them. 

    But Zosia was here, inspecting beans by some ridiculous internal standard Carol would never access, and Carol was here, and the fights hadn't made either of them leave. Carol had been waiting for the walkout, but the door had opened and closed several times now and Zosia kept being on the inside of it. 

    She'd used up her luck with Helen. That was what she'd believed, that she'd got more than she deserved the first time. She'd never even imagined a second round. But Helen had apparently bet on Carol one last time, and Carol was starting to think she owed it to all three of them to stop treating every good thing like a test that was supposed to fail.

    The beans hit the grinder with a sound like gravel shifting underfoot, and Zosia's hand cupped the lid, palm curved. Carol stood in her destroyed hair with the groceries half-unpacked and thought about whether she could have this. The coffee frown, the cardigan theft, the sodium snobbery. Every stupid morning.

    Zosia blew a strand of hair out of her face, missed, blew again, Carol breathed out with her and the fear left too, easy as that. The most disorienting part wasn't that it didn't scare her, it was that she was suddenly glad. Happy to realize she wanted more time. To live again, after all.

    Between unpacking the paprika and the peanut butter, Zosia's hand stopped on a jar. She turned it in her fingers to read the back label, and Carol saw her nose wrinkle. 

    "Have you had it?" Carol asked.

    "I've read the label. That's enough."

    Carol took the jar from her and placed it on the shelf where Helen's Marmite had always lived, second shelf, because she'd eaten enough of it to wear a groove in the wood. Her fingers held the shelf and she left them there for a second. 

    "Fun fact," Carol said, and watched Zosia smile at the phrase. "Helen was obsessed with it. She'd eat it on toast with an amount of pale American butter that would make your European heart sink."

    For the first time she hadn't braced for it to hurt—the past tense—and the kitchen stayed ordinary around her. Zosia looked at her with such dignified horror, effortful in its composure, that Carol huffed a laugh, and that was the whole of it. Zosia had turned back to the bag, hadn't made it a thing, and so it wasn't one. It made it easy to keep going. Carol shelved two more cans and Zosia lined them up, rearranging, alphabetizing, heights descending. She had opinions about everything now—and the thought caught on something Carol had been assuming without examining. 

    Zosia no longer had a million Wycaro readers in her head. Somewhere between her correction of a fantasy author's fake physics and recognizing a dagger from a shitty sketch, she'd started assuming Zosia's encyclopedic familiarity was a whole readership's supplement. It hadn't been. Every time I re-read.

    "Wait," Carol said. "All that Wycaro trivia. That was just you, knowing it. How many times did you read them?"

    Zosia turned with her back to the counter and looked at the ceiling. "I had a lot of spare time, and a professional interest in fact-checking."

    Carol grinned. "A professional interest." She leaned against the counter. "In romance novels."

    "I had opinions."

    "You had opinions multiple times." 

    Zosia's blush deepened and she pushed hair behind her ear with impatience that Carol was about to read as stop—but Zosia's gaze came back down to her, dark and embarrassed, and Carol remembered. I like how you look at me. Said with Carol's fingers inside her.

    "What else did you fact-check?" Carol managed, meant to sound teasing and instead came out like she'd been hit in the head. Zosia was still looking at her and the ratio of eye contact to functioning brain cells was becoming untenable.

    "The ships slow after dark." Zosia's voice had steadied but her blush hadn't. "Sand does pack tighter at low temperatures. Did you research that?"

    She had not. She had written 'the slipsand thickened in the cold' because it sounded moody. 

    "It's fantasy," Carol shrugged, her brain half mush. "I just imagine it." The words came slower and lower than she'd planned, and Carol felt the sentence reshape itself in the air between them. Zosia's lips parted, and the kitchen was quiet. 

    Carol broke first, ending a dare neither of them could win without touching. She forced herself to turn back to the groceries, able to form a sentence now she wasn't looking. "Well enough to convince a sailor I know what I'm writing about."

    "But—the displacement," Zosia said, reaching for solid ground. "The granular sheer—"

    "I needed a word that wasn't splash."

    Zosia closed her eyes. "The hull resonance—"

    "I hit a pan with a wooden spoon and described the sound."

    Zosia opened her eyes to look at her, stricken, and a laugh broke out of Carol, graceless and snorty, and it cracked the tension. Zosia's composure buckled into a half-smile.

    Carol was a landlocked fraud who'd imagined it all from a thesaurus, Zosia had lived inside the real sound and been seemingly stirred by Carol's saucepan. All that world under her boots, and she'd still found Carol's worth taking with her. She didn't know whether that said more about her or Zosia. There was probably no helping either of them. They'd just lived on opposite sides of the same sea, one inventing it and one crossing it, each apparently convinced the other had the more admirable job.

    Her face was getting hot again. Ridiculous.

    Zosia's read of it all was more generous than the text deserved, because she had no insider knowledge now, either. "Did you ever look up interviews? Behind-the-scenes stuff?"

    "I read the books," Zosia said, as if this distinction mattered. "I didn't follow the—what is it, fandom. There's no wi-fi at sea."

    She'd read the books so carefully and never once Googled her. Carol found this unbearably charming. She was well aware that charming was not the word and turned to the cabinet before it could show on her face.

    "The original ending of Stormshadow," Carol said instead, sliding the dark roast onto the shelf. "Raban dies."

    Zosia's hand stopped on the can she was holding. "What?"

    "First draft. He went down with the enemy ship. I'd already written the second draft of it with the plank instead, because I knew Val would shoot it down, obviously, and she lost her mind, but I was serious."

    "Who's Val?"

    Carol turned and Zosia was looking at her blankly, hand still mid-air holding a can of soup not knowing who Val was anymore. Carol smiled again. "My publicist."

    Zosia set the can down, label forward. "Why did you want to kill him?"

    The question was so direct, and so genuinely curious, and Carol let it loose. "Because I didn't think he deserved to survive," she said. "At the time."

    Zosia held her gaze and didn't flinch, and Carol watched her not flinch and opened the next cabinet and kept talking.

    They made a very late lunch. Carol stopped thinking about where her hands were relative to Zosia's and just let them be hands doing a job, making a meal, which was either progress or exhaustion and she'd take either. After they'd eaten and washed up, they stood at the counter with the dishes behind them and Zosia set her hand down near Carol's and left it there.

    The inch was a canyon and nothing. Carol's pinky twitched and she locked it still. She didn't look down. She let it exist, the most deliberate inch of countertop in the western hemisphere, and was deciding whether to say something or die when three knocks hit the front door. 

    Except this time they kept going—four, five, six—and kept going. "For fuck's sake," Carol muttered, and carefully pushed off the counter and went down the hallway. 

    She pulled the door open and Manousos arranged his face into a smile. "May I come in, please?"

    "What the—I take it back. This is worse. Barge in next time—mi casa su fucking casa, I don't care anymore."

    Manny stepped past her with no response, which was so predictable Carol had already left the doorway wide enough. He had sand on his boots he didn't dust off and he set his dirty fucking backpack on the living room couch, asshole, and unzipped it. 

    "How was the recce? Make any friends?" Carol asked.

    He took out two chunky black devices. Walkie-talkies. Carol stared at them like he'd produced two live fish.

    "Good," Manny said, which was all he intended to say about it right now, clearly. "We talk about it later. First this." He placed one device in front of Carol and one in front of Zosia, who had appeared through the dining room entryway, posture up like she'd been called back to duty. "From the ambulance," he said. "When we go, these are the link when we separate." He tapped the one nearest Carol. 

    "When we separate," she repeated.

    "Any plan has too many steps. We don't stay together." 

    Carol opened her mouth, closed it, and conceded the point with a flick of her jaw. She looked at the walkie-talkie and saw approximately fourteen buttons, two dials, two switches, the only Spanish word she recognised was MENU. "Great."

    Zosia had already picked hers up. She turned it over once, checked the battery compartment, flicked a switch.

    Manny was already zipping his backpack and looked at Carol. "Test. Learn. You need to be able to use under pressure." He shouldered his bag and turned toward the door.

    "Wait, that's it? You're not going to give me a tutorial? Maybe a pamphlet?"

    "Zosia knows radio." He glanced at her for confirmation. Zosia gave a nod. "She teaches you. I have work." He left and the front door shut behind him.

    Carol turned to Zosia. "Right," she said. "So you've used these before."

    "Every day. Have you?"

    "No," Carol said. "I mean—I used the wired one in the police car. I've seen them on TV. How hard can it be?" She picked it up. It weighed more than she expected. The plastic was warm. The button layout defied all logic. "Which button is… the talk one."

    "Push to talk is here." Zosia's index finger found the button on the side. "Hold it down while you speak. Do you want me to show you?"

    Carol's first instinct was yes, put your hands on mine. That wouldn't be happening. Zosia had called her resourceful once—but show me right now would be a near-contact sport. She forced a shrug. "I can figure it out." Carol pointed at a dial. "What's this one?"

    "Squelch. Don't touch it."

    "Squelch?"

    "It filters static. It's set correctly."

    "Squelch," Carol repeated. "That's a word."

    Zosia's lips did the thing where they settled for the corner twitch. "It is."

    "What does this switch do?"

    "Monitoring mode. Don't touch it."

    "And this one?"

    "Sub-channel tone. Don't touch it."

    Carol turned the device over. The back had a label in Spanish she couldn't read.

    "We should test range," Zosia said. "If you go to the balcony and I go down the hill—"

    "How far?"

    "Far enough that we can't talk normally." Zosia looked toward the front windows. "I'll walk past Manny's. You stay upstairs."

    "Alright." Carol clipped the walkie against her hip like she'd seen people do in movies and went upstairs.

    Carol stepped out onto the balcony, squinting. The late sun put a gilded edge on everything, and the cul-de-sac looked almost habitable—the brush lit to copper, the dust suspended and glowing like the air had been shaken. 

    She watched Zosia emerge from the front door and walk, leather jacket catching the light. Her stride was even, the gait of being trained to walk rolling decks—and maybe a runway model. 

    Zosia passed the shipping container and her head turned toward it briefly. Manousos moved around the ambulance, opened a side door, rummaging. It was parked at the curb, dull under red dust.  He didn't look up as Zosia turned to walk past it, backwards, facing Carol, and she raised the walkie to her ear.

    Carol raised hers too. She pressed the talk button. Static erupted, loud enough to make her jump. "Jesus—" She jerked the device away from her head, and tried again. "Okay," Carol said into the walkie. "Testing."

    Silence.

    Maybe the volume was too low, or too high, or— she twisted the dial and the thing emitted an angry chirp. She smacked it and pressed the button. "Zosia? Can you hear me?"

    Only static answered her, crackling, and then her own voice echoed back faintly.

    Zosia's voice came through a second later, with a tinny compression. "You're on channel six. Go back to four."

    Carol looked down. "I was trying to turn the volume up."

    "That's not the volume," Zosia said, calmly. 

    "I know that now." The screen showed more numbers than six that could have been a channel or a frequency or the meaning of life for all Carol knew. "I'm on channel—" The static surged as she twisted the other dial— "fucking—" More static— "How do people use these?"

    She squinted down the street. From the balcony, the helicopter's shadow cut a long score across the pavement. Zosia walked backwards past it without pausing, though she looked up at the rotors for a second. "You moved to channel three."

    "How the hell do you know that?"

    "Because I've found you, broadcasting on channel three." 

    Carol stared at the little screen. She was an adult with two degrees. "I'm a novelist."

    Zosia's voice warmed. "Yes."

    "I'm allowed to be bad at modern technology."

    "This isn't modern." Zosia was further down the street now, holding the radio to her ear with the ease of taking a phone call.  

    "Okay, see, that's worse," Carol said. "You're telling me we used these in, what, Vietnam? And I still can't—" Static swallowed the rest and Carol's hand clenched. She glared at the plastic rectangle and smacked it again. 

    "Carol," Zosia said, and her voice had a different quality through the speaker now—the trained calm of real responsibility for other people's lives. "Stop slapping. Press, release."

    Carol raised her walkie and let out a breath she hadn't noticed she was holding. Found the button. "Hello," she said, formal, like she was leaving a voicemail for a doctor's office. "Are you there?"

    "I can hear you. Turn the volume dial down."

    Carol fumbled the dial. "How about now?"

    "Better. You're holding too hard. Lighter touch."

    She was, in fact, strangling the device. Maybe it deserved it. She relaxed her fingers and tried again. "Is this—can you hear me?"

    "Clearly."

    "Clearly good or clearly I can hear you making a fool of yourself from two hundred feet away?"

    "Both."

    Carol snorted. "Great," she said, "Because I'm about to throw this thing off the balcony."

    "Do not," Zosia said, instantly.

    Carol could just about see the entrance to the community garden, and if she squinted hard, Zosia standing next to it. At this distance she was a figure, details lost.

    "Can you see me?"

    "Yes."

    "Wave." Zosia's figure lifted one hand. Carol waved back, feeling ridiculous. "This is weird." Her hands were sweaty. She wiped them on her jeans.

    "Now go to four."

    Carol carefully returned the dial to four. She pressed the button and felt the small red light against her finger. "There. I'm on four."

    "You're coming through. Well done."

    Carol could hear something warm under the briskness, and unable to shut herself up: "Tell me you're proud of me."

    Static. "Don't push your luck."

    Carol laughed. Zosia had shifted—she'd draped the leather jacket over the fence and stood in the white t-shirt with one hand resting on the post, her weight easy on her back foot, chin lifted. 

    Raban at the rail, overcoat slung over one shoulder, watching the horizon. Carol had drawn a crappy reference sketch herself—the posture, the angle of the head. She'd been writing from imagination then. She hadn't met the model yet.

    "You're good at this," Carol said.

    "I use radios," Zosia said, and it was almost a dodge.

    Carol leaned against the balcony. "I know, I meant… the teaching part. Dealing with me."

    Zosia was quiet for a moment. "I was put here for it."

    She meant her naval calling, training juniors through instrumentation. Or maybe the other thing.

    "This is weird," Carol said again, quieter this time. "Talking like this."

    "Like what?"

    Zosia was a figure against the garden, and Carol was a figure on a balcony, and the only thing connecting them was sound.

    "I don't know. Just voices. I can't see your face."

    "Is that bad?"

    It was easier because the face was a weapon of mass distraction and without it, Carol could actually think. It was harder because she couldn't confirm what Zosia was doing—no jaw to track, no flush to interpret, the corner-twitch or the full smile. Every signal Carol had been reading into all day, gone dark, replaced by two hundred feet of cooling air. "I can't see you judging me for holding this thing upside down."

    "I wasn't judging."

    "Bullshit."

    "Okay, a little," Zosia admitted. "But fondly."

    Fondly. She knew what face Zosia was doing—the left corner, the slight narrowing, the tilt. She knew and couldn't see it and the absence gnawed. "Your poker face is terrible, by the way." Shut up shut up shut up shut up. "Every time you're trying not to smile, you do that thing."

    "What?"

    "The corner lifts. On the left side."

    Silence through the static. "You've been paying attention."

    "Yeah. Well." I like how you look at me. Carol cleared her throat. "Okay. So. We should have codenames."

    "Codenames?"

    "Yeah, for the mission. We can't just use our real names over the radio. That's—that's not secure. What if they're listening?"

    "They aren't,"  Zosia said, and Carol could hear the smile in her voice.

    "They might have scanners now. We should be smart about this."

    A longer pause. "Okay. What are our codenames?"

    Carol hadn't actually thought this far ahead, she'd just wanted to redirect her train of thought and keep talking. She wracked her brain. Barbarossa, Desert Storm, Eagle One? 

    She looked at the mountains in the distance turning pink in the late afternoon light. "I'm... Desert Rose."

    The pause was judgmental. "Desert Rose?"

    "It's a real plant," Carol said defensively. "They grow here."

    "It's cheesy."

    "I write romantasy," Carol pointed out. "It's—fine, it's shit, I know." Carol drummed her fingers on the ledge, casting around for something less crap. Simple, military, mission-y. "Captain," she said, and pressed the button with the confidence of recovering from a fumble. "I'm Captain." She leaned on the balcony, the concrete cold against her hip. "Now you pick."

    "I'm not picking a codename."

    "Okay, you can be 'Commander', because you are one." Carol stared at Zosia's dark silhouette, holding the walkie like it was an extension of her hand. She gulped.

    Manousos opened a side compartment on the ambulance and pulled something out—tools, maybe, a med kit, Carol couldn't tell. He glanced briefly at Zosia, then at the house, then went back to work. He'd probably rather chew glass than participate in codenames.

    Zosia still didn't reply. Carol held the talk button again. "Commander." Carol's pulse kicked up and her belly dipped low and she told it to stop. "Do you read me?"

    Carol waited. Below, she could see Zosia's figure shift stance against the fence rail. "I read you. Don't—" A brief crackle— "call me that." 

    "You choose then."

    Carol watched the distant figure shift again. Zosia's free hand went to her hair—the impatient tuck. She was thinking about it. "Raban."

    Carol's hand tightened on the walkie so hard the plastic creaked, her heart doing something crazy and her brain doing less than nothing. She made herself press the button. "Raban?"

    "Is that okay?"

    "Yep." Too fast. "That's—it's—very fitting, obviously." She released the button and pressed her forehead against the walkie. The hot plastic burned. She deserved it.

    "Better than Desert Rose." Carol smiled. Zosia's voice came through, and Carol could hear a note of smugness. "Raban copies, Captain."

    "Ugh, don't say copy."

    "It's correct procedure."

    "It makes me feel like I'm in a bad action movie."

    "You would survive a bad action movie. You have the right instincts."

    Huh. "You think I have good instincts?"

    "I think you have very good instincts and very bad impulse control."

    Carol smiled into the walkie and was grateful nobody could see it because it was huge and pathetic. Above the mesa, the sky softened—peach into lavender into a deep bruised violet. Carol huffed at herself and then, because the radio made it easier, said the other thing that had been pressing. "When we're separated. The plan. How bad is it going to be?"

    Zosia didn't answer immediately. "The VLA isn't complex, but it's big. Manousos will brief us. There will be positions to hold, timing to coordinate."

    "But I have no spatial awareness. I get lost in grocery stores bigger than my Sprouts."

    Zosia let out a laugh and Carol froze. 

    She'd heard this one before. 

    Glarsh wah-zonk-a, Carol had said, and the same laugh had escaped, surfacing for a half-second. Unable to do anything inside what steered her, Carol had made her happy, despite everything. Here was the proof. Carol had made her happy.

    The laugh had already faded from the speaker, but not from her. She tried to replay the sound in her head, unwilling to let it dissolve. Zosia had laughed, then and now, and Carol had caused both, and she was holding four ounces of plastic when she wanted to be holding the source of that laugh—the whole beautiful person. She'd have to settle for static.

    "You'll be fine. I'll walk you through it," Zosia said, and her voice had settled. "You won't be alone."

    Helen's laugh was gone. She would never hear it again. She hadn't recorded it, had never thought to, because she'd thought it would always be there. Carol pressed the walkie against her heart and held it with both hands as if the sound of Zosia's laugh was still inside, something she could keep, and looked out at the cold desert. 

    "You'll stay with me?" Carol asked, and meant the channel, and more, pressing the button hard enough to bruise.

    "Yes."

    The last streak of stubborn sun gilded the horizon, and then Carol watched it let go.

    She leaned forward against the balcony wall. Zosia still had one hand on the post, the jacket thrown over her shoulder. Raban at the taffrail. Captain on the quarterdeck.

    Carol closed her eyes and exhaled hard. "Okay," she said. "Okay, I believe you." She swallowed. "Captain acknowledges no need to worry. I'll be fine."

    "You will."

    It should've ended there. The test was done, the channels understood. They could go back inside, resume the careful proximity. 

    Carol stayed on the balcony and held the walkie and said nothing. Below, Zosia didn't move either. The impulse came and Carol recklessly let it run. "I'm glad you're here," she said, releasing the button. 

    She watched Zosia's figure shift and Carol thought maybe she should clarify. She didn't mean the whole improbable chain she'd already admitted she was glad for. She meant here, in the real and difficult world, unjoined and opinionated and dreaming things and choosing to stay with Carol and be a person anyway. A whole, flawed person, who she couldn't touch and had been falling for in fragments—a shipyard memory and a surfacing laugh and a sound in the dark—since before she knew there was anyone to fall toward.

    "Me too."

    Carol closed her eyes again and when she opened them the light had gone another shade. The air had cooled enough that goosebumps climbed her arms. The walkie was still pressed against her chest with both hands, plastic damp in her grip, and she scoffed at herself. "Getting cold out here."

    "Go inside."

    "Yeah."

    Neither moved.

    Above them, too soon, a crescent moon—a fingernail of white visible hours before it should be, hung above the garden. Carol looked at it and then at Zosia's figure below it.

    She could say it now. She could press the button and say: I love you. I love this you, who fights with me about chickpeas and corrects my fantasy physics and handles ropes and radios with twenty years of muscle memory and still blushes when I say your rank. I wrote you before I knew you existed and I'm afraid of the mission and I'm afraid that the best thing in my miserable new life is a love story I'm too much of a coward to finish. I love you, and it started with mango ice cream, and I somehow knew it then.

    She could say all of it. The radio made it possible. The anonymity of voice without face, the merciful absence of Zosia's eyes—it was the safest she'd ever be. Her lips parted. Her lungs were full. The words were there, three of them, ordinary and annihilating, they would travel the distance and reach the person they'd belonged to all along.

    "Zosia." 

    "Hm?"

    She'd never been a words person. The irony of this was not lost on her, given the career. But the big things, the real ones—

    "Nothing," she said. "See you inside." She released the button, exhaled and pressed the walkie against her thigh, hard, the plastic edge digging into denim.

    She watched Zosia push off the fence toward the house, until she passed below the balcony and out of sight. The moon hung over the garden. Carol looked at it and felt an idea form. She stood there for another minute in the cold, and then went inside.

    Zosia was filling the kettle, and she didn't look up when Carol entered, but the line of her shoulders was soft. Carol set her own walkie beside Zosia's on the counter—side by side, like two sleeping animals—and then Manny barged through the front door with his map rolled under his arm and a look on his face that was, for him, animated.

    "Findings," he said. "Sit down. Both."

    Carol looked back at Zosia who had already straightened, hands leaving the kettle. "We just got in," Carol complained.

    "Bring your coffee." Manny was already at the table. Carol exhaled through her nose. She picked up Shrek, already filled with decaf without Carol noticing or asking, and followed. 

    Manny spread everything on the table and Zosia came to sit beside her, six inches between their elbows, and all three of them went through it together. His map of the site was hand-drawn, sketched in pencil—lines of circles arranged in a Y-shape across the page, three arms radiating from a hub, then access roads, fencing, what might be power lines.

    "Three arms," he said, tapping each in turn. He pulled out a second sheet showing a sketch of a building from two angles. "Center is the control building. One road in, one road out." 

    Carol looked at the map and saw herself alone on one of those arms with a walkie-talkie and no sense of direction and her shoulders climbed.

    Zosia's hand moved to the map. She was telling him about sightlines. Her finger pointed to the central building and traced outward along the northern arm, and the gesture was so steady Carol's breathing slowed without deciding to. Zosia told him about timing—how quickly someone could move between arms on foot. Manny asked another question and Carol listened to the rhythm of their exchange and felt the panic thin. 

    "Is there power?" Carol asked. They both looked at her.

    He frowned. "The array is transmitting. Power is on."

    "Right, but is there power for us? Lights in the building, outlets for your equipment or whatever? If they cleared the facility, then they don't need it, and they conserve power. They might have shut down everything except the dishes."

    Manny's pen stopped. He hadn't considered this.

    "We need a generator," Carol said. "Just in case." She could hear the difference in her own voice. Last week she would have said fine, tell me what to do. Today she was arguing for contingencies, a plan that accounted for things going wrong, because she wanted to be on the other side of it now more than ever.

    Manny wrote something and glanced at Carol with an expression she suspected was approval.

    They talked through timing, positions, sequence—nothing locked, everything provisional. Carol made herself speak. She argued for buffers between each phase. Manny resisted the margins. Zosia backed Carol without fanfare. It almost felt like a plan, or something half-formed, at least.

    The conversation shifted and another sheet was unfolded—his own signal recordings, annotated—and Zosia was already cross-referencing them against the existing notes, her finger tracking between two pages. They started talking about what could replace or disrupt the signal, and the source, and Carol followed for about twenty seconds before the vocabulary outpaced her.

    Carol sat with her decaf and let them go. 

    She watched Zosia's hand trace a waveform, and Manny leaning in with that grudging nod when something had earned it. A few days ago this would have stung—the shared language she couldn't speak and the science she couldn't touch. She looked at Zosia now, absorbed, one hand anchoring the page while the other waved in the air, and felt something simpler. 

    She let them run for another few minutes, then pushed her chair back. "I'm gonna leave you to it."

    Zosia glanced up. "You don't have to go." 

    "I know, but you're about to say 'heterodyne' again and I can feel my soul leaving my body. I've never understood hetero anything." Carol picked up her mug. "Getting some air." 

    Manny didn't acknowledge her departure. Zosia stared at her and Carol gave her a look that meant to say it's okay and probably gave away closer to I'm going to go do something and you can't ask what. Zosia watched her for a second longer, then turned back to the readings. 

    Carol rinsed Shrek in the kitchen, set him on the rack and stood there, listening to their voices from the table; Polish-accented English and Colombian-accented English meeting in the middle. Then she went upstairs.

    The telescope was heavier than it looked.

    Carol had forgotten, which was dumb, because she'd insisted on hauling it with no help from Helen, from an antiques fair in Connecticut to the rental car, with both arms and a bruised hip five years ago. It had lived on the windowsill since, accumulating the fine desert grit that got into everything. She wiped the eyepiece with her shirt sleeve and set it on the blanket.

    The community garden occupied the start of the cul-de-sac and garden was generous. A few raised planters held the holdouts: stubborn herbs turned silver, some brittlebush curling at the tips, a line of palo verde whose bare branches made a lattice against the last of the light. The rest was gravel and chippings.

    Carol unclipped the walkie from her belt. Zosia would be in the kitchen by now—Manny gone thirty seconds down the street and the kettle already filling. Carol could've set a clock by it. She pressed the button and held it and thought of every awkward thing she'd ever said into a phone receiver.

    "Hey." She released the button, pushed it again. "Come back to the garden. Whenever you want. I've got a—thing. Outside." She closed her eyes. A thing. Outside. Hemingway wept.

    The walkie crackled. The reply came faster than expected.  "A thing?"

    "Whenever you want," Carol said again, which she'd already said, and fooling nobody. Carol clipped the walkie back before she could make it worse.

    She moved the cooler to the left of the blanket, then to the right. She adjusted the angle of the telescope, which she'd pointed at nothing in an artisan fashion, and smoothed a wrinkle from the wool that would come back the second it was sat on. She smoothed it again.

    The ice cream had been in the back of the freezer since yesterday afternoon. Zosia across the street at Manny's for hours, and Carol alone in the house again, ears still ringing with everything they'd said, too wired to write, too guilty to drink, her hands needing a job. The mango had been cut up in the freezer since the day before it had gained any significance, from their first trip to Sprouts. Then the fight happened and Zosia left and Carol stayed in her kitchen with her hands stained gold and sticky to the elbows, eaten none of it.

    Footsteps on pavement. She wiped her hands on her jeans and sat down too fast and banged her knee on the telescope. "Ow, fuck."

    Zosia came around the fence in the jacket, hands in her pockets, and slowed when she saw.

    Carol had never been a saying words person. She'd made a mixtape instead of telling Helen first. She'd written Wycaro because she couldn't even say my teens were a pile of shit to a therapist. She slept in hospital waiting rooms, ate food she hated, stopped planes on the tarmac, survived church wedding services, driven through tropical storms. Carol did things, made things, lugged heavy brass objects across a gravel lot at sunset and arranged them on wool blankets and hoped to God the message got across.

    "It's not earning its keep collecting dust." Carol arranged herself with elbows on her knees, attempting to act normal. "There's stuff in the cooler. Whenever."

    Zosia stood at the edge of the blanket, studying the telescope, and then she sat, cross-legged, leaving the careful gap. The wool creased. Carol didn't smooth it.

    "You set this up," Zosia said, mostly a statement.

    "While you and Manny were talking about propagation curves. Nobody noticed."
