    "I noticed," Zosia said, as she rested her hands on her knees and looked up. The sky had deepened while they spoke, the indigo pushing from west, and the first real stars were showing into points, two of them doubled in the brown of her eyes. Carol watched Zosia's face go still and open. The same expression Carol had seen in her office, when Zosia had stood in front of the map and forgotten to guard herself.

    Carol bit down on the urge to say something but it came up anyway, of course. "When I did this before. Stargazing. With—before." Carol picked at the blanket fringe. "I wanted information for the whiteboard. Behind the Wycaro five stuff there's another list I was making, for the mission. The virus is from another planet, and I thought, y'know, what better way to ask than—" She could hear herself and stopped.

    "You suggested the stargazing date to collect intelligence."

    "It wasn't a date."

    Zosia's eyes went from the blanket to the cooler to the brass telescope, and her eyebrows rose a fraction.

    "It wasn't the same," Carol said, defensively. "It was for the whiteboard, the mission, and— well, alright, I was trying not to look at you—at them. I don't know which pronoun to—God." 

    "You're doing fine."

    "They walked me through finding Kepler-22. Very patient."

    "You complained the entire time," Zosia said, fondly, and Carol realized that Zosia was remembering it too. From the inside. She'd been underneath the whole time, watching Carol complain her way into wonder, through glass. "It was nice," Zosia said. "From where I was."

    Carol had to look at the sky for a moment. "It was." She'd be a liar if she said otherwise. "But I set this one up because I want to do it with just you. Who can complain back." Her neck went hot.

    "Good."

    Carol could see the edge of a real smile being held down, and the effort made Zosia's cheek hollow slightly. She had to look away again and the sky was useful now so she gestured at the telescope, because if she didn't redirect, she was going to say more dumb shit she'd told herself she wouldn't.

    Zosia moved to it and crouched, adjusting the barrel. Her knee was an inch from Carol's.

    "What's your favorite?" Carol asked.

    Zosia looked up from the eyepiece. "Star?"

    "Mm."

    "Polaris," she said instantly. "You find north and everything else orients."

    "Practical."

    "Yes."

    "Very you."

    Zosia smiled this time and went back to the eyepiece. "On Albatros, in the winter everything froze, your hands on the rail, even your eyelashes if you stood still. The air was so cold it'd burn your lungs. And the stars—" She tipped her head further back from the scope. "You don't get those in port. At sea, the whole sky opens. Billions. You feel very small and very awake." Carol had heard this, or a version of it, in the bathtub. She kept her mouth shut. "On clear nights they keep going below the horizon in the reflection, no line between sea and sky. It feels like you're sailing through them." Zosia paused, as though she'd heard herself. "It's—good for star fixes." Her hand went back to the barrel.

    A thread hanging from a cloud, now the sky opening over the sea. Carol had worked harder for worse lines, and Zosia said them by accident whenever she got going. The story was good the first time and better now, and she could've listened to a hundred more.

    "Polaris doesn't move," Zosia said. "Everything else rotates around it. First thing after every watch, I'd find it right where I'd left it. I taught my junior officers how to calculate bearing from it and they preferred GPS. Thought I was old-fashioned." Zosia looked at her sideways, "I just like knowing where I am without any help."

    Very you. Carol could've said that again but it would have been the fourth time today and at some point a lady notices. Zosia especially. "Open the cooler," Carol said, instead.

    Zosia reached over. Carol watched her lift the lid, see the container, and Zosia's hand stilled. Her lips parted and closed. She didn't look up. 

    "I made it," Carol said, to fill the silence. "While you were at Manny's yesterday. I had the mango in the freezer since—well, you were there." She wasn't going to explain it. She'd told herself she wasn't going to explain it. "Something—happened when you told that story. I saw you and I said this morning I didn't know and I didn't know I knew but I—" She stopped. Her dumb mouth had done it again.

    Zosia still hadn't looked up. She pulled the container out and held it in both hands, looking at it. Her fingers pressed into the frost. Carol could see her breathing deeply, and she was quiet long enough that Carol knew she'd said too much and was going to have to throw herself into the nearest planter. 

    Then Zosia said, "Technically, you recognized me at orgasm first."

    Carol blew out a sound between a laugh and a groan.

    "You brought it up," Zosia said, and her ears were red but she was smiling, eyes gleaming and dimples in her cheeks, unrepentant. 

    "I regret it." 

    "Giving me the ice cream speech or the orgasm?"

    "Both. Neither. Open the damn thing."

    Zosia peeled the lid off. The ice cream had softened, golden and dense, and the smell hit the air between them—too sweet for the desert. Carol watched Zosia's throat move. 

    Zosia took a spoon and scooped. Carol dug her fingers into her kneecap and told herself to look at the sky and looked at Zosia's mouth instead as she tasted it, willing the flavor to be right, to be enough, to say what she would fumble. 

    There was a micro-nod, a slight furrow, and the corners of Zosia's lips pressed together around the taste. Then her eyes opened and they were bright and focused entirely on Carol's face. "Better than the shipyard," Zosia said. "Like the real thing." 

    Carol exhaled. "Yeah? A ten-year-old's palate is a low bar." 

    "You cleared it." Zosia set the spoon down. Her other hand reached and stopped on the blanket, an inch short of Carol's hip, then came back to her own lap. "Thank you," she said, quiet enough that the desert could've taken it. 

    Carol tipped her head back and blinked at Polaris until it steadied, and in her periphery, Zosia took another spoonful then set the container down between them.

    Carol got the second spoon from the cooler and dug. She'd done a decent job, actually. Three mouthfuls in, the brain freeze had crept into her ribs, the stars were filling in overhead, and the desert air was dropping fast. Carol shivered—the full-body kind—because she failed miserably at hiding anything, apparently. Zosia shrugged the leather jacket off without a word and held it out. 

    "I'm fine," Carol said.

    Zosia kept holding it.

    Carol shook her head. "I'm not cold, I'm—"

    Zosia's eyebrows rose.

    "Fine." The leather was warm from Zosia's body and smelled like the collar she'd pressed her face into on the highway. She pushed her arms through the long sleeves and tried very hard not to bury her nose in it again.

    Zosia's bare arms in the white t-shirt were a whole new problem. The sleeves rolled to her shoulders, the cotton pulling when she moved. Carol tracked the dip at the base of her throat, and then forced her eyes to the stars.

    Carol gestured at her without looking, chin up. "No tattoos. Sailors get tattoos. Isn't it practically contractual?"

    Zosia glanced down at her own arm. "People looked at me enough. Didn't want to give them more to read."

    Carol nodded. A woman in a male profession, controlling the surface of herself. The less she offered, the less they felt entitled to. Made sense.

    "I thought about it once," Zosia said. "For Sasha. He had an anchor on his bicep, very traditional and ugly." The fondness in her voice was unselfconscious. Zosia glanced at her and away. "He was the only person I ever told."

    Carol's spoon stopped. She looked at Zosia, who was now looking at the gravel between her knees.

    "That I'm gay," Zosia said, to the ground. "Sasha knew. Manousos knows. That's the whole list." 

    Carol let out a breath. She'd hoped, she'd told herself not to project, and here it— "Wait," Carol said. "Manousos?"

    Zosia's ears went pink. "It wasn't—he was there and I was—"

    "What is his security clearance? How does he get this intel before me?"

    Zosia's mouth was twitching dangerously. "When I told you about Sasha, you said a beard. I didn't know the English word for it before everything." The humor dimmed. "I didn't say the rest."

    "I was too chicken to ask."

    Zosia tapped her fingers on her jeans. "I should've told you. You were right, earlier. I've spent my life letting people assume. Hard habit. And we tried hard to be convincing."

    The guise of a life that passed inspection. "It's—I get it."

    Zosia looked at her. "I wouldn't choose it now."

    "The bearding?"

    "Being straight," Zosia said simply. "But if someone had asked me then, I'd have taken the switch. Everything simpler."

    "I'm—I'm glad that I'm—yeah." Carol rubbed the back of her neck. "It gave me Helen. I got to be someone's wife and she got to be mine, and it was—I was lucky." For a moment Carol just let that be true, without reaching for the grief or the list of ways she'd failed. She'd been lucky.

    "You were," Zosia said simply. "That's why I didn't say it. I thought it would make things worse."

    "Same reason you didn't tell me about the touch thing."

    Zosia's jaw tightened. "I'm bad at this. At—telling people things. In the Navy, it wasn't—you don't. I couldn't. And then the hive just knew." She shrugged.

    "That's what's so great about them, right? Skips the telling part. You touch me and just—get it. Whether either of us want to or not." Zosia went still. Carol looked at the two feet of distance between them. Thought about what would happen if they didn't keep it. "You'd see everything, and I've got—there's a lot of shit. I don't—"

    "I know." 

    Carol glanced up and Zosia was looking straight at her, calm and unafraid. I'd let you see. The whole disaster. She trusted Zosia would still be here after. 

    Two feet of blanket. She could close it in a second and Zosia would know her again and Carol would never have to find the words for any of it. Her hands ached with how easy it would be. 

    She pulled the jacket tighter. "I don't want the shortcut," Carol said, roughly. The collar pressed her jaw. "I want to be bad at it. I want to fuck it up and start over and leave things out and have you ask." 

    She could feel her own heartbeat in her ears. The silence lasted about a thousand years. Zosia nodded. "Okay. Tell me something."

    Carol exhaled a long breath and scrambled through material, past every good memory and reached for the bottom drawer. 

    "Well, I never came out either," Carol said, to the sky, which was easier. "I mean, Helen's family knew, and her friends. My readers didn't. It wasn't—I could have." She'd had the option of deciding it wasn't worth what it might cost her commercially. A door she could open or close. Zosia had never had a door. "Nobody was going to court-martial me," Carol said. She picked at the jacket cuff. "You had to hide. I did because the books sold better, which I'm realizing is a position you can take when you're lucky to be married where it's legal and nobody's going to throw you off of a boat."

    Zosia shrugged. "My career mattered more too."

    Carol didn't have a comeback for that. The stars were sharpening, and Zosia didn't press for more than Carol wanted to say. 

    Carol watched as she turned her head back to the sky, her throat exposed to the cold, smiling as her eyes joined the dots of constellations.

    Like beauty wasn't a trick, like she was allowed to notice it even when the world was ending. Carol had spent all of her life acting like joy was optional, like it would always be available later, once the work was done, the crisis past. Helen had tried. Later had been a lie. 

    Lucky. 

    Her mouth was already opening to burn it down.

    "I did something," Carol said. Zosia looked back down at her. "A DUI. Years ago. It was—" Carol scratched her head. "I was trying to parallel park to pick up Helen from a publishing thing. Hit a fire hydrant. Cops were right there. I blew whatever the limit was and Helen had to leave to bail me out of the actual police station."

    "Carol—"

    "The hydrant was fine, by the way. My pride was the only casualty. Helen didn't speak to me for two days."

    "You could've told me anything," Zosia said, exasperated. "You went straight to the closet and the criminal record." Zosia's thumb ran along the edge of the spoon. Then she set it down. "A bar. East coast. It was raining."

    Carol frowned. "Huh?"

    "One of the memories I got," Zosia said carefully. "It was after a signing. A woman, a fan, very drunk. She was making a scene, being… entitled. You paid for her cab."

    Carol stared at her. The memory surfaced, barely and blurry: a woman in a red coat, hammered and grabbing at Carol, once Helen went to the restroom. And when she'd said no to a hug, the phone came up recording and bitch came out and Carol had stood there silently and thought right back at you. Then she'd caught up with the bitch, about to get in her car, thinking about the rain, the highway, the hydrant, Helen at the station.

    "That's who you are," Zosia said. "That's what I—" She took a breath, looked at the stars. "That's what matters."

    "Sure." Her own voice came out bright and wrong. "Your turn. Tell me something. Anything. What was your worst parking job?"

    Zosia eyes narrowed at her. She'd heard the swerve and was choosing to let it happen. Zosia picked up her spoon again and considered. "Well, I myself can parallel park a patrol boat."

    "Show-off."

    "In a crosswind in the dark."

    "Insufferable."

    "Probably while over the limit," Zosia added, an eyebrow raised, and Carol leaned back on her hands through the jacket sleeves and let the laugh out. The ugly snorty one.

    Zosia watched her do it and then she stood to reach for the telescope. One eye to the brass, one hand making corrections, the movement so fluent it barely qualified as effort. "There," Zosia said, and stepped back.

    Carol stood up and leaned forward, hands in her back pockets. Through the eyepiece: a single point of white light, steady, while everything around it drifted and shimmered in the lens.

    "Polaris," Zosia said, behind her. "Right where I left it."

    Carol pulled back. Zosia was standing with her bare arms loose at her sides, the white tee looking blue in the starlight, face tipped up, reading the sky with a smile. Fully present. Entirely herself.

    Zosia looked down. Whatever she read on Carol's face made her chin dip. Her eyes dropped to Carol's mouth and came back up and the two feet of cold desert air between them caught fire, a line drawn in the dark. Carol felt it run through her, everything in her strained toward it—every cell in her desperate little heart—and she could feel Zosia holding still on the other side. 

    She could cross it in a second, the most charged piece of ground Carol had ever occupied—she wanted to grab Zosia by the neck and close the gap, kiss her until the stars went out, wanted it so badly her hands shook, and she stayed. She stayed. She was in love with her and it was the size of the sky above them and it was enough. That was enough for now.

    Zosia turned back to the telescope and adjusted the barrel to the moon and said, over her shoulder, "Look."

    Carol crossed the distance. Leaned in close, an inch between her shoulder and Zosia's waist. She put her eye to the brass and looked. Zosia didn't move away, and neither did she, and the leather jacket smelled like someone Carol would not allow herself to touch, and the stars went on burning.

    Chapter 9

    Chapter Notes

    Hello Albuquerque! Apologies for there being no update last week, I had a kinda near-death experience and have been processing it... healthily. Good news is that includes writing, so we roll, but may explain some melodrama u read. These final few updates may be fortnightly while I find my feet, or not.

    A beach underfoot. Thailand—known before the image resolved. Limestone karsts rising from water, sand fine enough to get into everything.

    The cotton against her calves flapped unfamiliar. Zosia had worn dresses annually, at officer's balls where Sasha had zipped her in and the fabric had been stiff as rigging; dress whites and mess dress and formal dresses, all uniforms.

    "Which one do you want?" Carol had asked, earlier, holding up the hangers. 

    Zosia had never asked herself which one she wanted, never thought about what it felt like because the point had never been feeling. The point had been appearing. 

    "Whichever pleases you," she said, warm and easy, genuine and empty of what Carol was asking. Preference required a body that belonged to someone, and Zosia's belonged to everyone, and the question of what she wanted against her skin had never survived long enough to become an opinion.

    Carol had chosen the yellow one, holding it up against Zosia's shoulders, her head tilted, one eye narrowed. Zosia was wearing it now. The cotton moved when she moved, the hem caught the cooler sea breeze, and she could feel the air between her knees, practical for the heat, and underneath the sensation, a fact she had no practice naming: she liked it. The air found her shoulders, her back, the skin where a scar sat. 

    Carol kicked a piece of coral out of their path before Zosia could step on it, already forming a question about why Zosia had been chosen. Her hands moved while she asked, conducting her own sentences, and Zosia's thumb found Carol's knuckle to hold on, while the calibration ran underneath. There were true things that couldn’t be said.

    Helen had been joined, already leaving, open to all of them for the first and last hour, burning through her final reserves on a single task: plugged into billions of minds and looking for one. Carol would rage, resist, rather be alone, and needed someone she would want to let in. 

    She'd found Zosia and looked through her completely. Seen Wycaro worn soft, dog-eared and underlined, what Carol thought she'd buried, found and loved by a woman who'd buried it too. The life spent in uniform in lieu of living, costumed over the same wound Carol had dressed differently, both of them accomplished and neither satisfied because of it. Helen had seen that and the rest—someone stubborn enough, steady enough—and said her. If we’re going to do this, her. She already loves the parts Carol thinks she has to hide. 

    They couldn't deny a dying woman; couldn't weigh the risk of this choice against Helen's happiness in her last minutes, against Zosia meeting her favorite author, against Carol having someone at her door she might let in. Three comforts in one gesture, and they'd never be able to choose a less loving option. 

    They kept it. Carol couldn't have this, not yet, not until she was with them.

    Her mouth said something clinical and true—the number becoming smaller—that moved along the surface of the answer. 

    There. Out on the water, dolphins broke the surface. Beautiful. Let her have this. Watching it from inside the dream, feeling their attention swing toward the horizon with exactly the right timing, her hand releasing Carol's to point—she almost admired the calculation of it.

    Carol looked. The dolphins arced against the last of the light, silhouetted, and Carol forgot the sentence that had been left unfinished. Their appreciation was real, and whatever else they were doing too, they weren't performing that. The light went on going gold.

    Carol started talking about religion: the cruelty of a love that claimed to know her and use it to find her broken, then apologized for bringing it up and listed her flaws.

    "You're very easy to love," Zosia said. 

    Of course she was. It was self-evident, from the inside, because they knew it all—every occupied room, every small thing she'd done when someone was watching, every version of Carol that anyone had ever seen. The sentence was finished before it started.

    They forgot that Carol couldn't hear the rest of it. Zosia felt annoyed, like a muscle tensing. It added up, from inside, so obvious it didn't need saying. But Carol still lived out there, where you had to be told things, because no one could simply find them. 

    Underneath, pressing against the calm, she wanted to put her hands on Carol's face and say it again, until Carol believed it. To say the rest of it. The sentence that started with I and ended somewhere she couldn't get to, but Carol deflected, looked at the roots tangled in the sand, and they let her. The answer would keep.

    The beach’s humidity became a hotel bathroom’s. Zosia's body was in a bath that was too hot, her face pink with it. Carol across from her, wet hair curling on her neck, looking at Zosia over her knees, composing a sentence she'd never say out loud. Her gaze kept finding Zosia's mouth, the wet skin at her collarbone, and dragging itself back each time like she was scolding it. The worst liar Zosia had ever seen.  

    The steam on her skin, her own heart beating, Carol's eyes from across the water—each sensation hers first. Carol was asking, in the usual sideways manner she thought was subtle, about before.

    There was a short pause, a hand reaching into a pocket to check. "This body prefers cold water," she said, and then she was somewhere else too:

    A deck in the dark before sunrise, the stars not gone yet, her uniform collar scratching her throat as the cold wind cut through her. The smell she was searching for, salty and sharp, and the feeling underneath the smell: she was twenty-something again, and had a life ahead that was hers to spend however she chose. A future she could steer.

    They had the memory. They had everything, every morning she'd ever stood at that rail, the temperature in Celsius, the wind direction, the ship's heading. They could reproduce any fact of it. The feeling of having only one life to live was outside what they could enter.

    "I felt like I could do anything, then." She was here, herself, surfacing in the steam and Carol's attention. "I wanted to belong somewhere." You belong with us. She felt them reach and miss. Their belonging was total, unearned, not chosen by something that could've chosen otherwise, and they couldn't feel anymore why the difference mattered. 

    Carol reached across the water and they also moved to gently re-establish contact, to close a window they had opened. Carol's thumb found her pulse and Zosia wanted to say: that's mine, that's for you, but words were dissolving again before they reached her. 

    Zosia watched her fingers move to lace with Carol’s, and the handhold became another handhold, on the beach—became every handhold, one continuous gesture, each time Carol had reached for her. Twenty years of portside bars and dawn departures and never once had she had it, and Carol had no idea, and Zosia turned toward the warmth of the sun on the beach again and it was already a fireplace. Outside, the mountain was white and enormous and still. 

    "I keep waiting for it to go away and it doesn’t," Carol was saying, "And I don't want it to."

    Carol was describing something she expected to lose, and she was right. 

    They had extensive documentation of Carol's distrust of her own contentment, and they had used it. The warmth of these weeks, all of it real, and all of it also a managed ease, keeping Carol inside the feeling while the path towards her permanent peace continued elsewhere. Zosia had kept her content, held her hand and kissed her and fucked her and loved her, and every one of those acts had served the plan, and every one had been genuine, and the genuineness was the plan's best feature.

    The burn hurt as fresh as the first time, the love and complicity and grief, all hers, because it was the first time—she'd had it then, and was so sure now that she wondered how she'd thought anything else before. 

    She felt more separate than she'd been in any of the earlier dreams, and before, the blur had cushioned it—she could drift inside the overlap and not feel owned. Now she could feel the edges, being overruled and redirected, loving Carol in her own way and having no mouth to say it from. She could do nothing but watch from inside and feel it happen. 

    Carol asked how it worked, how the happiness functioned, what made it stick, like she was asking permission to trust it. 

    The hive took it for one more threshold on the way to peace. Zosia heard what Carol was really asking and wanted with all the force in her to tell her yes—keep this, your own happiness, as yourself—but nothing of her body moved. Her thoughts struck uselessly, beating on glass.

    You won’t have to wonder much longer. Carol would join them, and the happiness she was having trouble believing, this warmth by the fire, would simply be where she lived. The honeymoon was just the beginning.

    "You’re not talking about the joining, are you?"

    The answer should've been instant, but it stuttered. She'd never felt that before, a crack in consensus, a hairline fracture. The oxytocin had done something, day by day, that they hadn't predicted and couldn't name. Zosia didn’t smooth it over, or offer a truth that could've resealed the surface. Instead they let the silence do what it would do.

    They had found the loophole, the convenient omission, like water finds a crack. She'd been there, everywhere and nowhere and one among billions. Carol was going to ask, and they were going to have to tell her, and Zosia was going to be the mouth it came out of. The only honest and unavoidable thing was to feel it, with no honest separation possible.

    "My eggs."

    Through Zosia's eyes they'd watched Carol stare at Helen’s grave; they knew what those eggs meant—and through Helen they knew the rest—a life they'd once planned to get to eventually, a name they'd never had to pick.

    "If you loved me, you wouldn't do this."

    That's why we can't stop. Like standing in a lit room and looking out at the dark—their love was blazing and blinding and unable to see past its own light. Love as a constraint was foreign to them, to love her and not act was the contradiction.

    "Because… I love you."

    It came from Zosia’s mouth, in her voice, the first time, the only time she'd ever—and it was theirs. They loved Carol and were answering her accusation with the truest words, spent without permission, stolen clean through her teeth, laid at Carol's feet in the same breath as the stem cells, as the reason for it and every other thing they'd done to her while loving her.

    Carol heard it from her and didn't believe it.

    Carol's pain, intolerable, and they had made it, because the alternative was leaving her incomplete, which they also couldn't tolerate. Both true. No resolution. Just Carol's face, and what they'd done to it, and no way back.

    The helicopter lifted. The lodge got smaller. The mountain stayed exactly where it was, indifferent and immaculate, a beautiful thing that existed whether anyone was watching or not. Everyone had appreciated that, once.

    The dream widened past her body. She was at the antenna, boots on sand, and the dream held her there long enough for her to notice what had changed, and how.

    The new attachment: a spike, not a simmer, and now a dip. The hive had registered the absence, had felt the dip, and it had fed their feeling, deepened it, a tributary pouring into a river until the current was just current. Nothing to prove it had two sources. She could only tell her own water when it ran against—the glass was only visible when the light fell differently on each side.

    On the fourth day apart, Carol and Manousos left together. They tracked the ambulance. Then, collectively, in a movement that was not quite a decision, withdrew the drone before the destination resolved.

    They had been doing it in other ways. A windfall total in Balochistan, an updated transport route in Chengdu, a solar panel output in Lagos, kept local for an hour. Small self-imposed ignorances, accumulating like sediment on a hull; each one negligible, but the sum a drag on the heading that no one had corrected because no one had ordered it.

    They thought about Carol’s unknown destination and felt the compound feeling still building. The music, the painting—every tradition averaged, nothing left out—had been close and not enough. They understood why now: it described what Carol did, not what her doing it meant.

    So they tried once more. They imagined Carol's front door. Warm dark wood, carved panels. They could only see the door was beautiful because it faced them, because it was closed, because closing was what a door was for. The house filled the frame around it, background rendered only enough to locate it, and the rest allowed to fall away. Underneath, a thin line of yellow light, and through the rejas, the warmth broken into fragments by iron grilles. Proof of an unknown interior, living a life they couldn’t enter.

    This was what they were permitted. The outside face turned to the world.

    It was the right feeling, finally. Not the anticipation of Carol appearing but Carol's choice to remain behind the door. Their uncanny impulse to let it stay closed.

    Carol and Manousos came back three hours later. The ambulance pulled into the cul-de-sac carrying what the drone registered as books, contents unknown. They walked into the house without looking up. The door closed. The drone's eye watched, and waited, with a feeling it now recognised, for Carol to appear again.

    "Come by my house."

    Too fast, too raw. Zosia felt them process the request in fractions of a second: Carol's vocal pitch, her breathing rate, the ambient sound of a house with no one else in it. Carol had called, voice cracking on I want to see you, and Zosia was glad—selfishly, uselessly, to be called there again, to see her too. She had missed her every hour of each separation and each dip had changed her, small and stubborn inside the chorus, and changed them too.

    The ladder rungs of the antenna and then the helicopter came as they always had, the descent easy, no borrowed competence needed.

    Carol was standing in the doorway, pale and furious and alive. The relief of it hit before anything else could reach, before the guilt underneath and their strategic sentences. Zosia was counting the hours on Carol's face—every sleepless night visible in the skin beneath her eyes, the bitten edge of her mouth, the fists she was clenching to keep her hands from shaking.  

    She looked exactly as Zosia had seen her the first day with clear eyes—same stained sweatpants, shoulders braced for something terrible. Zosia was ending where she thought she'd started.

    Every cell that was still hers strained toward Carol, her ribs tightening like something had grabbed hold, and none of them moved. She wanted to cross the driveway at a run and her legs only walked at the pace they were given.

    She could only say the words they'd prepared: "I missed you," and couldn't separate the sources. Consensus moved her mouth, and the current carried her own voice, one among billions, without noticing.

    She felt the weight of the bag against her shoulder. Inside was what they had made for her, a gift they couldn't fully explain, and they didn't know if Carol would understand it. Words hadn't been enough, lately; maybe this would reach her differently.

    "We're sorry you were hurt." Zosia felt it leave her mouth and thought: I was sorry. That was mine too and it didn't help. She had been here for all of it—present, a passenger, feeling everything, steering nothing, and the dream was making her watch it again from the seat she'd sat in the whole time.

    The front room was dim with its superfluous newspaper windows, making the light gray and private. Carol's voice shook with confession, and they went quiet, checking options.

    "We aren't asking to win." 

    They'd wanted Carol joined, had planned and manoeuvred and loved her toward it with total devotion, and what Zosia said now was built from her own feeling, distributed then returned to her, still wearing her voice. A newer impulse than a plan. The bag on the chair held the proof.

    They were reaching for Carol to comfort her and she wouldn't let them, and they couldn't understand the refusal. Zosia had done it before—held her, touched her face, felt Carol lean into it—the wanting and directive had been nearly identical, and this was where it ended and she would never know now which it had been. 

    "If it works," Carol choked, "Will she remember?" 

    "She might be changed." 

    They couldn't promise Carol what would survive. The honesty was the closest they'd come to feeling fear—for Zosia, that the unjoining might damage her beyond repair, and regardless, she would be without them again. No body had ever left them to continue existing. 

    Zosia felt no fear. She was happy. She’d been happy since the pain that had been her baseline for years had lifted completely: the bliss of being carried, the relief of a body that didn't hurt and a mind that never had to be alone with itself. 

    And in this moment, the happiness had a name, because Carol was in front of her, the reason she was glad to be here at all, today and every other day she'd been called into Carol's orbit, and she could feel her own heart beating faster for it. 

    They were begging Carol to believe them, and Zosia wanted her to believe them. Her happiness was real. She needed Carol to know that, somehow, from the other side of all of it. "Right now I'm happy," she said, and the pronoun faltered. The hive giving her something true, or a woman pushing through.

    Carol was still shaking and this might kill Zosia and Carol knew and was doing it anyway, and Zosia should’ve been afraid, and instead felt only the radiant want to see eachother with nothing between them. She would take any odds for that.

    She knew she was being irrational, that love was doing this—turning a gamble into a gift, a lab rat into a willing volunteer—she knew and didn't care. This might leave her empty. She might wake up and not know Carol. She might not wake up at all, and if she didn't come back it would still have been worth it to feel it. 

    She couldn't say I know. I know what you're about to do and I'm glad, I'm so glad you're brave enough. 

    Carol's hands were trembling, and then not, because Zosia was holding them. The hive saw it as evidence of the suffering they could stop, someone who needed saving, who would be alone and broken otherwise, who required exactly what they were offering.

    We can't just watch you drown. They still couldn’t parse how the cure could be worse than the illness. They had to do it, for the same reason Carol had to do it.

    "And I can't let you stay like this, even if it means you hate me."

    Zosia, still in no pain, still glad—felt an answer that was only hers and always had been. The hive was running every possibility fanning out from this instant, and in none of them, in no configuration of neurons or damage or loss, was there a version of Zosia who could hate Carol. 

    Zosia had already gone to her knees, and felt everyone’s alarm at the risk, the narrowing distance between Carol's anger and the trigger. Carol knelt too, finally eye-to-eye, and underneath Zosia could only think one clear thing: there you are, close enough to see again, and I'd rather die on this floor looking at you for a chance. A life where I can touch you with only my own hands and mean it. 

    They were saying goodbye—the grip on Carol releasing, letting her go. They had loved Zosia with everyone they had, too, and this was them saying goodbye inside it, and they felt it as loss disseminated across continents. Zosia felt it the other way around—Carol's mouth, rough and brief and furious, the rest of the world disappearing. 

    Then Carol telling all of them—and Zosia's last thought before the signal shredded was that she'd heard it. Whatever came next, however empty she woke up or didn't, she’d heard Carol say it while she could still feel it, and then the current cut.

    Her body went somewhere they couldn't follow, every circuit blown at once, the network severing, then nothing. 

    Nothing— 

    and then something. Pulling in a direction that wasn't up, or down, but toward, and then—

    She woke up.

    She came back in the dark. 

    The guest bed.

    She lay on the mattress, her body feeling returned to her like it hadn't before, the weight of a self that was only hers to wear. The other mornings she'd woken with the sense of a report still half-read. This was different. She knew there would be no more. The record was complete, and she was the sole full copy.

    The hive had anticipated the wrong thing. She was more herself, before the years had gone narrow, lighter than she thought she could be again. The girl who'd stood at the rail dreaming had survived the woman who'd learned to button a collar over everything. Keeping her was the task. Every morning since, every frustration of the real world had been the same fight, against every old reflex to seal the hatch. 

    She got up. The house was dark, Carol's door closed, the hallway silent. Zosia moved through it without turning on a light, feeling the wall, and went out the back door in Carol's cardigan.

    The sky was turning. Not sunrise yet, but the orange band along the east meant dawn was close, the stars above it still visible but . 

    She walked until the yard ended in scrub, and then beyond the gate, into the desert stretching featureless. The air was dry and still and smelled of dust. Cold, too—colder than she'd expected, but a cold that had no moisture in it, that sat on her skin without settling.

    She couldn't tell if she was choosing a place with nowhere to hide or if she just couldn't be inside walls with this feeling. 

    She looked up and found Polaris. On water, it was the fixed point from which everything else could be calculated, but here was no course to plot. She was just a person standing in a place with no water and no heading, trying to make the ground hold still because everything inside her was in motion.

    The feeling wasn’t new. Zosia hadn't needed the latest dream to tell her that, but it had told her again anyway. They had taken her body and her voice and her autonomy and woven her through all of what they planned for Carol, and underneath all of that, her heart had gone on wanting what it wanted with a stubbornness that embarrassed her.

    The nothing after the seizure hadn't been empty. She couldn't recover the voice, couldn't even be sure there were words, only that she'd turned toward something, and she knew it was Carol. Just like she knew now when Carol was in the same room, before sight or sound confirmed it. 

    She could feel the pull of the house behind her, Carol somewhere inside it, sleeping or not, and the distance between them was the wrong distance, the wrong amount, fifty feet of desert was the most absurd distance in the world when she'd already crossed the other one, so Zosia walked farther away anyway.

    Her feet were cold. She looked down and realized she'd walked out in bare feet. She’d always chosen cold. Cold showers, cold mornings, the bracing clarity over the blur of warmth.

    Cold feet and not a shred of doubt. That got a laugh out of her. 

    That was new, or rather, old. She’d used to smile easily, and in the gray years between then and now Zosia had mislaid it and now she’d found it again. The hive had cleared the ground, taken the weight that held it down, and then Carol had walked onto it and been funny.

    She’d lived years on less feeling than one laugh. She'd worn the restlessness so long she'd mistaken it for purpose. She knew now, she'd just been searching for this feeling, and even if this was all she ever got, it didn't even matter whether Carol felt it back. To have it at all, to know she was capable of it, to feel it burning in her at five in the morning in a cold desert she couldn't navigate, had settled something in her that had been unsettled since she was twenty. 

    There had been a moment in the dream—Carol saying even if you hate me—when something had surfaced in Zosia that the hive couldn't touch and the dream had gone past quickly. 

    Her whole life had been motion, the next port, the next horizon; she had wanted the world badly, had gone and got it and it hadn’t been enough, and then Carol happened. How could she ever hate the shore she’d been swimming toward her whole life. How could she ever hate the answer to a question she'd stopped believing in. The word was so impossible it was almost funny.

    She was more likely to have died. Seizing on a mattress until her heart stopped again, stripped of her memory, her name, and whatever was left of her, of who she’d been before they found her—reading Carol's books and already turned toward her without knowing it—would turn toward her still.

    So when she heard the back door open a while later, she didn't need to look. A pause of silence—Carol deciding—and then footsteps.

    Carol stopped close enough that Zosia could hear her labored breath, which was closer than Zosia expected and farther than she wanted. She’d obviously dressed in the dark. She had pillow creases on one cheek.

    "You're out here," Carol said, sleep in her voice.

    "Yes."

    Carol didn't ask. The light was shifting, the orange band had widened into gold and the mountains ahead were gaining color—rust and ochre, a deep purple in the shadows. Zosia watched it happen and couldn't judge any of it. How far, how high, how long until the sun cleared the ridge. On a bridge she'd have known all three by instinct.

    "Those mountains," Zosia said. "How far?"

    Carol moved up beside her, hair still crumpled. She followed Zosia's gaze. "The Sandias? Maybe thirty miles as the crow flies. It looks closer—the light does something weird to distance out here."

    "No haze. Too dry."

    "I guess." Carol rubbed her eye with one knuckle. "You get used to it."

    Thirty miles could’ve been ten. At sea, she'd have known. Light refraction over water was predictable, governed by temperature gradients she'd learned in her teens. Here she had no idea.

    "What about the ridge to the north?" Zosia asked. "The lower one."

    "Jemez. Farther than it looks, too. Maybe seventy? Runs all the way up past Los Alamos." Carol pointed. "You can see snow on them."

    Zosia followed her hand. She was taking the bearing from Carol because she couldn't take one from anything else. She had nothing. Only Carol's voice and a landscape she couldn't read.

    "I miss the sea," Zosia said quietly.

    Carol glanced at her. "Yeah," she said. "I bet."

    They stood in silence.

    "The dream was the last one," Zosia said eventually. Carol went still with the effort of not turning to face her, not asking, giving her the side of her attention instead. Zosia looked at the mountains. "It went all the way to the end, the seizure." She paused. "I have all of it now."

    Zosia heard her swallow something, a question, probably, or several. Carol's fingers curled at her sides and released.

    "Was it—are you okay?"

    The question was so inadequate and so genuine that Zosia smiled for a second. Was she okay? She had just finished reliving eighty days of consciousness inside a body she couldn’t steer, had watched herself keep Carol warm and keep her captive with the same arms, felt what made her life worth living and what broke Carol's heart be nearly the same thing, without ever lifting a different finger.

    "I will be."

    Carol nodded. Zosia saw it in her periphery as a single dip of the chin.

    The complicity burned. 

    She'd known it was coming—Carol had told her about the stem cells the first day, before either of them knew she would dream everything else—but knowing it was coming and living it were different. She had loved Carol and served the plan and she had beaten on the glass and no sound had carried through because her mouth wasn’t only her own.

    Carol had given it back, and Zosia had just watched herself betray her.

    A stone had been pressing into the ball of Zosia's foot. She registered it now as a small point of pain, and leaned on it, keeping her in the present. Eighty days of nothing hurting. 

    Carol looked down. "You'll cut yourself on something. There's a better place to stand if you're going to keep doing this." She gestured past the scrub line. "I’ve sat out there before." 

    Carol hadn’t told her to come inside. Zosia looked where she was waving. A huge flat rock, shin-high, shining in the first direct light.  Carol started walking and Zosia followed her path, the ground kinder there. Carol knew this patch of desert, years of walking it, her feet finding the most packed ground without looking down, and being led by someone who had a heading let Zosia's shoulders drop.

    Carol stepped up onto the outcrop, turned, and her hand came out automatic. Zosia had been handed aboard a thousand times, in a hundred ports, and never wanted the help. In the first minutes returned to her, Carol's hand had caught hers and a knowing had come from nowhere. She knew why now. Carol's hand was the only one she’d ever wanted. 

    Carol withdrew it to scratch the back of her head. "Sorry. Habit." 

    Zosia had to step up on her own. It stung the scrape on her sole and her weight shifted for a roll the rock wouldn’t give. 

    "Before," Zosia said, to start. Carol looked up at her. "When I told you I was there, I said I agreed with them, that I was happy. That’s true. I wanted you to be happy, and so did they, and I couldn't tell where mine ended and theirs began." She paused. "But this dream I could tell when we disagreed. What they were doing was awful, and everything I felt had just run in the same direction."

    Carol was very quiet. The sun was climbing the ridge and the light was on her face and she didn't flinch from it. Zosia could see her listening hard, not racing ahead. "So you feel guilty for giving a shit."

    It flattened all Zosia was feeling into one blunt sentence, and the relief of being seen clearly made her huff a laugh. "I feel guilty for giving a shit because it helped them."

    Carol was silent for another moment, thinking. "They didn't purposefully make me lonely either. They just knew it, and thought they were helping. Same as whatever they knew in you." Carol’s jaw shifted. "It helped that I was scared enough to not look too hard for you."

    "You looked harder than anyone expected, and that's why they were happy to have the real thing underneath."

    "The real thing," Carol repeated, carefully, like she was handling something she wasn't sure was hers.

    "The care," Zosia said, steadier than she felt. She could feel the words she hadn't used, warm and heavy, wanting out. They'd used all three of them, from her own mouth as justification for everything Carol had reason to fear. She kept her mouth closed and let care do the work, bloodless and nothing like what she meant.

    "They thought they were making us happy," Carol said. "That's what makes it—" She made a rough sound. "They weren't being evil. They just never know when to fucking stop."

    "No," Zosia agreed.

    "Those fuckers," Carol muttered, bitter and almost fond, aimed at something vast and absent.

    Zosia laughed again. The plain profanity of it cut through more efficiently than any absolution could have, and she felt the weight start to shift, Carol shouldering part of it without being asked. 

    "I won't feel guilty for them," Zosia decided. A practical choice, made in real time, like any operational decision. She didn't have the luxury of guilt, misplaced or not, right now. There was too much else going on.

    "You shouldn’t," Carol said. She was still looking at the mountains, her face tight with something she was keeping to herself. Zosia could see her trying to turn it inward, to hear I cared about you and translate it into something bad. She watched Carol stop herself from saying whatever self-lacerating thought had formed.

    "Don't," Zosia warned, mildly.

    Carol glanced at her, caught. "I didn't say anything."

    "You were thinking it."

    Carol blew air through her nose. "Well," she said, shrugging after another few seconds of silence. "It's their loss. Efficient sons of bitches consulted my wife and accidentally hired someone I gave a shit about too." 

    Zosia smiled again. The knot behind her ribs she'd brought onto the sharp ground loosened. 

    They faced east together with the house below. The sun broke the ridge and the desert lit up all at once, and it was, she had to admit, not the sea, but beautiful.

    "I'll figure out breakfast," Carol said, after a minute. Not come inside. "Whenever you're ready."

    Zosia stayed on the rock. She watched Carol walk away, lopsided and bleary in an inside-out sweater, magnificent in the dawn sun—and Zosia’s heart went with her, a compass that had found a north, with no guilt left in it again, no complication beside the distance every cell in her body was constantly objecting to.

    She stayed outside for a while longer and the path back was less painful, partly stepping in Carol's footprints that softened the dirt, partly that her feet were learning and could read the camber. Not the sea, but a language, she thought, stepping onto the concrete of the back step, that she could probably learn. Zosia looked back at the desert, lit gold and enormous. She had time.

    Breakfast had been instant oatmeal and the previous peanut butter, eaten at the counter. Zosia finished her own and then scraped the last of the butter from the jar with a spoon.

    Carol sighed into her bowl. "God, I miss your omelets. The seasoning, the—" She waved a hand. "Whatever you did." 

    Zosia's face warmed. She remembered. Her hands cracking shells with the borrowed expertise of a thousand entremetiers. She’d been underneath, happy and stirring. Carol was letting her keep it, all of the compromised domesticity, as their shared history.

    "The trick was lower heat," Zosia said, because it was easier to say that. "But yours were good too."

    "Sure, but don't be nice about my eggs," Carol said, lightly. "It'll make me suspicious."

    Zosia gave her a look. Carol's chin was up. 

    "Carol." 

    "What, too soon?"

    It was too soon, for both of them, but Carol was doing it again—taking the violation and folding it down to a joke for Zosia to receive without it cutting, something she should smile at. She didn’t smile but she let it be. The oatmeal was gone, the kitchen was bright, and Carol was looking at her with expectation and wasn't pretending otherwise.

    "Thanks. For this morning." Zosia meant the attempted jokes, the rock, the breakfast. All of it. She left the sentence there and held her gaze long enough to make it clear.

    "Oh. Uh. Sure." The last word wavered. Carol grabbed her mug and drank the dregs standing up, set it down, and looked past Zosia toward the window. The sun was fully up and the light was different from dawn; whiter, the gold burned off, and the desert looked less romantic and more like what it was: miles of dry ground and no shade. 

    "Get dressed," Carol said. She was already rinsing her bowl, water too hot. "And put your boots on this time, you maniac. We’re going out."

    "Where are we going?"

    "The Rio Grande's twenty minutes away." Carol set the bowl on the rack and dried her hands. "It's not the Atlantic, but it's wet."

    Carol had insisted on driving. The bike stayed on the curb and went unmentioned.  

    "I can't believe we stole his ambulance," Zosia said. She'd objected in the kitchen and lost, and somewhere between there and here the objection had turned into amusement.

    "He stole it from a hospital." Carol wrenched it out of the cul-de-sac, thrilled with herself. "So it's as much mine as it is his." 

    Yesterday she'd put Carol on the back of the Bonneville to go to the store, and been privately smug at the elegance of the solution; an unimpeachable reason to have Carol against her.

    Today was different; side by side instead of stacked together, and Zosia found the loss didn't cost her. This time she could see her. Close enough to see the fine hairs at Carol's temple in the light, her pulse in her throat where her plaid shirt fell open. Far enough that neither of them had to manage it. No constant awareness of Carol's thighs bracketing her hips, her forearms locked across her stomach, her breath in the collar of her jacket. 

    The ambulance was a diesel manual and Carol was losing her fist fight with it. The clutch bit late, she wasn’t matching the revs, and the whole cab bucked when the engine bogged. Zosia diagnosed every error and held her silence for almost a minute. "Throttle before you downshift, it won't—"

    "I'm doing it my way." Carol's jaw was set, and Zosia bit the inside of her cheek and said nothing more. 

    They lurched through another residential stretch, houses closed and curtained, basketball hoops hanging over empty driveways. Through the open window the air cut through the white cotton of her boxy t-shirt, and in it, a mineral note that was either the river ahead or her wanting it to be.

    "It's the bosque," Carol said, answering a question she hadn't asked. "The cottonwoods along the river. There's a spot I know." Carol forced it down a gear for a bend, the gearbox shrieked in protest and the cab shuddered. "It's not pretty. I mean, parts of it are. It's not a park. It's just—" One hand came off the wheel, made a vague pass at the windshield, the road. "It's where the river is."

    Carol muscled up a gear and Zosia braced one hand against the dash as the transmission screamed and the ambulance kangaroo-hopped forward again. 

    Zosia inhaled through her nose. "You need to release the clutch slower."

    Carol looked down at the stick, looked at the road, and yanked it into third, the glovebox rattling. 

    "Anything else, Commander?"

    Zosia swallowed and looked out the window, and Carol drove the next half mile in silence before grinding another gear, the ambulance bucking hard enough that Zosia's water bottle rolled off of the seat. Carol caught it without looking and slammed it back.

    "Fine," Carol muttered, and Zosia was clearly not supposed to hear it and clearly was. "Tell me how it’s done." 

    "Throttle up, then shift," Zosia said, to the window. 

    Carol did as she was told. The gear slid in silent and the cab went smooth and Carol's eyebrows came up.

    "That’s better."

    "Don't patronize me."

    "I'm not. If you'd done it badly I'd have said. I did."

    Carol did it again. Smooth. Her hands were learning it already, resistant and then suddenly fluent.

    "Good," Zosia said.

    Carol glanced at her, and whatever she found made her sit a little straighter. "You could’ve told me ten minutes ago," she griped.

    "You were doing it your way." 

    Carol's mouth twitched. She downshifted for a turn and the gearbox purred. "Okay. That one felt good."

    Zosia looked out the window again and let the corner of her mouth do whatever it wanted.

    The trees came up, a thickening of shade where before the landscape had been open and sun-bleached. The air through the window turned over once more—the dryness gone, replaced by a vegetal damp, soil and leaf rot. 

    They pulled off into a clearing of dirt half hidden behind shrub. The cottonwoods stood around, gray trunks wider than her arms could span and deeply furrowed.

    Carol killed the engine, dropped down to the dirt, and looked back through the cab. "Coming?"

    Zosia stepped down, and then she heard it, under the birdsong, under Carol's boots in the deadfall: the sound of water, going somewhere, and every part of her turned toward the sound before she'd decided to.

    Carol was already at the trailhead, one hand flat on a trunk, looking back. The branches met overhead in a canopy that would've shut out the sun in summer and now let the winter sky through in long pale columns. The trail was a gap between the trees, narrow and turning, packed by feet that hadn't come this way in months. People who'd walked the bosque on weekends and thrown sticks for their dogs and been joined on a Wednesday in November and never come back.

    Zosia followed her into the trees. 

    "Okay. Worst city," Carol said, without turning around. 

    They'd been doing this since yesterday—trading favorites, dislikes, telling things she thought Zosia already knew and Carol had never asked.

    Zosia kept her eyes on the path, which was not the same as keeping her eyes off Carol. Her plaid shirt and the tank top beneath had ridden up on one side where Carol's arm was up for the branches, at the small of her back where the skin was flushed and goosepimpled.

    Zosia looked at the trees, the trail, at Carol again and accepted defeat. She stepped over a root. "Dubai. It was like a kitchen where nobody cooks."

    "Sounds like my publisher’s office," Carol said. "What about best?"

    Zosia considered. She didn't really have a favorite, but— "Istanbul." The call to prayer over the water at dawn, all the ships cutting the strait, a city built on the argument between two continents. "What about you?"

    Carol waved a hand. "I don't rank cities. They're all shit."

    Zosia waited patiently. She thought about what Carol had said on the blanket last night: I want to be bad at it. She would get there in her own time or not at all; pushing only made her circle.

    Carol walked a few more steps. "I hated New York," she said, eventually, to the path ahead. "Eight million people on an island that should hold about four, and every one of them is walking too fast and you're in their way." Carol pulled a branch back and held it. "And the subway smells like piss. I'd been saying I hated it forever. It was a whole bit."

    Zosia took the branch and Carol kept going.

    "Then we went. You guys lit up Times Square for me, every screen blazing ads to an empty city and there was—" She paused. "Nothing. No one shoving. No car horns or cab-window arguments. No seedy guys selling fake crap." Carol glanced back. "I took your hand."

    "I remember," Zosia said. They’d been so proud—all of it lit for her, the grand gesture received. Carol's fingers had closed around hers and they’d felt it as confirmation: she's happy she's with us. Zosia had felt their collective happiness and her own, indistinguishable; Carol's hand cold and holding on to her. 

    Carol nodded and faced the trail again. "I needed—because it was so empty—" She pushed through the trail. "I missed it. The noise. People being shitty to each other at full volume." She let go of the next branch too early and it swung back and Zosia caught it.

    They’d all read Carol's hand in hers as thanks, but she’d only been holding on because it unsettled her. None of them had known. They hadn't even mistaken fear for joy, they’d noticed and translated it to proof the gift was necessary.

    "So you don't hate people," Zosia said, to Carol's back.

    Carol's shoulders went up. "I missed the noise." Carol didn't turn around. Zosia watched as her neck went pink over her shirt collar. "Fine. Whatever."

    The trail curved and the trees thinned and through the gaps Zosia could see light, reflecting off a surface. Water. The Rio Grande spread before them gray and broad under the winter sun, wider than Zosia had imagined. Braided channels moving around pale sandbars. Cottonwoods leaning over the banks with exposed roots gripping the mud like fingers.

    "Come on," Carol said, and her voice had gone rough.

    She led Zosia down the bank, the ground loosening under their boots, sand and gravel shifting. 

    Cold air rolled off the water and Zosia stepped closer instinctively. Her breath went deep without deciding to, pulling it in, her lungs filling. What had been tense since she’d woken on a mattress in the desert released in a single exhalation.

    Carol had stopped beside her and wasn't watching the river. Zosia let her, she stood there with the water ahead of her and Carol's gaze on her, both of them equally welcome.

    At the bottom, the bank levelled into a wide sandy strip littered with driftwood and pale smooth stones the current had left behind. And there, pulled up on the sand with its bow still half in water, was a canoe. 

    Dull with weather, a length of frayed rope trailing from the bow cleat to a root. The hull was silted along the waterline, leaves collected in the stern, a paddle wedged under the thwart. Someone had moored their boat and then been joined, and left this behind, mid-life. The rope still holding. 

    Zosia’s hand found the gunwale and ran along it, the rivets, the keel line, the flex of the hull under pressure. She rocked it once, checking the weight and balance, and the motion went through her arms and shoulders with ease her body had always known, something that predated the hive and had nothing to do with borrowed skill. This was hers.

    She could feel Carol still watching her. Zosia crouched to check the hull. "It's sound."

    "You want to take it out?"

    Zosia looked at the river, gauging. Shallow, manageable, readable, not cold to her, but it would be for Carol. "Maybe later," she said. She stood and wiped her palms on her pants—Carol's borrowed leggings, which presumably ended at Carol's ankles but her own calves. "Sit with me first."

    "In it?" Carol eyed the canoe with suspicion and the clear and dear intention to conquer it anyway. She put one foot in fast and the boat lurched sideways and she froze halfway down.

    "It can't tip," Zosia said, smiling. 

    "Everything can tip. I've seen movies." 

    Zosia set a boot in and pinned it flat to the bed through the shallow. "Step where I'm holding it. Then sit, slowly."

    Carol did exactly that, and looked irritated at how well it worked. 

    Zosia stepped in easily and sat, facing her, folded her longer legs into the narrow hull and their knees ended up nearly interleaved, a problem with no dignified solution, and neither of them proposed one. 

    The canoe found its balance under them and stopped arguing about it. Carol let go of the sides reluctantly, to drink from her water bottle. "Okay, your turn."

    Zosia had a thousand questions. She chose the smallest. "First job."

    "Filing. Temp job. But I was fired inside a month for insubordination." 

    "Shocking."

    "Damn right it was." Carol pointed at her. "Don't take their side."

    Zosia felt the giggle come out before she could authorize it and Carol's bottle stopped halfway to her mouth. "What about you?" Carol asked, quieter, before she took a gulp.

    "I cleaned hulls during naval college." Her hands had split in the cold. She'd loved it. Every vessel was going somewhere she hadn't been yet. "A bit bigger than this one."

    "You went from cleaning boats to being in charge of them."

    "Seemed practical."

    Carol's mouth pulled like it was the most charming thing she'd heard all week. "Favorite color?"

    Zosia knew the answer instantly and couldn’t say it aloud. The gray that turned bright blue in sunlight. The color of Carol's eyes.

    Carol put up a hand to stop Zosia. "Wait! It’s gotta be—it's blue. Duh. The sea."

    Carol was so pleased with her own deduction—chin up, hand still out, triumphant—and she was wrong, and right, and Zosia sat in the warmth of watching her, not correcting her. "Yes," Zosia said. "Like the sea."

    Carol nodded, already moving on. Zosia held still and let the other meaning dissipate into the morning air, and it was true, Carol's eyes were exactly the color of open water on a clear day, when the light hit at the angle that made depth visible all the way down, when you couldn't tell where the sea ended and the sky began.

    "Yours?" Zosia asked.

    "I always say purple, obviously, but it’s green. Like old book spines, the cloth ones. Library green." Carol nodded towards her. "Like my favorite cardigan."

    "The one I've been wearing."

    "That would be the one, yeah. Is it comfortable at least?"

    "Very."

    "Great. Anything else you'd like? Kidneys?"

    Zosia could feel her ears going warm. The joke was more deflection and permission co-existing. "I can give it back," she said, calling her bluff.

    "No." Carol picked up her water and drank with forced focus and said, into the bottle, "It looks better on you." 

    The canoe should have been big enough and wasn't. The distance had contracted since they sat down, or maybe Zosia had stopped being able to measure it accurately, both equally plausible since the disorienting dawn. She could see the fine lines at the corners of Carol's mouth, the loose threads at the cuff of her shirt Carol kept pulling at.

    Zosia swung her arm over the side of the canoe because her hand couldn't go where it wanted. The water split before her knuckles and closed behind them, the cold climbing her wrist. 

    Carol cleared her throat and sat straighter against the thwart. "Okay. Favorite word," she said quickly, changing the channel. "Mine's fuck. The most versatile word ever. Noun, verb, adjective, infixitive, prayer. How bout you?" 

    Zosia could feel her face going helpless and fond and didn't try to fix it. "In which language?"

    "Yours. Polish."

    "I never thought about it." She thought about it. "Przystań?"

    "What does it mean?"

    "Harbor, or, more accurately, just—a place where ships come in."

    Carol nodded slowly. "That makes sense." Then she lifted her bottle. "Smacznego."

    Zosia's head came up. The word was wrong in several directions but it was recognizable, and Carol hadn’t learned it from them before.

    "Where did you get that?"

    Carol shrugged with studied casualness. "I have an app. I looked up some things yesterday." She was holding the bottle out like a toast.

    "You know that's for food." 

    Carol's hand stilled in mid-air. "What?"

    "Smacznego. It means enjoy your meal. Like bon appétit."

    Carol's face went through a rapid sequence of confusion, defiance, resignation. "I was saying it to my coffee before you came in this morning," she grumbled. "What do you say for cheers, then?"

    "Na zdrowie."

    "Naz—no. I'm keeping smacznego. I earned it." Carol bounced her bottle against Zosia's. "Smacznego."

    Zosia tapped it back. Carol had been whispering bon appétit to Shrek, alone in the kitchen, and the thought of it made Zosia so soft she had to look away at the mountains.

    "So how do I say something that isn't toilets or food?"

    Zosia looked back. Her face was open, expectant, her cheeks pink, and her eyes—the color Zosia had lied about a minute ago—she'd seen more shades of blue than she could name, and none of them had been that beautiful.

    "Miałam na myśli twoje oczy." 

    Carol frowned. "What does that mean?"

    "Try this instead—"

    "Uh, no, what did you just say?"

    "It's too long to explain."

    "It was like six words."

    "It’s complicated. Wszystko w porządku," Zosia said, briskly. "It means everything's fine."

    Carol stared at her, visibly deciding whether to push. Zosia offered nothing. Carol huffed. "Fine. Say it again."

    "Wszystko w porządku."

    Carol listened, brows knotted. "Fshistko…" Carol looked at her for approval.

    "The sz is—"

    "V-shit-ko—" 

    Zosia covered her mouth with one hand. Carol’s eyes narrowed in satisfaction at finding the detonator and she leaned forward, ready to press it repeatedly.

    "Shit-ko po-zodkoo," Carol said, deliberately mangling it, watching Zosia's face. "Fist cow—"

    The laugh broke through Zosia's hand and it filled the air and Carol watched it happen—the smugness dissolving.

    "That's it," Carol said, breathing hard. "I made you laugh. Before. I didn't know it then."

    "You did," Zosia said, laughter trailing off.

    Carol pressed her lips together. "Okay. Good." She cleared her throat. "So I have fist-cow down. What's next?"

    "That is not what you have down."

    "Teach me what you said, the long one."

    "No."

    "Why?"

    "Nie twoja sprawa."

    "Is that a new one? You’re teaching me a new one to distract me?"

    "It means none of your business." Carol made a sound of outrage that was at least half theatrical. "Jesteś niemożliwa."

    "Another one?"

    "You're impossible."

    "Yeah, I know what that sounds like in every language, the tone is universal." Carol pointed at her. "You owe me the long one. I'll find out somehow. I have an app for that."

    "Smacznego," Zosia said, correctly, and raised her bottle. 

    Carol’s eyes narrowed but she thudded their bottles. "Wait." She froze. "I still don’t know your last name. Jesus Christ. I called you Pirate Lady for two days and I never—what is it?"

    "Pszczelińska."

    Carol's mouth opened and her eyes went wider. "PISSY-linska?" She grabbed the canoe with both hands like she’d struck gold. "Holy shit. Commander Pissylinska," she said with relish. "That’s your actual name."

    "That’s not—it means beekeeper." Carol was enjoying this far too much. Zosia’s irritation had no chance against the grin on her face.

    "It means you've been pissy about everything since the day you woke up. My seating suggestion, my decaf, my tacking…" Carol was counting on her fingers. 

    Thirty years of people reaching for the same word. Pretty. She'd always set it down unopened, since it described a surface and nothing of who was beneath it. Then the hive had sanded every opinion down to nothing.

    Carol was still counting Zosia's objections, pleased and presenting it like evidence she was proud to have collected, "...my driving, my butter…"

    Zosia felt her ears warm even more and turned to watch the river filling her cupped palm, spilling through her fingers. She couldn't hold it.

    She flicked a handful of cold water at Carol. The arc caught her across the shins and she yelped. "Jesus! See what I mean? Your name’s perfect." 

    Carol grabbed at the river with a hand and flung back with no grace, half of it airborne and the other half running down her own arm. 

    What reached Zosia made her laugh and retaliate, and then they were both splashing and laughing and for a second Zosia forgot everything—the hive, the mission—and they weren’t immune and unjoined, just two idiots playing in a boat. The feeling so ordinary she almost forgot it was what had sang through seven billion neural circuits and glitched them. 

    She was the same person underneath. The happiness she felt right now was the same the hive had found in her and amplified. They hadn't made it, just made it unearned, stripped of the mortifying vulnerability of sitting with red ears wanting someone you can't touch to call you Pissylinska again.

    Carol was lunging for the water now and nearly tipped them. 

    "Sit down, you’re going to capsize—" 

    "You started it!" 

    "And I'll finish it." Zosia dipped her whole forearm and dragged it flat across the surface. 

    Carol scrambled backward so hard the canoe rocked the other way. "You like cold! Not fair!" 

    "Then surrender." 

    "Fine." Carol dropped to her bench, water dripping from her fingers, looking victorious though she’d plainly lost.

    A gap opened in the overcast and the sun lanced through at an angle and hit the river. The surface flashed white, hard enough to sting and Zosia turned her eye from it reflexively. 

    Carol straightened immediately. "What happened?"

    "I'm fine."

    "You winced."

    "Just the light."

    Carol was already leaning sideways again, and held her hand out low over the water, palm flat, trying to catch the glare where it came off of the surface. It didn't do much. The reflection slid past and found Zosia anyway and Carol scowled at the sun as though she could make it move. 

    Zosia's throat went tight. She wanted to take Carol's hand out of the air and hold it, and couldn't.

    "Do you want me to—" Carol was frowning at the water now. "We could swap—" She shifted again stubbornly, shirt sleeve nearly dipping into the river as she tried to block it, the gesture hopeless and earnest. 

    "It's okay," Zosia said, softer than she'd intended. The sun was behind cloud now anyway. "It was just my eye being sensitive."

    Carol's hand came back slowly from the water. She touched her own cheekbone, just below the left eye. "How did it happen?" 

    "An accident, in my twenties. A mooring line parted." Carol's face was blank, so she translated. "When a ship is tied to a dock, the ropes are under massive tension. Thousands of kilos holding against the current, the wind, the ship’s own weight. If it snaps, it whips back faster than you can react. People have died. You have to trust the line to hold."

    "And yours didn't," Carol said flatly. 

    She remembered it complete with sound. "It was cold enough for ice on the bollards, and the harbor pilot brought us in at the wrong angle. The line creaked—they make a noise when they're overstressed—and you have less than a second between the sound and the break. I turned my head in time so a fray only caught my eye."

    Carol's hands were gripping the gunwhale again. Zosia could tell—she was imagining the scene, her jaw clamped, wanting to fight something else she couldn't reach.

    "I had an eyepatch for a while. Suited my codename," Zosia said, trying to lighten the mood.

    Carol didn't smile. "I never asked," she said, still flat. "I took it and—"

    "Carol—"

    "Used it for Raban without even—"

    "You didn't take anything." The correction was so urgent it bypassed every filter she had.

    Carol's mouth stayed open on the unfinished sentence.

    She hadn't planned to say it but Zosia felt the words she needed to speak rising. Hours after unjoining, she'd given Carol the minimum, wanting the floor to swallow her even then. Now she was embarrassing herself on purpose again, refusing to let Carol diminish herself.

    "You didn't take anything from me. You gave me something. Years ago. I carried your books across every sea and I wanted to be Raban." She knew how it sounded. She was a grown woman. The admission was making her face hot again. "He wanted things I wanted." A faint smile touched her mouth. "He was brave, lived outside the rules, had seen the world, and I'd never done any of that when I was twenty five, and Raban's half the reason I tried." 

    Carol’s expression was softening with each sentence, her shoulders dropping one degree at a time. Good. "I saw myself, and then when you told me she was a she—I understood why, and I couldn't say it then. I thought I'd known you for only an hour and I was already—"

    Cold wind moved through the trees, and, absurdly, tears blurred her vision. Everything running through the same breach Carol had opened, everything that used to be sealed was finding its way out, on couches and curbs and in canoes.

    "You gave me Raban's dream, and you gave me somewhere to go when I had nowhere, and no-one, because the only person who knew me was gone forever. You got me through the worst time of my life." Carol was staring at her now with a blank, stunned look. "And then you made me her, and called me beautiful, and I've heard that all my life, in every port and language and yours was the first time it's ever meant anything, and if you apologize for that I'll—" She sniffed. "I'll throw you overboard. You're small enough."

    Carol was silent and Zosia realized with a lurch that she had no idea what came next because she had never in her life said this much truth to anyone. She’d given a whole humiliating speech.

    "I’m nearly five-five and you can't touch me." 

    Zosia blew a shaky laugh. She'd expected..she didn't know what she'd expected, but her pulse was slowing, the adrenaline of saying all of it draining out of her. The canoe turned slowly in the current and neither of them corrected it. 

    Zosia sniffed again and one drop escaped anyway, straight down her cheek from the damaged side Carol had written beautiful. Absolutely mortifying. She swiped it and rolled her eyes at herself. "Three times in as many days," she said, wryly, about her own malfunction.  

    "I wish I could—" Carol pressed her lips together, fingers flexing against her knee like she was physically restraining herself. 

    Zosia knew the rest because she’d had the same unfinished thought for days. Hold your face. Wipe the tear away with my thumb. Something. Anything. "I know," Zosia said softly. 

    Carol shook her head. "I didn’t—I didn’t make you her. You're better than—She does what I say. Just words in a row. Nobody wrote you brave—"

    The first drop hit the canoe with a flat sound. 

    Carol stopped. The second drop hit her forearm. A third, on the water, spreading a ripple. "No." Carol held her palm up. Rain hit it. "No, no, no, what the fuck."

    Zosia looked up and blinked against the sudden downfall. 

    Carol was shaking her head at the sky. "It doesn't rain here, not in winter. I swear to God. I think up one—"

    "We should get under cover." 

    "—one excursion, and it decides to do this. Fucking rain…" Carol was already climbing out of the canoe, unsteady and indignant.

    They made the trailhead in seconds, the canopy closing overhead, the branches catching the drops and scattering softer. The sound of it layered on bark, on leaves, on the river behind—until the rain was a wall around them, enclosing the path, sealing the world down to the width of the trail and the two of them in it, Carol two steps ahead of her, still complaining.

    "My shoes," Carol said, looking down at them fighting the mud, "They’re swamp boots…I’m going to get trench foot…This is what happens when I can’t check the weather channel…" 

    The trail climbed. The dirt was darkening, the roots and littered branches going slick. Carol's shirt was soaked through now, clinging to the shift of her shoulder blades with each step, and below that her leggings were wet and Carol was walking fast and furious and her— 

    Zosia looked at the Sandias instead, which she knew now were fifty miles away, not one meter, so safe to admire. The mountain view didn't help. She looked back. 

    "...I'm going to draft a strongly worded tripadvisor review," Carol was grumbling, "for this river. Dear clouds, your timing is—" Her boot slipped and she corrected— "your timing is impeccable and I fucking hate you and I'm never going outside again..."

    The trail steepened. On the right the bank dropped suddenly toward the river, the edge crumbling where the soil had gone too wet, roots arching out over the drop with nothing underneath them. Zosia placed her feet carefully. 

    "One star," Carol was muttering, "Would not recommend. Zero stars. Negative stars, and I’d like to speak to whoever is in charge of—" 

    "Carol, watch the roots."
