    Chapter 11

    Chapter Notes

    By the time Carol came back from the bedroom with pants on, Zosia had already briefed Manousos. He'd arrived, looked at both of them—Carol in Zosia's shirt, Zosia in Carol's cardigan, neither making eye contact—slung a bag on the table and not asked a single question about it, thank fuck.

    "Sit," Manny said, without turning around.

    Carol grabbed the chair she'd been using for every briefing, the one with the uneven leg that rocked when she leaned back, and set Shrek on the table, beside a biro and some kind of frequency chart that looked like an EKG of a heart attack.

    He reached into his bag and out came bottled water and three packets of gas station almonds that looked old enough to vote. "Eat while I talk." His arms folded. "Original plan is dead. No time."

    Carol gulped. "Okay, what is it now?"

    "Zosia says they have doubt. We argue."

    "Argue?"

    "As Plan A."

    "And what's the argument?"

    Manousos made eye contact with Zosia, then looked at her. "You," he said. Carol's mug stalled on the way to her mouth. "You talk to them. If it doesn't work, we pull the plug. Plan B." 

    "Everyone seizing?" 

    "That is the alternative." Not looking pleased about any of this, he tapped the map once. The little box labeled CONTROL, where presumably she'd be sitting with a microphone. "I can hold frequency, run hardware. That is it. This part is yours."

    "Peachy. No pressure, then." The world's best high, and she was supposed to convince them all into a hangover? That was a book ending, not a real-life thing. She would know.

    "You talked Zosia out," Manny said, looking up.

    "That was different. That was—" One woman at point-blank range in a cage, stumbling and stammering. This was a stadium gig for everyone alive. "I need to write something this time," Carol said. "I can't just…ad lib at a telescope."

    "So write." Manny penciled it on the list. "Today."

    Carol thought about the print, proof they'd already painted themselves into their own corner. "Is there a way to send an image? While I'm talking?"

    Manny looked up again. "If you have a digital camera."

    "That's it?"

    "Photograph is data, signal is data. You take a photo, we encode it. Multiplex. Their signal is much more than two streams."

    "I want to send their art back to them," Carol said.

    "We can do that." He said it with the same flat assurance he used to say the ambulancio would reach the library on fumes, and Carol wanted to believe him with the same irritated faith. 

    She sighed. "Walk me through the rest."

    Manny tapped the map again. "Positions." He pointed to the dish nearest the hub. "Up the dish, we install hardware at the relay point: the junction where data meets carrier."

    "Who climbs?"

    Zosia said it before Manny could. "I do."

    She'd told Carol about the tall ship, Iskra, with the masts, and she'd been up those same dishes.

    "Twenty five meters," Carol said anyway, knee bouncing, reading from the notes. "How many feet is that?"

    "I've climbed in worse weather." Zosia traced a line on the sketch from the base of the dish to the relay junction. "I go up to the panel and connect it. Five minutes if everything cooperates." She traced back down to the base of it. "Manousos is here. Frequency lock, timing synchronization. It has to match or they'll detect interference before you've said a word. When its injected, you start."

    Carol looked at the map: Zosia on the dish, Carol in the building, Manny between them at the base. The control hub had a window, she'd seen it in his sketches, so she'd be able to see. Carol pulled Shrek closer by the handle. She could live with a hundred feet and one pane when she'd been imagining a thousand.

    "So how long for everything?"

    Manny held up three fingers, then corrected to four. "Setup, five minutes. Frequency lock, one. Injection, seconds once in position. Then, you talk for as long as you can." 

    "So I'm writing a speech against a clock I can't see."

    "You already know what to say." 

    "Knowing and writing are different. Writing and making someone believe you is even harder."

    "With Zosia we had nothing and it worked," Manousos said firmly. "This time we have the argument and the evidence. It is not worse odds." 

    Zosia straightened. "There's something I should say," she said, to the map. "The modifications the virus made are still in me. At ambient levels, nothing happens, but the signal at the VLA is orders of magnitude stronger. There may be a risk of re-joining."

    Carol set her coffee down hard. "So we get you out again."

    "There's no Faraday cage at the array."

    Manousos was already nodding at his own idea. "We get angry every time, you seize every time."

    "It's not safely repeatable." She looked at Manny. "It causes cumulative injury. That's why they had to leave. White matter lesions, haemorrhage, progressive loss. Each time carries a higher risk of permanent damage, so if I keep seizing…"

    Carol's hands had gone cold around the mug. "So we can't stop you from joining?"

    "I'm saying it's not safe to keep me seizing."

    "That's the same thing."

    "It's a different sentence."

    "Zosia."

    "I'm telling you the risk. I won't hurt you, obviously, but they could use me to stop you another way; unplug a cable, or destroy equipment." She paused. "Gently."

    "Okay," Carol said, tight. "We build a Faraday cage out of the ambulance and tinfoil. We find another—"

    "There's no time for leeway." Zosia's voice stayed level. "This is the plan. There isn't a version where I stay out of danger and it still works."

    "There has to be."

    "There isn't."

    Manny wrote something on his list and Carol couldn't tell if it was real or if he was giving them a moment. She opened her mouth for the next debate point and found she'd run out. 

    Zosia looked at him. "Martin has a sidearm in his closet. Can you use one?"

    "Yes," he said, but the answer came too slowly.

    "Will you bring it?"

    His pencil stopped. "In case of what?"

    "In case of me."

    Carol's head turned so fast her neck cracked. No, that wasn't what—no. She could feel her pulse in the wrong places.

    He shook his head. "We restrain instead. Tie-downs from the ambulance—"

    "Manousos." Zosia said his name how she'd said sir on the first day, with rank behind it. "You need something to use from distance, for when you have to hold position."

    Carol looked at Manny's face and saw it there, what she was trying not to see, then looked at Zosia's face which was worse because there was nothing on it at all. 

    His pencil was pressing into the page. He'd said better off dead about all of them, but he knew better now, he would—

    "Say what you are asking me," he said.

    Carol rounded on him. "Are you fucking kidding?"

    "No. I'm making sure it is her choice."

    Zosia was resolute. "If I rejoin and interfere, you stop me."

    His jaw worked once, grinding toward the certitude that had always followed, but he swallowed instead. "How much?"

    "As much as necessary."

    Carol said her name like a reflex, like when someone steps into traffic. Zosia's eyes closed for half a second, the only concession she'd made, and then she was looking at Manousos again. 

    "Then yes. If it comes…" His fingers went to the cross at his throat. "If it comes to that," he finished. Carol watched him write the fucking thing down on his checklist and his handwriting had gone to hell.

    Carol pushed back from the table. "No. Stop. You'd—with a dentist's gun?" Which was the stupidest possible thing to say. "Are we seriously…" It was right there, the panicked fight that started with you're not going and ended with her losing because three people were needed for any of this to work and they all knew it.

    Zosia could've said it yesterday, or earlier, Manny's ear only, Carol upstairs and none the wiser. She'd have written it that way; the secret to save her withheld till the most dramatic moment. Stop smoothing all the road for me, she'd told her. Zosia had taken the note and Carol wanted to burn it now.

    Manousos cleared his throat. "I can go up the dish myself," he said to Zosia. "If it comes to it."

    Zosia went rigid. "No."

    "It is just cables, brackets. I will be fine—"

    "You're not going up unclipped." The force of it turned both their heads. "I lost someone that way," Zosia said, softer. Her hands were flat on the table again, blanched.

    Sasha. Carol hadn't asked how. She saw her own panic looking back at her, smaller and older, and every angry word she'd had left loaded folded. 

    Manny looked at Zosia's hands, then at the height marked on the map. "Then I find clips," he said simply. He put it on his much shorter parts list and shouldered his bag. "I go to Dick's, for that and…other things, but it will not be long." He pointed at Carol with the pencil. "Write."

    The door clapped shut behind him, and Carol went to the sink with Shrek and looked out at the backyard, felt Zosia's eyes on her as she ran the hot tap until it steamed. 

    "I never asked," Carol said. "About Sasha."

    "He fell." Flat. "From the foremast."

    Carol's hands tightened on the porcelain, trying very hard to let her own fear wait its turn. "He sounds like a guy who'd go up even when someone told him not to."

    "Every time."

    "And you're the same."

    "Yes." 

    But all the fury she'd lost at Zosia's trembling chin was returning, lodged in her. Carol wrung the dish towel hard and turned around. 

    Zosia had squared herself and took one breath that was too conscious before she looked at Carol.  "You're going to be fine," she said.

    The mooring line creaked. That was how Zosia had described it on the river, the sound a rope makes under too much tension, the second of warning before it snaps and takes somebody's head off. 

    "Don't. Don't tell me I'll be fine. Tell me you'll be fine."

    "I can't—"

    "Then don't tell me I'll be fine. Because I won't be, if you're not." She'd done this once, months in the crater, and she'd come out of the pit onto the far uphill side only just. There wasn't a second crossing in her. "A fucking gun. In a voice like you've already decided and you're just tying off the ropes."

    "If I use a different voice, I'm not useful. One of us being scared is enough—"

    "No, it's not, because I'm the one being scared but you're the one being fucking shot." Carol heard her own voice climbing. "And I can't even be fully angry because I know you're doing what I told you and I know you're being practical because the whole fucking planet is at stake, and what am I doing? What am I actually doing?"

    "You're writing a broadcast, and everything I'm planning is for one thing. You staying yourself."

    "And if it costs you—"

    "Worth it."

    "Don't. Don't be fucking noble. Don't be—Jesus. Be fucking selfish."

    Zosia's jaw worked once. "I'm not asking permission." It left no room for dispute. "If they take me and I have to be stopped, that's a consequence I've already weighed." 

    Carol's voice dropped off its ledge. "Fuck you. You've weighed your life? I've weighed the world and you win. You've won every time." 

    Zosia's hand opened and closed once at her hip. "The world is downstream of you too. That's how it happens to be for the mission and how it is for me." She tucked her hair with the same steady hand, and Carol wanted to slap it loose, wanted to find the shaking she knew had to be there somewhere. "I'm sorry I can't say it in a different voice, I don't have another one right now."

    Carol opened her mouth to say stay alive, whatever it takes and it died on her tongue because she'd eat the gun herself before letting them tune her to the chorus. She'd written over my dead body on the whiteboard and meant every letter, and there was no light between that and what Zosia was willing to do. She had nothing left that wasn't a lie, and Zosia could see it.

    "If something happens," Zosia said carefully, "you have to keep talking. That's what the world needs from you."

    Carol sagged against the counter, pressing cold into her back. "I don't give a shit what the world needs."

    "Yes, you do. That's why you're the one, why they have doubt, why I—because you give a shit, even when you're pretending you don't."

    Zosia's eyes were bright as she finally crossed the kitchen, and Carol's hands were already there, hauling her the last stride, and she pressed into her cardigan covered collarbone and could not get close enough, and Carol loved her and wanted to kill her and could scarcely sort the two apart.

    "I hate you," Carol said, into the knit, petulant.

    "I know." Zosia's arms came around her, chin to Carol's crown, and Carol had been planning to stay angry for at least another minute, but Zosia's heartbeat was there, slamming faster than the voice had ever let on. Every measured word backed by a hammer clocking a hundred and forty, at least, a heart that had been afraid through the whole briefing and just better at hiding it.

    She pressed her ear flat and listened to the fear she'd been shouting for and found she didn't want it, after all.

    The house went quiet for the first time in ten minutes, and Carol's breathing slowed, against her will and Zosia's chest, pulse coming down now.

    Her knuckles ached from gripping and she loosened, finally pulled back, wiped her nose on her sleeve. "God. I'm going to write something that saves the world in this mood and it's going to read like a divorce filing." Zosia's mouth pulled. "Don't smile. I'm furious at you." Zosia looked down at her and the smile she was suppressing was in her eyes instead, which was much worse. "I'm going to be furious at you for the whole drive there," Carol informed her, folding her arms.

    "That's fine." Zosia dipped her head and kissed right where her pout was sharpest, quick and soft.

    Carol's scowl softened. "And when we get back I'm going to be angry for even longer," she lobbed out anyway.

    Zosia's arm tightened around her. "Looking forward to it."

    Carol's shoulders started dropping, then stopped. Looking forward. Present tense, aimed at a time Zosia hadn't promised would come. She huffed. "Yeah," Carol said, rough. "Me too."

    Her legs had gone weak. She leaned into Zosia and let the counter do the rest, hollow.

    "I should write," Carol said.

    "You should." Zosia didn't move.

    "Stop looking at me like that."

    "Like what?"

    Carol gestured at Zosia's face without looking, knowing what it was doing. "With your eyes. Quit it. I won't type a usable word before he's back if you keep doing that. Go away."

    She felt Zosia pause for a moment, then withdraw.

    "What are you doing?"

    "Removing the distraction," Zosia said mildly. "You need to write." She went to collect her mug, and her free hand opened and closed once before it found the handle, talked out of reaching back. 

    "That's not—" Carol sighed. Now she had no excuse.

    She crossed to the table and pulled the laptop toward her, opened it, sat her butt in the wonky chair and her fingers on the keys. She stared at the blank document, feeling Zosia's attention on her spine like sun through the window.

    She typed The argument for and deleted it.

    The house was quiet except for a drawer opening behind her now, the freezer seal pulling loose.

    Her pulse was being unreasonable for sitting still. The cursor blinked in a beat she couldn't match. 

    Zosia reappeared with two dishes of the leftover mango ice cream and set one beside Carol's laptop without looking, walked to the living room carrying the other and a notebook under her arm. Carol heard the couch receive her, and then nothing.

    Carol slumped lower in the chair.

    Somewhere a lab had her cells in it, growing the thing that would worm into her skull and turn the lights on and leave nobody home, and she was procrastinating the only stay of execution. Carol leaned back on the uneven leg and rubbed her face. "Fuck." 

    She lowered her hands and glared at the screen that waited with saintly patience. She typed What I Want to Say and stared at it. 

    Carol ate from the bowl so she wouldn't have to type more and the spoonfuls were sweet and gave her brain freeze and that was something. That was part of the argument. What she had to find words for. 

    She'd made and given it instead of the sentence she still couldn't get her mouth around: that she'd been a goner since that morning Zosia surfaced. Zosia had a favorite to tell her because Carol had asked, and the nearest she could come to why Zosia loved it was this, her own tongue, reaching as near as the gap let her.

    She thought about Zosia on the blanket with the telescope, stars in her eyes, holding still across two feet of gravel she didn't dare cross, and how the hell was that only last night? The mango tasted identical, which felt fraudulent, because nothing else between that spoon and this one was the same, and what the fuck was time, anyway? Fifteen hours. Fifteen hours was a hangover, a transatlantic flight with a layover, and this time felt like fifteen weeks.

    She deleted What I Want to Say and typed A door is. Looked at it, tucked her chin into her stolen shirt, and smelled Zosia. A door was distance, the sacred fact of an interior life, and what she should've put in the living room entryway and barred with a chair.

    Carol closed the laptop and went. Zosia was on the couch, notebook open on her knee, and glanced up.

    "I know," Carol said. "I'm coming back to it." She rubbed her forehead. New approach. She dropped into the armchair opposite and set the laptop on the side table where it could judge in her peripheral vision. She needed to get her brain working in a different direction so she could come back to it fresh.

    Carol's eyes moved around the room looking for the different direction and stopped on Bloodsong, face down on the table where Zosia had left it last week. She leaned and picked it up, opened it to where it fell. Lucasia descending the well to where the sirens' song met the moonlight.

    The twin moons, those wine-green tyrants, crept behind the shadow of the earth, and their glow guttered. Nine minutes, no more, Madam Asclepius had said, and already the seconds were running through her fingers like the amaranthine sand of seas she might never see again. Aurora would return the light and the Moonsburn curse with it. 

    Oh, damnable duty! Lucasia had done harder things than speak. She was a captain of the line. Hesitation was for lesser women and dead men. To have come four hundred leagues and have herself go to ground at the final step! She now found, at the lip of the Moonwell, that courage was not a thing one had but a thing one chose. 

    She turned the book over, to look at the cover she knew fans would hate since the day it came back from the printer. The cheapest authorship, writing a version of yourself who didn't fail. 

    Except Zosia had confessed in the canoe that she'd wanted to be Raban, and used her character as a compass. Carol had managed, before the rain cut everything off, only a few stupid words back. Another sentence still incomplete.

    So much for a different direction. She'd gone looking for time away from writing and walked straight into more wearing a corset, and now the only other channel her brain was offering was the one it always defaulted to nowadays, currently sitting six feet across from her. 

    She glanced up at Zosia, who was studiously revising the mission sequence. "I stole the eclipse idea, y'know. The one-window trope, dark as the only chance. I didn't come up with any of it." 

    Zosia didn't look up. Her thumb moved the corner of a page without turning it. "You wrote her talking the sirens down. It's in your hands."

    "It's fiction. It worked because I decided it would." Because the alternative was no fucking book. "Here there's no—" She vaguely waved up at nothing— "God in the rafters deciding I find the words." 

    "I'm not worried about that." Zosia looked up at last. "I'm proof of it." She went back to reading and wasn't going to debate, which was the most annoying possible response. 

    Carol watched Zosia not watch her. Spine straight, feet tucked, every muscle aligned toward the task in her lap, pen tapping her lip. The cardigan had slipped off one shoulder, showing the bare skin beneath it, and every cell in Carol's body was suddenly campaigning for a repeat of this morning.

    She shut her eyes and tried to think about privacy and personhood and instead thought about Zosia prone between her thighs earlier, feet kicked up and ankles crossed, perfectly content going down on Carol like she was a damn bowl of ice cream on a sunny afternoon, taking her sweet fucking time. 

    Carol leaned back and pressed her knuckles into her eye sockets. "Fuck." 

    She wanted to throw a cushion at her.

    She wanted to cross the six feet of living room rug and climb into Zosia's lap and ruin her concentration like Zosia had ruined hers by simply existing perfectly in her own damn cardigan. She wanted to rip the notebook out of her hands and put her mouth where the pen had been and feel the infuriatingly noble and responsible Commander Pissylinska under her. 

    The space was less than six feet. The length of Zosia lying down. They could do it right here on the floor. But that would be the writing time gone, the only way out of this gone, and the worst part was how tempted she was. The whole world for more. She'd already sold it once.

    "I need…I need to do something else. A distraction, so I can come back to it. That's…that's how this works…."

    Zosia's lips pulled at one corner. She closed the notebook and Carol looked at the top of her head, the parting she'd chosen, and felt a twist in her chest not anything to do with the unwritten essay. What she'd been angling for ebbed, and left in its place a need with no use for twenty minutes, or one afternoon, aimed instead at watching that messy part go gray, at the unremarkable rest of it. She'd known on fragments alone. If it wasn't her, then it wouldn't be anyone.

    If it worked. If tomorrow went the way it was supposed to and the hive heard her and nobody joined and none of them died and the world came back. If all of that happened, then the day after tomorrow would be—what? Friday. The mission was the cliff they were both walking toward and beyond it was the far side of a Friday she couldn't see, either nothing or everything.

    "What happens after?" Carol asked. "If people come back, and the world is…whatever the world is after this."

    "I haven't thought about it."

    "I call bullshit on that."

    Zosia gave an amused exhale. "I haven't thought about it productively."

    "So think about it. What do you—what was your dream?" Carol asked, instead of the other thing. "Before all this."

    "Iskra was my dream," Zosia said, simply. "Then I got it and nothing changed." 

    Carol nodded. She thought of the first time she held a printed copy of Winds, how it had been what she'd wanted and still not enough. 

    "And then, I had a number," Zosia said. "What I needed for a sloop that could make offshore passages." One shoulder lifted. "Something to do with the rest of life."

    "You were saving for a boat?"

    "I was always going to have a boat," Zosia said, like saying she was always going to sleep or eat. "Something small enough to single-hand. The plan was to retire and sail until I ran out of money or coastline." She gave a small smile. "Sasha said I'd be bored in a week."

    "Would you?"

    She shrugged again.

    Single-hand. Carol got green on cruises, cold at night, itchy anywhere without a roof and a desk. Or that was the bit, anyway. None of it had ever been tested past a deck chair and being hungover. 

    Carol chewed her sore lip and said none of it. She could see Zosia choosing what to say next and then not. 

    "What about you, would you finish Wycaro five? You said you had ideas."

    Carol pulled at a thread on the arm of the chair. "I've been..." she gulped down the rest. She'd been writing. Wycaro five: fifty lines of Raban sleeping on her stomach, another seventy five of what Raban might've been thinking staring out a window, coffee cooling in a clay mug.

    She supposed there'd have to be a plot in this one too, the usual turbulence of cut throats and burning cities—and all Carol wanted, what had her scrawling at four in the morning, was Raban eating oatmeal with a wooden spoon, apparently. Raban putting her hand into sand that lit wherever she touched it. Standing on a frozen deck with ice in her eyelashes navigating by constellations.

    She wound the loose thread around her finger until the tip went white. "Yeah." She unwound the thread. "I'd write. Would you read it?"

    Zosia rolled her eyes. "That might be the silliest question you've ever asked. So you'd write and I'd read." She shrugged. "On opposite ends of something."

    "Of what?"

    Zosia looked down at the notebook in her lap. "I don't know. Whatever the distance is."

    Carol didn't know if that distance could be none, if Carol asked, if the cliff had land not sea on the other side and they were both standing. The only ground Carol could picture under her own feet was sandy; where her house was, her life was, her wife was. She wasn't about to tell Zosia to come ashore and call it enough. She pressed her thumbnail into the armchair and felt the weave give.

    "What about you?" Zosia said, turning it around again. She reached for her own bowl of ice cream. "What was your dream?"

    Carol's shoulders came up to her ears. "The usual. Bestseller list, movie deal, awards and whatnot. Oprah's book club, which doesn't even do fantasy."

    "Mm." Zosia took a spoonful and her eyebrows lifted at Carol, waiting.

    "Fine," Carol huffed. "Fine. It was—" She pulled the thread harder. "Making Helen happy, and proud." Which was the true one, that she couldn't say at panels and drinks mixers she was dragged to. "I wanted her to feel like it had been worth it. The years of me." She swallowed the lump and picked at the wool. "And being read properly," she added. "Something that actually mattered." 

    "Then you got it," Zosia said, sure. "You got it. Someone read you properly, and it mattered, in a bunk in the Baltic. And Helen was proud. She was happy."

    "You don't know anymore—"

    "I do."

    Helen's Norway, somewhere in Zosia's head. Her throat thickened.

    Helen loved her, she'd never once doubted, because why the hell would she put up with Carol's shit otherwise. Helen had been happy, and that was the worst part. 

    Zosia had been to Norway with Helen. Carol hadn't. 

    Carol had been complaining, shit-talking, her phone confiscated and she'd still found somehow to avoid being there fully, to avoid feeling happy completely. The gorgeous aurora moved across the sky and Carol sat shivering under reindeer pelts thinking about review aggregators.

    How about the hot tub, Helen had said. You can see even better out there. Carol had kept grumbling that she was too cold to go outside and watched through the glass door: Helen in the steam, leaning on the railing, face tipped up to the full display of it, greens bleeding into violet. 

    Carol had forced herself to go, furs around her shoulders, and pushed through the door into the freezing air. Helen was at the rail and the sky was still moving, beautiful, and Carol was thinking where she'd made the Times list, then about the next book, and then about Helen's hand on the rail and how she should hold it. By the time her own hand got around to reaching, Helen's was already gone. Already saying I'm pruning, coming in.

    She'd had the dream, and she'd appreciated the aurora more in photos, afterwards. Loved the memory of it more than she'd loved being there.

    "I'm—" Her eyes were burning. She didn't want to list all the ways she'd fucking failed.

    Losing her, then the hive cracking something open, and then Zosia sitting as herself on that couch, and in a canoe, and on gravel someone called a garden, had Carol noticing she'd actually been sitting still in time and not running ahead and ruining things. She hadn't been thinking the worst, or if she had, she'd been able to make herself stop and be present. That was either growth, or grief, or both, and either way, Helen had deserved it all first.

    She'd bought the hot tub for the backyard when they got home. Helen had been delighted, called it an extravagance, used it every evening that first winter. Carol had never told her why. Now she'd never know.

    Carol's face crumpled, she couldn't stop it. "I didn't—I wasn't good enough for her. I was a miserable fucking piece of shit and she deserved better. She was happier dying than any moment with me." Zosia started shaking her head and Carol wasn't having it. "I'm serious. She deserved—"

    "Shut up," Zosia snapped. Her expression was suddenly severe, and Carol went quiet. "Why do you do that? Talk about someone loving you like they're stupid or trapped?" She was plainly offended. "Why do you act like loving you is punishment? An endurance test?"

    Carol scoffed. "Because it is."

    "It isn't. It's the easiest thing I've ever done."

    Carol's mouth opened and nothing came out, a hundred sarcastic deflections on tap and not one of them would fire. Easiest thing I've ever done. She ran it again, and her internal vaudeville act tripped over it and face-planted.

    Zosia watched the failure and her jaw set. "You weren't listening last night," she said. "When I told you what matters. You dodged, like you're trying to do now." The notebook slid off her knee and she left it where it fell. "Do you remember what I said to you on the beach in Thailand?"

    Carol's mouth was still agape. 

    "I said you were easy to love, and then we just stopped, like that explained itself. They forgot you couldn't hear the rest. Everyone so used to being inside." Her nostrils flared. "I was annoyed about that, when I remembered. And at the time."

    "Zosia—"

    "Do you know how many times the world tried to change you? Before all this. Every time someone told you to be easier, quieter."

    Carol could feel the resistance finally shouldering up, thank fuck. "I wasn't brave about it. I just couldn't not."

    "I know." Zosia's voice softened. "You kept being… this." She nodded her head at her. "Doing what you're doing now. Being difficult. I don't mean you're easy. You make things harder than they need to be."

    Carol huffed. "You're really selling me." 

    "I'm trying to be precise. Do you understand what I'm saying?"

    "You're saying you have shitty judgment."

    Zosia exhaled a laugh, and then Carol watched her try a different tack. "The memories I saw. Ones you've obviously forgotten, because you weren't trying to be good, you just were. I was a boy on a playing field." Zosia's voice had gone plain. "You told him he hadn't made the team. Said it fast and badly."

    Carol's stomach sank. She knew this. She'd been—eight? And he'd been holding a copy of the paper they'd pinned and Carol could see from his face he hadn't read it yet, or he had and hadn't understood, and she'd said it because she thought someone should, before he walked into the crowd and found out in front of everyone. 

    He'd cried. She remembered his tears and the flush of knowing she'd caused it and the lurch of wanting to take it back but also not wanting to, because it was true. His mom had called her mom and Carol had listened to her mother apologizing in the voice she used for other people: honeyed, so embarrassed, you know what she's like.

    "Yeah. I made him cry."

    "He didn't remember the crying much after forty years. He remembered you told him, and everyone else made him walk."

    Carol shook her head. She'd carried that boy's crying face had been exhibit A in the long casefile she'd built against her own mouth. She'd hurt him and then bought him off with chocolate. "Everyone thought I was a nightmare," Carol said, rough. "Everyone. Teachers, parents, all the kids—"

    "You gave him candy after. He remembered it as the one nice thing in the whole day."

    Carol wanted to say something about self-interest, but nothing came, all the garbage jammed at the exit. She blew air through her nose, hard, and her eyes skated off—to the book on the table, the rug on the floor, the O'Keefe on the wall, anywhere but Zosia six feet away saying this shit. 

    Zosia came up off the couch, crossed the rug Carol had been staring at, and went down onto knees in front of her, taking Carol's face in both hands, refusing to be dodged again, firm enough to stop the turn Carol had already begun. "Listen to me." 

    She was so close and so beautiful that Carol forgot for a full second to pre-emptively deflect what more was about to be said.

    "There was another one ten years later, and you were still fighting. Had stayed yourself through it all." Zosia tilted her head. "It was a college party, a group laughing at someone, and you ruined the room. Told the leader how stupid he sounded."

    Carol had only gone for the free booze in the basement, some of it spilled on the carpet tiles, the sour stink near the laundry room. "Brian," she said, hating that the name survived. She remembered unhinging her drunken jaw, calling him a varsity dipshit, DJ Jazzy Jeff still playing through the awkward silence after.

    She'd told herself she'd done it because she was angry, because he was a moron and she hated morons, because anything was better than admitting the sound scared her. The sound of collective derision at one person. She'd heard her mother's voice, the counsellors' contempt, the corridor ridicule: wanting was selfish, wanting women was worse, wanting to be wanted back was the funniest joke in the whole goddamned cafeteria.

    "That doesn't make me…" The rest dissolved on a sigh. She was too exhausted to finish the sentence and too honest to mean it. She was being narrated with nowhere to run. Her shoulders came up again. Her hands found Zosia's wrists and pulled. She dropped her chin and Zosia's palm was already there. "Will you—" Carol struggled, and then didn't finish because she didn't actually want Zosia to let go. Fucking infuriating. 

    "And then Brian needed help later."

    Carol remembered that too, three sheets to the wind and staggering as she'd been by then. "Yeah. The asshole was going blue on the lawn." She'd only done the first-aid course for the credits, knew alcohol poisoning all too well, hadn't thought about it in thirty years. Probably because she'd had to willingly put her mouth on a man.

    "You cursed at him until the ambulance came," Zosia said, smiling. "I saw a few like that. You heard something break, someone shout, and you didn't think about whether you liked them, whether they deserved it. You just went." 

    Carol shut her eyes. She knew what that looked like. What happened when you ran to the stranger while your wife fell behind you. If she'd been the selfish person she'd spent her life being told she was, Helen would still be alive. 

    She almost said it, laid Helen out—here, counter this one, tell me this was the right thing too. But using her for this was a kind of obscenity that rendered the whole rebuttal moot. She couldn't argue she was unlovable by using the person who had loved her the longest, who'd spent their whole life together trying to convince her.

    She could squabble the point or she could believe them. She couldn't do both. 

    Her chin wobbled and she stopped fighting it, and it felt like putting down a heavy weight she'd been carrying uphill for three months. Helen, somewhere, was helping to win a debate she'd started in 1998. Carol opened her eyes and Zosia's thumbs hadn't moved. Carol wondered if her knees hurt.

    "Your whole life you helped people and complained about it loudly and never once pretended to be nice, which is how I know it counted. You've been a pain in the ass remarkably consistently."

    "Wow, thanks," Carol muttered, rolling her blurry eyes. "Put that on my dust jacket."

    Zosia smiled. "See what I mean?"

    Carol made a dismissive sound and looked past her to the tree through the window, the ceiling beams above, anywhere but Zosia, her shoulders dropping an inch anyway. The light had gone longer while she was forced to listen, laid in bars and climbing the wall.

    "And then you were left alone." Zosia's mouth tightened. "You saw something that wasn't right and you tried anyway. You did it as a kid, at twenty, after the world ended. You did it for me. It was always going to be what you did."

    Carol felt exposed and raw. She exhaled through her teeth. "Alright," Carol said, voice rough, "I get it, that's enough." She tried to turn her face again. "Zosia—"

    "I'm not finished," Zosia said, digging the heels of her palms in. Carol clamped her jaw and realized she'd become one of the topics Zosia wasn't reticent on, that she'd go for fifteen minutes about without breathing. With her hands there Carol couldn't do any of the things she normally did when her face was in mutiny.

    "I've known you freely for a week, and we've fought through half of it." Carol's mouth twitched, barely, her lips trembling. "That's not thirty years, or everyone's memories. All I have is—" she searched for the word and found it— "friction. It tells you how something holds up. Helen, the hive, me; we all found the same thing. It's not a coincidence." She held Carol's face and eyes firmly. "You're not someone to be suffered, you've always been good enough, and the fact that it might take the end of the world to convince you is the only thing about you that I find actually annoying."

    The burn that had been building behind her eyes reached the front. Her breath had gone shallow, pulling back from her chest in thin retreats, and she couldn't look at Zosia and couldn't look away.

    "That's why I can't—it's the thing I most—" Zosia was frustrated with her own words, like she was translating something that should be effortless. "I was in there and I had to feel them want to join you." Her voice wasn't steady anymore. "I couldn't do anything and the whole time I was thinking—don't. Don't touch her. So when you talk about yourself like that—I can't hear it. I won't." 

    Zosia's face finished searching, brow finally smoothing, and she said it blunt and glad. "I love you difficult. I want every complaint and argument because that means you're you, and I know what they would do to the part of you that kept you as you are through everything, that makes you fight, that saved me. They'd take all the scars, the splinters, all the stubborn ways you hold yourself against everything and smooth all of it away, and you'd be easy, and who I'm in love with wouldn't be there." 

    Carol heaved a shaky breath as the room went to water. "Stop," she croaked.

    Zosia finally relented. "Okay. I'm done. That's what I would've said on the beach. What I've been trying to say all day." She let her hands slide from Carol's face. "So yes, tomorrow, whatever it costs. Keeping you as you are is what I'd die for."

    God knows she had no words this afternoon so Carol gave the reply she did have: instead of letting Zosia rise she came down and kissed her.

    Carol broke away with a wet breath and a glare she couldn't hold. "What the hell is wrong with you?" she said against Zosia's mouth, going straight back in. "Why would you say all that?" Another kiss, her thumbs swiping at Zosia's cheekbones, her own tears getting onto both. "What the fuck."

    Zosia kissed her back, taking the storm of it, one hand coming up to cradle the back of Carol's head while Carol shook against her mouth and complained between every kiss.

    Zosia broke away. "You said to be selfish," she said, her mouth still soft from the kisses. 

    "I say a lot of stupid shit."

    "Yes." Zosia's eyes warmed. "Remember, last week, when I told you that being joined was the happiest I've ever been?" Zosia took Carol's hand and pressed it against her own heart. "I didn't remember this yet. If they take you then the best thing I've ever felt goes too. I don't know a more selfish reason to do anything."

    "Jesus Christ, shut the fuck up," but she said it into Zosia's mouth, and Carol's breath fell out of her in one pathetic rush that turned into a laugh by accident.  

    Carol pulled a hand free just long enough to swipe at her face, then took Zosia's hand again like she hadn't let go at all and squeezed hard, too hard probably, and held it against her own chest, right over the hammering evidence.

    "Do you feel that? Never do any of that again," she said, fiercely. "I'm too old for this, I have blood pressure."

    Zosia's smile reached the corners of her eyes and stayed there. "Sorry."

    "No, you're not." Carol sniffed and stared at her, wet-eyed. "You're insane."

    Zosia's brows rose.

    "You navy-brained lunatic. You had a perfectly good life of repression and boats and whatever the fuck, and this is your port of call?" Carol jabbed a thumb at herself.

    "Yes."

    "I hate how fast you answered." Carol's voice cracked on the last word and she was furious about it. "Obviously I love you, you maniac, and this was not how I was going to say it."

    "I know," Zosia said. "You've told me three different ways already, you're not subtle. And you said it in your sleep earlier, when you drooled on me."

    For fuck's sake. Carol took a breath that shuddered. 

    "I love you," Carol said again, to hear it exist outside her own head. The sentence sounded small and huge at once and she'd written millions of the fucking things and this was still the only one that mattered. "I love you," half-choked half-laughing, like a cough she'd been holding. She huffed another breath, and wiped her face with her shoulder because both hands were occupied  "Okay. I'm done," Carol said, voice clearing. "I'm done being weird for—" she checked nothing— "at least ten minutes."

    "That seems ambitious."

    "And how many minutes did you get, hm? You gave a damn monologue and I've got three words and hypertension. That's what I've got. I'm a writer, allegedly."

    "Yes. My favorite." Zosia put Carol's hand briefly against her heart again, like a receipt.

    Carol pressed their hands flat on Zosia's sternum, pushing, already thinking again about the rug and the length of Zosia laid out on it, and how fast—

    The front door opened and boots shuffled on the mat and Carol came up off the chair so fast the whole maneuver was finished before her brain signed off. Upright by another console table with no bug to blame this time, nothing to wave away, all for the one man alive who couldn't possibly be keeping the score that she was still reflexively keeping. 

    Manny's throat cleared too late to be any use to anyone. He stood in the entryway with a Dick's bag in one hand and a hard black case in the other. He looked at Zosia, who was getting to her feet in no hurry. "I have the clips," he said, "and the other thing." He raised the case an inch, in case the other thing needed naming. It didn't. Manny's glance tracked to the laptop, then to Carol. "You wrote it."

    "Working on it."

    "Hm."

    And the fuller answer Carol had been about to give Zosia had to stay ungiven. She'd said a speech off-the-cuff and Carol could only spit one sentence out. Pathetic. She still had a due appointment with the blinking cursor, and she understood the opus that she owed the world and the one she owed Zosia were the same words now, or she'd manage neither. 

    The microwave counted down green numbers, and Carol waited for the bag to swell. A stutter of corn started popping apart in the dark.

    A movie had been Manny's idea, which was to say, his prescription. The dining room still smelled of burnt metal from their afternoon with the soldering iron that Carol had spent pacing her office. Now the hardware was built, sequencing tested, plan set, broadcast written, nothing left. He'd drawn a line through the penultimate item and looked at them both until it was understood that the last one—eight hours of sleep, adrenalin off the boil, decompress first—wasn't a suggestion. 

    Carol had wanted, very badly, to say no. As soon as she'd come downstairs she'd wanted to take Zosia upstairs, and had already opened her mouth to find some way to break it. Then she'd thought of him crossing the street all day, every day, and how her thank you had been telling him to pound sand and fuck off to Radioshack.

    So when he asked for two hours of normality on the last night any of them might have, she shut the hell up and got popcorn.

    In the den, he was working through her DVDs in the TV stand, each case opening and closing with a plastic snap. Tomorrow they would drive to the array and Carol would say her piece to seven billion and find out whether words could undo a god. Tonight there was just another movie, and the three of them being very normal about it all.

    She dug the scoop into the decaf and Zosia caught her wrist before it cleared the bag.

    Since she'd come down, Zosia had not stopped touching her. She stood at Carol's back with a thumb hooked over her waistband, against the skin above it, and didn't take it away. She got the kettle one-handed, keeping her place. Carol gripped the press and let herself be pinned to the counter by one warm knuckle and felt every nerve reporting the slow steady siege that hadn't let up since Manny left the room. She wasn't about to mention it.

    "Too much."

    "You said it barely counts as coffee."

    "It counts." Zosia returned a pinch. "You don't need so much if you do the rest right. You rush the rest."

    "I don't."

    "You do." Low, fond, and it went through Carol on a wire. Zosia smoothed the scoop level and then clicked the kettle off before it bubbled. "Boiling burns it—you lose the oils, it's bitter with nothing underneath. You need to wet the grounds first a little, then wait."

    "For what?"

    "The bloom." The word came warm against the shell of her ear, soft and round, bloom, opening on the breath like the thing it named. "Thirty seconds. They swell, they let go, they open. Then they'll take the rest of the water properly. Slow, from the middle out. Then you leave it alone."

    All of it true probably, the snobbery completely sincere, and she was getting wet over a water temperature lecture like some Pavlovian disgrace.

    She tipped the grounds in. Zosia reached past her for the kettle again, her forearm dragging across the front of Carol's shirt, and poured a thin spiral of water, her wrist steady enough for surgery.

    The grounds darkened and rose, and the smell did bloom up between them, sweet on the steam.

    Thirty seconds. Nothing to do but be ass-over-teakettle turned on, and over what. A forearm.

    Zosia's mouth found the side of her neck, oh Jesus.

    "That's—not in the drill," Carol said. 

    "Mm." Zosia's thumb moved once along her hipbone and Carol needed it to go lower or higher, either, she really wasn't picky.

    She needed to be sedated. Manousos was twenty feet away alphabetizing her DVDs. 

    "We can't," Carol breathed, mostly to convince herself.

    "Can't what?" Like the word was a small puzzle she might enjoy solving.

    Carol gulped as Zosia's thumb found more bare skin. "He's right there."

    "He's reading." Quiet and reasonable. "We have ten more seconds of bloom. Then four minutes for the steep," Zosia said, like a generous offer, like she wasn't being a goddamn menace on purpose. Perhaps the last night of her life and she was going to spend some of it learning to brew coffee she might not drink again, felt up by her teacher to a timer. 

    The dread was waiting to have her too, and she tried to keep Zosia's hand on her and tomorrow nowhere. The microwave popped, soft and far.

    The bloom finished. Zosia filled the press around her, steering the spiral tight to center, not one tremor in her hands, inconsiderate of Carol's plans to panic.

    Zosia set the kettle down and a hand came over Carol's on the plunger and pressed, slow and even, the mesh sinking through dark water, every line of Zosia sealed to her and well, so much for not turning around. Her back met the counter's edge and she fisted the front of Zosia and pulled, was going to kiss her in the kitchen with Manny mere meters away, and she didn't give a fuck, she didn't—

    "It says it is a heist movie."

    Carol's forehead dropped to Zosia's collarbone.

    "I am not watching Bound with you," she called, and her voice was impressively level.

    "Neo-noir."

    "Put it down."

    "Hm." 

    The microwave beeped.

    Zosia uncurled Carol's hand from her, turned it palm-up between them, and kissed the heart of it, a dog-eared page to come back to. 

    Carol heaved a sigh. She carried the warmth of it cupped in her hand along with the press and mugs through to the den, and Zosia carried the bowl, and they found Manny on the floor with her films fanned around his knees.

    Out of the whole cabinet he'd surfaced Desert Hearts. He still had Bound on the floor like unfinished business. Xena in his hands, for Christ's sake.

    He turned the box set over. "You have all of them."

    "It's culturally significant," Carol said, putting the press down, hard. "It's—" She heard herself about to defend the dramaturgy. 

    "Six seasons," he said, reading the back, "and it ends how?"

    "Give me that." She snatched it from him. "You picked these?" she asked, watching his face.

    "They were in front." He didn't look up.

    Which told her nothing. With anyone else it could've been a message in the only dialect he had, or, he just sorted DVDs by some unknown rubric that didn't include who might be kissing whom. She lifted the only two straight selections from his shortlist and returned the rest, like pushing a letter back in an envelope, and knew, as she did, what she was doing. The thing she'd been doing all day. 

    "This one." Moonstruck. "Or this one." Ladyhawke, the case cracked at the corners. 

    Manousos took one in each hand, weighing them like produce. "Moonstruck is better."

    "Says who?"

    "Cher won an Oscar."

    "That's not—that's a roomful of people congratulating themselves."

    He turned Moonstruck over and read the back of it. "It is a good film about family," he said, quieter.

    "Ladyhawke," Carol declared, with less and not more conviction, because she had no good reason to prefer it. The only true one right now—the eclipse she'd stolen, two people cursed to be in the same world and never touch, until the day the curse breaks—she was not going to say out loud.

    They both turned to Zosia to be judge, who had the popcorn bowl in her lap and was already munching. She took the cases, appraising both, as though the cover copy might tip a truly balanced scale.

    "This one," she said, lifting Moonstruck. "Won Oscars."

    "Three," Manousos nodded.

    She weighed it another moment. Then handed Manousos the cracked case. "Ladyhawke."

    Manny took it with a flat look, unfooled. "Next time," he said, feeding the disc in, "Moonstruck."

    He sat down at the far end of the sofa and left the rest open. Carol recalled the last time, the two of them pinned to the arms, Manousos fortified between them as their very own chaperone.

    Carol yanked the blanket off the back of the couch, sat in the center and covered their laps, and the toss happened to bring her shoulder flush to Zosia's, and she stayed there because retreating in front of Manny would be more conspicuous than staying, she told herself.

    Zosia simply lifted her half of the blanket and arranged it without being told, accepting every fumbled overture Carol had made or otherwise contemplated. She could fake a stretch. Do the old yawn-to-shoulder move, hadn't attempted it herself since she was twenty-two and drunk at a showing of Aliens. She pictured it and felt her elbow twitch, then imagined Manny watching it happen from two feet away, and folded her hands.

    The synth came up over the opening credits, an indefensible wall of eighties keytar. "The score was experimental," Carol said anyway, louder than needed. Her cold feet migrated under the warm weight of Zosia's leg.

    The popcorn bowl made its way to Manousos, and by the end of the first act, he had eaten most of it and was a hundred percent committed to the screen. 

    Carol stopped reaching for the bowl and reached for Zosia's hand instead, ate a piece of popcorn from her open palm, did it again, and Zosia fed her absently without looking away from Michelle Pfeiffer. Understandable.

    Then the popcorn was gone and the hand didn't come back up. It found Carol's under the wool and stayed there. The bowl, the blanket, the cooling mug, every errand of the evening went to Zosia's other one. This one she kept, fingers laced, and it never once came free for anything the world wanted. 

    Somewhere in the second act Carol noticed Zosia's fingers tapping a rhythm under the blanket, percussion through the cushion and her own hand where they were pressed together. She'd been up since dawn, since the dream and the river and everything after, stayed awake while Carol napped, and tapping was the tell—Carol learned—a small coup she staged when the rest of her was losing the fight. Zosia's head listed. Caught. 

    "You can sleep," Carol murmured.

    "Don't want to," but her eyes were heavy, and she listed again. Carol caught her with a shoulder. "Want to see how it ends."

    "You know how. The curse breaks."

    "Good," Zosia said, already half-gone, and Carol felt her relinquishing exhale as her hand went slack and warm in Carol's and stayed there. 

    On screen the hawk crossed a valley at dawn, alone, banking itself down the wind.

    "I finished your book," Manousos said, quietly, to the TV. "It would make a good movie." 

    She'd thought it ten thousand times. 

    "They'd ruin it," she muttered, because she had to say something. "Netflix would set it in space. They'd cast a couple of tanned teenagers. They'd never—" They'd never get Raban, was the end of the sentence, because the right one was here with popcorn salt on her fingers. "They never find the right person," she said instead.

    She'd given Zosia Raban to steer by without knowing it. Carol felt her hand in hers, and thought about the backspace key and the safe bet she'd made, her palms sticky. Lucasia had to choose courage. Carol had been standing at her own lip for thirty years and flinching.

    She lifted both their hands, Zosia's grip loose now with sleep, and brought them on top of the blanket. Out. Visible where the light reached and where Manny, had he looked over, would've seen.

    On screen the evil Bishop moved through torchlit rooms in red. 

    Her nerve lasted about ninety seconds before she caught him glance and panicked.

    "Do you mind?" she blurted, as if offended.

    "Do you?" Manny looked up from their hands, his face cool. She opened her mouth and he went on, "All day. Hiding." He'd seen all of it; of course he had. "You think I am that man," he nodded to the bishop on the screen, "because of this." The cross between his fingers.

    "That's not—I didn't—" 

    "They took her soul." He let the pendant drop. "That is the sin." He looked back at the screen. "Now it is hers again and she chose you. Why would I mind grace? It is the only good thing since this began." He picked up a kernel of popcorn from the cushion.  "I've prayed every night for that, for all of them. For the souls to come home."

    Carol thought of him in the rearview, getting smaller, left standing in a dead-end street so she could follow the hand she was holding. She wanted to let his misread stand, take the coward's way out, but she was trying to choose courage. 

    "I left you alone," she said. "Just…drove off like an idiot."

    "You came home too." He shrugged, the matter closed.

    It didn't help. "You did everything, though. The hardware, the recon, all of it. You've been planning all week while I was…you've been saving the world and I've been…" She heard it and kept going anyway. "Getting the girl. Again. If this works tomorrow, it's you. Not me. You should be in the history books."

    He watched the final duel without moving except to pick the last kernels from the popcorn bowl solemnly.

    "I came a long way to get here," he said, eventually. "Your name kept mine company. I did not come to be in books. I came to see if you were still a real person, with your own will, and all that comes with. You were. You are. Tomorrow everyone will hear because of it. The books can say whatever they like, only get that right. That I believed in you first."

    Carol stared at the screen and felt the urge to make a joke about sainthood, but she couldn't sneer him away. He had spent actual effort on her—miles, risk, gas, hunger, his stubborn bones in that ambulance, her name riding shotgun—with no evidence she deserved it, before anything had proved anything, and she supposed that was the crux of it. There was probably some bullshit Catholic word.

    The credits started rolling over the last blast of unforgivable synth and Carol grabbed the remote with her free hand and pressed mute to spare everyone.

    He read every name. Carol almost mocked him, then didn't. Each one of those people had spent some unrecoverable sliver of their life making this ridiculous thing. Two hours, years behind it, gone and still here.

    The names turned into logos and the screen went back to the menu, and Manousos unfolded from the sofa. He picked up his baseball cap and held it, not putting it on. Carol braced for some statement about tomorrow; God, courage, duty, or the sacred obligation to drink bottled water.

    "Sleep," he said.

    "That's rich, coming from you."

    "I am sleeping in ten minutes."

    "Bullshit."

    "Maybe twenty. I'll be back before dawn."

    Carol decided she hated the phrase before dawn. It was for executions, foxhunts, doomed cavalry, and she gave him a look that said this and probably also that she needed a beta blocker.

    "Carol."

    "What?"

    "It will work."

    You don't know that. Stop pretending. She rubbed both eyes and kept the words in. He had believed in her first, the bastard.

    He nodded once, accepting no objection, and went. His boots went soft on the rug, then harder on the tile. The door shut with a blunt little clap, and the house sealed itself around the two of them.

    The screen washed a cool pool across the sofa. "Hey," Carol said quietly, bending her head near Zosia. 

    Nothing.

    She brought her free hand up and brushed Zosia's cheek, soft as a whisper. "Hey, sailor."

    A twitch. Zosia's eyes opened halfway and she looked around with dazed suspicion. "He's gone."

    "Yeah. Movie's over." 

    Her lids closed again, pleased, and she didn't lift her head from Carol. If anything she sank further, other hand sliding to rest flat against Carol, anchoring. Her feet, which had been tucked, stretched until her toes found the arm of the sofa.

    "Really? The couch? We should be in bed," Carol said, though the stairs felt like a mile away. "We have two, both less lumpy."

    Zosia's arm tightened around her. "But here I have a pillow that complains."

    Carol huffed. The sofa was taking them on a diagonal descent and the arrangement was uncomfortable, technically. Carol's hip pressed into the sink between cushions, her foot had lost circulation beyond numbness and one of them had a knee in the wrong place and none of it was enough to make her move. Carol let the minute become two, shoulder tucked against the sofa back and Zosia slung across the front of her, and Carol thought she had gone under again until she spoke.

    "I owe you an apology," she said, accent syrupy with sleep.

    "Yipee. For what?"

    "I know I've been clingy. Testing."

    "Testing?"

    "That it's still only you," Zosia said into Carol, the low words coming up through the collarbone before they reached her ears. 

    Now it made sense. A broken touch meant a next one to risk. "I'd noticed you've been a menace, yeah. And this pillow isn't complaining, to be clear."

    "It stopped." She should've sounded pleased. Instead Zosia said it as Carol imagined she might report that a patched ship had survived the night, relieved about the floating but thinking about the leak. "I don't know why."

    "That's good, though. That's—"

    "I don't know why," Zosia said again. She tucked her hair with her free hand, impatient at herself. "I keep waiting for it to return, mid… mid-anything. That the next time it'll be back, or I'll wake up and it will be."

    "That's why you didn't want to sleep," Carol said slowly.

    "It's not rational. I'm aware."

    Carol brushed some hair off Zosia's forehead. "I'll tell you my theory."

    "You have a theory?"

    "I have a hundred theories, I'm a professional."

    "You weren't interested in mine."

    "I was interested in other things then." Carol smiled weakly, then lost the joke. "I think it stopped because you've let them go." She shifted them, got an arm braced so she could look into the tired face turned to her. "I'm no neurologist, but you had this…this back channel. Free trial of being joined again, running while you sleep, no charge. The warmest place in the world to go at night. And maybe, you liked that because letting it go meant it was really gone, and being alone again is—" She sighed. "I dunno. I'm projecting." 

    "No," Zosia said. "Keep going." 

    "Well, then you wake up and the real deal's here stealing your popcorn. You told me that—" She heard the old self-review crank up, one star, would not recommend, recoil from believing anyone might look at perfect belonging and pick her. "You said that this—" She gestured at the two of them, wedged sideways now, Zosia half over her— "was better than being joined." Zosia nodded, and how a cranky widow's couch and a cracked DVD case could outbid paradise, Carol had no idea. "So, the thing, the cut wire, the neurons or whatever it was leaking, just… closed, because you stopped wanting the last tether, the dreams, whatever. You'd rather just be you. Be here."

    Zosia didn't say anything.

    "It's a crappy theory. I make things up for a living. I don't know how any of it works."

    "It isn't," Zosia said, quietly. The experiment continued anyway; thumb against wrist, palm against palm.

    Carol cleared her throat. "Anyways, I'll keep watch. I'll be right here so there's no next time to worry about yet. You can sleep."

    When Zosia looked up again the fear had been set down, if not gone. A whole afternoon cursing at the cursor, and here, Carol must've somehow said the right thing first try. 

    "I finished it," Carol said.

    Zosia lifted her head. "The broadcast?"

    "Speech. Suicide note to civilization. Whatever it'll be. Done enough that I stopped wanting to delete it." Carol rubbed a knuckle on her temple. "I just… have to make them feel it, not just know it."

    "They'll feel it." Zosia gathered her closer, curled above her in the cramped remaining strip, their joined hands trapped between them. "You made me feel it."

    Carol lay under the truth that it had already worked more than once. "Yeah?"

    "Yeah." Zosia pressed the answer into her hair.

    The TV had become too bright. Carol reached around her for the remote and clicked it off.

    The dark dropped over them and Carol couldn't see an inch in front of her face. She could hear Zosia breathing, could feel the heat of her in the narrow bank between them, and the world went out with the light, everything past the edge of the couch ceasing to exist.

    Zosia shuffled nearer. "Come here," she said, barely voiced, the black absorbing it.

    Carol found her mouth by breath and guesswork, caught the corner first, the kiss clumsy and blind and Zosia's hand came up to the side of her face and steadied it.

    Sightless, the rest of her senses sharpened to compensate. The plush of Zosia's mouth, the scrape of teeth when she caught Carol's lower lip and tugged. 

    "Here?" Carol said against her mouth.

    "Here." Zosia's hand found the hem of Carol's shirt, burrowed under, spread warm and flat against her ribs. The blanket slid off them both.

    The sofa shifted under their weight. Carol tipped back the last few inches and Zosia followed, hip to shoulder, fitting along her front on what was left of the narrow cushion.

    Zosia's mouth left hers and Carol almost objected, but then she was at Carol's cheek, her jaw, the exposed line of her neck. Carol felt herself tilt with it, stupidly obedient to pressure no stronger than a sigh. She got one hand into Zosia's hair by accident or divine intervention, her elbow wedged by the sofa back.

    Carol turned her head and gave Zosia the commentary she would've edited out, let every word loose into the dark, where Zosia alone could hear them and wanted them. "My shoulder is going to be fucked for a week," she said to the ceiling, and she could feel every spring in the thing besides.

    She felt Zosia's mouth curve. 

    "When this is over," Carol said, because the dark made it sayable, "I'm buying a bed that doesn't fucking creak. A stupid hotel-sized mattress. Big enough to spread your insanely long legs."

    Zosia pushed her warming face into Carol's neck, and that had been the point: to make her want it, the after, to build a room in the dark they both had to live to walk into. 

    "What else?" Muffled.

    "I'll eat you out on it until you can only speak Polish." 

    Zosia laughed against her, startled, and her thighs clenched around Carol's. Zosia's hand traveled down, over Carol's tit through the cotton, thumb grazing, along her ribs, her stomach, her abs jumping at each new inch, and Carol's hips lifted to meet it before it arrived, embarrassingly wet already.

    "Your turn," Carol said. Zosia was quiet. Carol could feel the heat of her blush against her neck, pink she couldn't see. "You've got one. I can feel you thinking."

    Silence. Zosia's hand stopped at the crease of her thigh, too far and too close to where she needed.

    "I want to have coffee with you."

    Carol waited. That was all of it. "That's not a sex thing, that's—we just did that."

    "Somewhere else." Quieter. "It's what I want," she said, and stopped there, short of a promise.

    "Okay." Zosia drew a circle on her hip with her thumb and Carol covered her hand and held it there. "I'll take you out." Coffee, somewhere else—while Carol was offering filthy thoughts, Zosia wanted to sit across from her in public and hold a cup with one hand and hers in the other. Carol kissed the nearest part of her she could find, her hairline, clumsy in the dark. "It's a date."

    Zosia traced the waistband of Carol's jeans and Carol reached between them and fumbled her own button because she couldn't stand the patience of it any longer, Zosia's unshaking hand while her own hips were ten seconds ahead. Zosia brushed her fingers aside and somehow popped it one-handed in the pitch black, and between the two of them they shoved everything down past one knee. Carol kicked her other leg free, felt the fabric bunching at the ankle against the armrest.

    Carol still couldn't see, had to read Zosia by hand, got them up and under the cardigan where the wool had Zosia's heat and the woody scent had gone fully to salt, to her waist, the small of her back. She found the bare skin at the base of Zosia's spine, damp, and pinned her palm flat to feel her move.

    Zosia slid her fingers through her, playing her open, and Carol moaned at the feel of them, the length of them, the sureness. Zosia groaned low against her throat at how easy she went, the sound vibrating into Carol's pulse, but didn't speed up, just pressed with patience that made Carol want to scream.

    Zosia's mouth found the hollow behind Carol's ear. "You're so wet." Her accent was thicker. "I want to—" She stalled, barely audible, her face burning Carol's neck. "Clear everything off your desk and lay you on the map." Carol's hips jerked and her thighs fell wider and Zosia exhaled, freed: "I've wanted that since you let me in. I want to fuck you where you wrote it."

    Carol fluttered on nothing and got wetter. "Fuck," Carol groaned. "Yes. We'll do all of that."

    Zosia's mouth left her ear and traveled south, and her teeth closed on the collar of the shirt. Her shirt. It smelled of her, and now she was breathing over Carol while the ghost of her clung to the cotton, Zosia above and Zosia in the weave, Carol surrounded on every side. Zosia dragged the collar down, baring one breast to the cool air, and covered the nipple with her lips. She laved it, tongued it stiff, sucked with her cheeks hollowing until a whimper wrenched loose.

    Zosia stroked through her, withdrew, stroked again, thumb rolling over Carol's clit on every return, circling with maddening precision, and her deft fingers explored the rest, dipping and retreating, tracing the entrance but withholding, until Carol's hips tilted and she begged with enough urgency that Zosia stopped being patient, gave her what she'd been pleading for.

    Two long fingers, and Carol's head dropped back onto the cushion and her eyes rolled shut at how fucking good it felt.

    "Tell me another," Zosia mumbled, back at the crook of Carol's neck, her thumb curling and dragging forward on every next stroke.

    Carol groaned through her teeth as Zosia grazed her swollen clit, her voice gone open-mouthed and unedited at the soaked give of herself around Zosia's fingers. "You—you'll be insufferable about coffee in the morning with that, fuck, that goddamn smug look on your face." Zosia's fingers scissored and she gasped, the stretch of it exactly right. "And you'll—you'll bend me over before I finish telling you to go to hell."

    Zosia's breath broke on her shoulder, each exhale hotter, wetting Carol's skin, and then her hips ground against Carol's thigh, and Carol knew Zosia was picturing it: the counter, her mouth running, the shutting-up, and the thought of that and being bent over on a random goddamn Monday did almost as much as her hand. 

    Carol hooked a hand behind her neck and yanked her mouth down, and the kiss was a mess, no finesse. Carol groaned into her and felt Zosia's hand flex inside her at the sound, fingers spreading. She wanted it deeper and Zosia sank further before the thought had finished forming. Carol felt her forearm flex against her thigh with each thrust, her whole body behind it now.

    Her shirt had ridden up past her ribs and the collar hung loose where Zosia's teeth had been, left the whole front of her bare against the rough knit that raked her bare stomach and caught on her chest with every drive. "I want you first thing, before coffee," Zosia grunted, pushing deeper still. "I want to wake you up every day with my mouth."

    "Every—" Carol's voice cracked. Her heel dug into the back of Zosia's thigh, still not close enough. "Fuck. That's a lot of—that's—" Zosia's thumb circled harder and Carol couldn't finish the sentence. Every morning. Her other hand was flat on Zosia's bare back, riding the muscles as they worked, and she was close, and the words came because she couldn't hold them and the lack of light still made it sayable:

    "I want—I want to watch you read and—and I'll—pretend to write and look at you instead, for—for years, for forever, I want—" The rest faded because Zosia was making it impossible to think, every nerve narrowing, every thought contracting. Zosia dropped her forehead to Carol's temple. Her hand slowed, each stroke the full length of her, like she was touching Carol for years, each press a morning and each drag back a night.

    She caught Zosia's mouth somewhere in the dark, or Zosia found hers, and the kiss was past saving, mouths too slack to close, tasting breath, but she could feel Zosia smiling into it. Carol rocked into the roll of her hand, climbing, and her groans had gone to rags; she was close, had been close, everything they'd built strung in her, the knot in her belly pulled so tight she couldn't breathe.

    "Carol," Zosia said, so close, her lips at Carol's ear now, just her name, in that voice, said like it was the whole answer, and what had been hauled wire-tight in her all evening slipped. It poured from the center of her, a long plunge down through her her skull, her fingers, hips to the soles of her feet, and she shoved her open mouth to Zosia's skin and gave it to her—all sound, no language.

    Zosia rode it down with her, patient through every second, like they had every night still coming and this was only the first. She slowed as Carol slowed, until Carol caught her wrist and held her hand still for a second, too much now, to bear and to lose.

    Zosia kissed her temple, then her cheekbone, then the bridge of her nose as she eased her fingers out, and Carol clutched at them going and ached the second they were gone. Zosia rested her wet palm flat on Carol's thigh, and her other arm folded and she dropped onto her side in the narrow space.

    The couch had stopped protesting. Carol had stopped panting. She slid down, her fingers already at Zosia's waistband—

    Zosia caught her hand. "No. Just this." Soft and certain, eyelids already drooping. "Want this to be the last thing, before I sleep." Zosia got Carol's palm on her chest, over the slowing knock of her heart.

    "Okay."

    Last. Carol caught on it and couldn't let go, felt her mind leave the room, climb the stairs, cross the hall to the art room, her phone left on the worktable after taking the photograph of the print.

    Her brain went there before she could stop it. She had no photos of Zosia. No proof she'd existed, in this house, alive and undocumented. No Zosia saying fun fact, mouth gone wry, eyes sparkling. No Zosia in the kitchen, furious and still making Carol's coffee perfectly. None of the look on her face when she'd said mango ice cream and surprised herself, ten years old for two seconds.

    Just memories, most of them tainted.

    The need was so sharp she nearly got up, her hand flexing under Zosia's. She shut her eyes, but the phone remained, waiting with its little lens and untrue promise that something could be kept forever.

    Photograph is data, Manny'd said. That was all a picture was. A piss-poor substitute. She'd stood on the other side of glass once. She'd rather have felt the cold.

    Carol stayed where she was.

    Zosia's thumb moved over her knuckles, reading her like braille. "You're thinking."

    "It's nothing." Zosia didn't push, until the silence left nowhere to hide. "Just—I don't have any photos of you."

    Quiet. Long enough that Carol thought she'd lost her to sleep after all, then Zosia's fingers laced more firmly through hers. "When we get back," she said, "I'll let you take one."

    Carol froze at the first future tense promise she'd made all day.

    Zosia didn't open her eyes. "A terrible one, probably."

    Her huffed laugh hurt. "Bullshit." As if a bad photo of Zosia could possibly exist. She could be captured mid-sneeze at the DMV and still come out perfect.

    "We will see."

    Carol would do anything to make it true. "Okay," she said, like a vow. "Tomorrow." 

    Carol listened to Zosia's breathing go toward sleep. In and out, the most ordinary sound in the world. She caught herself counting it, unwilling to lose a single one, each rise and fall, an arm around Zosia's back, the other trapped at an angle she'd regret, which would be the least of her worries in the morning.

    The reflex clawed upward, tallying everything she stood to lose. She could feel—

    Heat on her forearm, the sofa cushion scratching under it. Zosia's pulse in her palm, resting, maybe seventy-something. A strand of Zosia's hair caught on her lip, and she didn't move it. She was here, and that was the truth of this minute.

    This minute. Only this one.

    Dawn waited outside the window, and the pull was there, a drink she could sink into like she used to. Carol glanced to the glass once, but in the dark it showed only where she was. Dim and doubled. The sofa too small, Zosia asleep against her by stubborn choice. She was breathing deeply now, and Carol listened until the rhythm became the room's only clock.
