    Chapter 12

    Chapter Notes

    Looks like melodrama's back on the menu, boys.

    Carol's arm was dead.

    For one stupid second, that was the whole world. Sofa seam welting her hip, jeans still twisted around her ankle, Zosia's hair in her mouth.

    Zosia shifted and her breathing changed, too small to have caught before and now grossly precious to Carol, who'd turned into some deranged breathing accountant overnight. 

    One dark eye opened against her shoulder, and fingers tightened once in the fabric at Carol's waist. "Morning," Zosia mumbled.

    "That's debatable." Outside, the atrium had returned only in silver scraps and shadow.

    Zosia pushed herself upright. "Did you sleep?"

    "Parts of me did." Carol shook her arm as blood swarmed in pins and needles from elbow to fingertip.

    Zosia's feet found the floor silently and her shoulders lifted back, chin tucked, and there she was, reporting for duty. Carol wanted to pull Zosia back down and keep her in the cramped den of them for another hour, and realistically, had less than a minute, probably. Her hand moved to the hem of Zosia's shirt and stopped there, two fingers hooked in the cotton, before the mission pulled her loose.

    As if on cue, the knock that must've woken her up came again at the front door. The sound was patient, a hotel porter rather than a battering ram, and therefore Manousos at his most paranoid of what he might find beyond, and thank god for that. Her shirt was still rucked under one tit and she got a sleeve caught on her thumb and nearly punched herself in the face fixing it.

    A third knock came, at a shorter interval now, Morse code for move your asses. "Jesus, give me a minute!"

    Carol pulled her jeans up and limped across the cold tile to the door, where Manny stood in his newly adopted baseball cap and the same clothes as yesterday too. He carried a plastic document sleeve and a tupperware of foiled cylinders.

    Carol looked at it. "Tell me that's breakfast and not home-made dynamite." 

    She could hear herself. Meiosis, the literary term, if you wanted to be a dick about it. Shrink the fear until it fits in a burrito and call it comedy.

    "Breakfast." He came in. "Dynamite is in the ambulance."

    "Funny."

    "No." Manny handed the plastic sleeve to Carol. "Your page. I made two more copies."

    "Don't you think that's overkill?"

    He proffered the tupperware. "Eat."

    Carol took one and the smell hit her and her stomach, traitorous fucker, rolled and contracted in two directions at once, queasy and starving. She'd thought fear would be more dignified at this hour; a minor key, operatic cavities, violins and whatnot. Instead pepper and potatoes were making her want to puke, and she needed to pee, and none of this was how the hero was supposed to feel before the final threshold.

    Manny checked his watch for the fourth time. "We go in eight minutes."

    "Eight? What the fuck—I need to shower, I need to—my jeans are—"

    "Eat in one. Wash in five. Dress in two."

    Carol flapped her lagging hand in irritation, pins and needles still biting. Zosia took it without asking, worked her thumb into Carol's palm, then left her hand there, checking. 

    "Seven minutes," Manny said.

    Carol squeezed and let her go. "Great," she huffed, and tried to finish breakfast.

    The streetlights died behind them one by one.

    Manousos drove. He'd taken the wheel while Carol climbed into the passenger side, like old times, meaning: last week. The heater came on and burned off dust through the vents. They drove for twenty minutes before he started the timing checks yet a-fucking-gain.

    "Radio one."

    "Receiving," Zosia said from the back.

    "Radio two."

    Carol lifted her walkie. "This is Ground Control to Major Pain-in-the-Ass."

    His face didn't change. "Do not call me that on channel."

    "Receiving, Regional Manager." 

    Zosia's voice came dry from behind her, fondly exasperated. "Carol."

    "What? I'm rallying morale." She was attempting to treat a drive toward possible annihilation with the narrative framework of a caper, the only genre she had for this absurdity. The engine cover between the seats put its heat onto her calf, and left the rest of her cold.

    In the back, Zosia was moving through the gear, had wedged herself on the bench along the wall, a boot braced against the opposite cabinet, penlight between her teeth while she checked a connector. Every few seconds, metal clicked.

    No headlights came toward them. The traffic lights changed over empty intersections for an audience of three and one unfinished burrito. The city shrank in the side mirror until a turn took it. Her house, her yard, all gone.

    Carol watched the desert brush go green from gray, low ridges lined in the yellow distance. None of the cinematic wreckage from disaster movies and paperback covers she'd judged in Barnes and Noble. They'd kept the planet tidy, everyone in peace; done what every government and god and H.O.A. had promised and failed. The world could've at least had the manners to look doomed while it was being saved.

    She looked down at the translucent plastic sleeve, at the first line of her speech visible under her thumb. Her pathetic little soul in twelve-point Times New Roman, much neater than she felt. 

    The nearer they got, the more it looked less like an argument and more like begging. The first plan had required less than a handful of memories and one lie. A page waited in her lap now, every sentence true, and she trusted them less. The words bounced in time with the ambulance and her stomach rolled again.

    "Why didn't we take the helicopter?" She'd been chewing on it since they loaded. "It'd get us there in, what, twenty minutes? Instead of this Oregon Trail horseshit."

    Manousos didn't answer, his hands fixed at ten and two. Road noise filled the pause.

    "I'm the only one who could pilot us back," Zosia said.

    Carol stared ahead at the ruled line she was riding straight to the vanishing point. "Right." Her face floated over the road in the windshield faintly. Jesus, she looked embalmed. "Stupid question."

    She pulled down the visor. The little mirror showed the same corpse and Carol tilted it until Zosia came into view, bent over the gear. Better.

    There'd be no drink today, obviously, but past the last streetlight it occurred to her there'd been no coffee either. No time to put the kettle on. The beginning of the end and she'd face it caffeine-free and stone sober, running only on adrenalin and potato like some Mormon storming Normandy. Christ.

    She'd have given a lot right then for one lousy cup and Zosia lording it over. Carol stared at her in the mirror, and could only think of the four minutes thirty seconds they hadn't spent together. 

    Zosia had resumed her checks, hands busy among the cables. Clip. Tug. Click. Clip. Tug. Click. A sailor's rosary. The same hands that had held Carol's face fifteen hours ago and told her she was loved and that it was easy, and it felt like fifteen minutes ago. She should've held them longer.

    The ambulance rattled over a bump in the road. The gun case knocked Carol's ankle, and she moved her foot away.

    They crested a rise and at first the dishes looked too white to be real, scattered across the plain in the distance. Then the road dipped and rose again, and more of them appeared, each one turned in the same cold attention, into forty miles of unobstructed gusts and not moving an inch for it. 

    The road curved and a blue sign for the visitor center rose from the scrub.

    ARE WE ALONE?

    Carol shrugged. "Complicated."

    A meadowlark on the fence wire had ran through its dawn song and started again, and the wind took most of it away. Manny's hand left the wheel long enough to press his pendant as he slowed through the unlocked gate. The ambulance vibrated over the cattle grid and the tremor climbed the seat into Carol's spine. 

    The next sign appeared a quarter mile later.

    TOGETHER, WE HEAR FARTHER.

    "Okay. A little on the nose."

    Then:

    OPEN YOUR MIND TO THE UNIVERSE.

    "Absolutely not."

    The final sign had an arrow beneath it.

    RESTROOMS

    "Oh, thank God." The plastic sleeve in her lap had collected fog where her thumb was pressing. She wiped it on her jeans and made a worse smear. "Well," Carol said, taking a page out. "At least the parking's free."

    Neither of them laughed. Right. Her comedy act concluded and had carried her as far as it could. The visitor signs were behind them. The dishes rose larger with each turn. Ahead was the stronger signal and the risk of Zosia entering a country Carol couldn't follow.

    Behind her, the clips and small metal tugs had stopped. 

    She twisted around. "Still with me?" If the answer was ever no, Carol couldn't do a goddamn thing but hear it.

    "Yes," Zosia said, gentler than it needed to be, and held her eyes past the word. Carol chose to believe the look and not the odds. 

    She heaved a sigh and faced front again, folding the page in half, too careful for what only needed to survive the next hour. The crease still came out crooked. She opened it, smoothed it flat against her thigh, and left it alone.

    Okay. Okay, Sturka. Showtime. She'd done this once already, in sweatpants. Manny had climbed into that container without a scrap of drama, dragged the mattress across, clanged the door. No future talk. Do steps.

    She looked at the building where she'd be, at the dish Zosia would climb, at the hundred feet between them she couldn't cross.


    Zosia had the rear door open before the ambulance stopped moving. Her boots crunched on the packed dirt, and she started pulling equipment out, stacking the cases downwind of the wheel. 

    She'd worked here. Only last week the body had stood in this dust, and it felt more like resuming than recalling. The cabinet on antenna twelve had two spare BNC adapters taped inside the left panel. The seventeenth rung on the nearest dish had a split rubber tread. The base tuner's upper gain dial pulled slightly left when released.

    Memory could come back through place. Ships did the same. A smell, a footfall, and she remembered. If the world woke from this, someone would need to dismantle what had been built. She might be the only one who'd know where every bolt was. 

    "Five minutes for setup," Manousos said.

    The walkie slipped in Carol's grip before she trapped it against herself. Zosia watched the back of her head and the line of her shoulder through the gap between the seats. Her hair had dried badly after the fast shower, one side lifting in a stubborn wing.

    Zosia forced her gaze away and took inventory again. Hands steady, balance good, vision clear.

    Manousos began unloading too; the climbing gear first, then the converter case, then Carol's rig, the slim mic and its box that would transmit her voice into the carrier. He clipped a walkie to Zosia without being asked. Last out was the smaller black case he'd never named aloud. Zosia saw Carol see it. Her mouth went flat.

    Zosia looked up at the dish. In every version of the plan made before yesterday, going up had been hers. She'd climbed worse in worse weather. She had no fear of the height.

    Manny pulled the gear out of the bag. "We move."

    "You climb," Zosia said.

    His head came up. "What?"

    "You climb. I stay at the base."

    "Why?"

    "I don't know." She had a gut feeling she'd be less useful above. "Inside the dish, the signal will be worse."

    He held the look long enough to read her, then shouldered the gear. He handed her a case without protest. "Okay, base unit is yours."

    He opened the gun case and Carol finally snapped. "She feels fine. Why is that out?"

    Manousos checked the chamber and Carol turned away from the sight. "Insurance is purchased before the accident," he said. He clipped the holster onto his belt and began coiling the climbing line over one shoulder.

    Carol was staring at the control building. The window was dark from outside, but Zosia could see a desk inside, the dull green reflection of old monitor glass. The door opened outward and had been left on just a latch.

    She tasted metal, or imagined she did. Her mouth had gone too wet. Nerves, maybe. She'd been in storms, fires, blood on deck, and her mouth had never done this. She pressed her tongue behind her teeth and ignored it.

    "Final positions," Manousos said. "Carol, here, microphone. Me, relay, five minutes. Zosia, dish base, frequency lock, one minute. I call when sync is matched."

    Manousos took two steps toward the dish, then stopped with visible irritation at himself.

    Carol saw it. "Oh no."

    He looked at her. "You are good at this."

    "At what?"

    "At talking when angry."

    "Sure," Carol said, flat. Her gaze went to the holster, then the building.

    "You do your part. I do mine. Now we go."

    Zosia should've been checking her base unit, or confirming Manny's clips, or walking the path between building and base to mark her footing. Instead she was measuring the small shake in Carol's hand, a vibration too fast to be cold. 

    She stepped closer to her. "Manousos, give us a minute," she said. His eyebrows rose. "One minute."

    He looked between them. "No goodbyes. It is bad practice." Carol's mouth opened. "No," he said. "Later, you joke. Now, you do. Zosia, one minute. Then I climb." He clipped his walkie and left.

    Carol watched him go, breathing too high in her chest. "Bad practice. Listen to Emily Post over there." She looked back at Zosia with immediate suspicion. "If this is another practical conversation about how he may have to shoot you, I'm going to start biting."

    Zosia ignored that and nodded toward the control room. "Go in. Put the page down. Deep breaths before he calls, or you'll start too high and waste your voice."

    "Bossy."

    "You need it."

    Carol gulped in concession. "I need a drink."

    "If the power changes, if the signal goes, you wait for his read before deciding what it means."
