    Zosia managed to raise an exhausted eyebrow. "You looked out of the window," she rasped. 

    "Of course I fucking looked at you. Thank god I did."

    Carol was shaking still. Zosia lifted a hand, her arm heavy and her fingers slow, and set two knuckles under Carol's streaming eye, wiping the wet sideways. "What happened?"

    "Your heart stopped." The words made the last minute real again. "I couldn't—I couldn't find a pulse. I did the—" she mimed it, two stacked hands, "I breathed into you, and then you came back."

    Zosia looked at her mouth.

    "What?"

    "They made me infectious to you. My mouth."

    "What? Wait—so... they could've joined me?" Zosia nodded slowly. "But they didn't?"

    "No," Zosia coughed.

    Carol huffed a laugh through the remains of panic. "Huh." 

    Zosia's arm came around her slowly. Carol's next breath finally made it all the way down. "Your crap version was good." 

    Carol's face crumpled further. "Shut up."

    "I'm... I'm thirsty," Zosia said, marveling at it. 

    A minute ago Carol had forced her own breath into her and prayed it took, now Zosia was breathing on her own, in and out, spectacular, a fucking miracle. She hovered over Zosia's filthy forehead and kissed her there instead, hard enough to leave dust on her lips. "God. Yeah. Water. I'll give you water." Neither of them moved. "They let everyone go. Manny says the signal's dead." 

    "Maybe," he called.

    Carol lifted her head. "Oh, for fuck's sake."

    He came toward them without sharing their relief. Sweat had darkened his collar. He looked at Zosia, then at Carol's hand still cupping her face.

    "No signal," he said. "From here. It does not prove the network is gone. It does not prove they can't restart it."

    "You are a fucking delight," Carol said.

    Manny didn't answer. He unclipped his radio and extended its antenna. "Silence I don't trust," he said. "I want a stranger. Someone they don't have now." He kept turning the dial.

    Carol left him to it and worked an arm under Zosia. "Come here. I've got you." 

    They rose in stages and Zosia unfolded until Carol's cheek ended up against her shoulder, her weight distributed with insulting steadiness despite having been dead five minutes ago.

    "You're doing too much," Carol said.

    "You're short."

    "Well, you came back just as mean." Carol's arm closed harder around her waist. 

    They crossed to Manousos and he turned the dial in increments, his face closed against hope, and the radio spat nothing but static. He listened past one hiss, then another.

    Carol could feel Zosia's pulse now, but she kept checking it anyway.

    A woman's voice broke through.

    "Hello? Hello? Help. Where I am. Please—"

    Manny stopped turning the dial and lifted the handset. "Hello?"

    The channel crackled.

    "Hello? Please, you no go. I no have telephone. Please—" 

    Carol had half-expected proof to sound triumphant. A voice announcing that they had done it and everyone could clap. Instead some woman somewhere was frightened, her English failing, begging the first stranger she found not to disappear. 

    "My name is Manousos Oviedo. Tell me what you see."

    "Manousos." She held the name. "My name is Elena. I wake in truck. I no know this place, the sign is English. Is nothing here, only road. Truck lights go tick-tick. I have key. I wake, is stopped." 

    "They pulled her over," Zosia said quietly, before a swallow of dry air. "Set everyone down softly."

    "Even her," Carol said, meaning the whole waking world.

    "Everyone but me." Zosia's mouth pulled wry. "I wouldn't be parked."

    Elena spoke again. "We in vacation. My family. Then…" The radio carried her breathing while she searched. "People. Many people. I was…" She gave a small, bewildered sound. "I no say. Then truck. I no have bag, no have documents. Doamne… Where is my family?" The English ran out and she kept going anyway, faster, in her own tongue, the words shaking and opaque and vaguely Russian or Italian or something.

    She looked at Zosia, who only shrugged a shoulder.

    Manny waited until she paused. "Elena." The one word he was sure of. "I don't have your language. I'm sorry. Only English."

    Dredged back into the broken, shared words, she said, "My feet hurt. The shoes is too small. Not my shoes." Fabric rustled. "The clothes not mine. In the door is card, say Travis Bell. He take me? I am… kidnap?"

    Here was the sound of Carol getting what she wanted. Wrong country, wrong clothes, no family. A life months up the road with no handhold between one blink and the next.

    "No." Manny leaned into the handset, choosing each word plainly so it would carry the distance. "Something happened to everyone. You are safe. You are speaking to a person, and you are Elena. That is the first thing."

    Elena breathed on the far side of the world.

    Then she started to cry. The sound came through ragged, private, and they couldn't lift it from her.

    Manny began again, patient. "Elena. I'm here."

    Chapter 13

    The radio had talked to itself all the way home, and at first it'd been what they'd heard at the VLA: single, bewildered people waking up lost. A dad in Juárez looking for his daughter, and two young guys on a ham radio channel, laughing at each other with stunned hilarity.

    By the time they got back, it'd changed:

    "—all units, FEMA Region Six activating, requesting status from all posts, acknowledge on—"

    Manny turned the dial and found another.

    "—Kirtland Air Force Base is operational, repeat, Kirtland operational, all military personnel report—"

    And another.

    "—Interstate 25 checkpoint at mile marker 194, all traffic routed through—"

    He clicked the radio off. The kitchen went quiet except for the kettle boiling and Zosia breathing from the living room, where she'd fallen asleep with her wrist bound in a dish towel of ice.

    "Checkpoints," Manousos said.

    From the north, so low the window vibrated in the frame, a helicopter crossed overhead. Manny's head turned, tracking the sound until it faded, and by the time he looked back to Carol, his jaw had set.

    "How do we explain any of this?" Carol asked. "Who would we even tell? The military? Hi, hello, my name is Carol Sturka, I'm a fantasy novelist, I yelled at a telescope and everyone woke up. Here's my team, a Paraguayan prepper and a Polish sailor, we'd like a medal and a couple of green cards." She paced the kitchen. "They'll think I'm a crank."

    "You should not tell the military anything."

    "So what, we just—sit here?"

    "You need…" He tapped the counter. "El abogado." 

    "There are no lawyers, Manny. There's nobody yet."

    "Then wait. I have seen what happens when your government has questions. Do not volunteer for interrogation." His eyes moved to the living room. "Either of you."

    The couch creaked. Zosia appeared in the kitchen doorway with the towel around her wrist and a bruise on her cheek already gone plum. She'd heard all of it—you couldn't breathe in this house without the tile selling you out. 

    "I should report," Zosia said.

    Carol's stomach pitched. "Report to who?"

    "My command. The transmitters have to be decommissioned. I might be the only person who knows, if those—"

    "They're gone," Carol said, too fast. "The signal is dead, you said—"

    "The signal is gone but the hardware to send it again isn't." The same voice she'd used to tell them about the re-joining risk, already past the part where anyone argued, unwilling to leave a loose line untied. 

    Carol felt her fight forming again, all the words loading into the chambers. "You died today."

    "And I'm alive now, and I remember things." Zosia's thumb pressed against the swelling, reading her own pulse. "Thanks to you." She had the gall to smile, god damn her, and there went half the arsenal.

    Manousos cleared his throat. "I'm leaving," he said. Carol turned on him. "Today. South. Before the checkpoints."

    "We just—" She looked at Zosia, then back. "We just did it. And you're leaving already?" 

    "I'm not a citizen of this country."

    "You're not even going to—what, stay a few days? See what happens?"

    He folded his arms. "I know what happens. Your military will sort foreigners. They go into a system that doesn't know their name, in a language they do not speak, run by people who did not ask for them. Elena is near Las Cruces and she knows my name. I will not leave her standing."

    Carol's throat went thick. She hadn't expected goodbye so fast. "Manny."

    "It is your name for me, yes."

    "Don't be fucking flip."

    "Carol," he said, gentler than her current tone earned. "You have a country." He nodded toward Zosia. "She has a navy. You have a people." 

    "You have—you can have us." She scowled at how it sounded, and huffed into the wonky chair for the last time with that company, apparently.

    Manousos reached into his bag on her porch and produced her colander.

    "I used it to rinse soldering flux with acid. Clean now."

    Carol turned it in her hands, a new scorch mark along the steel handle, then looked past him at the street which was as empty as it'd ever been.

    There were humvees on the interstate, but no one had come for the helicopter, or the atom bomb, yet. Authority sputtered in bursts of static, a voice reading instructions, static again.

    The ambulance waited at the curb with rear doors open. The mic transmitter still lay on the bench, its antenna collapsed, a strip of white tape showing his block-lettered label: CAROL. Beside it, tucked under the edge of his sleeping bag, was the library copy of Winds he'd finished, barcode and all.

    Fucking thief. Carol stepped back. "Get in here. We made you coffee for the road."

    The cable modem had found the world two hours ago. She finally took her cell phone out of airplane mode, but it still displayed NO SERVICE. Walls and wires worked while the air remained useless.

    Manny came in behind her and Zosia looked at him, and he looked at her, and some exchange passed between them that Carol couldn't read and didn't try to, she was too exhausted. 

    She handed Manousos her ancient UNM travel mug. "So," Carol said, "Panama?"

    "The hospital needs its ambulance. Then a flight, if one to Asunción exists then."

    "Call me when you get somewhere with a roof," Carol demanded. "I don't care what time it is."

    He reached into the pocket of his shirt and produced a pen with the logo of a dental office. "Number."

    "You got paper?"

    Manny tore the blank margin from one of the maps still on the table, removing a narrow strip of Nevada. Carol wrote the landline.

    Manny examined the strip.

    "What?" Carol asked.

    "Is this five?"

    "It's a six."

    "It does not close."

    "Jesus." She took the paper back and corrected the six until it resembled a small, angry snail. "Happy?"

    He copied it into his pocket notebook anyway, then peeled two post-its from another page and set them down separately. Yellow squares, the same number starting +595, one by her mug and one by Zosia's notebook. She stared at Zosia's too long as he made for the door. Zosia followed and Carol scrambled to catch up.

    "There's a checkpoint in Truth or Consequences," she said to his back.

    "I know."

    "The state website says one lane."

    "I saw."

    "The rear tire looked low."

    "It is not."

    "You have aspirin?"

    "Yes."

    "Okay," Carol said, as they got to the porch. "You could stay," she tried one last time.

    "No," was all he said, and that was that.

    Zosia offered her hand. He clasped her forearm, his grip firm, like Carol imagined sailors did, or soldiers. Respect earned at altitude. It lasted two seconds and Carol watched whatever it was happen again.

    He nodded to the phone inside. "You will have to call."

    "Eventually."

    "They need you."

    "So does she."

    "I'm right here, by the way," Carol said.

    Manny's expression loosened as he turned to her. "That is why we didn't speak in Spanish."

    She'd prepared several acceptable forms of goodbye while he finished packing. Don't die had been leading. A sincere thank you remained unusable. See you soon sounded too much like a request the returning world might hear and punish. 

    He'd come to her when every other survivor considered her a bitch best kept outside. He'd trampled through her house, sifted through her shit, driven while she was drunk, fed her stale granola and faith in her with uniform force. Now he was going back to somewhere she couldn't even find on an unlabelled map, and she hadn't said any of that and wasn't going to.

    "Don't get sentimental," she warned, as if he was going to. 

    He clapped her on the shoulder. "You did good work."

    Carol weighed the colander still in her hand and looked past him through the open door, at the white tape on the transmitter beside the book, to what had broadcast it farther than any binding or blurb.

    "Yeah." Her grip shifted. "You too. Just—call. And drink your stupid bottled water. If the ambulance breaks down in Honduras or whatever, I'll be pissed." His mouth had pulled. "Wait." She held up her free hand. "Do you want Tootsie? The DVD? I mean, you ordered it."

    "No, I have my tape. You keep it. Something to remember me."

    "I don't need—" She pressed her lips together hard and dropped her hand. "Alright," she managed. "Go. Call me." 

    He walked down the driveway then turned at the container. "Write it," he called. "What we did."

    Carol shook her head. "That's not—"

    "You asked what I wanted to be in the books. I want to be in yours."

    Carol couldn't speak. She gave him a look that was supposed to be glowering and flapped the colander at the ambulance. "Shoo. Go."

    He opened the door and the diesel engine caught on the second attempt, loud enough to travel over every empty yard.

    "He'll make it home," Zosia said.

    "Yeah." Carol folded her arms. "He'll make it, and he'll never call. He doesn't even own a goddamn cell phone." Zosia's bad hand came to Carol's back and her spine went cold. 

    You're going to leave too. She didn't say it.

    Carol kept watching the ambulance. The sound of it pulled away through the cul-de-sac, the yellow roof disappeared downhill and she listened to the quiet it left behind.

    The helicopter crossed the ridge again, or a second one.

    Zosia sighed. "I'm going to call. Tell them everything." 

    Carol's stomach dropped and she turned. "No—not—not yet. What about—what about the other chaperones? Maybe they'll remember too, and you won't have to—"

    "I don't know," Zosia said. Her eyes softened at Carol's stammer, as though her panic was another difficult thing she'd weirdly decided was endearing. "I was an outlier. I fell in love." She looked faintly amused by the diagnosis.

    Carol narrowed her eyes. She was getting very schmoopy lately. Carol wanted to kiss the bruise and then every stubborn inch of her mouth—and couldn't—Zosia's rule, an overabundance of ridiculous caution she wouldn't relax yet.

    Zosia caught her staring, and instead of pretending otherwise, said, "I have to call eventually because I'd like to kiss you again too," and Carol steadied by half. Very unfair. A prospect of future kissing could accomplish what reason, duty, and the continued existence of civilization couldn't. "Whether chaperones remember or not, there's no way to know today."

    Zosia's thumb was moving, patient enough to make Carol's next breath come out easier. Cheap tactics. Highly effective cheap tactics. The future retreated one grudging inch. 

    Carol huffed. "Right. Stay in the room." Zosia looked down at her with tenderness so undisguised Carol had to raise the colander between their faces. "I'll make pasta. Apparently this has been through a chemical bath, so." 

    "I'm sure we'll be fine."

    The phone had kept ringing for the wrong number, her landline one of millions people were panicking and pressing wrong. Every working phone had become a bottle thrown into an oceanful of bottles.

    Then Val had called. Val had said Helen's name first, Carol had said hers, and the conversation broke there. Val had accepted the facts, with bewildering calm, in the sequence Carol could force them out: Helen, the virus, Zosia sent, the VLA, the release.

    Val and Helen had held a Friday call for fifteen years, including the ones Carol had no book coming out. They discussed Carol in tonalities of coordinating freight through hostile territory; covering reviews, humiliating sales figures, then less humiliating sales figures Carol had also found a reason to resent, then drinking, and whatever Carol had been bossed into doing that week. Helen would pace with the phone against her ear and make faces at Carol whenever Val said something accurate.

    "I think I knew," Val said.

    Carol's thumbnail dug into the seam between two tiles on the backsplash. "What do you mean?"

    "Before you told me," Val said carefully, "I had a feeling she was gone. I don't remember anything, but there's a peace in me I can't—" Her breath caught. "I think I said goodbye to her, Carol, and she heard me. I wish I knew what we said."

    Carol had stared ahead until the grout stayed square, her throat burning with envy. "She probably corrected your grammar," Carol said. Val laughed once, and by the end of the call, she knew her oldest client had saved the world, and was about to be the only one that mattered.

    The call today Carol answered on the second ring, sprinting down the stairs from the shower to catch it.

    "Hi?"

    "Oh my God, Carol!" Val's voice went in her ear too loud, high and fast, none of the calm of the last call; this was the one she used for news that needed both hands in the air. "I've been calling, I've been—" Val took a breath that was audible across state lines. "Someone found me."

    "What do you mean?"

    "Through the website, which is somehow up, don't ask me how. The hosting company is probably a box in a basement right now. He emailed my contact form. A man named Diabate, he says he knows you."

    "Eh, not so much."

    "Really? Because he says he was immune, like you." Val's voice had shifted from champagne-launch to a pitch like a story was about to break. "There's a group of them, and they want to make a statement, do a press conference, and they want to tell everyone what you did."

    Carol leaned against the hallway wall. Zosia was watching through the frame, the laptop's light on her face. She'd put on the cardigan, and her hair was down, and she looked like she lived here, which she did, for now. The screen reflected in the cabinet glass beside her: a map that was mostly blue. 

    "Carol? Are you there?"

    "I'm here." She rubbed her cheekbone. "What exactly does he want?"

    "He asked if I could connect you. He was very charming, I liked him immediately, which I know you'll hold against me." Val cleared her throat. "Can you hop on a Zoom?"

    She imagined Koumba and the others in their confortable little windows, on Tuesdays and Fridays, while she'd been in this house with the blinds drawn.

    "No."

    "Carol, the office only has power for another three hours. I woke up wearing only one earring. Don't tell me I climbed, like, sixteen flights for nothing."

    "Why the crap did you climb all that? You have asthma!"

    "Elevators are reserved for people with healing injuries. Zoom."

    Carol huffed. "Fine." 

    "Give me five minutes, I'll send you the link."

    Carol walked into the kitchen. "Val's setting up a Zoom. Koumba found her through Wycaro. He wants to talk about a press statement already."

    Zosia's expression didn't change, but her hand moved to open the tab, and Carol caught it before it disappeared—the page in Polish. She'd kept returning every few minutes to a message from the Polish Ministry of Defence. The recall order had been issued overnight, Poland's day; naval personnel were instructed to report.

    Zosia hadn't answered. She was already pushing her chair back. "I'll refill."

    Carol sat down. Her hands were cold. She opened the email, clicked the link that Val had just sent and then the little circle was spinning, struggling through whatever there was of the internet.

    The screen connected and Val appeared in a black silk blouse. Her face was bare of makeup for the first time Carol could remember. 

    "Hi, Carol, you look—" Her eyes moved to the edge of the frame where Zosia crossed behind her carrying two mugs.

    Zosia put coffee beside Carol, her thumb brushing Carol's nape as she leaned to look into the camera. "Hello again."

    "Commander."

    Carol turned. "What the—"

    "We've spoken," Val said, eyes still on Zosia. 

    "When the—"

    "While you were in the shower," Zosia said. "The phone kept ringing."

    Val adjusted one cuff. "I had questions."

    "I answered," Zosia said.

    "She did," Val agreed. "I can see why Helen liked her." And Val gave Carol a look then, Val who'd been selling a bearded heartthrob for a decade and a half, having just seen the original walk across the kitchen in a white button-up. Several things were clicking together behind that one pearl earring. "Carol, you neglected to mention she looks like—"

    "Can we fucking not—and can we postpone the mutual performance review until after I've rejected international fame?" She reached for the laptop power cable and dragged it across the table for something to do. 

    Val's eyes dropped to the green mug at her elbow. "Oh my God. Is that thing still kicking?"

    Carol put a protective hand around Shrek. "Show some respect."

    Val grinned. "I still remember her caption. 'Found Carol's Soulmate'. She cackled about that mug for like an hour on our call."

    Carol smiled but her throat bobbed. "Yeah. I remember." She remembered where Helen had stood to take the photo too, six feet in front of where Carol was sitting currently, one hip against the counter. Seven billion other witnesses to it gone, now. 

    Val touched her ear. "Okay. I have a man waiting."

    "Only one?"

    "Shush. I'm adding him."

    A square opened in a hotel lobby. The chandeliers were dark and folding tables filled the floor. Koumba wore a white shirt open at the throat and a silk neckerchief. People moved behind him carrying clipboards. ROOMS AVAILABLE UPSTAIRS was taped beside the elevators, but mattresses lined the far wall anyway.

    "Ah, Carol. There you are."

    "Here I am. Looks like you're still in Vegas."

    "I am. The fountains still work. Everything else is—" He made a gesture. The video stalled on his face, resumed, and his mouth moved half a second ahead of the sound. "You told me I would remain myself."

    "And you're still wearing that, so I assume it worked."

    His laugh returned. "You did it. I knew you had a plan, and I still could not imagine this."

    Carol reached for a joke and a change of subject. Zosia's knee touched hers under the table.

    "We did it." Carol answered instead. "Three of us."

    "Then I owe all three of you my thanks. We are making a statement this afternoon and this is, as you might imagine, somewhat complicated, but this happened to everyone, so the world should hear from us before it becomes the account of one country or another. We have to tell them what we know, and I only know you had a plan. We all agreed your names should be said only with your permission."

    Carol glanced at Val who gave one small nod: keep him talking.

    "What does the statement say so far?"

    "That we were given anything we wanted but there were few of us, so we were isolated around the world."

    "Isolated?" Inside her, a folding chair scraped backward. "What does it say about you keeping me out?"

    Koumba's smile faded. "It can say whatever you would like, Carol." 

    "I want it to say the truth."

    "Mm, that you succeeded without our help."

    "In spite of it," Zosia said. "You excluded Carol intentionally and now you want to ride her coattails."

    Val lifted one eyebrow.

    Koumba tipped his head. "I accept your point, as I did before. I could have objected more strongly. I'm sorry, Carol." Zosia leaned back. "I confess, the old world was not especially generous to me, and now it is back, I'd like to make certain there is a place for me in it this time."

    Carol looked at him, small in the square. "Sure." She'd driven across the desert for him and then resented him for wanting peace without her. That was what she'd done to Manny too, called herself every epithet over. "I—uh…forgive you, or whatever." 

    Zosia's hand found hers below the table and Carol gripped it. She breathed, and said, "I want you to say that I was immune too and you left me out on purpose, because I was difficult, because I wanted to fix it."

    "Some of the others will find that uncomfortable."

    "Good. They should be. I was uncomfortable for weeks."

    Val surfaced from her silence. "They can describe a group in New Mexico and leave you out. I can issue a written statement of your own, you can be unavailable, I can say you're recovering."

    Koumba looked past Carol. "Zosia, would you permit us to use your name?" 

    "No."

    "Okay." He didn't ask why. "I have no means to reach Manousos, and we would ask first."

    Zosia turned to Carol. "You can say no to all of it."

    Her face offered neither noble expectation nor a promise that visibility would be good or bad. The choice remained hers, and Carol's pulse had begun speeding. She could already hear the questions piling: how she'd done it, what she'd said. Millions of strangers would reach toward the part of her that had kept its door, but she'd begged the world to live separately, and that was what separate people did.

    She heaved a sigh. "Fine."

    Val's pencil stopped, then resumed. "Fine, as in?"

    "Fine as in you can use my name, and I retain the right to hate every second of it."

    "Standard terms, then."

    "They can choose not to be named," Carol said, "but it has to credit three of us, don't make it sound like I did this alone."  

    Koumba leaned forward. "And the press conference? Will you join—"

    "No."

    Val stirred in her box. "Carol, I think you should consider, if you're being named—"

    "Val. Let me think."

    Carol looked at the tiny lens above the screen.

    Being public had once meant warm bottled water and a microphone that smelled of the last author's lipstick. Val in the aisle checking the clock and Helen against the back wall, ready with their rescue signal if Carol's answers started deteriorating.

    The woman in the author bio had smooth hair and no sweat stains. She answered questions about Raban's appeal with the same three anecdotes, and never mentioned what she was. They love a version of me that doesn't exist, she'd sulked, and Helen had told her to tolerate some love from the world. The version of her they'd know this time was real. She'd written the damn broadcast, as herself. No beard stitched over the bones. 

    Koumba waited. Even Val waited patiently, which may have been the first recorded instance.

    "I'll be public," Carol said. The words sounded strange and true. Val's image jumped, froze with her mouth open, then resumed. "Later. My own press, my own terms. When I'm ready."

    "Carol—" Val said, recalibrating. "When you say your own, do you mean—"

    "I mean I'll tell them the truth."

    Val stared at her. Carol saw her running the implications; the publicity, the exposure, what Val understood better than anyone she'd spent decades resisting. 

    Koumba was nodding, so Carol continued, "You do yours, name me, and when the world knocks on my door, I'll answer it. Eventually."

    Val's eyebrows climbed, already writing, Carol could hear the pen scratching through the speaker, her mind racing ahead.

    "Carol," Koumba said. His voice had the warmth back, that he'd used when he told them to take care of each other. "Thank you. For this, and for what you did." He glanced to where Zosia sat half off-screen. "Both of you."

    Val clapped once. "Great."

    "À tout à l'heure, Valerie."

    Val snorted and waved goodbye with both hands. "Call me directly next time."

    Koumba smiled and his square went dark.

    Val lingered and she was alone on the screen now, a mess of an office behind her, the collapsed world she was trying to rebuild already with two pens and a singular professional will.

    "Carol."

    "What?"

    "Hel would be so proud of you."

    Carol's eyes welled even as she rolled them. "Yeah, well. She always wanted me to stop being chickenshit."

    "She didn't say that."

    "Same difference." Carol sniffed. "I'm sorry I told you on the phone. I should've…I dunno. There's no good way—" 

    "There's no good way," Val agreed. "You told me. That was enough." Her voice steadied, and she clapped again, brisk and final. "Now. I have a press conference to plan from a high rise that doesn't have working plumbing yet, and you have an alarmingly gorgeous girlfriend beside you who looks proud enough to burst."

    "Jesus Christ, Val—"

    Val blew a kiss, and the screen went dark. 

    Carol sat back and felt herself tilt on the uneven leg. "Huh." She kept looking at the screen. "Is uh—is that what we are?"

    Zosia's hand remained in hers. "Is it inaccurate?" 

    Carol rubbed her free hand over her eyes. "It sounds so—"

    "Young?" 

    Carol squinted through her fingers. Zosia's mouth had a curve at the corner. "Insufficient."

    "We saved the world together," Zosia said drily. "I think that accelerates the timeline." 

    "Further than girlfriend?"

    Zosia's eyebrows rose. "Forever was mentioned."

    Carol huffed a laugh. "We skipped the middle."

    "You can call me whatever you want," Zosia said, shrugging. "I'll know what you mean."

    Carol could feel her face warming. "I've never called anyone girlfriend. Helen was—Helen was my wife."

    Zosia's jaw had tightened and she was watching their hands instead of Carol, and her own blush had started. "I've never called anyone anything. Sasha was my cover. The rest—" She lifted one shoulder. "I've forgotten their names." 

    "So neither of us has ever done this," Carol said.

    Zosia's grip shifted in hers. "Girlfriend," she said, like fixing a course. Her eyes came up. "I've wanted to be someone's. I'd like to be yours."

    Carol blinked her vision clear. "Where do you get these lines from?"

    Zosia's mouth twitched. "You say it."

    "Girlfriend," Carol said, testing the word. It sounded absurd for all they'd already said and done, made her feel sixteen and sixty, and still embarrassingly pleased. "My girlfriend." Her face hurt from restraining a smile.

    Zosia kissed her hand. "My girlfriend was very brave."

    "Don't get schmoopy."

    Zosia smiled but looked at the laptop screen, still dark. Her fingers started tapping Carol's. "Braver than me, I think. I should've called Poland already."

    Zosia picked up the pen again, and looked at the notebook margin, at whatever she'd written in Polish, with the same expression Carol had worn five minutes ago. "You'll have to tell them."

    "They'll ask why I retained memory. If I skirt around the truth, they might misunderstand the only evidence." 

    "And if they decide they've got a problem with it?" 

    She met Carol's eyes. "I won't protect myself by making you less safe. I'm going to call."

    The container had begun collecting sand along its base, a little dune building against the steel wall, trying to slowly bury it. Zosia was on the phone and Carol stood on the porch with her arms folded thinking about the atom bomb inside. For an hour, Carol had understood nothing but her own name among the Polish. 

    The door swung. Zosia came out with the landline still in her hand. 

    Carol's arms tightened. "How'd it go?"

    "They had me as missing. Presumed," she said without inflection. "I told them everything. Then a rear admiral got on."

    "They believed you?"

    "They asked me to repeat my service number about a hundred times, but they believed me." Zosia's thumb moved on the handset. "I gave them the transmitter sites. NATO will have at least the European ones decommissioned today."

    "That fast?"

    "Militaries are functioning," she shrugged and looked out at the street. "It means you won't be asked."

    Carol turned her head. "Huh?"

    "The operational account is complete and went up a chain that governments trust." Zosia's eyes came back to her. "No one's going to put you in an interrogation room. There's no reason to. They'll have the version from an officer."

    All day she'd been furnishing the room in her head: windowless, shut door, the man waiting for details, pen poised until she finished. "You did that on purpose."

    Zosia's mouth pulled. "I did it because it's my job."

    "What did they say? About you being gay."

    Zosia quoted. "They consider it a private matter, provided it remains private and does not interfere."

    "It interfered so hard you saved the world, so… so what? They're keeping you in the closet?"

    "They never considered me outside it."

    Carol looked at the container. "And they still want you back?"

    "More than they did yesterday. They've given me leave."

    "But you're going to leave," Carol said, to the container, and stayed looking at it, stubbornly, even as Zosia came to stand in front of her.

    Zosia tapped beneath Carol's chin and waited until the container lost the argument. "I'm not leaving you again." 

    "You're reading Polish news," Carol grumbled.

    "I'm not leaving you."

    Later, Carol found the browser on a Gdynia port bulletin: two rescue arrivals listed beneath it. Carol remembered her barefoot at dawn last Wednesday, staring at mountains she couldn't read. I miss the sea.

    By morning, corporations had found one voice and were promising Carol a life in which she'd never have to ask for anything again.  

    Val sent one email with eighty-one attached, subject line PEOPLE WANT TO GIVE YOU THINGS?

    Carol scrolled through them, some she couldn't even read—Arabic, Japanese—an airline whose planes still remained mostly grounded, saying whenever they flew again, she could go anywhere, first class, for free. Hotel groups offered permanent access to any room in any building they owned, including the ones currently serving as temporary accommodation. A grocery chain offered free food delivered for life, and it wasn't Sprouts so she ignored it. 

    Cars, security, clothes, furniture, prescription glasses she didn't even use. The laptop heated her forearms while a real estate company offered her a beachfront mansion she didn't want. 

    She knew this. Unconditional abundance aimed at her from every direction, generosity that asked for nothing back. 

    Zosia noticed her balled fists. "Carol."

    "I'm fine." She left the laptop to make breakfast.

    Zosia clicked back from a supplement company offering a lifetime supply. "These are people."

    "Are they? I can't tell the difference. Between this and that. It feels like the same damn thing." 

    Then cameras found the house.

    They parked at the curb and remained on it. One photographer unfolded a chair, opened a paperback of Winds and read with her gloves still on.

    No one knocked or shouted Carol's name.

    Carol peered through the blind. "What are they waiting for?"

    "You." Zosia stood behind her, close enough that Carol could feel her attention moving over the street. When one angled toward the bay window, Zosia went outside and spoke to him. The camera moved back to pointing at her door before Zosia came back in.

    "Did you threaten him?"

    "I asked him to respect your privacy. He agreed."

    Of course he had. They kept their shoes exactly on the public side of the property line. Carol stared at that invisible border and wished one of them would put a toe across it.

    "I'd know what to do if they were assholes. This is the same goddamn thing."

    By the end of the day, Carol resented the woman reading.

    "She's going too fast," Carol muttered.

    Zosia glanced through the blind and squared her shoulders. "You're watching her read?"

    "No."

    "I can tell them to go, if you like?"

    Carol imagined the photographers dissolving into apologies and she could see it clearly. It would work. Zosia would do it without shouting, unlike Carol, and they'd go, and Carol would be left inside feeling like she'd sent her girlfriend to fight her battles.

    "No," Carol said. "I'll deal with it."

    She didn't deal with it. She closed the blinds and went back to the sofa, to the keyboard and the mess of paragraphs refusing to become a chapter. Her feet disappeared under Zosia's legs while Zosia stole her phone and scrolled through news, and the sound of typing filled the house again, and outside, the cameras waited with infinite patience.

    Carol watched the street through the peephole. Nineteen of them now. Nineteen reporters occupied the sidewalk. Carol had counted through the blinds twice. A police block at the mouth of the cul-de-sac had kept everyone else out, though several cars waited beyond it. Val had called this a press conference. A press conference generally involved at least a podium and a function room. 

    What this was, in practice, was Carol opening her front door.

    A woman in a trench coat was checking a mic against her palm. The rest milled about, like waiting for a bus they'd been told was coming.

    "You don't have to do this today," Zosia said from the kitchen.

    Carol turned. Zosia was at the island with her phone, scrolling as usual. One in eight people had died during the joining, and the appeals ran constantly, on every channel, every news website, for what the world had run short of, or needed more of. Pilots, translators, doctors. Zosia never mentioned it.

    "If I put it off today, I'll put it off tomorrow, then the next day, then I die in this house and they find me mummified in a free La-Z-Boy."

    "That's dramatic." Zosia set the phone down. "Do you know what you're going to say?"

    Carol took a sip that scalded her tongue. "Nope. I'm gonna open the door and see what comes out."

    Zosia stood and stopped in front of her, straightened the collar of Carol's flannel, which didn't need straightening, and tucked a strand of hair behind Carol's ear, which did. "You okay?"

    "I'm agreeing to be famous. On purpose. The books don't count."

    "They counted."

    Carol huffed. 

    You're kinda famous now, Helen had said, twenty years ago. It was time to say it, and she knew it like she knew when a chapter was done.

    Carol took a breath, another sip that burned less, and turned back to the door. "If anyone asks about you—"

    "I wasn't here."

    "You were never here."

    Zosia put one hand on Carol's nape. Her thumb rested below Carol's ear, over the pulse hammering there, and it lessened. "I'll be here," she said.

    Carol nodded, Zosia let go, and Carol opened the door.

    The light was bright, and the nineteen of them looked up as one, so synchronized Carol's skin prickled. Then a cameraman fumbled his focus, the trench coat woman mouthed sorry and backed off Carol's yard, another reporter removed his glove with his teeth and dropped his pen onto one of the many camping chairs.

    Individuals, badly coordinated. Thank god. 

    She stopped at the end of the driveway with the container doors as backdrop with her flannel, jeans, coffee. Val could call it a press conference if she wanted. 

    A woman spoke first. "Ms. Sturka, thank you for—"

    "Carol's fine."

    "Carol." The woman adjusted the mic. "The immune coalition credited you with initiating the release. Can you tell us, in your own words, what happened at the Very Large Array?"

    Carol wrapped both hands around Shrek. In her own words. She'd used her own words, and none of these people had heard them, and all of these people had heard them, were standing here because of them.

    "Three of us drove out there in an ambulance," Carol said. "Plan A went to shit. Plan B went to shit. So I talked." She took a sip. "I talked, you listened, and you let go of each other."

    The silence after was strange. She was expecting six follow-ups before the sip finished. These reporters patiently waited, and they took turns, one question at a time.

    A man in a fleece vest: "What did you say?"

    Carol shifted her weight. "I asked to give everyone back their individuality. I explained why what would be lost was worth losing."

    "Can you be more specific?"

    "I was specific at the time, but I was also fucking terrified, so my memory is…" She gestured Shrek. "There's a transcript somewhere. Maybe it'll be published in the future."

    A woman with a CNN mic asked whether she'd been in contact with government agencies, whether she had information about the global coordination effort. Carol said she'd had one phone call from a man at Homeland Security who'd been very polite and very confused about his own politeness. 

    "Mostly he wanted to know whether I had possession of any alien technology."

    "Do you?"

    "Not unless the toaster's been holding out on me."

    Soft laughter moved through the group. Carol waited for the ridicule hidden inside it and found none. They liked her. That was the problem.

    An older guy asked: "There are reports of displacement on an unprecedented scale. Families separated. People waking up in cities they've never visited. FEMA is estimating forty million Americans are currently outside their home state. Do you have any message for those people?"

    Carol chewed her lips. They were asking her to address America like she was Roosevelt at a fireside. "I don't have a message," she said. "I'm not a leader. I've never been good with people."

    "You saved all of us."

    "I argued into a microphone. That's what I'm good at. Running my mouth."

    A British woman with a BBC press badge: "There are discussions at the UN about whether the joining constitutes a crime against a humanity, whether we should be treated as victims, legally. Do you have a view?"

    "That's above my pay grade. I write fantasy books." She sipped.

    "But you—"

    "I'm not a lawyer or a diplomat or anyone who should be making those calls." The concrete was cold through her socks. She'd forgotten shoes. "I'll say this. You weren't there by choice. I don't know what you call that in a courtroom. I know what I call it."

    "What's that?"

    "Love without asking, which isn't love. It's—another thing."

    The woman wrote something and didn't follow up.

    A man with glasses, soft-voiced: "Some people have described the joining as… they've used the word 'dream.' A good one. Do you have any response to that?"

    Carol looked at him closer. He was in his forties, light jacket, and he was crying, and it confused him visibly.

    "Yeah," Carol said, slower. "I've heard that. I think it felt good, but you can miss something and still accept it's over."

    The man nodded. He pressed his thumb and forefinger against the bridge of his nose and his shoulders dropped.

    A reporter from the Albuquerque Journal, notebook open on his palm: "The immune coalition said two others were with you. A man from South America who ran the technical side and a woman they described as previously joined, a naval officer. Can you tell us about them?"

    "The other immune people, I was trying to get us to talk, work together, whatever, and nobody cared but him. He drove all the way up here." Carol's grip on the mug tightened. "And I fucked him over, by the way. I left him alone to go on vacation. But he found the signal, how to screw with it, built the equipment, and kept me pointed at the job. He believed I could do my part before I did." Carol looked across the cameras. "So when you write I saved the world, put him in the same sentence or you're lying."

    The reporter checked his notes. "And the officer?"

    "Before the VLA, we unjoined her right here in my driveway, with that thing." She waved toward the container. 

    The pens moved faster. "And what did she do during the final attempt?" 

    "She went back in. When you all tried to use her to stop me arguing, she fought. She got my words to you and kept herself from me long enough, and she died to keep me free. She came back, but it killed her. She knew that might happen before we went." Carol rubbed her thumb over the handle. "She's the bravest person I've ever met. That's all you're getting."

    "Can you give us her name or nationality?"

    "Nope. That's hers to tell. Leave her alone."

    Camera shutters clicked. A younger reporter raised two fingers and Carol nodded. "What was it like for you to remain immune?"

    She looked past the reporters to the police cars at the end of the street. An officer had turned away to give her privacy from forty yards. Beyond him, the city spread under a hard blue sky. Three months of empty roads. The wind picked up and Carol could feel the cold through her shirt. The reporters' breath appeared in pale clouds. 

    "Lonely," Carol said. Her voice thinned. The microphones found it. "It was lonely." The mug trembled between her hands. "My wife died on joining day."

    A gray-bearded reporter, gently: "Your wife?"

    Carol looked directly at him. "Helen Umstead."

    Her name entered the cameras, to nineteen strangers and whoever was able to watch. Her wife.

    She knew folding chairs, she could feel the door behind her, closed, and there was a man with a pen in front of her. But she wasn't in a windowless room. She was on her own front step. Zosia was in the house, and Helen in the yard and in the mug and in the name she'd just said aloud to a camera for the first time. She was shaking so hard the coffee was circling and she wasn't going to hide it, and hell, she was in for a penny.

    "I'm gay," Carol said, because she couldn't say the other word. "I've been gay since I was twelve." She could hear her own heart. "And the guy in my books? He's a woman and he always should've been. I'm fixing it. I won't make a song-and-dance about it because I've made enough speeches." They didn't balk away, or lean forward. "So. There you go. Any more questions?"

    Near the back, a young man in a beanie who hadn't spoken lowered his phone. He looked scarcely older than the kids in those folding chairs had been. 

    "Carol?"

    "Yeah?"

    "What's with the mug?"

    Carol glanced down at the green face grinning up at her from the cooling coffee. "This is my emotional support ogre." 

    The whole group exhaled and smiled. "Helen gave it to me," she said, and her voice was steady now, and she was smiling talking about her wife to a group of strangers with microphones. 

    She had no idea what to do next.

    "Thank you," the trench-coat woman said eventually. "Seriously. Thank you."

    Carol's mouth twisted. "Sure," she said. "My coffee's cold and my feet are freezing—" several reporters chuckled— "so I'm uh, going back inside now." She thumbed backward. 

    No one objected. The cameras followed her to the threshold and stopped.

    Carol opened the door, stepped through, and closed it on their patient faces. Zosia was standing in the hallway, arms folded, face unreadable.

    "They asked about you," Carol said. 

    "I heard."

    "Yeah." The mug had begun to slip in her damp hands. Zosia took it and placed it on the console. "Well, don't leave me hanging, did that go ok—"

    Her startled noise broke against Zosia's lips and the knob dug in her back. Zosia's fingers curved along her jaw, placement worked out in advance and used once before in this hallway, with the sun through the front windows doing exactly this to the tile. 

    When Zosia drew back, Carol followed before dignity caught up. 

    "Okay," Carol said. Her smile had escaped containment. "Are you going to lead with the part where this won't potentially kill us all?"

    "The last array's reversed." Carol got a briefer kiss at the corner of her mouth. "I got confirmation while you were outside." Carol glanced at the phone left on the console. "And I looked up the extracellular half-life of glycan coated viruses and calculated the decay. The residual viral load in my saliva fell below infectious dose eleven hours ago."

    Carol's eyes returned to her lips. "Hot."

    A soft breath of laughter kissed Carol's cheek.

    She'd used every good word on the cameras. Zosia got the dregs, and didn't seem to mind, which made Carol push her face into a shoulder that smelled woody.

    "You told them who you are."

    "I said gay. It's one syllable."

    "Not just that." Zosia's hand stayed on her face. "I'm proud of you."

    It had taken the end of the world, but she'd done it. "Thanks."

    The shaking stopped. Zosia didn't comment on it. Her hands moved to Carol's collar instead, and the flannel came open button by button, each one given the same focused dexterity Carol imagined she'd given a knot in a line or a live wire or anything she knew how to disarm.

    The shirt slid off Carol's shoulders and Zosia caught it and let it fall. The pilled plaid puddled at Carol's feet and she stood there in a sweaty bra and dirty socks.

    "I forgot shoes," Carol said.

    "I noticed."

    Zosia kissed her once more, soft at first. Carol got two fistfuls and made it less soft. Outside, someone snapped a case shut. The cameras remained pointed at a closed door that had already given them everything they were getting today.

    Carol pulled Zosia down again and turned them away from it.

    The volunteer mail carrier arrived the next day.

    Carol heard the knock and expected a lens, and opened the door with her jaw set and ready to do damage.

    She stared.

    He didn't know her. His eyes were clear, his smile polite. "Ms. Sturka? I've got two bundles here for you. Want me to leave them on the porch?" 

    Carol opened the door wider and leaned against the frame. He had no idea, no memory of sitting in the hospital waiting room with her. "You, uh, you're delivering mail again?" 

    He smiled, uncertain. "Volunteering." He indicated the bag he was hefting. "Sorting center's running two routes a day. Aid goes first, then personal mail where we've got space." He looked down at the bundles. "You've got a lot of personal." 

    Carol looked at the man who had known her then. He had known every fact available, every medical update from inside the operating theater, worn their patience in one borrowed body and remained beside her while she waited to learn whether Zosia would live.

    "We—" There was nothing useful she could do with that sentence. "Were you working when it happened?" 

    "Yeah. I was on my route, and then I woke up in a warehouse wearing a Saints jersey." He scratched his stubble. "Couldn't tell you anything about what happened in between."

    "Nothing?"

    "Nothing I can put words to. Just a feeling." He looked at the bag of mail, then back at Carol. "People seem to know you saved us. I don't remember it, but I believe them." He shrugged. "I just wanted to say thank you, if that's not too weird."

    "Everything's a little weird."

    He smiled, guileless, and held out his hand. "Thanks."

    His palm was sweaty. He released her hand.

    "Do you want coffee?" Carol asked.

    The invitation surprised both of them. He glanced at the van. "I've got another four hours before they close the west sorting dock."

    "Right."

    He started down the driveway. "Maybe tomorrow. You're getting a lot of mail, Ms. Sturka."

    "Carol."

    "Carol. I'm Anthony." He glanced toward the two cameras, then back at her. "They bothering you? Want me to say something?"

    Carol nearly laughed. The DHL guy, her accidental knight errant, offering to joust with photographers in cargo shorts. "No. But thanks."

    She went inside. Zosia was at the island, reading. The shipping news first. Ahead of the headlines, the reconstruction updates, before the weather she wouldn't need. A grid of vessel movements—arrivals, departures, tonnage, port of call—and she read it like Carol would read the bestseller list: with professional attention and private hunger. Carol tried to ignore it.

    "I just invited the mailman in for coffee," Carol said, putting the envelopes down. "He doesn't know we've met."

    Zosia left the laptop and gathered the mail into a neater pile. "How did he seem?"

    Carol thought about the sweat on his forehead. "Like a person." 

    Most mail was simply addressed to CAROL STURKA, NEW MEXICO.

    Mailed flat in a manila envelope from an address in rural Vermont there was a single pressed flower between two pieces of cardboard. Chicory, blue, dried. The letter was from a typewriter:

    This was growing in the median of I-89 when I drove home in a strange car. The whole highway for miles was wildflowers up to the windows! Queen Anne's lace, goldenrod, everything the state usually mows. I pulled over and stood in the middle of it and it came up to my chest. I picked this flo one for you, I hope it travels okay. Thank you for bringing me back!

    Carol laid the flower on top of Zosia's hand on the counter. "For you."

    Zosia lifted it to her nose, which was pointless, it would only smell like paper, but the blush hit her cheekbones anyway.

    An envelope from Oklahoma contained a blurry photo. The photographer had moved. A woman was in a hospital bed holding a newborn against her chest, and beside her stood two people in scrubs and blood, cheering. The mother's note said they had woken with no idea what was happening and delivered the baby anyway. The accountant held my hand and did the counting and the lunch lady caught her, she wrote. I named her Carol.

    Carol brushed a finger over Carol. "Poor kid," she said. "Stuck with that."

    A teacher in Baton Rouge had sent drawings: crayon suns, stick figures holding hands, one with yellow hair and CAROL written in wobbly capitals. She was significantly taller than the house.

    "You wish," Zosia said, over her shoulder.

    The wax softened beneath Carol's thumb. At the bottom, in adult's handwriting: Lily, 6. She told me to tell you the green circle is your cup. Carol put it down beside a pink crocheted scarf from Portland, one end four inches wider than the other. 

    "Man, the world is so fucking weird," Carol said, and let the pile of art on the counter grow.

    Val forwarded a link with a single line above it: You should see this.

    CAROL STURKA'S "BRAVEST PERSON": WHO IS COMMANDER PSZCZELIŃSKA?

    Poland has identified the naval officer credited by Carol Sturka during the operation that ended the Global Joining. Online readers have already found another connection. 

    "Oh no."

    A red banner crossed the top of the article: DEVELOPING. Carol rotated the laptop. Zosia's face didn't change, she simply squared her shoulders and read downward without comment.

    Beneath the first paragraph, Zosia clicked a link. The page loaded in Polish.

    "When did they post it?"

    "Overnight." Warsaw had already been awake for seven hours. 

    Carol watched her face give less and less away. "What does it say?"

    "They released my service record. Qualifications, commands, commendations." Another scroll. Carol came around to see the screen and Zosia clicked translate.

    Komandor Porucznik Pszczelińska demonstrated—

    "What's the poruz thing?"

    "My full rank."

    …exceptional courage, technical discipline, endurance, and devotion to human life under conditions of extreme danger. Her conduct reflects the finest traditions and enduring readiness of the Republic of Poland to serve humanity.

    Poland hadn't played a role. Poland had been joined, along with its ministry and its ranks and every other chair-warmer.

    Komandor Porucznik Pszczelińska will return to serve in the reconstruction effort. The Ministry remains in contact with allied authorities and will provide further information when operational conditions permit.

    It ended there and Carol stopped. "Return."

    Zosia's index finger was tapping against the table. "The Polish is worse. It implies I've placed myself at their disposal."

    "How long did you talk to them? An hour? Jesus. You've been useful for a day and they're already owning it." Carol pulled the laptop back and found the article again. "This is Koumba's trick."

    "Koumba asked permission."

    "Right." Carol began to read. The article was quoting the Navy's press release.

    A still image from her press conference accompanied the article along with a second photo, of Zosia, captioned Several days earlier, a woman now identified as Pszczelińska was captured addressing a photographer who had approached Sturka's Albuquerque property.

    Pszczelińska's apparent continued residence at Sturka's address has prompted speculation. A defence ministry spokesperson declined to explain why she is staying at a private residence despite the reopening of Allied Air Force Bases and the restoration of consular services. 

    Sturka described Pszczelińska during remarks outside her Albuquerque home as "the bravest person I've ever met", said the officer carried her words into the collective after equipment failed, "died to keep [her] free" and told reporters to "leave [Pszczelińska] alone."

    Carol pressed her thumbs into her eye sockets. She'd meant it all, aimed at the door as much as the cameras, and it hadn't occurred to her until this moment that it might be revealing.

    Online, the identification of Pszczelińska has collided with the aftershock of Sturka's public coming out, and proven sufficient for readers of her bestselling Winds of Wycaro book series to speculate on the nature of their relationship. Already processing the discovery that the series' central romantic fantasy originated as a closeted one, news of Sturka's sexuality has altered decades of interpretation almost overnight. 

    Readers quickly circulated side-by-side images of Pszczelińska and several official illustrations of Raban, the dashing corsair at the center of Sturka's stories. The most viral thread, captioned "TELL ME THIS ISN'T FEM RABAN??" has passed 80,000 comments. 

    "Oh, Christ." 

    Pszczelińska's connection to Wycaro predates her meeting Sturka. A former bunkmate, who requested anonymity, described Pszczelińska as "quiet, good at her job, and obsessed with those books." 

    Zosia's hand stopped tapping. 

    "Who?" Carol asked.

    "Doesn't matter." Zosia's mouth thinned. "Everyone reads in their bunks. That was—"

    "Private," Carol said. 

    Our source told the Reconstruction Desk that Pszczelińska has been a fan of the Wycaro books for years: "We all knew better than to call them bad in front of her". She was described as a demanding watch officer and an excellent navigator, "always first awake when anyone needed help".

    Little is known of Pszczelińska's personal life, beyond being married to Aleksander "Sasha" Sowiński, a fellow naval officer who died in a sailing accident in 2014: "Sasha used to call the Wycaro books her navigation manuals." An archived memorial notice described him as her "best friend".

    Sturka's representative was unavailable for comment before publication. The Polish Ministry of National Defence said Pszczelińska's "private affairs are outside the scope of the present announcement."

    Below the imaginary fold, a polling widget: 

    Do you think Commander Pszczelińska and Carol Sturka may be in a relationship? Yes / No / It's none of our business.

    Sixty-three percent had voted for the third option, which was reassuring and infuriating.

    They sat with the article between them like an overdue bill.

    "Val can draft—"

    "Don't." Zosia's voice was sharp. "Don't reduce it to a press release." The small muscle beside Zosia's ear was pulsing.

    "They didn't tell you," Carol said.

    "No."

    "You cooperated, and they didn't even—" Carol gestured at the laptop. "Not a phone call, an email, a fucking carrier pigeon? Nothing."

    "It's not personal. This is their version of gratitude."

    "Bullshit," Carol said. "It's extremely personal. Fucking decades of don't ask don't tell and now they're proud of you? You should sue them, or fucking court-martial someone, is that a thing?"

    The corner of Zosia's mouth twitched. "No." She straightened and folded her arms. "I'm proud of you, for all of it, I am, but—" Carol could see her processing: the chain of command, the tabloids, the naval brass below NATO Top Secret clearance who'd read and recalibrate everything they knew about their most visible officer.

    "Yeah, I get it. I don't want to hide you but it's—it's all shit. Every option is." Carol rubbed her eyes. "We don't confirm. We don't deny. We let them write whatever they write and misread whatever they read and we don't read it."

    "Okay," Zosia said. "We don't comment."

    "We don't comment."

    For two days they found an easy life between crises. Zosia pressed her perfect coffee. Carol cooked breakfast with wet hair while Zosia leaned against the counter, both hands around her cup. Carol read out the funniest mail while the pan sizzled until Zosia laughed into her coffee and accused her of inventing half of it.

    After breakfast Zosia washed while Carol dried. Zosia hummed under her breath, one foot braced behind the other against a roll the tile would never make. 

    They watched The Princess Bride and Muppet Treasure Island under one blanket, Zosia correcting every sailing detail until Carol climbed over her to shut her up. They had sex in every room with all the doors open and slept late with Carol's cold feet trapped between Zosia's long legs. For forty-eight hours, the hardest question was what to eat next. 

    On the third day, the tide table was still open on Zosia's laptop.

    Carol had seen it yesterday. Gulf of Gdańsk, four columns on a webpage out of the nineties, high water 06:14, low 12:40. Carol had passed it twice and said nothing both times. The tab stayed open, refreshed in the background, an open line to a world that moved with the water.

    She took an onion from the counter and started chopping.

    She'd heard the conversation in her sleep for days. The plan was to retire and sail until I ran out of money or coastline. She wanted the sea. She'd always wanted the sea. The navy had been the means to it and the joining had been the interruption and the sea was still there, and Zosia was five thousand feet above sea level watching tide tables for harbors oceans away and saying nothing.

    Zosia stood at the sink in one of Carol's stolen shirts, sleeves shoved past the elbows because the cuffs fell short, with both hands in the running water, rinsing a mug.

    "Do we still have black pepper?"

    Nothing. She was staring out of the window.

    "Zosia."

    "No." Late, and no use by then. 

    Carol stopped cutting, her eyes were already stinging, and felt the knife twist. 

    She was so present in Carol's kitchen and Carol's clothes, after two good days, and so visibly elsewhere. Her eyes remained outside, on fifty miles of desert running up to the mountains. 

    Carol had one job, and it was to be bigger and smaller than that.

    "You don't have to stay."

    Zosia's hands went still.

    "The sea, the reconstruction, whatever you want to call it. You should go." Open hands, she'd told the whole fucking world. "There's a chart open on the table for water five thousand miles from here. I'm not going to be what stands in front of it."

    Zosia pulled her hands from the water and dried them on the towel, slowly, folding the towel in thirds. She turned. Carol could see the assessment happening behind her eyes: what Carol was doing, why she was doing it, whether to fight it. 

    "You miss it," Carol said, before she could get a word in.

    Zosia stared at her, fond and furious. "Yes."

    "You want to go help."

    "Yes."

    "They're begging for you." Carol gestured toward the black screen in the den, the laptop. "Everyone needs anybody, but they keep describing you personally." Her hand dropped. "You had a life before you walked into my yard."

    "I have one here. I won't leave you alone."

    Carol's heart seized and her resolve wavered. "I'll be fine. We promised to miss each other, remember? I want you to live a life where you remain yourself too." Even if it killed Carol.

    Zosia came closer with her mouth set hard and her eyes too soft and Carol couldn't tell which one made her move. "You'd rather I leave wanting to stay than stay and wonder if I should've left. You've decided—"

    "I haven't decided anything. I'm giving you—"

    "A door, I see it." Zosia folded the towel once more and set it on the counter next to Carol. "You're good at doors now."

    Carol's anger rose, welcome and useless. "What do you want me to say? Abandon your duty and spend your days holed up here?" 

    "You could. You could ask me to stay." 

    Saying that meant becoming what kept her, what the hive had done, the exact crime—and calling it love. "I won't. I won't be the reason you won't go."

    "You already are."

    "That's fucking why, don't you get it? Look around, there's nothing but sand, cameras, people camping on the sidewalk to photograph me carrying out trash. I won't keep you hostage. That's what they did."

    "They never asked me anything."

    Zosia got a hand under Carol's jaw, and waited. Carol stood there with nothing but her eyes stinging. "You're so difficult," Zosia said eventually. Carol's jaw unclenched into her palm, though the rest of her remained unconvinced. Zosia kissed her and her face softened, resigned. "There's a transport to Ramstein I can pilot."

    Carol's chin dropped. She'd known. The world needed her and she wanted to go and Carol was going to be alone in this house again, and that it was the right thing didn't make it any better.

    "Okay," Carol said. "When?"

    "Thursday."

    Carol did the math twice in case it improved. "You should call." 

    Zosia left her and picked up the phone. She dialed and spoke, clipped and formal, and when she hung up she looked at Carol across the kitchen. Her eyes were bright and her chin was level.

    "I guess I need a car," Carol said, to say something. "There's a helicopter in my cul-de-sac and nothing to drive in my driveway."

    "I can fly it."

    "I can't fly it back."

    She found one, scrolling through the offer emails Val forwarded: I've killed all the pasta sauces and mattress companies that had a six-page rider. Her shoulders loosened at six pages. Endorsement rights and photo ops meant these people had the usual motives. She scrolled, scrolled, and finally gave up and just searched "car". One dealership had sent five follow-ups, another had rendered a Carol Sturka Edition pick-up, the VLA co-ordinates embroidered into the headrests, a chrome plaque on the tailgate.

    She found one short email. Ms. Sturka, we'd like to offer you any vehicle, no strings. If this isn't wanted, no reply is necessary. Thank you for what you did.

    She forwarded it to Val and typed: I don't want a new one. There's an old blue Corolla parked on the tarmac at the Sunport. I want that car. Tell them to spend whatever they were going to on buying that legally, and donate the rest.

    The dealership delivered it Wednesday. A kid in a polo handed over the keys, said congratulations on the world, ma'am, and got into the flat-bed without asking for a selfie.

    Zosia came out in Carol's coat and stopped halfway down the path. She opened the driver's door and folded herself behind the wheel. The seat was still pushed to her reach. 

    Carol saw it all at once: Zosia driving her home through the dawn, one long hand on the wheel, turning toward her after every impossible date with that pleased little breath before goodbye.

    Zosia's thumb moved across the worn leather of the steering wheel. Then she got out, moved the driver's seat forward six inches and set both mirrors for Carol without being asked. She went back into the house and returned with a blanket and the flashlight from the junk drawer, and put them in the trunk.

    Carol watched from the porch and said nothing about why she had wanted this car, out of all the cars in the world.

    Thursday was cold and cloudless. The sun hadn't cleared the mountains, and the Corolla's windshield wore a skin of frost too thin to justify how long she took to scrape. The duffel waited by the door, the same one she'd returned with, and Carol carried it to the car before Zosia could.

    They drove to Kirtland with the heater on, neither of them touching the radio, and the roads were bad again. A stoplight was out at the university intersection, there was a detour around a bridge. Carol drove with both hands on the wheel.

    The frontage road went by, the Circle K, a checkpoint down to two cones and a bored guy in a reflective vest who waved them through without looking. Headlights still burned along Central, though the eastern sky had begun bleaching them useless. 

    Their faces stayed dim in the car. 

    Nearer the base, a transport crossed low above them, gray belly filling the windshield, and its roar shook loose a flock of birds from a power line. Zosia followed it with her head until the road curved.

    "C-130," she said.

    "Yours?"

    "Probably." Zosia looked out of her window for a while. "You still owe me a coffee."

    "I do."

    "Somewhere else." She was watching the fence go past. 

    Name a place. Carol had the words in her mouth but she let the exit come up on the right instead. "The heater's making that noise again."

    Zosia reached over and put her hand on Carol's thigh and let it drop.

    The joke was that she'd already left once, back when the planet was empty. She would've followed Zosia anywhere, and they'd gone to the library at midnight for beach reads. Now the lights were back on in every building, and leaving meant arriving in a real place, a barista who'd look twice, a table that wasn't hers, and everywhere else was somewhere her life hadn't been. The apocalypse had paradoxically been safe.

    Somebody had put a hand-lettered sign on the fence outside the base. WELCOME BACK. As though the whole species had come home from a long trip and they were the only ones who hadn't unpacked.

    At the security gate, the airman did a double take. Clipboard checked, waved through, and Carol couldn't tell if he was saluting her or Zosia.

    On the runway the C-130 had its ramp down. Personnel in winter gear moved between pallets, breath streaming from them as they shouted over the engines. Carol parked in the designated row and shut off their engine.

    Zosia unbuckled. She didn't reach for the duffel. She looked at Carol, who looked ahead.

    "One thing, then I'll go." She kept her eyes on the windshield. "I'm not leaving because you gave me permission. The work is real and I can do it and you're right they need me. But I want you to know that you could've asked."

    Carol's fingers hurt around the wheel. "I know."

    "And I would've stayed."

    "Okay."

    "And being somewhere else doesn't mean I've left you."

    "It literally does."

    "It doesn't." Quieter, and firmer, her own damn argument, returned to sender. She hated when she was right.

    Zosia leaned across the console and kissed her. Carol let go of the wheel. The clock on the dash changed once.

    When Zosia came back an inch she stopped there, her mouth hot, her breath coffee-sweet, and her thumb moved under Carol's eye.

    "Kocham cię."

    "Yeah. You too. Go."

    Zosia's hand stayed there for two seconds and let go. "I'll call from Ramstein."

    Carol's voice broke. "You better."

    Carol released her and Zosia opened the door on jet fuel and January. She took the duffel and the last of the warmth from the car, shut the door and tapped the roof twice with two fingers, and Carol nearly said it.

    Stay.

    She could stop her. She'd done it once. 

    But now Zosia stood beside an open door of her own choosing. Carol held the wheel and Zosia walked away. At the foot of the ramp, she paused while a crew member spoke to her.

    Every movie had this scene in it. A hundred feet and a name at the top of her lungs, rain, a run.

    She could sound the horn. She could get out, shout her name, make every head on the tarmac turn. Zosia would stop and stay, Carol knew it with the same terrible certainty as before.

    Zosia adjusted the duffel, and looked toward the aircraft, back straight.

    Turn around. Just—look back once. Turn around and I'll do the whole ridiculous thing again, I'll shout it in front of the forklifts and the flight crew and ruin your life with it.

    Zosia went up the ramp, her stride even, and didn't turn. The dark interior took her and the ramp rose, sealing her in.

    Carol sat and watched crew clear the area. The engines climbed, the plane taxied, and for one wild second she imagined driving to the front and stopping her at the nose, airplane screeching to a halt like before, the door opening, Zosia crossing the tarmac toward her smiling.

    The plane lifted. It climbed into the clear morning light, its belly turning white and east, and got smaller, and became a dot, and then the sky had nothing in it at all.
