The afternoon sun off the Sea of Cortez hit her full in the fucking face, Jesus Christ, it was late October and still warm enough here to justify heading south after three weeks at the house, though Carol missed the shelf of foreign edition covers she could rage at from a chair that didn't pitch.

    Carol kept messing up the line and trying again, tying again, and it defeated her five times.

    The sun was on her bare shoulders and she could feel her arms being watched with an expression Carol had learned to provoke but not put on paper. Carol pulled the line taut, one foot on the rail, not above flexing to make up for her ineptitude. Zosia was barefoot, hair loose, one hand on the wheel, wearing a faded navy pullover that pressed against her front by the wind. She looked like she'd been born at the helm and Carol looked like a novelist on a boat, which was exactly the situation and always would be.

    On the sixth attempt she tried with her tongue between her teeth and inched the bunny ears through and the loop finally fucking held.

    She raised it into the air like a trophy.

    "That's a bowline," Zosia confirmed.

    "Damn right. Tell me you're proud of me."

    "You could climb through that loop, though."

    "Maybe I will. Maybe it's a portal bowline, to a dimension where you congratulate me." Carol threw the thing at her face, but of course Zosia caught it one-handed and pulled the loop snug with a finger.

    The line ran taut between them and Zosia pulled the line shorter. "Come here."

    Carol was tugged along and Zosia reeled the last, took her face in both hands and kissed her. Carol laughed against her mouth, hands full of coiled line.

    Zosia pulled back. "Congratulations."

    Carol was smiling into her palms. "If I'd known that was the reward, I'd have tried harder."

    "You were trying very hard."

    Carol elbowed her.

    Zosia corrected the wheel around the impact without losing the grin and then stepped sideways. "Why don't you take the controls?"

    Carol narrowed her eyes and could see through the plan instantly. The last time she'd accepted that lesson, Zosia had corrected her grip, then her stance, then her hips, and the lesson had ended below deck with the jib luffing and the boat turning circles.

    "You tried that in Mazatlán and I almost killed us both."

    Carol sat in the helm seat instead, needing to finish this goddamn paragraph before any distractions, and she let the sun shine against her closed eyelids.

    She loved this boat. She'd spent thirty years imagining the sound of sails and the feel of a hull, and now that she had the creak, the lean, the salt and sand crusting her keyboard—the gap between imagination and reality was only the width of her own incompetence.

    She'd once needed a desert to keep the world far enough away, now forty feet of boat was plenty. It'd made the world smaller by letting them cross it and bigger by giving Carol reasons to want to. She wanted to see where Zosia had sailed, then every random lighthouse or rock formation she knew a fact about, and one place kept leading to another.

    They could spend a week tied up among a thousand noisy strangers, being fed incredible food Carol couldn't pronounce, being told stories she needed translated, and whenever the world got too crowded, they could cast off, sail until it was only sea, sky, Zosia and her. The boat had made the world exactly the right size and distance because it was theirs to choose.

    She just couldn't tie a fucking knot.

    "Your page," Zosia said, nodding to the laptop she'd put on the side to not tie a knot. "What's wrong with it?"

    Carol picked it up and read the passage aloud. Zosia tried to interrupt when Raban entered the cave at high tide, but Carol held up a finger to her until she was done.

    "She'll suffocate in the sand," Carol said, pointing out the problem anyway. "How about the charm that saved her after the plank?"

    "It only lasted five minutes."

    "Oh, for fuck's sake, why did I write that?"

    Zosia adjusted the wheel a quarter-turn starboard, considering. "Fun fact: some sea caves breathe. Waves and pressure force air through cracks, so you can hear an entrance before you see it."

    "Huh." Carol adjusted her hold on the laptop. "Cool." She typed a note in the margin: CAVE BREATHES. "You just saved Raban from a very stupid death."

    "Yes."

    "Don't be so smug about it."

    Zosia looked very smug about it. "What's inside the cave?"

    "You'll have to wonder and see," Carol said, equally smug, and went below deck.

    She sat and took a sip of the fresh coffee from the galley. Goddamn it. Perfect. Worse, she could taste the altitude now. This morning Zosia had ground the beans with the copper contraption clamped between her knees, both hands turning the crank, and Carol had watched from the berth and thought about three things at once, none of them coffee. The result was so offensively good she'd been forced to retire an entire category of complaint.

    Carol wrote it, grand theft. Re-read one line. Air pulsed through the hidden fissure and Raban followed the breath of the mountain toward the light.

    "Eh, better," she admitted, begrudgingly. Zosia told her a pressure differential and Carol made a cliff have lungs. Same as always, she supplied the impossible part and Zosia kept it from killing anybody. She closed the laptop on whatever that made them and was about to go back up for more when her phone buzzed.

    Manny and his giant nostril filled the screen. She picked up. "What?"

    "Carol." In the background, the sound of whatever generator he was oiling today. She pictured the rows of shelving he'd reorganized three times in three months, the emergency supplies he still rotated on a monthly schedule despite the emergency being over. "How is the boat?"

    "Wet and tilty. How's the bunker?"

    "It's not a bunker."

    "You have eight months of canned human food."

    "I have the space. It is insurance." He paused. "I was thinking of visiting." Carol sat up straighter. "You said I could."

    "Come over whenever, Manny, that's what I said." The bark in her voice had gone. "We're in Baja through fall. Back in Albuquerque for the holidays. Come for Christmas."

    "I don't want to impose—"

    "Good, because you're coming for work."

    He perked up immediately. "Work?"

    "They're making the Wycaro movie and I told them film it in Colombia and you run the production, or they can make some other asshole's book for the relief fund. I trust Hollywood people as far as I can throw this boat."

    "Not far."

    "Exactly. You love movies and I need somebody producing it who can keep a budget and a schedule. You're the only one I trust. You already made one impossible plan happen."

    "Colombia?"

    She shrugged. "You know it, and Zosh and I can sail there. She wants to see your hometown coffee farms or whatever."

    "Yes. Huila has desert, and Cartagena has the old streets, but traffic will complicate. Which season?"

    "No idea."

    "I will make a list of what you have failed to ask."

    Carol smiled. "See? Hired."

    "We have not discussed salary."

    "Jesus Christ. Fine. Come for Christmas and extort me in person. Zosia'll make this fish thing. You can organize my DVDs and I'll complain about it. It'll be like old times."

    She heard him exhale. "Hm."

    "Great. You're welcome."

    She was expecting him to grunt a goodbye and he didn't.

    "Carol."

    "What?"

    "Gracias."

    "Oh god, don't actually thank me. I'm hanging up."

    "No, I hang up."

    She held the phone for a second after he got there first, the bastard. Through the companionway hatch, she could see Zosia's bare feet shift on the sole. Carol climbed back up.

    "Manny's coming for Christmas." The wind was steady and warm out of the south. Carol sat again beside her, close enough that her knee pressed against Zosia's long bare leg.

    "You used your gentle voice," Zosia said.

    Carol rolled her eyes. "Don't start. The spice rack needs alphabetizing." Zosia touched her knee. "Keep patronizing me and you can sleep on deck tonight."

    "You'd come out for me."

    Carol huffed and looked out at the water. "Maybe. Eventually."

    "Before midnight."

    "Shut up."

    Somewhere east, Zosia's mom was expecting a phone call before midnight—her Tuesday morning, always Tuesday—and Zosia would make it from the well deck, phone tucked between ear and shoulder while she trimmed the jib, her Polish softer and younger than she used while sailing. Carol would sit below and listen to the cadence of it without understanding a word.

    After Zosia handed in her notice they'd visited her mom. She was nearly eighty and had been watching the news. She'd taped newspaper clippings of Zosia to the refrigerator beside a laminated prayer card. God and the television had apparently signed off on an American girlfriend and a boat with no proper kitchen and who was she to overrule. She'd spent the first hour treating Carol with the reverence reserved for world saviors and the next fussing over her posture but feeding her four courses.

    At the end of the second evening, she'd taken both their hands and called them córeczki—little daughters. Carol, who'd been thanked by every head of state but never once been warmly called daughter, had studied the lace doilies on the table until the patterns no longer doubled.

    Zosia's hand left the wheel and found the back of Carol's neck. Her thumb traced the tendon there idly, as if she were reading the tension in it. Carol leaned into the touch and Zosia's fingers moved up into her hair, loosening a knot the wind had made, and Carol tipped her head back against Zosia's hip and looked up at her from below.

    Zosia was already looking at her, the light behind her, her face another one Carol still couldn't turn into words but hadn't given up trying. "You okay?"

    She was. She was more than okay. She had been more than okay for so long it was no longer suspicious.

    "Yeah. I'm happy."

    Zosia smiled. "Good." She had to correct course and murmured something in Polish to the wind, too fast to catch, and Carol watched her mouth move through words she'd never know. Still more of her. Thank God. Carol stood and pulled her down by the face.

    Zosia made a small sound against her mouth, surprised and pleased, and abandoned the wheel to put her arms around her. Carol rose onto her tiptoes to close the last inch of height between them, and the boat heeled slightly and neither of them corrected for it. Zosia's lips were warm and dry and tasted like salt and coffee, and the kiss was slow, and Sasha sailed herself for a while.

    Carol's heels eventually sank back to the deck. "Jesus, you're tall."

    Zosia laughed a big one, head tipped back, throat bare to the sun. Carol hadn't even made a joke. That was how easy she had it now. Zosia bent lower to save her the reach, and one hand left Carol's waist to spread across her back, pressure enough to hold her upright and out to the sea and the sun and anyone with binoculars, probably.

    Carol eventually leaned into her side and watched the water and felt the smallness that came with open sea as far as the eye could see, a useful kind that made the whole flailing endeavor of writing feel both ridiculous and necessary.

    "I need to look something up," she said, and went below again.

    Above the galley berth, wedged between the nautical almanac and a Spanish phrasebook Carol had bought and Zosia had corrected in pencil throughout, was Wycaro five. The spine was already cracked from rereading—Zosia several times and Carol twice since publication, which was two more than she'd reread any of the others.

    She opened it to the front matter, because what she needed was there and she still liked seeing it.

    For Helen, who got me here.

    For Zosia, who made here too small. Every line is yours.

    The page had them both and so did she. Carol gripped the book and here she was, bigger than she'd been, her heart grown larger around all of them. Helen, Zosia, Wycaro: the loves of her life.

    She turned to the back flap and looked at herself. The photo was taken on this deck, Carol squinting mid-sentence with her hair across her face. She was not posed, or poised, she looked like she was arguing with the wind and losing. It was the worst photo she'd ever approved for publication and the only one that had felt like her.

    ABOUT THE AUTHOR

    Carol Sturka is the author of the best-selling Wycaro series and part of the team who restored individual consciousness to the global population. She is a lesbian who lives and works wherever the coffee is perfect.

    Through the companionway hatch, Zosia's bare feet crossed her own deck. Carol slid her book back into place on their shelf and climbed up to bother her again.

    The sun had gone lower now, the sea turning the color of beaten gold. Zosia smiled at her from the helm, so absurdly beautiful in the light that Carol's heart did what it always did—a sort of capsize, there was probably a sentence—and Carol sat down beside her again and felt the unruliness right itself as Zosia's free hand came back into her hair.

    The bow had turned and the light ran along the water in a broad, molten road and Sasha sailed straight down the center of it. Carol watched the most obvious happily ever after she'd ever seen and didn't want to edit a thing.

    Ahead, there was only open water, and plenty of world if they wanted it. The boat sailed west, and Carol closed her eyes and let it carry them both.
